chapters.title: Historical Underpinnings, Evolution and Making of Indian Constitution

elements.text: Historical Underpinnings, Evolution and Making of Indian Constitution
1.1 Indian Constitution: Historical Underpinnings

The Indian Constitution, which came into force on January 26, 1950, represents a complex historical fusion of inherited colonial structures and the nation's own ambitions. As Dr B.R. Ambedkar famously stated, it is a synthesis derived from "the experience gained through the ages".
Why did the Constitution makers borrow heavily from the 1935 Act?
• Administrative Familiarity: Indian politicians and administrators were already familiar with the administrative machinery
(foundational framework for the Parliamentary and federal system) established by the 1935 Act.
 It made sense to adopt an existing, functional system rather than experiment with a completely alien structure.
• Detailed Institutional Framework: The 1935 Act provided a highly detailed blueprint for complex administrative systems
like the Federal layout, the Judiciary, the Public Service Commissions, and Emergency provisions, which suited the vast
and diverse Indian landscape.
• Need for a Strong Centre: The 1935 Act had provisions for a strong federal framework which the framers found necessary
to hold the newly independent, geographically vast, and socially diverse nation together and prevent balkanisation.
How does the Constitution of 1950 fundamentally differ from the 1935 Act?

A "Bag of Borrowings" or a Tailored Masterpiece?

The debate over whether the Indian Constitution is a "Bag of Borrowings" or a "Tailored Masterpiece" is as old as the document itself. While critics often dismiss it as a "patchwork" of foreign laws, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar famously argued that there is no shame in "ransacking" the best features of existing constitutions to suit the needs of a new nation.
The reality lies in the adaptation: the framers didn't just copy-paste; they modified global concepts to fit India's unique socio-political diversity.

By pragmatically assimilating the best administrative lessons from the past, the Assembly transformed a history of colonial concessions into a durable, sovereign charter of justice and democratic rights.
1.2 Making of the Constitution

The institutional framework of the Indian Constitution was heavily drawn from the administrative machinery established during British rule. The process shifted from centralisation to gradual decentralisation and limited representation.

elements.text: Demand for Constitution
• M.N. Roy’s Proposal (1934): M.N. Roy, a pioneer of the communist movement in India, was the first to formally put forward the idea of a Constituent Assembly.
• INC’s Official Stand (1935): The Indian National Congress (INC) officially demanded a Constituent Assembly to frame the Constitution of India.

• Nehru’s Declaration (1938): Jawaharlal Nehru declared on behalf of the INC that the Constitution of a free India must be framed "without outside interference by a Constituent Assembly elected on the basis of adult franchise."
• British Acceptance: The demand was accepted in principle by the British in the August Offer (1940) and later formed the core of the failed Cripps Mission (1942).
Constitution Drafted (1946–1949)

• Constituent Assembly: The Assembly met for the first time on December 9, 1946. The Muslim League boycotted the meeting, insisting on a separate state of Pakistan. Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha was elected as the temporary President, later replaced by Dr. Rajendra Prasad.

• Objective Resolution: On December 13, 1946, Nehru moved the historic "Objective Resolution", laying down the philosophical fundamentals of the constitutional structure. This eventually became the Preamble.

• Impact of Partition: After the Indian Independence Act of 1947, the Muslim League members from Pakistani territories withdrew. The Assembly's strength was reduced from the original 389 to 299 members.

• The Drafting Committee: Set up on August 29, 1947, under the chairmanship of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. It scrutinised the reports of various sub-committees and prepared the first draft, which was published in February 1948.
• The Assembly held 11 sessions spanning 2 years, 11 months, and 18 days.

Acknowledging the colonial origins of our Constitution does not diminish its greatness but rather highlights the intellectual maturity of its framers. By pragmatically assimilating the best administrative lessons from the past, the Assembly transformed a history of colonial concessions into a durable, sovereign charter of justice and democratic rights.
Salient Features of Indian Constitution

The Indian Constitution is a uniquely comprehensive document that blends provisions borrowed from global constitutions with India's specific administrative needs. This synthesis has resulted in a dynamic framework equipped with several distinct features designed to unite and govern an immensely diverse nation.

rows.text: Features
Description
Lengthiest Written Constitution

It is the most detailed constitution globally, driven by India's vast geography, historical influences (1935 Act), and the inclusion of both fundamental principles and administrative details → It originally contained 395 Articles and 8 Schedules, but today, through multiple amendments, the Indian Constitution has expanded and now contains 448 Articles (grouped into 25 Parts) and 12 Schedules.
Drawn from Various Sources
Its structural, philosophical, and political frameworks borrow heavily from the Government of India Act 1935, as well as the US, Irish, British, and other global constitutions.
Blend of Rigidity and Flexibility
It synthesises both; some provisions require a special parliamentary majority (Article 368) or state ratification, while others can be amended via simple legislative processes.
Federal System with Unitary Bias
It combines standard federal features (division of powers, bicameralism) with strong unitary traits (single citizenship, a strong Centre, all-India services), often described as "quasi-federal".
Parliamentary Form of Government
Based on the Westminster model, it features a nominal and real executive, majority party rule, and collective responsibility of the executive to the legislature at both the Centre and State levels.
Judicial Review

Judicial review is the power of the Courts to examine the actions of the legislative and executive branches of government to determine whether they are constitutional. If a court finds that a law, policy, or government action violates the constitution, it can declare it null, void, and unenforceable
Integrated and Independent Judiciary
A single hierarchy of courts (with the Supreme Court at the top) enforces both central and state laws, protected by constitutional safeguards to ensure complete independence.
Fundamental Rights

Part III guarantees six justiciable rights to protect citizens against state tyranny, though they are subject to reasonable restrictions and can be suspended during emergencies (except Articles 20 and 21).
Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)
Enshrined in Part IV, these are non-justiciable directives aimed at establishing a "welfare state" and promoting social and economic democracy.
Fundamental Duties
Added by the 42nd Amendment (Part IVA), these serve as non-justiciable moral obligations for citizens to maintain unity and respect national ideals.
A Secular State
It embodies a "positive" concept of secularism by giving equal respect and protection to all religions, without upholding any official state religion.
Universal Adult Franchise
Grants voting rights to all citizens over 18 without discrimination, a bold experiment that made Indian democracy broad-based.
Single Citizenship
Despite its federal structure, it provides uniform national citizenship to foster unity and fraternity among all Indians.

elements.text: Independent Bodies It establishes autonomous institutions like the Election Commission, CAG, and UPSC to serve as bulwarks for the democratic system.
Emergency Provisions Contains unique mechanisms that allow the federal structure to temporarily convert into a unitary one during National, State, or Financial emergencies to safeguard the nation.
Three-tier Government
The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) constitutionally recognised local rural (Panchayats) and urban (Municipalities) governments, a unique feature globally.
2.1 Why is the Constitution called a Living Document?

A constitution is termed a "living document" when it is not a static, frozen piece of legislation but a dynamic, evolving entity that responds to the changing socio-economic, technological, and political realities of a nation. The Indian Constitution has survived for over seven decades precisely because its framers built mechanisms for its continuous evolution without destroying its foundational ideals.
“If you make a constitution too rigid, you stop a nation’s growth and the progress of a living,
vital people.” - Jawaharlal Nehru.
Mechanisms through which the Indian Constitution evolves

rows.text: Aspect
Explanation
Blend of Rigidity and Flexibility (Article 368)

• Adaptability: Over 100 amendments have been passed to reflect changing times. ♦The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) restructured grassroots democracy, and the 101st Amendment (2016) overhauled the nation's indirect taxation system to introduce the GST.
• Example: The 106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023), reserving seats for women in legislatures, demonstrates its ongoing capacity to address contemporary demands for gender equity.
• Article 368 itself reflects the framers’ intent to balance continuity with change
Transformative Constitutionalism

• The Supreme Court of India is not just the guardian of the Constitution but also its most active interpreter. Through its power of judicial review, it continuously expands the scope of constitutional text to cover modern issues.
• Expansion of Article 21 (Right to Life): Originally interpreted narrowly, the Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) case expanded Article 21 by transforming "procedure established by law" into a substantive requirement of fairness, justice, and reasonableness. ♦The judiciary has expanded "Life and Personal Liberty" to include the Right to a Clean Environment (M.C. Mehta Case, 1986), the Right to Education (Unnikrishnan Case, 1993) and, crucially, the Right to Privacy (K.S. Puttaswamy Case, 2017) - adapting a 1950 document to the digital age.
• The Basic Structure Doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati Case, 1973): This judicial innovation ensures that while the Constitution is "living" and can be amended, its "soul" (secularism, federalism, and judicial review) remains immortal and immune to destruction.
Laws by the Parliament

• The Constituent Assembly deliberately left many administrative and procedural details out of the Constitution, delegating them to the future Parliament to legislate as per the needs of the time.
• Examples: Voting is a constitutional/statutory right under Article 326, but the exact mechanism of elections, disqualifications, and political funding is dynamically managed by the Representation of the People Act (1950 & 1951). Similarly, the Citizenship Act (1955) has been amended multiple times to reflect shifting geopolitical and domestic realities.
Evolution of Constitutional Conventions

• Unwritten conventions and practices have organically grown to supplement the written text, adapting to political realities (such as the era of coalition politics). (conventions are non-binding political practices.)
• Example: The President's practice of inviting the leader of the largest pre-poll alliance to form the government in the event of a hung parliament is an evolved convention, not a strictly written constitutional rule.
Evolving with Societal Values

• The framework adapts to shifting cultural morals without needing a brand-new Constitution.
• Example: The decriminalisation of Section 377 in 2018 aligned the law with modern understandings of equality and dignity.

elements.text: Constitutionalism and Constitutional Morality: The Twin Pillars of Indian Democracy

While the Constitution is the written legal framework of a state, Constitutionalism is the political philosophy of "limited government", ensuring that state power is restrained by law. Constitutional Morality, on the other hand, is the ethical compass of the document, ensuring that the government and citizens adhere not just to the letter of the law but to its underlying values of justice, liberty, and equality.
Constitutionalism (The Structural Restraint)
Definition: The idea that government authority is derived from and legally limited by a body of fundamental law. It is the antithesis of arbitrary, authoritarian rule.
Key Manifestations in the Indian Polity:

• Limited Government & Fundamental Rights: The state is not absolute. Part III (Fundamental Rights) acts as a negative injunction against the state, preventing it from encroaching upon individual liberties (e.g., Article 13 voids laws that violate Fundamental Rights).

• Rule of Law (Article 14): Borrowed from A.V. Dicey, it establishes that law is supreme, not the ruler. It ensures equality before the law and equal protection of the laws, subjecting executive discretion to constitutional limitations and judicial scrutiny.
• Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: The Constitution prevents the concentration of power by dividing it between the Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary (Article 50).

• Judicial Review & Basic Structure: The Supreme Court serves as the ultimate arbiter. Through the Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973), the judiciary established that Parliament cannot alter the "Basic Structure", structurally enforcing Constitutionalism even against a super-majority government.
Constitutional Morality (The Ethical Compass)

Definition: The adherence to the core principles of the constitutional text. It dictates that societal norms, biases, and majoritarian views must bow down to the egalitarian values of the Constitution.
Evolution:

• Dr. B.R. Ambedkar’s Vision: Dr. Ambedkar introduced this term in the Constituent Assembly (borrowing from historian George Grote). He warned that democracy in India was only a "top-dressing" on an essentially undemocratic soil, arguing that Constitutional Morality- meaning peaceful conflict resolution and paramount reverence for the Constitution - had to be deliberately cultivated.
• Triumph over "Public/Social Morality": In recent years, the Supreme Court has resurrected this concept against majoritarian and orthodox societal norms.

 Navtej Singh Johar Case (2018): While decriminalizing homosexuality (Section 377), the Court ruled that "Constitutional Morality" trumps "Social Morality." The rights of a minority cannot be denied merely because the majority disapproves.

 Sabarimala Temple Case (2018): The Court struck down the ban on the entry of women, stating that religious practices cannot subvert the constitutional morality of gender equality and dignity (Article 14 and 21).

 NCT of Delhi vs. Union of India (2018): The Court applied the concept to the federal structure, stating that constitutional functionaries (like the LG and the elected government) must act with mutual respect and constitutional morality, avoiding power struggles.
Key Elements of Constitutional Morality
• Protection of diversity and pluralism.
• Commitment to individual dignity and liberty.
• Non-violence and peaceful resolution of political disputes.
• Eradication of systemic discrimination (caste, gender, religion).
Application of Constitutional Morality: The Judicial Fulcrum

While Constitutional Morality protects citizens from majoritarianism, it also acts as a vital internal check on high constitutional functionaries. The Supreme Court uses it as a fulcrum to balance the delicate tension between Judicial Independence and Judicial Accountability:
1. Upholding Judicial Independence (Protection from Executive):
 Constitutional morality dictates strict adherence to the Separation of Powers (Article 50).
 It requires the judiciary to act as a fearless guardian of the Constitution, completely insulated from executive or political pressure.

 Example: In the NJAC Judgement (2015), the Court struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission, ruling that executive interference in the appointment of judges violates the "Basic Structure" and the constitutional morality of an independent judiciary.
2. Ensuring Judicial Accountability (Protection from Overreach):
 Conversely, independence is not a license for judicial dictatorship. Constitutional morality demands that judges practice Self-Restraint and remain accountable to the constitutional text.
 It prevents "Judicial Overreach" by ensuring courts do not usurp the policy-making powers of the legislature or executive.

 Example: The push for administrative transparency (like bringing the CJI's office under the RTI Act) and the reliance on "In-house procedures" to investigate judicial misconduct are driven by the constitutional morality of public accountability.

The Indian Constitution derives its enduring strength from its ability to reconcile competing democratic ideals through a pragmatic and balanced framework rather than rigid absolutism. This constitutional synthesis has enabled India to preserve unity, liberty, justice and democratic stability while adapting to changing socio-political realities.
2.2 The Basic Structure Doctrine

The Basic Structure Doctrine is a judicial innovation stipulating that Parliament, through its constituent power under Article 368, cannot alter or destroy the essential framework or "soul" of the Constitution.

As eminent jurist Nani Palkhivala noted, Parliament is a "creature of the Constitution and cannot become its master". Coined in the historic Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), scholar Granville Austin famously termed this doctrine the "bedrock of constitutional interpretation in India".
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. “Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution is a limited power and it cannot be
enlarged into absolute power.” In the light of this statement explain whether Parliament
under Article 368 of the Constitution can destroy the Basic Structure of the Constitution
by expanding its amending power? (2019)
2. What was held in the Coelho case? In this context, can you say that judicial review is of
key importance amongst the basic features of the Constitution? (2016)
Evolution of the Doctrine
Phases Description
Phase of Absolute Parliamentary Power (1951-1965)
• Shankari Prasad Case (1951): Following the 1st Constitutional Amendment Act (which added the
9th Schedule to protect land reform laws from judicial review), ♦The Supreme Court ruled → Parliament enjoys absolute constituent power to amend any

part of the Constitution, including FRs → A constitutional amendment was not considered a 'law' under Article 13(2).
• Sajjan Singh Case (1965): A 5-judge bench upheld the Shankari Prasad judgement, though some
doubts were raised regarding the absolute amendability of the Constitution.
Phase of Fundamental Right Supremacy (1967)
• Golak Nath Case (1967): 11-judge bench (6:5 majority) ruled → Parliament does not have absolute
power and cannot abridge or take away any Fundamental Right.
♦It categorically stated that constitutional amendments are considered 'law' under Article 13(2).
Birth of the Doctrine (1971-1973)
• Government's Reaction: Parliament enacted the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments to nullify the

Golak Nath ruling and re-establish its supreme amending power. → The 24th Amendment explicitly stated that Parliament can abridge FRs.
• Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973): (13 judges) → The Supreme Court performed a balancing act.
♦It upheld the 24th Amendment, overruling Golak Nath, and declared that Parliament can amend
any part of the Constitution. ♦However, it propounded the Doctrine of Basic Structure, ruling that the constituent power
under Article 368 does not enable Parliament to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution.
Cementing the Doctrine (1975-2007)
• Indira Nehru Gandhi Case (1975): The SC reaffirmed the doctrine by striking down a provision of

the 39th Amendment Act (which kept the Prime Minister's election disputes outside the jurisdiction of all courts) as it violated basic features like free and fair elections and the rule of law.
• Minerva Mills Case (1980): During the Emergency, Parliament passed the 42nd Amendment (1976),
declaring that there is no limitation on its amending.powers, attempting to exclude judicial review over Constitutional amendments.
♦In Minerva Mills, the SC struck this down, stating that a "limited amending power" and

"judicial review" are themselves basic features of the Constitution.
• Waman Rao Case (1981): The SC clarified that the Basic Structure doctrine applies retrospectively

only to constitutional amendments enacted after April 24, 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgement).
• I.R. Coelho Case (2007): The SC ruled that there is no blanket immunity from judicial review for
laws placed in the 9th Schedule. Any law added to the 9th Schedule after April 24, 1973, is open to challenge if it violates Fundamental Rights (Articles 14, 15, 19, 21) or the basic structure.
Implications of the Doctrine
• Expansive Judicial Review: The doctrine marked the beginning of strong Judicial Review in

constitutional interpretation. A key example is the striking down of the 99th Constitutional Amendment (National Judicial Appointments Commission - NJAC).
• Present-day constitutional challenges, such as the 103rd Amendment (EWS reservation) and the
abrogation of Article 370, are tested against the touchstone of the Basic Structure.

elements.text: Significance of the Doctrine
• Promotes Constitutional Ideals: Basic Structure Seeks to preserve constitutional principles and

Basic ideals envisioned by the founding fathers.
• Granville Austin argues that with Basic Structure Doctrine, a balance has been reached between the

responsibilities of Parliament and the Supreme Court for protecting the seamless web of the Indian Constitution.
• Protects Fundamental Rights: Basic Structure protects the citizens' fundamental rights against the

legislature's arbitrariness and authoritarianism.
• Constitution as a living document: Being dynamic in nature, it is more progressive and open to

changes in time, making the Constitution a living document.
• Safeguarding Constitutionalism: If Parliament is bestowed with unlimited powers to amend the

Constitution, it defeats the very purpose of having a Constitution.
• Check on Majoritarianism: Governments have historically enacted questionable amendments to suit
ulterior motives, especially during the Emergency Era (e.g., 42nd Amendment). The doctrine ensures that absolute power does not corrupt absolutely.
Comparative Constitutionalism
• India's doctrine is a judicial invention, but similar concepts exist globally, either in text or through

judicial routes.
• Germany's 'Eternity Clause' (Art 79(3)): A Textual ban on amending human dignity/federalism.
• Bangladesh: Adopted India's doctrine in 1989.

While the Basic Structure Doctrine is a product of high judicial creativity, it acts as the ultimate bedrock of Indian democracy. However, while wielding this doctrine, the Supreme Court must also respect the democratic mandate attained by the Government, ensuring that the Constitutional values and democratic accountability remain harmoniously balanced.
The Preamble
The Preamble serves as the introduction or preface to the Constitution, containing its summary and essence.
• Origin: It is based on the 'Objectives Resolution', which was drafted and moved by Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru on December 13, 1946, and adopted by the Constituent Assembly on January 22, 1947.

 The Preamble itself was enacted at the very end of the drafting process (November 1949) to ensure it aligned with the finalised Constitution.
• "Identity Card": Eminent jurist N.A. Palkhivala referred to the Preamble as the "identity card of the Constitution".

3.2 Nature of the Indian State: The Five Adjectives
Sovereign
• India is an independent state, neither a dependency nor a dominion, free to conduct its internal and
external affairs.
♦Membership in the UN or Commonwealth does not limit this sovereignty.

Socialist (Added by 42nd Amendment,
1976)
• India follows "democratic socialism" (a mixed economy where public and private sectors co-exist),

not "communistic socialism".
• It aims to end poverty, ignorance, disease, and inequality.
• Contemporary Dimension: While the 1991 LPG (Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation) reforms
diluted strict socialist credentials, the core aim of distributive justice remains intact.

Secular (Added by 42nd Amendment,
1976)
India embodies "positive secularism". Unlike the Western concept (complete separation of religion and state), the Indian state treats all religions with equal respect and provides equal support.
Democratic
• Based on popular sovereignty, India practices a representative parliamentary democracy.
♦Dr. B.R. Ambedkar emphasized that political democracy must be rooted in social democracy
(liberty, equality, and fraternity as a "union of trinity")
Republic
• Indicates that the head of the state (President) is elected (indirectly for a fixed term), rather than
hereditary as in a monarchy.
♦It also signifies that political sovereignty vests in the people and that all public offices are open to
citizens without discrimination.

rows.text: Justice (Social, Economic, Political)

• Social: Equal treatment without discrimination based on caste, race, religion, or sex.
• Economic: Elimination of glaring inequalities in wealth and income.
• Political: Equal access to political offices and equal voice in government.
Liberty (Thought, Expression, Belief, Faith, Worship)
• Taken from the French Revolution. Liberty is essential for democracy but is not absolute; it is qualified and must be exercised within constitutional limits.
Equality (Status and Opportunity)
• Ensures civic (Articles 14-18), political (Articles 325, 326), and economic (Article 39) equality by eliminating special privileges for any section of society.
Fraternity (Dignity of Individual & Unity/ Integrity of Nation)

• Promoted through single citizenship and Fundamental Duties (Article 51-A). "Integrity" was added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). It aims to overcome hindrances like communalism, regionalism, and secessionism.

3.4 Key Constitutional Debates
Is Preamble a Part of the Constitution?

This evolved through landmark Supreme Court judgements:
1. Berubari Union Case (1960): The Supreme Court stated that while the Preamble is a key to the minds of the makers, it is not part of the Constitution.
2. Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973): The Supreme Court rejected its earlier view and held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution and is of extreme importance for interpreting the Constitution.
3. LIC of India Case (1995): The Court reaffirmed that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.
Enforceability (Legal Status)

• The Preamble is non-justiciable, meaning its provisions are not directly enforceable in courts of law.
• It is neither a source of power to the legislature nor a prohibition upon the powers of the legislature.
Amendability of the Preamble

• Under Article 368, the Preamble can be amended.
• However, in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court ruled that such amendments

are subject to the condition that they do not alter or destroy the "basic features" or "basic structure" of the Constitution contained within the Preamble.
• It has been amended only once: the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1976) added "Socialist",
"Secular", and "Integrity".

Munshi termed it, it is the "horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic," and according to former CJI M. Citizenship

Citizenship is the legal status of a person recognised by custom or law as being a legal member of a sovereign state. It entails a relationship of allegiance to the State and, in return, the State provides protection and certain civil and political rights.
Enshrined in Part II of the Constitution, covering Articles 5 to 11.
The Indian State recognises two kinds of people:

• Citizens: Full members of the Indian State who owe allegiance to it. They enjoy all civil and political rights (e.g., Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30 are available only to citizens).
• Aliens: Citizens of some other state. They do not enjoy all Fundamental Rights. They are categorised into friendly aliens and enemy aliens (who are not entitled to protection against arrest and detention under Article 22).

4.1 The Citizenship Act, 1955
Acquisition of Citizenship (5 Ways)
• By Birth (Jus Soli - Right of Soil): Originally, anyone born in India was a citizen.
♦Due to illegal immigration, this was tightened. Currently, a person born in India on or after Dec 3,

2004, is considered a citizen only if both parents are citizens, or one is a citizen and the other is not an illegal migrant.
• By Descent (Jus Sanguinis - Right of Blood): For persons born outside India.
♦Originally tracked through the father. Post-1992, either parent being an Indian citizen suffices.

Post-2004, the birth must be registered at an Indian consulate within one year.
• By Registration: For Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs) ordinarily resident in India for 7 years, or persons

married to an Indian citizen residing in India for 7 years.
• By Naturalization: For foreigners who have resided in India for a specific period (usually 11 of the past

14 years + 1 continuous year before applying), possess good character, and have adequate knowledge of a language in the 8th Schedule.
• By Incorporation of Territory: If any foreign territory becomes a part of India, the Government of India
specifies the persons who shall be citizens (e.g., Puducherry, Goa, Sikkim).
Loss of Citizenship (3 Ways)
• By Renunciation: A voluntary act by a citizen of full age and capacity declaring their intent to surrender

Indian citizenship.
• By Termination: Occurs automatically by operation of law when an Indian citizen voluntarily

(consciously and willingly) acquires the citizenship of another country.
• By Deprivation: A compulsory termination by the Central Government if the citizenship was acquired by
fraud, if the citizen has shown disloyalty to the Constitution, or if the citizen has been ordinarily resident out of India for 7 continuous years.
4.2 Key Debates
Debates Description
Single Citizenship in a Federal Structure
• Unlike the USA or Switzerland (where a person is a citizen of the nation and their specific state),

India follows the Canadian model of Single Citizenship.
• Objective: To forge a united Indian nation and prevent regionalism or parochialism in a highly

diverse society.
• The "Residence" Exception: While Article 15 prohibits discrimination based on place of birth, it
does not explicitly prohibit discrimination based on residence. Under Article 16(3), Parliament (not state legislatures) can prescribe residence within a state as a condition for certain employment.
The Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), 2019

It amends the 1955 Act to state that Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan, who entered India on or before December 31, 2014, shall not be treated as illegal migrants. It also reduces their naturalisation residency requirement from 11 years to 5 years.
• Arguments in Favour:
♦Protects persecuted minorities from neighboring Islamic states. ♦Uses "intelligible differentia" (historical context of partition and specific state religions of those

3 countries), therefore defending it against Article 14 violations.
• Arguments Against (Criticism):
♦Critics argue it violates the secular fabric by making religion a criterion for citizenship. ♦It excludes persecuted groups from other neighboring countries (e.g., Tamil Hindus from Sri
Lanka, Rohingyas from Myanmar, Ahmadiyyas from Pakistan).
Assam Accord and Section 6A
• Section 6A was inserted into the Citizenship Act to implement the Assam Accord (1985), which was

signed to end the agitation against illegal immigrants from Bangladesh.
• It set March 24, 1971 (the start of the Bangladesh Liberation War) as the cut-off date for citizenship

in Assam.
• Recent Update: In late 2024, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional
validity of Section 6A, recognising the unique historical and demographic burden borne by Assam, validating the separate cut-off date as a reasonable classification under Article 14.
4.3 Domicile and Citizenship

While citizenship signifies the political relationship between an individual and the State, domicile implies a permanent home or a place where a person resides with the intention of staying there indefinitely. A person can have only one domicile at a time.

• Constitutional Link (Article 5): At the commencement of the Constitution (January 26, 1950), citizenship was granted to persons based on their domicile. A person became a citizen if they had a domicile in India and fulfilled at least one of three conditions: (a) born in India, (b) either parent was born in India, or (c) ordinarily resident in India for five years immediately preceding the commencement of the Constitution.
• Single Citizenship vs. State Domicile: India has a federal structure but provides for Single Citizenship (no separate state citizenship). However, under Article 16(3), Parliament can prescribe residence (domicile) within a state as a condition for certain public employment. Additionally, states can use domicile to offer special benefits, such as educational fee concessions to their residents, without violating Article 15

4.5 The Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025
Previously, India’s immigration framework was highly fragmented, relying on archaic laws. The new Act aims to modernise, simplify,
and digitise immigration rules, ensuring national security while promoting operational efficiency. Acts Repealed: It repeals four older
laws:
1. The Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920
2. The Registration of Foreigners Act, 1939
3. The Foreigners Act, 1946
4. The Immigration (Carriers' Liability) Act, 2000

rows.text: Domain
Specific Provisions & Mechanisms
Impact
Institutional Framework Entry & Exit Controls

• Bureau of Immigration: Formally establishes the Bureau to oversee visa issuance, regulate entry/ transit/stay, and advise on immigration policies.
• Designated Posts: Entry and exit are permitted only through notified immigration posts (airports, seaports, and land borders) manned by Immigration Officers.

• Centralises authority. The Centre may delegate functions to States, but retains absolute overriding authority over exemptions and permits.
• Grants Immigration Officers the final authority to validate or refuse entry based on national security, sovereignty, or public health grounds.
Digital Reporting & Accountability

• Accommodation Providers: Hotels, hostels, and religious institutions must electronically register foreign guests (including OCI cardholders) within 24 hours of arrival/departure.
• Universities: Must electronically report the admission of foreign students.
• Medical Institutions: Must report the indoor treatment, births, and deaths of foreigners within 7 days.

• Shifts from manual, paper-based tracking to a real-time, centralised biometric database.
• Ensures tight monitoring of individuals overstaying their visas.
Employment & Activities

• Restricted Sectors: Requires prior Central Government approval for foreigners seeking employment in sensitive private sectors (defence, space, nuclear energy, and human rights).
• Expression: Mandates prior approval before a foreigner can produce films or digital content in India.
• Prioritises national security and counters espionage or internal interference, though it raises concerns regarding freedom of expression.
Carriers' Liability
• General Declarations: Expands "carriers" to include air, water, and land transport. Operators must submit passenger/crew details prior to departure and cannot leave without clearance.
• Increases accountability for airlines and shipping companies, curbing human trafficking and illegal smuggling.
Exemptions Enforcement & Penalties

• Protected Categories: Exempts certain groups from standard visa rules, including citizens of Nepal and Bhutan, Tibetan refugees, registered Sri Lankan Tamils, and minority refugees (Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, Christians) from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan who entered before Dec 31, 2014.
• Arrest Powers: Empowers police officers (not below the rank of Head Constable) to arrest violators without a warrant.
• Graduated Fines: Fines range from ₹10,000 to ₹5 lakh. Entering without a valid passport attracts up to 5 years imprisonment.
• Compounding: Certain offences can be compounded via fines.

• Aligns with India's broader refugee policy and the spirit of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act (CAA).
• Faster Resolution: Compounding offences reduces the judicial burden. However, lower fines apply to certain refugee and monk groups, showing humanitarian leniency.

elements.text: Citizenship is the connective tissue between the individual and the Constitution. While India’s foundational ethos of single citizenship and secularism ensures a unifying identity across a diverse subcontinent, the evolving statutory framework from the 1955 Act to the CAA 2019- reflects the complex socio-political realities of illegal immigration, historical borders, and demographic anxieties. The ultimate touchstone for these evolving laws remains the delicate balance between sovereign security and constitutional morality under Article 14.
Fundamental Rights

Enshrined in Part III (Articles 12-35) of the Constitution and often referred to as the 'Magna Carta of India', Fundamental Rights serve as the bedrock of Indian democracy. They act as a vital shield against State encroachment on individual liberty, establishing a "government of laws and not of men" to ensure the triumph of political democracy over authoritarian rule.

5.1 Foundational Articles
• Article 12 (Definition of State): FRs are primarily available against the 'State'.

 Article 12 defines the State broadly to include the Union and State governments, Parliament, State Legislatures, all local authorities (municipalities, panchayats), and statutory/non-statutory authorities (LIC, ONGC, SAIL, etc.).

 The Supreme Court has ruled that even a private body working as an instrument of the State falls under Article 12.
• Article 13 (Laws Inconsistent with FRs): This article explicitly provides for the Doctrine of Judicial Review.
 It declares that all laws that are inconsistent with or in derogation of any of the fundamental rights shall be void.

• It ruled that Parliament has broad powers to
amend the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot rewrite its core identity or framework.
5.2 Rights
Fundamental Rights Description

Article 14 (Equality before Law & Equal Protection of Laws) Exceptions: Article 31-C: Laws implementing DPSP 39(b) & (c). Article 361: Immunity for the President and Governors. Article 361-A: Protection for true media reports of legislative proceedings. Article 105 & 194: Privileges and immunities for MPs and MLAs. Foreign Dignitaries: Immunity for foreign rulers, ambassadors, and diplomats. International Bodies: Diplomatic immunity for the UNO and its agencies.
• Equality before Law (British concept): Absence of special privileges for anyone; no

one is above the law.
• Equal Protection of Laws (American concept): Equals should be treated equally. Article
14 prohibits class legislation but permits reasonable classification. (must be based on "intelligible differentia" and have a "rational nexus" to the objective).
Article 15 (Prohibition of Discrimination)
• The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race,

caste, sex, or place of birth.
• Exceptions: Special provisions for women, children, SCs, STs, and Socially and

Educationally Backward Classes (SEBCs), including the 103rd Amendment (EWS reservation).
• In a landmark 6:1 majority verdict (State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh 2024), the
Supreme Court ruled that states have the Constitutional power to sub-classify Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) to grant separate quotas for the most backward within these categories.
Constitutional Perspective on Gender Justice in India
The Preamble: Sets the philosophical bedrock by securing to all citizens Justice (social, economic, and political), Equality of status and opportunity, and promoting Dignity of the individual.
Fundamental Rights (The Enforceable Guarantees)

• Article 14: Guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of laws to all persons.
• Article 15(1) & (2): Prohibits discrimination by the State solely on the grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
• Article 15(3): Empowers the State to make special provisions (affirmative action) for women and children, recognising historical disadvantages.
• Article 16: Guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment, prohibiting discrimination based on sex.
• Article 21: The Right to Life and Personal Liberty, which has been expansively interpreted by the judiciary to include the right to live with human dignity, bodily autonomy, and reproductive choices.
Directive Principles of State Policy (State Obligations)

• Article 39(a): Directs the State to ensure that men and women equally have the right to an adequate means of livelihood.
• Article 39(d): Mandates equal pay for equal work for both men and women.
• Article 42: Instructs the State to make provisions for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief.
Fundamental Duties
• Article 51A(e): Imposes a duty on every citizen to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.
Landmark Judicial Interventions

rows.text: Area of Intervention
Landmark Judgment Constitutional Significance & Impact
Workplace Safety & Harassment

Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) Filled a legislative void by establishing legally binding guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace, drawing upon Articles 14, 15, 19, 21, and international conventions (CEDAW).
Employment Equality & Anti-Discrimination

Air India v. Nargesh Meerza (1981) Struck down discriminatory service rules that mandated termination of air hostesses upon their first pregnancy, ruling it a violation of Article 14 and an affront to human dignity.
Right to Livelihood & Protective Discrimination

Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association of India (2008) Struck down a law barring women from working on premises serving liquor. The Court ruled that "protective discrimination" cannot be used to restrict women's employment opportunities and autonomy.
Command & Institutional Equality

Secretary, Ministry of Defence v. Babita Puniya (2020) Directed the government to grant Permanent Commission to women officers in the Army, dismantling gender stereotypes regarding physiological limitations and domestic obligations.
Dignity & Marital Autonomy

Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) Decriminalised adultery (Section 497 IPC), ruling that the law treated women as the "chattel" of their husbands, thereby violating their right to equality (Art 14) and dignity (Art 21).
Reproductive Rights & Bodily Autonomy Right to Life & Demographics

X v. Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare (2022) Granted equal abortion rights to unmarried women under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act. Crucially, it recognized marital rape solely for the purpose of the MTP Act, upholding a woman's bodily autonomy. Voluntary Health Association of Punjab v. UoI (2013) Issued strict directions for the effective implementation of the PCPNDT Act to curb the systemic issue of female foeticide and sex-selective abortion.
Adoption Rights, Reproductive and Decisional Autonomy, Maternity Benefits

Hamsaanandini Nanduri v. Union of India (March 2026) Recognised adoption as an aspect of reproductive and decisional autonomy under Article 21 and struck down the restriction limiting adoption maternity benefits to children below three months of age, thereby expanding maternity rights for adoptive mothers.
Right to use menstrual pads

Dr. Jaya Thakur v. GoI and others (2026) Menstrual pads is a matter of bodily dignity and health under Article 21, which serves as a necessary prerequisite to fully exercising the right to education under Article 21A.

elements.text: Article 16 (Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment)
• No discrimination in state employment on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place

of birth, or residence.
• Exceptions: Reservation of appointments or posts for any backward class (Mandal
Commission/Indra Sawhney Case) and EWS.
♦Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) [The Mandal Case] → Upheld the 27%
reservation for OBCs but established the "Creamy Layer" exclusion. It also capped total reservations at 50% and ruled that reservations cannot be applied in promotions.
Effectiveness of Reservation and Sub categorisation

rows.text: Dimension
Present Status
Challenges / Issues
Way Forward
Effectiveness of Reservation Policy

• Improved educational attainment, income and social mobility of SC/ST/ OBC beneficiaries.
• According to AISHE reports, SC enrollment in higher education increased from 46.07 lakh to 69.72 lakh over a recent decade.
• Political reservation has ensured continuous representation since 1950.
• Helped break hereditary occupational barriers.
• Greatest gains among rural and less-educated SC communities.

• Benefits unevenly distributed across communities.
• Reservation alone cannot eliminate structural inequalities in education and employment.

• Continue affirmative action while strengthening education, skilling and livelihood interventions.
• Example: Over 5.65 crore SC beneficiaries have been supported under the Post-Matric Scholarship scheme, heavily supported by Aadhaar-based Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT)
Intra category stratification

• Elite capture: 25% OBC castes received 97% of benefits (Rohini Commission).
• 983 of ~2600 OBC castes received no benefits; 994 castes shared only
2.68%.
• Less than 1% OBC groups cornered 50% of benefits.
• Similar concentration among SC/ST (basis of Davinder Singh).
• 40–50% reserved vacancies remain unfilled in many recruitments.

• Weak creamy-layer enforcement.
• Vacancy backlog.
• Merit vs affirmative action debate
• Demand for proportional reservation after Bihar caste survey.
• Political agitations (Jat, Gujjar).
• Continuing EWS debate after Janhit Abhiyan.

• Fill backlog vacancies on mission mode.
• Strengthen verification of creamy layer.
• Evidence-based recalibration using updated caste data.
• Focus on school-level inequalities along with reservation.
SC/ST Sub-Categorisation

• E.V. Chinnaiah (2004): SCs treated as homogeneous class.
• State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024): 7-judge Bench (6:1) allowed sub-classification based on empirical data.
• Court also endorsed applying creamy layer principle to SC/ST (concurring opinion).

• Centre has not implemented creamy layer for SC/ST.
• Lack of uniform empirical data.
• Risk of political fragmentation and litigation.
• Debate whether economic advancement removes caste-based discrimination.

• National empirical database/caste census.
• Uniform criteria for sub-classification.
• Legislative clarity on creamy layer for SC/ST.
• Periodic review of beneficiary groups.
OBC Sub-Categorisation (Rohini Commission)

• Constituted 2017; Report submitted 2023 but not made public
• Found extreme concentration of benefits among few OBC communities.
• 11 States/UTs already practice OBC sub-categorisation (e.g., Bihar, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka).

• Report remains unimplemented.
• Lack of national caste data.
• Political sensitivity and vote-bank concerns.
• Risk of arbitrary categorisation.

• Publish Rohini Commission Report.
• Use scientific socio-economic indicators for categorisation.
• Develop a uniform national framework while allowing state flexibility.

elements.text: Article 17 (Abolition of Untouchability)
Abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. It is available against private individuals as well. Enforced via the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.
Article 18 (Abolition of Titles)
Prohibits the State from conferring any title (except military or academic). Note: Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, etc., are not 'titles' within the meaning of Article 18 (Balaji Raghavan case).
Article 19 (Protection of Six Rights)
• Guarantees six freedoms to all citizens:

♦Freedom of speech and expression (includes press, commercial ads, right to know). ♦Freedom of assembly (peaceful and without arms). ♦Freedom to form associations/unions/cooperative societies. ♦Freedom of movement throughout India.
• Note: The right to travel abroad (external mobility) is not covered here; it is protected under Article 21

(Right to Life and Liberty - Maneka Gandhi Case). ♦Freedom of residence in any part of India. ♦Freedom of profession, occupation, trade, or business.
• These are NOT absolute. The State can impose "Reasonable Restrictions" on grounds of sovereignty and integrity of India,

security of the state, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency, or morality - Article 19(2)
• Hate Speech: It is not protected. It falls under the reasonable restrictions of Article 19(2), specifically "public order,"

"incitement to an offence," and "friendly relations with foreign states".
• Films: Prior censorship is constitutionally valid for films (unlike print media). K.A. Abbas v. UoI upheld the

Cinematograph Act, empowering the CBFC to pre-censor movies to prevent public disorder.
• Amit Sahni v. Delhi Police Commissioner (2020) (Shaheen Bagh Case): Upheld the right to protest but established that

there is "no right to protest indefinitely" in public spaces; it must be balanced with the commuting rights of others.
• T.K. Rangarajan v. Govt of Tamil Nadu (2003): Clarified that government employees have no fundamental or statutory
right to strike.
Facets of Free Speech under Article 19(1)(a)

rows.text: Right Description Freedom of the Press Implicitly embedded in the right to free speech; not explicitly stated in the Constitution. It is the freedom of citizens to express themselves through the media. Right to Silence The negative freedom of speech. The right to express oneself inherently includes the right not to be forced to speak or express. Right to Information & Know The right to receive and impart information freely. Essential for an informed citizenry and forms the basis of the RTI Act.

Case Discussed in Constituent Assembly (Damodar S. Seth). The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed its implicit inclusion (Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras, 1950). Bijoe Emmanuel & Ors. v. State of Kerala (upheld the right to remain respectfully silent during the national anthem). Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (Established voters' right to know the antecedents of electoral candidates).
Right to Report & Broadcast The right to circulate, publish, and broadcast information, including reporting on legislative and court proceedings to ensure transparency.
The Supreme Court has recognised airwaves as public property, making telecasting a facet of free speech.
Commercial Speech Protection for advertisements and commercial communications that disseminate vital information about products and services to the public.
Tata Press Ltd. v. MTNL (Recognised commercial speech as a protected right).

Right Against Pre-censorship Protection against prior restraint. The government generally cannot prevent the publication of material beforehand. Right to Demonstrate Protection for peaceful picketing and demonstrations as a form of expression.

Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (struck down pre-censorship as a fatal blow to press freedom). Note: This specifically does not extend to a fundamental right to strike (Kameshwar Prasad v. State of Bihar (1962)).

elements.text: Section 69A (IT Act, 2000): Rights, Restrictions & Case Law

rows.text: Aspect
Legal Basis Principle and Judicial Position
Power to Block Content
Section 69A, IT Act, 2000 Empowers the Central Government to block online information in the interests of sovereignty, integrity, security of State, defence, foreign relations and public order.
Procedure & Confidentiality
Blocking Rules, 2009 (Rules 8, 9 & 16) Provides committee-based review and emergency blocking mechanism; Rule 16 maintains confidentiality of blocking orders.
Freedom of Speech Equality & Natural Justice Life & Personal Liberty

Articles 19(1)(a) & 19(2) Digital speech is protected, but may be restricted through reasonable limitations similar to those expressly permitted under Article 19(2). Article 14 Confidential blocking orders raise concerns regarding transparency, fairness and potential arbitrariness, though courts have not invalidated Section 69A on this ground. Article 21 Restrictions affecting digital access must satisfy necessity, proportionality and procedural fairness.
Right to Profession/ Trade
Article 19(1)(g) Platform restrictions impacting businesses and livelihoods must demonstrate a legitimate purpose and proportionality.
Constitutional Validity of Section 69A
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) Supreme Court upheld Section 69A due to narrowly defined grounds, written reasons, review mechanisms and availability of judicial review.
Internet Freedom & Proportionality
Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) Internet-based expression enjoys constitutional protection; restrictions must be necessary, proportionate and subject to judicial scrutiny.
Blocking Orders & Intermediaries Temporary Platform Restrictions

X Corp. (Twitter) v. Union of India (2023) Karnataka HC largely upheld government blocking orders and recognized the State's authority to direct content/account blocking under Section 69A. Telegram Matter (Delhi HC, June 2026)
• The Delhi High Court officially dismissed Telegram FZ LLV's plea against the nationwide restriction.
• The Court upheld the suspension, ruling that the Centre strictly adhered to Section 69A of the IT Act and employed the "least restrictive measure" to secure the integrity of the upcoming NEET-UG 2026 re-examination.

elements.text: Freedom of Speech vs. State Restrictions

rows.text: Aspect
Sedition vs. Freedom of Speech
Hate Speech vs. Freedom of Speech
Core Concept
• Penalises words, actions, or visual representations that attempt to bring hatred, contempt, or disaffection against the established government or endanger the nation's sovereignty.
• Penalizes communication that creates divisions in society by belittling, insulting, or inciting violence against specific groups based on religion, race, caste, gender, sexual orientation, etc.
Relation to Fundamental Rights
• Often criticised as a colonial-era restriction on political free speech. Lawful criticism with a view of obtaining change (without inciting violence) does not amount to sedition.
• Runs contrary to the liberating objective of free speech. It threatens constitutional fraternity and the fundamental duty (Article 51A-h) to develop humanism and scientific temper.
Essential Ingredients for Offense
• There must be a clear intention to cause public disorder, disturb peace, or incite violence/armed rebellion against the State.
• Often relies on stereotypes and is used as a tool to gain popularity (e.g., post-election anti-minority incitement). It requires malicious intent to arouse communal disharmony
Primary Legal Provisions (Old vs. New Law)

• Old: Section 124A, Indian Penal Code (IPC).
• New: Section 152, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023. (The word "sedition" is dropped, but the section penalises acts that endanger the "sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India" or encourage "subversive activities").

• Old: Sections 153A, 295A, and 505 of the IPC.
• New: Sections 196 & 299, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 (Penalizes promoting enmity between groups and outraging religious feelings).

elements.text: Historical & Foundational Case Laws

1. Dr. Das Rao Deshmukh v. Kamal Kishore (1995): The SC struck down an election poster saying "teach a lesson to Muslims", ruling it threatened communal feelings and violated India's secular structure.
2. Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan v. UOI (2014): SC urged the Law Commission to define hate speech to prevent its delivery under the garb of free speech.

1. Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962): Put a strict limit on Sedition; only individuals using speech to incite violence and disrupt public order can be penalised.
2. Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015): Emphasised there must be a "degree of proximity" between the words spoken and the public disorder that takes place.
Latest Judgments & Contemporary Context

1. Shaheen Abdulla v. Union of India (2022/2023): In a major ruling to curb rising hate crimes, the Supreme Court directed police across all states to take suo motu (proactive) action to register FIRs against hate speech without waiting for formal complaints, irrespective of the religion of the speaker.
2. Election Commission Guidelines: Continuous crackdowns on hate speech used for political mobilization and violence.

1. S.G. Vombatkere v. Union of India (2022): The Supreme Court put the colonial-era Section 124A (Sedition) in abeyance (suspended its use) due to rampant abuse against critics and journalists.
2. Vinod Dua v. Union of India (2021): The SC quashed an FIR filed against journalist Vinod Dua for criticizing the PM on YouTube, upholding journalistic freedom under the Kedar Nath guidelines.
3. Latest Position (2026): Pending sedition proceedings may continue with the accused's consent, but the constitutional validity of sedition remains undecided.
Current Challenges
• Despite the suspension of 124A, concerns persist
• It remains a highly profitable political tool.
that the new BNS Section 152 uses broad terms like "subversive activities", which critics fear could still be weaponised against legitimate dissenters and journalists.
Courts and police constantly struggle with the evidentiary challenge of proving "malicious intent" and drawing the fine line between offensive advocacy and illegal incitement.
Navigating the Boundaries of Article 19
Aspect of Article 19
Provisions Judicial Pronouncements
Latest Updates
Sedition
Kedarnath Singh (1962): Restricted sedition only to acts inciting violence. Shreya Singhal: Required proximity between words & disorder. Vinod Dua: Upheld journalistic freedom against arbitrary FIRs.
Sec 124A IPC: Penalised for attempting to bring hatred/ disaffection against Government Requires intent to cause public disorder.

Updated Law: The IPC has been replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023. Section 124A is gone, but a new provision (Section 152) penalises acts endangering the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India.
Hate Speech
Dr. Das Rao Deshmukh: Seeking votes by arousing communal feelings is offensive, illegal, and violates the secular structure.
Current Trend: Remains heavily linked to political polarization online. Tackled under new BNS provisions regarding communal harmony and strict Election Commission monitoring.
Belittles specific groups; contrary to Art 19 & Art 51A(h) (scientific temper). Penalised under various criminal laws.
Contempt of Court
Contempt of Courts Act, 1971: Civil (wilful disobedience) vs. Criminal (scandalizing the court). 2006 Amendment: Made "truth in public interest" a valid defence.
Het Ram Beniwal (2017): Held that contempt powers must be exercised sparingly and not in a routine manner.
Current Trend: The judiciary continues to balance the necessity of protecting institutional dignity against the right to fair criticism of judgments.
Fake News & Disinformation
Alakh Alok Srivastava (2020): SC recognised the problem of 'infodemics' and directed the government to curb the menace of fake news.
Addressed historically via the IT Act (2008), Disaster Management Act (Sec. 54), and IPC (Sec. 505). Often used as a political tool or to target minorities.

Under the IT Amendment Rules 2023, the Govt notified a Fact Check Unit (FCU). However, in Sept 2024, the Bombay High Court struck down the FCU as unconstitutional for violating free speech. The SC is currently hearing the appeal.
Censorship of Cinema
K.M. Shankarappa (2000): Held that the executive cannot override a CBFC clearance, as it violates the separation of powers.
Films undergo certification. The proposed 2021 Bill sought to give the govt. "revisionary powers" to re-examine CBFC-cleared films, triggering self-censorship fears.

The Cinematograph (Amendment) Act 2023 was passed. It introduced UA age categories (7+, 13+, 16+), granted perpetual certification, and removed the government's revisionary powers to ensure CBFC autonomy.
IT Rules 2021 (Social Media & OTT)
Tehseen S. Poonawalla (2018): Directed the govt to stop the dissemination of explosive mob-lynching videos on social media.
Ongoing Friction: WhatsApp and others challenged the traceability clause in the Delhi High Court, arguing it breaks end-to-end encryption and violates user privacy.
Mandates Grievance Redressal Officers (GRO), OTT self-classification, and "traceability" (identifying the first originator of a message).
Right to Internet
Anuradha Bhasin: Restrictions must pass the Puttaswamy Proportionality Test: legitimate aim, rational connection, necessity, and procedural safeguards.
A positive right to access the internet and a medium to express oneself, subject to Art 19(2) and 19(6) restrictions.
According to an Access Now report, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest among democracies, primarily deployed during protests and communal violence.
Article 20 (Protection in Respect of Conviction for Offences)
• Scope → Protects against arbitrary and excessive punishment in criminal matters • Available to

Citizens, Foreigners and Legal Entities → Applicable only in criminal proceedings.
• Article 20(1): Ex-Post-Facto Laws → No conviction for an act not an offence when committed → No

greater punishment than prescribed at the time of offence → Prohibits retrospective criminal laws → Does not prohibit retrospective civil or taxation laws → Applies to conviction and punishment, not procedure.
• Exceptions to Article 20(1) → Does not apply to Preventive Detention → Demand for Security →

Retrospective Vodafone taxation valid as Article 20(1) applies only to criminal laws.
• Article 20(2): Double Jeopardy → No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence
more than once → Protects against repeated prosecution and punishment for the same offence.
♦Scope of Double Jeopardy → Applicable only after prosecution and punishment by a Court/

Judicial Tribunal → Not applicable to Departmental Proceedings or Administrative Inquiries → Section 300 CrPC (BNSS equivalent) bars retrial on same facts.
• Article 20(3): Self-Incrimination → No accused shall be compelled to be a witness against himself •

Recognizes Right to Remain Silent • Applies only to accused persons in criminal proceedings • Covers oral and documentary evidence.
• Exceptions to Self-Incrimination → Does not cover production of material objects • Thumb
impressions • Blood samples/medical specimens • Specimen signatures/handwriting • Compulsory exhibition of body.
Article 21 (Protection of Life and Personal Liberty)
The most organic and expansive right. "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law."
• Evolution: Post-Maneka Gandhi Case (1978), the Supreme Court ruled that the procedure must be "right, just and fair", effectively bringing in the American concept of "Due Process of Law".
 It encompasses the right to live with human dignity, the right to a clean environment, the right to privacy (Puttaswamy case), the right to free legal aid, etc.

rows.text: Parameter Procedure Established by Law
Due Process of Law
Origin Derived from the British legal tradition.
Rooted in the American judicial system.

Scope of Judicial Review Narrow: The court only checks if the law was properly enacted by the legislature and if the prescribed procedure was followed. Focus Does not question the intent, fairness, or morality of the law. (If the procedure is correct, a harsh law is still valid).
Broad: The court checks procedural correctness and the substantive fairness of the law itself. Allows the judiciary to strike down laws that are unfair, unreasonable, or unjust.

elements.text: • Article 21A (Right to Education): Added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002). The state shall provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14 years.
• Khap Panchayats and honour killings: Extra-constitutional bodies issuing diktats (like honour killings) that violate Article 21 (Right to Life and Liberty).

 Legislative: No central anti-honour killing law yet, but prosecuted under BNS Sections 49 & 55 (Murder, Abetment). States like Rajasthan passed the Prohibition of Interference with the Freedom of Matrimonial Alliances Bill (2019).
 Executive: Establishment of police "safe houses" and protection cells for inter-caste/runaway couples.

 Judiciary: Shakti Vahini v. UoI (2018). The SC ruled that any attempt by Khap Panchayats to prevent consenting adults from marrying is absolutely illegal. It laid down preventive, remedial, and punitive guidelines.
• Clean Environment vs. Cracker Burning: Article 21 (Right to a clean environment) vs. Article 25 (Freedom of Religion/ Customs) and Article 19(1)(g) (Right to trade for cracker manufacturers).
 Article 21 takes precedence. The right to breathe clean air overrides the absolute right to trade or burst crackers.

 Arjun Gopal v. UoI (2018) → The SC heavily restricted fireworks, banning barium salts and allowing only "green crackers" within specific timeframes. Recent NGT/SC rulings continuously uphold total bans in areas with a "poor" or worse Air Quality Index (AQI).
The Expanding Horizons of Article 21
Following Maneka Gandhi, the Supreme Court treated Article 21 as a constitutional umbrella, recognising "penumbral rights" (implied rights) essential for a progressive society.
The Progressive
The Judicial Expansion
Landmark Case Law
Need
under Article 21
Socio-Economic Dignity
Olga Tellis v. BMC (1985) Francis Coralie Mullin (1981)
Right to Livelihood and Shelter. The Court recognised that "life" means more than mere animal existence
Environmental Justice
M.C. Mehta Cases Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991)
Right to a Clean Environment. Recognizing that industrialization must not compromise human survival or health.
Intellectual & Social Mobility
Unni Krishnan v. State of A.P. (1993)
Right to Free and Compulsory Education (later formalized by the 86th Amendment as Article 21A).
Technological & Informational Era
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
Right to Privacy. Acknowledging the digital age, bodily autonomy, and informational self-determination.
Bodily Autonomy & Progressive Morals
Navtej Singh Johar (2018)
The Right to choose one's sexual identity and the decriminalization of consensual same-sex relations.
Dignity in Death The Right to Die with Dignity, legally recognizing "living wills" and passive euthanasia for terminally ill patients.
Common Cause v. Union of India (2018)
Emergency medical care
SaveLIFE Foundation and Anr. vs Union of India and Ors. (2026)
Right to trauma and emergency medical care (2026) - SC recognised timely access to trauma and emergency medical care as fundamental right.
Article 21 now encompasses not just the right to live, but the right to travel safely, making road safety a constitutional obligation rather than a policy choice.

• Sexuality: It denotes an individual's inherent orientation regarding sexual preferences and intimate self-expression. It transcends mere biological acts, manifesting broadly through non-sexual external identifiers such as lifestyle, clothing, and overall disposition.
• Gender: In contrast, gender is a socio-cultural construct. It represents the normative roles, behaviours, and expectations structurally imposed by society, traditionally conditioning individuals into rigid binary frameworks of masculinity and femininity.
The Evolution of Privacy as a Fundamental Right (Article 21)

Although a single, universally accepted legal definition of privacy does not exist, it fundamentally refers to the ability to shield oneself from unwanted intrusion. It encompasses the various ways individuals keep their personal information, property, and decision-making processes inaccessible to others.
The core characteristics of this right are:
• An Inherent Human Right: It is a natural right that belongs to every individual simply by virtue of their existence, not a privilege granted by the state.

• A Constitutional Guarantee: In the Indian context, it is recognized as a Fundamental Right. It intrinsically flows from the guarantee of "life and personal liberty" enshrined under Article 21 of the Constitution.

• A Dynamic Concept: Because society, technology, and personal boundaries are constantly evolving, the exact meaning and scope of privacy are not rigidly fixed. Instead, the courts determine its application on a case-by-case basis.

rows.text: Year & Landmark Case
Significance
1954: M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra
Rejection of Privacy: An 8-judge bench held that the Constitution's drafters did not intend to include the Right to Privacy as a fundamental right. Search and seizure operations were upheld as valid.
1962: Kharak Singh v. State of UP

Partial Recognition: The SC invalidated nightly domiciliary visits by police as an "unauthorised intrusion into a person’s home". However, the majority maintained that the Right to Privacy was not explicitly guaranteed under Article 21.
1972: R.M. Malkani v. State of Maharashtra
Protection of Communication: The Supreme Court ruled that telephonic conversations are inherently private, establishing that unauthorised phone tapping constitutes a violation of privacy.
1975: Gobind v. State of M.P

Case-by-Case Evolution: The Court acknowledged privacy claims but stated they must be developed case-by-case. It held that privacy could only be infringed upon for "superior reasons" (compelling state interest).
1978: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India

The Due Process Shift: The SC Expanded Article 21 to mandate that any law or procedure interfering with personal liberty (and privacy) must be "just, fair, and reasonable" and not arbitrary or oppressive.
1983: Harvinder Kaur v. Harmander Singh

Gender & Domestic Privacy: Delhi HC upheld conjugal rights by ruling that their core purpose is marital companionship, not forced sexual intimacy. It held that expanding the right to privacy into the domestic sphere would destroy the sanctity and stability of marriage.
2011-12: Right to Privacy Bill & Justice A.P. Shah Committee
Legislative Groundwork: The government initiated drafting privacy legislation. The A.P. Shah Committee laid foundational principles emphasising user consent and institutional accountability.
2017: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India

The Watershed Moment: A 9-judge Constitutional bench unanimously declared the Right to Privacy as a fundamental right intrinsic to Life and Personal Liberty under Article 21, officially overruling the M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh judgements.
2018: Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee
Data Protection Framework: Formed post-Puttaswamy to draft a robust data protection framework, laying the groundwork for India's future data privacy laws.
2023: Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act
Current Statutory Reality: Enacted to govern the processing of digital personal data, balancing an individual's right to protect their data with the state's lawful need to process it.

elements.text: How has the Supreme Court interpreted Article 21 to operationalise the 'Right to
Die with Dignity' and Passive Euthanasia in India?

rows.text: Dimension
Judicial Pronouncements, Principles & Details
The Constitutional Premise Recent Landmark Application

Article 21: The "Right to Life" inherently encompasses the "Right to Die with Dignity."
• Common Cause Case (2018/2023): A Constitution Bench legally recognised passive euthanasia and validated "Living Wills" (Advance Medical Directives), with guidelines simplified in 2023 for better accessibility. Harish Rana v. Union of India (2026): Marked the first time the SC gave the green signal to apply the complete Common Cause guidelines.
• Allowed the withdrawal of life support for a patient in a permanent vegetative state (PVS) for over a decade.
The Litmus Test of Article 21

The core legal question is not whether death is in the patient's best interest, but whether it is in their "best interest" to have their life artificially prolonged by technological means when recovery is impossible.
The "Best Interest" Principle

• There is no straight-jacket formula. It demands a holistic assessment.
• Must include medical factors (chances of recovery) and non-medical factors (the patient's previously expressed values, beliefs, and what they would have chosen if mentally competent).
Right to Palliative Care

Principle of Non-Abandonment: Withdrawing treatment does not mean abandoning the patient.
• The withdrawal must be accompanied by a clear, humane, and step-by-step End of Life (EOL) palliative care plan to minimise suffering.
Active vs. Passive Euthanasia

Active Euthanasia (Impermissible): A positive, overt act to cause death (e.g., lethal injection).
• Passive Euthanasia (Permissible): The legal halting/withdrawal of medical treatment or life support, allowing the patient to succumb naturally to the underlying illness.

Article 21A
• Mandated that "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the ages of six to

fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine."
• Amended Article 45 (DPSP): Shifted the focus of this directive to Early Childhood Care and Education

(ECCE) for all children until they complete the age of 6 years.
• Added Article 51A(k) (Fundamental Duty): Made it the duty of every parent or guardian to provide

opportunities for education to their child or ward between the ages of 6 and 14.
• Article 21A is an enabling provision; it required legislation to define how this right would be executed. This
led to the enactment of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 (effective April 1, 2010).
Article 22 (Protection against Arrest and Detention)

Provides protection in cases of punitive detention (right to be informed of grounds, right to consult a lawyer, right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours) and establishes strict safeguards for preventive detention laws.
Preventive detention and procedural fairness
Dimension Framework SC Observations
The Core
Article 22(3)(b) permits preventive
Union of India v. Ranu Bhandari (2008): The SC reiterated that
Provision
preventive detention is an "evil necessity" and inherently repugnant to democratic ideals. Because normal trials are bypassed, strict procedural scrutiny is mandatory.
