rows.text: Right to Information (The Grounds)
Article 22(5) mandates that the detaining authority must communicate the grounds of detention "as soon as may be"

The Ruling: Simply stating the grounds is insufficient. The State must proactively supply all documents relied upon (including local language translations). Non-supply paralyses the detenu's legal defense.
Right to Representation
Article 22(5) also mandates that the detenu must be given the "earliest opportunity" to make a representation against the order.

Jaseela Shaji v. Union of India and Others (2024): The SC quashed the detention because prison authorities took 9 months to forward the representation via "ordinary post." The Court mandated the use of modern technology (email) for immediate processing.
Rule of Law vs. Executive Tyranny
The tension between State Security (Public Order) and Individual Liberty (Article 21).

Pramod Singla v. Union of India & Ors. (2023): Procedural fairness is the only Constitutional shield a citizen has here. The "subjective satisfaction" of a District Magistrate cannot morph into dictatorial power; it is checked by these procedural safeguards.
Constitutional Morality
The expectation that State institutions protect fundamental rights rather than hide behind bureaucratic red tape.

Jaseela Shaji v. Union of India and Others (2024): The SC slammed the "casual, callous, and negligent approach" of prison authorities. It established that institutional apathy that delays a representation directly violates Article 21 (Right to Life and Liberty).

elements.text: Article 23 Prohibits begar (forced labor) and human trafficking. Available to both citizens and non-citizens.
Article 24
• Prohibits employment of children below the age of 14 years in any factory, mine, or other hazardous
activities. Major Developments Strengthening Article 24
• 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 – Inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory

education for children aged 6–14 years a Fundamental Right, thereby reinforcing the objective of eliminating child labour.
• Factories Act, 1948 & Mines Act, 1952 – Prohibited employment of children in hazardous sectors; the

Mines Act barred persons below 18 years from working in mines.
• Beedi and Cigar Workers Act, 1966 – Prohibited employment of children below 14 years in beedi and

cigar manufacturing due to unsafe working conditions.
• Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 – Defined a child as below 14 years and

prohibited child labour in specified hazardous occupations and processes.
• Child and Adolescent Labour Amendment Act, 2016 – Banned employment of children below 14 years

in all occupations and introduced protection for adolescents (14–18 years) by prohibiting their employment in hazardous work.
• Stricter Penalties and Enforcement (2016 Amendment) – Enhanced punishments for employers

violating child labour laws, strengthening deterrence and compliance.
• Child Labour Rules, 2017 & Rehabilitation Measures – Established mechanisms for prevention, rescue,
rehabilitation, monitoring, and welfare of rescued child labourers, supported by judicial directives and welfare funds.
Article 25 (Freedom of Conscience and Free Profession, Practice, and Propagation of Religion)
All persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practise, and propagate religion.
Restriction: Subject to public order, morality, and health. The word 'propagate' does not include the right to forcibly convert another person.
Key Term Meaning Example
Freedom of Conscience
The absolute inner freedom of an individual to mold their own relationship with God or to shape their religious faith.
The choice to be an atheist or agnostic is fully protected.
Right to Profess
The right to openly and freely declare one's religious beliefs and faith to the world without fear.
A Sikh individual wearing and carrying a Kirpan as a declaration of their faith.
Right to Practice
The freedom to perform religious duties, worship, rituals, and ceremonies and visibly exhibit one's beliefs.
Performing Puja in a temple, offering Namaz, or participating in religious processions.
Right to Propagate
This does not include the right to convert another person.
The right to transmit, disseminate, and explain one's religious tenets to others (e.g., missionary work).
Conversion Limit
The Constitution prohibits forced or induced conversions.
Forcing a conversion directly violates the other person's fundamental "freedom of conscience".
Doctrine of Essentiality

Origin: Established in the Shirur Mutt Case (1954). Example: The Supreme Court ruled that using loudspeakers or beating drums is not an "essential" part of any religion and thus can be restricted to control noise pollution.
A judicial test to determine if a specific practice is fundamental and core to a religion's identity. Only "essential" practices are protected under Article 25.
Article 26 (Freedom to Manage Religious Affairs)
• Every religious denomination has the right to establish and maintain institutions for religious/charitable
purposes, manage its own affairs, and acquire property.

♦Article 26 (d) also includes the right to administer such property in accordance with law.
• The courts apply the "Essential Religious Practices" (ERP) Test to determine what religious practices are
protected. Essential Religious Practices (ERP) Doctrine
• Origin: Developed in Shirur Mutt Case (1954) to determine which religious practices are protected under

Articles 25 and 26.
• Core Principle: Only practices that are essential and integral to a religion receive constitutional protection;

secular activities can be regulated by the State.
• Major Applications: Used in cases such as Triple Talaq (Shayara Bano), Sabarimala, Hijab, and Ismail
Faruqui, where courts examined whether a practice was religiously essential.
♦Prevents every religious custom from claiming constitutional immunity and enables social reform

while balancing religious freedom with constitutional values.
• Criticism: Courts effectively become "theologians", deciding what is essential to a religion, leading to

inconsistency and allegations of judicial overreach.
• Current Debate: The Sabarimala Reference (9-Judge Bench) is reconsidering whether courts should
continue using the ERP test or shift towards a rights-based approach grounded in equality, dignity, and constitutional morality.
Article 27 The state cannot compel anyone to pay taxes for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion, but regulatory fees for administration of religious institutions are permissible.
Article 28
• No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institution wholly maintained out of State
funds.
Landmark Cases
• D.A.V. College v. State of Punjab (1971): Religious instruction cannot be imparted in institutions wholly

funded by the State.
• Aruna Roy v. Union of India (2002): Secular moral education is constitutional and does not amount to

religious instruction.
• Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986): No student can be compelled to act against sincere religious

beliefs.
• S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): Articles 25–28 embody secularism, which forms part of the
Constitution's Basic Structure.

Article 29
• (Protection of Interests of Minorities) : Any section of citizens residing in India having a distinct language,
script, or culture has the right to conserve the same. Protects both religious and linguistic minorities.
Article 30
Grants all minorities (religious and linguistic) the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

rows.text: Implications for Admissions & Reservations

Exemption from National Quotas: Minority institutions are exempt from the strict mandates of national reservation policies (SC/ST/OBC/EWS quotas) under Article 15(5). Sub-quotas: If recognised as a minority institution, AMU can legally reserve up to 50% of its seats exclusively for Muslim students (as per the St. Stephen's precedent), profoundly impacting its demographic intake.
The Broader Constitutional Balance

• Autonomy vs. State Regulation: The judgement highlights the delicate tension between protecting minority rights and ensuring state oversight.
• The SC clarified that while minorities have the right to administer, the State can still impose regulatory measures to ensure academic excellence and prevent maladministration.
• Reinforces the constitutional promise of pluralism. It ensures that minority communities are not penalised (by losing their constitutional rights) simply because they seek formal state recognition or university status.

elements.text: Article 32

It empowers every citizen to directly approach the Supreme Court of India if they believetheir fundamental rights have been violated by the government or any other authority. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called it the "heart and soul of the Constitution."
It makes FRs real and effectively justiciable by providing a mechanism for their enforcement.
The Supreme Court has the power to issue Writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo-Warranto) for the enforcement of FRs.
The Five Prerogative Writs
Type of Writ Application
Habeas Corpus ("To Have the Body")
• Inquires into the legality of a person's detention. The court orders immediate release if the

detention is found to be unlawful.
• Locus standi is the legal principle that determines whether a person has the right to approach

a court, requiring a sufficient interest or direct injury in the matter.
• Exception: In Habeas Corpus petitions, the rule of locus standi is relaxed- any person acting
in good faith (such as a relative, friend, or even a public-spirited individual) may file the petition on behalf of the detained person
Mandamus ("We Command")
Commands a public official, lower court, or public body to perform a specific public duty that they have failed or refused to perform.
Prohibition ("To Forbid")
Issued by a higher court to prevent a lower court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction or violating natural justice. It acts as an order to stop ongoing proceedings.
Certiorari ("To Be Certified")

Issued to a lower court or tribunal after a final decision has been made. It quashes the lower body's order if there is a legal error on the record, lack of jurisdiction, or violation of natural justice.
Quo Warranto ("By What Authority")
Challenges a person's authority to hold a public office to prevent illegal usurpation. It can be filed by any interested person, even if not directly affected.
Exceptions to Fundamental Rights
• Article 31A: Protects five categories of laws (mostly related to agricultural land reforms and industry

management) from being challenged on the grounds of contravention of Articles 14 and 19.
• Article 31B (Ninth Schedule): Protects acts and regulations included in the Ninth Schedule from being

challenged on the grounds of contravention of any of the fundamental rights. (Though constrained post-I.R. Coelho case, 2007).
• Article 31C: Protects laws made to implement Directive Principles under Article 39(b) and (c) from
being challenged on the grounds of Articles 14 and 19.
Article 33
• Empowers Parliament to restrict or abrogate the FRs of members of armed forces, paramilitary forces,
police forces, and intelligence agencies to ensure the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline.

Article 34
• Provides for the restriction of FRs while martial law (military rule) is in force in any area within the
territory of India.
Electoral Bonds Case: Article 19(1)(a) vs. Article 21
Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) v. Union of India (2024)

rows.text: Aspect Article 19(1)(a): Right to Information
Article 21: Right to Privacy
Supreme Court Ruling

The Core Claim Voter's Right to Know: Citizens have a fundamental right to know the source of political funding to make an informed electoral choice. Applicability (Individuals vs. Corporations) Applies fundamentally to the voting citizen who requires transparency for democratic participation. The "Double Proportionality" Test The scheme entirely sacrificed this right, blinding the voter to the flow of political money. Impact on Existing Laws Upheld the necessity of disclosure provisions in the Representation of the People Act and Companies Act. Final Directive Transparency restored. The Election Commission was ordered to publish the details for public scrutiny.

Donor's Informational Privacy: Donors have a right to keep their political affiliations and donations secret to avoid harassment or retribution. Applies to individual citizens (protecting personal political beliefs), but corporate political contributions can’t claim the same level of privacy protection as individual political beliefs. The scheme heavily favoured this right, granting absolute anonymity to the purchaser of the bond. Struck down the anonymity amendments made to the Income Tax Act, Companies Act, and RPA. Anonymity revoked. The SBI was ordered to stop issuing bonds and disclose all past purchase and encashment details.

The Court acknowledged both rights but found the Electoral Bonds Scheme unconstitutional for prioritizing privacy absolutely at the cost of transparency. Crucial Distinction: Companies do not vote. Massive corporate donations are often quid pro quo, so the voter's right to know heavily outweighs a corporation's claim to privacy. The scheme failed the double proportionality test because it did not balance the two rights; it completely extinguished the Right to Information. The Court struck down the removal of the 7.5% corporate donation cap, stating unlimited anonymous funding threatens democracy. The Electoral Bonds Scheme was struck down unanimously as unconstitutional.

elements.text: Right to Property in India

The Right to Property in India transitioned from a heavily litigated Fundamental Right to a standard legal right under the 44th Amendment Act of 1978. Below is a summary of its historical and current constitutional status.

rows.text: Aspect
Provisions
Original Position
A Fundamental Right under Part III; Article 19(1)(f) guaranteed the right to acquire/hold property, and Article 31protected against deprivation without public purpose and compensation.
Early Amendments
Parliament enacted several amendments (1st, 4th, 25th, etc.) adding Articles 31A, 31B, and 31C to protect land reform laws from judicial review and expedite welfare projects.
Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973)
The Supreme Court upheld Parliament’s power to amend property-related Fundamental Rights, while introducing the Basic Structure doctrine.
44th Amendment Act (1978)
The turning point: The 44th Amendment removed the Right to Property from Part III and inserted Article 300A in Part XII.
Current Status (Post-1978) Impact on Land Acquisition

It is now a legal/constitutional right under Article 300A ("no person shall be deprived of his property except by authority of law"). Property can now be deprived only through valid legal authority, and both executive and legislative actions remain subject to constitutional scrutiny. The government now has greater flexibility to acquire land for infrastructure and social welfare without the strict hurdles of Fundamental Right litigation.

elements.text: Exceptions (Compensation Guaranteed)
The State must still pay compensation when acquiring: 1) Property of minority educational institutions (Art. 30), or 2) Land under personal cultivation within statutory ceiling limits (Art. 31A).
Recent Supreme Court Stance

Kolkata Municipal Corporation & Anr. v. Bimal Kumar Shah & Ors. (May 2024): The Court reaffirmed protections under Article 300A, stressing that the rule of law mandates due process and timely, fair compensation when individuals are deprived of property.
The Three Pillars of Privacy (Puttaswamy Framework) - Paternity and Bodily autonomy
Dimension of Privacy Constitutional Application Relevance/ Medical Testing
Physical / Bodily Autonomy
The right to control one's own body and protect it from non-consensual state or private intrusion.
Force drawing of blood or amniotic fluid directly violates a woman’s physical autonomy.
Informational Privacy
The right to control the dissemination of personal, medical, and biological data.
DNA contains the ultimate biological blueprint. Forced extraction is a breach of informational privacy.
Decisional Autonomy
The freedom to make intimate personal choices regarding marriage, procreation, and family
A woman's choice to carry a pregnancy without being subjected to adversarial legal interrogations.
WHY PRE-NATAL DNA TESTING IS DENIED?
The Autonomy Defense: A pre-natal DNA test requires invasive procedures on the mother's body. Under the Puttaswamy doctrine,
no court can force a woman to undergo an invasive medical procedure solely to satisfy a husband's suspicion of infidelity, as it
constitutes a gross violation of her bodily integrity.
The Protection of Legitimacy Defense: The courts act as parens patriae (parent of the nation) for the unborn child. Ordering a
paternity test risks removing the legal legitimacy of the child, causing lifelong social stigma. The child's right to identity and dignity
(Article 21) outweighs the father's right to truth.
The Evidentiary Defense: A DNA test is not meant to be a shortcut for divorce proceedings. If a husband claims adultery, he must
prove it through independent evidence, not by forcing the State (Courts) to violate his wife's biological privacy.

rows.text: The Constitutional Trilemma: Health vs. Trade vs. Religion The Competing Right The Constitutional Argument The Constitutional Argument Article 25 (Freedom of Religion) Pro-cracker advocates argued that bursting fireworks during Diwali is a core religious custom protected under freedom of practice. The Health Caveat: Article 25 is explicitly subject to "public order, morality, and health". Furthermore, bursting crackers is a modern addition and fails the "Essential Religious Practices" (ERP) Test. Thus, it enjoys no absolute protection.
Article 19(1)(g) (Right to Trade/Business) Firecracker manufacturers in Sivakasi argued a ban destroys their fundamental right to a livelihood and creates mass unemployment.

The Survival Caveat: The SC ruled that Article 19(6) allows reasonable restrictions in the public interest. The economic livelihood of a few cannot be placed above the biological survival and respiratory health of millions.
Article 21 (Right to Life/Clean Air) Citizens (especially children and the elderly) argued that the toxic smog violates their right to live with human dignity and health.

The Ultimate Victor: The Court applied the Precautionary Principle, having generally prioritised public health and environmental concerns under Article 21 while balancing competing rights under Articles 19 and 25.

elements.text: Madras HC Ruling (2025): Balancing Free Movement, Protest, and Public Order

rows.text: Theme Constitutional / Statutory Provision
Madras High Court

Nature of Fundamental Rights Article 19(1)(a) – Freedom of Speech and Expression Article 19(1)(b) – Right to Assemble Peacefully Article 19(1)(d) – Freedom of Movement Rights vs. State's Regulatory Power Police regulations requiring prior permission for public demonstrations

• The Court held that the rights to move freely, assemble peacefully, and express grievances are integral to democratic participation.
• However, these rights are not absolute and remain subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order under Article 19(2) & 19(3).
• The Court observed that where the law requires prior permission for protests, participants must comply with the conditions imposed.
• Fundamental rights cannot be exercised in disregard of a valid regulatory framework.
Methods of Protest & Public Order Public order principles under Article 19(2) & 19(3) Check on Executive Arbitrariness Sections 55, 56 & 156, Railways Act, 1989

The Court held that methods such as climbing cellphone towers, life-threatening fasts involving senior citizens, and displaying human skulls and bones are inconsistent with the constitutional guarantee of peaceful protest.
• The Court held that railway authorities may deboard passengers only in limited circumstances - such as travelling without a ticket, suffering from an infectious disease, or occupying an unauthorised compartment.
• A passenger with a valid ticket cannot be removed merely because he intends to protest. Any such action would be unlawful and officials concerned may be held accountable.

elements.text: Fundamental Rights are not merely static constraints on the State; they are a dynamic framework that ensures the dignified existence of citizens. The Supreme Court's expansive interpretation, especially of Article 21, coupled with the Basic Structure Doctrine, ensures that the Fundamental Rights continue to evolve and adapt to modern challenges (e.g., cyber laws, privacy, and environmental protection), keeping the constitutional machinery vibrant and citizen-centric.
Directive Principles of State Policy

Enshrined in Part IV of the Constitution (Articles 36 to 51). Borrowed from the Irish Constitution. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described them as the "novel features" of the Constitution. Granville Austin called DPSP and Fundamental Rights the "Conscience of the Constitution". While Fundamental Rights establish political democracy, DPSPs aim to establish socio-economic democracy. They signify the transition from a colonial 'Police State' to a modern 'Welfare State'.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. Discuss the possible factors that inhibit India from enacting for its citizens a uniform
civil code as provided for in the Directive Principles of State Policy. (2015)
6.1 Dimensions of DPSP
Nature (Article 37)
• Non-Justiciable: They are not legally enforceable by the courts for their violation. The State cannot be

sued for failing to implement them.
• Fundamental in Governance: Article 37 explicitly declares that it shall be the duty of the State to apply
these principles in making laws.
♦They act as an "Instrument of Instructions" for all successive governments, regardless of their

political ideology.
• Judicial Compass: Though non-justiciable, the Supreme Court uses them to determine the constitutional
validity of laws. Courts often interpret laws implementing DPSPs sympathetically while balancing them with Fundamental Rights.
Socialistic Principles (Egalitarian Society)
• Article 38: Promote the welfare of people by securing a social order permeated by justice- social,

economic, and political and minimise inequalities in income, status, and opportunities.
• Article 39: Securing adequate livelihood, equitable distribution of material resources of the community
[39(b)], prevention of concentration of wealth [39(c)], equal pay for equal work for men and women.
♦Example: Abolition of the Zamindari system, Nationalization of Banks (1969), and enactment of the

Equal Remuneration Act, 1976.
• Article 39A: Equal justice and free legal aid to the poor.
♦Example: Enactment of the Legal Services Authorities Act (1987) and the establishment of Lok

Adalats.
• Article 41 & 42: Right to work, education, public assistance (old age, sickness), and provision for just/

humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
• Articles 43 & 43A: Securing a living wage, decent standard of life, and participation of workers in the
management of industries.
Gandhian Principles
• Article 40: Organise Village Panchayats and endow them with powers of self-government. (Implemented

via 73rd Amendment).
• Articles 43 & 43B: Promote cottage industries on an individual/cooperative basis in rural areas, and
promote voluntary formation of co-operative societies.
♦Example: Establishment of Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), Coir Board, Silk

Board, etc.
• Article 46: Promote educational and economic interests of SCs, STs, and other weaker sections, protecting

them from social injustice.
• Article 47: Prohibit the consumption of intoxicating drinks and drugs which are injurious to health.
• Article 48: Prohibit the slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch/draught cattle to improve their breeds.
Liberal-Intellectual Principles
• Article 44: Secure for all citizens a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) throughout the country.
♦The Supreme Court has repeatedly reminded the state to implement it (Shah Bano case, Sarla

Mudgal case). The debate centers on balancing gender justice/national integration with minority cultural autonomy. The recent Uttarakhand UCC act is a major case study.
• Article 45: Provide early childhood care and education (ECCE) for all children until they complete the age

of six years.
• Articles 48 & 48A: Organise agriculture/animal husbandry on modern, scientific lines, and protect/

improve the environment, forests, and wildlife.
• Article 49: Protect monuments, places, and objects of artistic or historic interest (national importance).
• Article 50: Separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
• Article 51: Promote international peace and security, maintain just relations between nations, and foster
respect for international law.
Evolution via Amendments
• 42nd Amendment (1976 - "Mini Constitution"): Added 39A (free legal aid), 39(f) (healthy development

of children), 43A (workers in management), and 48A (environment).
• 44th Amendment (1978): Added Article 38(2) requiring the State to minimise inequalities in income,

status, facilities, and opportunities.
• 86th Amendment (2002): Changed the subject matter of Article 45. Made elementary education a

Fundamental Right (Article 21A) and directed the State to provide early childhood care under Article 45.
• 97th Amendment (2011): Added Article 43B relating to co-operative societies.
Uniform Civil Code (UCC)

UCC: It is a proposed framework of laws designed to replace religion-based personal laws - which govern marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption - with a single, common set of laws that applies equally to all Indian citizens regardless of their religion, caste, or gender.
Landmark Supreme Court Verdicts The judiciary has frequently highlighted the need for a UCC:

• Shah Bano Case (1985): The Supreme Court emphasised the desirability of Article 44 implementation.
• Sarla Mudgal Case (1995): Addressed the issue of bigamy and the conflict between personal laws on matters of marriage.
• Shayara Bano vs. Union of India Case (2017): Challenged the practice of Triple Talaq and declared it unconstitutional.
Need and Significance of UCC

• Strengthening Secularism: A UCC aligns with India's secular principles by establishing a common set of laws for all citizens, irrespective of religion.
• Equality for All: It would eliminate discriminatory practices based on religion in personal laws, guaranteeing equal rights.
• Promoting Gender Equity: By overriding existing religious personal laws, a UCC could remove gender-based biases, leading to a more just society.
• Protecting Vulnerable Groups: It could offer stronger safeguards for the rights of women and religious minorities who might be disadvantaged by current personal laws.
• Freedom of Choice: It would provide greater freedom for individuals to choose their partners without religious or caste restrictions under civil law principles
Recent Developments & State Implementations

• Uttarakhand: Became the first Indian state post-independence to implement a UCC. It covers marriage, divorce, adoption, and inheritance with a strong emphasis on gender equality. It bans polygamy and child marriage, and notably mandates the registration of live-in relationships to safeguard partner and child rights. (Note: Goa has had a UCC since 1867).
• Gujarat: Has followed suit by forming a committee to draft a UCC, indicating growing momentum at the state level.
• 2018 Law Commission Recommendation: The 21st Law Commission previously recommended codifying existing personal laws rather than implementing a complete UCC, suggesting that the focus should be on universal principles of fairness and equality.
Challenges Way Forward
Religious Interference: May be perceived as an infringement on religious freedom, restricting personal matters.
Introduce the UCC gradually in stages (piecemeal approach) to minimize disruption and allow for smoother adaptation
Minority Apprehensions: Minorities may fear the imposition of majority-driven codes and the erosion of cultural traditions
Prioritize equity and equal treatment for all citizens during the codification process.
Threat to Diversity: Enforcing uniformity could undermine India's rich cultural and religious pluralism.
Foster public debate and open discussions to ensure transparency and address concerns.
Drafting Difficulties: Creating a universally acceptable code is complex due to diverse ethnic and regional traditions
Include legal and social experts from diverse backgrounds in the drafting process

Constitutional Conflict: Potential friction between Article 14 (Equality) and Article 25 (Freedom of Religion) Launch educational campaigns and engage with different communities to build awareness and garner support
6.2 Constitutional Tussle: FRs vs. DPSPs
The Evolution:

1. Champakam Dorairajan Case (1951): The Supreme Court ruled that in case of a conflict, FRs would prevail. DPSPs have to run as a subsidiary to FRs.
2. Golaknath Case (1967): The SC held that FRs cannot be amended for the implementation of DPSPs.
3. The Parliament's Pushback (24th & 25th Amendments): Parliament inserted Article 31C, stating that laws made to implement Article 39(b) and (c) (equitable distribution of resources) cannot be struck down even if they violate Articles 14 and 19.

4. Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973): The SC upheld the validity of the first provision of Article 31C, cementing the primacy of 39(b) and (c) over Articles 14 and 19.
5. 42nd Amendment Act (1976): The government attempted to give legal primacy and supremacy to all DPSPs over Articles 14 and 19.
6. Minerva Mills Case (1980) - The Final Settlement: The SC struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension. It ruled that the Indian Constitution is founded on the "bedrock of the balance between Part III (FRs) and Part IV (DPSPs)".

"To give absolute primacy to one over the other is to disturb the harmony of the Constitution. This harmony and balance is an essential feature of the Basic Structure." While Fundamental Rights act as injunctions against State tyranny, the Directive Principles are positive mandates for State action.Together, they form the core of transformative constitutionalism, ensuring that political liberty is not a hollow promise, but is firmly anchored in the reality of social equity and economic justice.
Fundamental Duties

The original Constitution (1950) contained only Fundamental Rights, not Duties. The framers assumed that citizens would naturally perform their duties. Rights and duties are correlative and inseparable. As Mahatma Gandhi famously said, "The true source of right is duty. If we all discharge our duties, rights will not be far to seek." Borrowed from the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR.
7.1 Dimensions of FDs

rows.text: Evolution and Nature

• The Swaran Singh Committee (1976): Formed during the Internal Emergency to make recommendations about fundamental duties. ♦The committee argued that citizens must realise that in addition to enjoying rights, they also have certain obligations.
• 42nd Amendment Act (1976): Inserted a new part, Part IVA, containing only one article: Article 51A. It initially codified 10 Fundamental Duties.
• 86th Amendment Act (2002): Added the 11th duty regarding the provision of educational opportunities for children.
• Restricted to Citizens: Unlike some Fundamental Rights (e.g., Articles 14 or 21), which apply to foreigners, FDs are strictly confined to Indian citizens.
• Non-Justiciable: Similar to DPSPs, they are not directly enforceable by courts. There is no constitutional provision for direct legal sanction for their violation.
Duties

• Civic & Patriotic Duties: ♦To abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, the National Flag, and the National Anthem [51A(a)]. ♦To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India [51A(c)]. ♦To defend the country and render national service when called upon [51A(d)].
• Moral & Social Duties: ♦To cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom [51A(b)]. ♦To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood; to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women [51A(e)]. ♦To value and preserve the rich heritage of the country's composite culture [51A(f)].
• Environmental Duties: ♦To protect and improve the natural environment (forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife) and have compassion for living creatures [51A(g)]. (Directly linked to DPSP Article 48A and FR Article 21).
• Intellectual & Progressive Duties: ♦To develop scientific temper, humanism, and the spirit of inquiry and reform [51A(h)]. ♦To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity [51A(j)].
• Public Property & Parental Duties: ♦To safeguard public property and abjure violence [51A(i)]. ♦To provide opportunities for education to one's child or ward between the ages of 6 and 14 years [51A(k) - Added in 2002].
Landmark Judicial Pronouncements

• AIIMS Students’ Union v. AIIMS (2001): The Supreme Court declared that Fundamental Duties are as important as Fundamental Rights. Though Part IVA is not enforceable by writs; it provides a valuable guide to constitutional interpretation.
• M.C. Mehta Case: The SC has heavily relied on Article 51A(g) (environmental duty) to order the closure of polluting industries, mandating that the state and citizens must jointly protect the environment.
• Shyam Narayan Chouksey v. Union of India (2016): The "National Anthem Case". The SC initially mandated playing the anthem in cinema halls to instil a sense of committed patriotism (Article 51A(a)), though it later made it optional.
• Ranganath Mishra Case (2003): The SC directed the Government of India to take steps to operationalise the recommendations of the Justice JS Verma Committee regarding the dissemination and enforcement of Fundamental Duties (Article 51-A) among citizens.

elements.text: 7.2 Statutory backing for Fundamental Duties
1. Upholding the Sovereignty, Integrity, and National Symbols

 Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971: Directly enforces the duty to respect the Constitution, the National Flag, and the National Anthem by penalising any disrespect or insult toward them.

 Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967: Strongly aligns with the duty to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India by strictly prosecuting unlawful and terror-related activities that threaten the nation.
2. Promoting Brotherhood and Social Harmony

 The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955: Reflects the duty to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood by strictly prohibiting untouchability and punishing discrimination based on religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
3. Safeguarding the Dignity of Women

 Women-Centric Legislations: The duty to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women is legally reinforced by statutes like the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, and the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act (formerly SITA, 1956).
4. Protecting and Improving the Environment

 Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972: Reinforces the citizen's duty to have compassion for living creatures by protecting rare and endangered species and criminalising illegal poaching and wildlife trade.

 Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980: Safeguards natural habitats and checks indiscriminate deforestation, directly echoing the constitutional duty to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, and rivers.
5. Safeguarding Public Property and Abjuring Violence

 Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984: Directly translates the moral duty of safeguarding public property and abjuring violence into a legal mandate by penalizing acts of vandalism and destruction.

 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023: Several penal sections within the newly enacted BNS regarding theft, mischief, and vandalism indirectly enforce the duty to respect the rights of others and protect public/state property.

While Fundamental Rights act as a shield against State tyranny, Fundamental Duties serve as a moral compass for the citizenry. In an era marked by environmental degradation, communal polarisation, and digital misinformation, Article 51A transitions democracy from a mere political mechanism into a participatory civic responsibility. As the Supreme Court has noted, a careful balancing of Part III (Rights) and Part IVA (Duties) is essential to realize the vibrant, progressive republic envisioned in the Preamble.
Constitutional Amendments and Article 368

Part XX, Article 368 grants Parliament the constituent power to amend the Constitution and lays down the procedure. The framers wanted a Constitution that could adapt to changing times but wasn't so fragile that ruling parties could alter its core for political gains. The Indian Constitution strikes a unique balance between extreme rigidity (like the USA, requiring a special convention) and extreme flexibility (like the UK, amended by ordinary law).
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. The Indian Constitution has conferred the amending power on the ordinary legislative
institutions with a few procedural hurdles. In view of this statement, examine the
procedural and substantive limitations on the amending power of Parliament to change
the Constitution. (2025)
2. Explain the significance of the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act. To what extent
does it reflect the accommodative spirit of federalism. (2023)
3. Explain the salient features of the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment)
Act, 2016. Do you think it is efficacious enough ‘to remove cascading effect of taxes and
provide for common national market for goods and services’? (2017)
8.1 Procedure and Classification

rows.text: Aspect
Details
Procedure for Amendment (Article 368) Classification of Amendments

• Initiation: A Constitutional Amendment bill can only be introduced in Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha). State legislatures cannot initiate an amendment.
• Introduction: Can be introduced by a Minister or a Private Member. No prior permission of the President is required.
• Majority Required: The bill must be passed in each House by a Special Majority (a majority of the total membership of the House and a majority of two-thirds of the members of the House present and voting).
• No Joint Sitting: Each House must pass the bill separately. If there is a deadlock, there is no provision for a joint sitting(unlike ordinary bills).
• The Ratification Clause: If the bill seeks to amend federal provisions of the Constitution, it must also be ratified by the legislatures of half of the states by a simple majority.
• Presidential Assent: After passage (and ratification, if needed), it goes to the President. The President must give assent. President cannot withhold it or return it for reconsideration (made obligatory by the 24th Amendment Act, 1971).
• Amendments by Simple Majority (Outside Article 368) → These are passed like ordinary legislative processes and are technically not deemed Constitutional Amendments under Article 368. ♦Examples: Admission/establishment of new states, altering boundaries (Articles 2, 3, 4). ♦Abolition/creation of State Legislative Councils (Article 169). ♦Second Schedule (Salaries of President, Governors, and Judges). ♦Fifth and Sixth Schedules (Scheduled areas and Tribal areas).
• Amendments by Special Majority (Under Article 368) ♦Most provisions of the Constitution fall here. ♦Examples: Fundamental Rights (Part III). ♦Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV). ♦All other provisions not covered in the first and third categories.
• Amendments by Special Majority + Ratification by Half the States ♦Provisions related to the federal structure (centre-state relations) require this rigid process. ♦Examples: Election of the President and its manner. ♦Extent of the executive power of the Union and states. ♦Supreme Court and High Courts. ♦Distribution of legislative powers (Union, State, and Concurrent lists). ♦Goods and Services Tax Council (Article 279A). ♦Article 368 itself.

elements.text: 8.2 Procedural vs. Substantive Limitations on Parliament's Amending Power

rows.text: Aspect Procedural Limitations
Substantive Limitations
Meaning Govern the process and conditions for amending the Constitution under Article 368.

Article 13 - power of judicial review
Focus Regulate how Constitutional amendments are made. Initiation of Amendment Amendment Bills can be introduced only in either House of Parliament.
Regulate what Parliament can amend. Parliament's amending power remains subject to preservation of the Constitution's fundamental framework.

Legislative Approval Requires a special majority in each House and, in specified cases, ratification by at least half of the States. Role of the President President is constitutionally bound to give assent to a duly passed Amendment Bill. Federal Safeguards Protect federal interests through mandatory State ratification for certain amendments. Judicial Evolution Rooted directly in the constitutional text of Article 368. Key Constitutional Principle Constitutional change must follow prescribed constitutional procedures. Illustrative Features Protected Special majority, separate approval by both Houses, no joint sitting, State ratification, and mandatory presidential assent. Objective Ensure broad political consensus and federal participation in constitutional amendments. Even a procedurally valid amendment can be reviewed for its impact on the Constitution's basic features. Presidential assent cannot validate an amendment that damages the Basic Structure. Protect federalism itself as a component of the Basic Structure. Developed through Shankari Prasad (1951), Golaknath (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), and Minerva Mills (1980). Constitutional change cannot destroy the Constitution's essential identity. Supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, judicial review, federalism, secularism, democracy, separation of powers, and judicial independence. Preserve the Constitution's fundamental character while permitting necessary evolution. Amendment may be struck down for violating the Basic Structure Doctrine.

Solution
Absence of a Dedicated Body
• 42nd Amendment (1976): It amended 59
India lacks a specialised body (like a Constitutional Convention in the USA) tasked with proposing or comprehensively reviewing amendments.
Establish a permanent Constitutional Review Commission or mandate specialised, non-partisan parliamentary committees to thoroughly vet proposals before introduction.

to Review the Working of the Constitution recommended creating a permanent constitutional review body, but the proposal remains unimplemented.
No Deadlock Resolution
• Women’s Reservation Bill (108th Amendment

dissolution of the 15th Lok Sabha, highlighting how a constitutional amendment can fail due to inter-house deadlock without any resolution mechanism.

rows.text: Ambiguous Ratification Timeframe
There is no prescribed time limit for state legislatures to ratify an amendment, nor clarity on whether they can withdraw their approval.
Stipulate a clear, fixed timeframe (e.g., 6 months) for states to communicate their ratification or rejection, and codify that consent, once given, cannot be withdrawn.

• 66th Amendment Bill (1989): Passed by Parliament but failed to secure the required state ratifications.
• Legislative Limbo: The Bill lapsed due to the absence of any time limit or mechanism to ensure state responses, exposing a gap in the amendment process.
Majoritarian Dominance
A central government with a strong majority can pass amendments swiftly, risking the override of minority interests or federal principles.
Introduce a higher threshold (e.g., three-fourths majority) for amendments affecting core federal provisions to ensure wider cross-party consensus.
• The One Nation, One Election proposal has faced criticism for potentially undermining regional autonomy.
Limited Public Participation
Amendments are often passed without broader public consultation or stakeholder involvement, reducing democratic legitimacy
Mandate a statutory public circulation period (e.g., 90 days) for all amendment bills to invite citizen feedback and expert scrutiny before a parliamentary vote.

• 97th Constitutional Amendment (2011): Enacted without adequate consultation and state ratification.
• Supreme Court Intervention (2021): In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah, the Court struck down key Part IXB provisions for failing to obtain the required state ratification, highlighting procedural lapses in the amendment process.
Limited State Legislature Role Frequent Amendments

States cannot initiate a constitutional amendment; their role is purely reactionary and limited only to provisions affecting federal structures. The exceptionally high number of amendments points to political expediency or a lack of foresight during drafting.

Empower state legislatures to jointly propose amendments (e.g., requiring a resolution passed by at least half the states) to be formally taken up by Parliament. Differentiate between routine administrative updates and core structural changes, potentially treating administrative provisions as “organic laws” that can be amended more easily than the Constitution itself.

• Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation (2014): Parliament created Telangana despite the Andhra Pradesh Assembly's opposition, showing that state consent is not binding under Article 3.
• 101st Constitutional Amendment (GST, 2016): States could only ratify the amendment and had no power to initiate, modify, or veto the restructuring of taxation powers.
• High Amendment Frequency: India has enacted 106 constitutional amendments in about 75 years, compared to only 27 amendments in the USA over 230+ years.
• Administrative Changes via Amendments: Several amendments (8th, 21st, 31st, 71st, 92nd, 96th, and 100th) dealt mainly with changes to the Eighth Schedule, indicating the absence of a differentiated amendment process and contributing to constitutional inflation.
Shift in Power Balance The Basic Structure Debate

Frequent structural changes risk disturbing the delicate institutional balance between the Centre and States, or Parliament and the Judiciary. While the "basic structure" doctrine safeguards core values, its undefined and evolving scope invites ongoing legal and political friction.

Strengthen institutional guardrails by requiring pre-legislative impact assessments on how proposed amendments affect federal and inter-institutional balance. Encourage collaborative dialogues between the Judiciary and Legislature to outline an indicative, clear list of principles that constitute the basic structure to guide future legislative drafting.

• 99th Constitutional Amendment (2014): Established the National Judicial Appointments Commission to replace the collegium system.
• Struck Down by Supreme Court (2015): In Advocates-on-Record Association v. UoI, the Court invalidated the amendment for violating judicial independence, highlighting the risks of major structural changes without adequate institutional assessment.
• Repeated Judicial Invalidations: The 39th Amendment (1975), parts of the 42nd Amendment (1980), and the 99th Amendment (NJAC, 2015) were struck down by the Supreme Court.
• Underlying Issue: These cases highlight the continuing tension between Parliament's amendment power and the judiciary's evolving Basic Structure Doctrine.

elements.text: Article 368 ensures that the Indian Constitution is neither a rigid monolith that breaks under the pressure of changing societal needs nor a malleable tool vulnerable to majoritarian whims. The Supreme Court's 'Basic Structure Doctrine' serves as the ultimate safety valve, ensuring that while the Constitution remains a 'living document' capable of reflecting progressive realities (like GST or Women's Reservation), its democratic, secular, and egalitarian soul remains immortal.

chapters.title: Parliamentary vs Presidential form of Government

elements.text: Parliamentary vs Presidential form of Government

The Constitution of India provides for a parliamentary form of government both at the Centre and in the states. Articles 74 and 75 deal with the parliamentary system at the Union level, while Articles 163 and 164 contain provisions for the states. The bedrock of the Indian political setup is the principle of collective responsibility of the Executive (Council of Ministers) to the popular house of the Legislature (Lok Sabha/Vidhan Sabha), ensuring a 'responsible government' over a merely 'stable' one.
9.1 Comparison of Parliamentary System and Presidential System

rows.text: Feature
Parliamentary System (Indian Context)
Presidential System (e.g., USA)
Executive Structure
Dual Executive: The President is the nominal executive (de jure head), while the Prime Minister is the real executive (de facto head).
Single Executive: The President is both the Head of State and the Head of Government.
Separation of Powers
Fusion of Powers: The executive is drawn from the legislature. Ministers must be Members of Parliament (or become one within 6 months).
Strict Separation: The executive and legislature are completely separate. The President's cabinet comprises non-legislators.
Accountability

High Accountability: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article
75). They remain in power only as long as they enjoy majority support.
Low Accountability: The executive is not responsible to the legislature. They cannot be removed by a simple vote of no-confidence.
Tenure
Uncertain: The government can fall at any time if it loses the majority (via a no-confidence motion).
Fixed: The President and legislature are elected for a fixed term and can only be removed via a rigorous, quasi-judicial impeachment process.
Dissolution of Lower House Merits Demerits

The Prime Minister can advise the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha before the expiry of its term to seek fresh elections.
• Harmony between Legislature & Executive: Reduces deadlocks as the executive is a part of the legislature and commands a majority.
• Prevents Despotism: Power is dispersed among the Council of Ministers, and their survival depends on parliamentary scrutiny, preventing a dictatorship.
• Ready Alternative Government: If the ruling party loses its majority, the President can invite the opposition to form the government without imposing immediate elections.
• Wide Representation: Allows representation of diverse regions, castes, and communities in the executive, which is crucial for India's pluralistic society.
• Unstable Government: Prone to collapse due to defections or coalition withdrawals (e.g., frequent government collapses in the 1990s in India).
• No Continuity of Policies: Frequent changes in government may lead to policy paralysis or reversal of previous policies.
• Executive dominance over legislature: If a party enjoys an absolute majority, the cabinet can bypass rigorous legislative scrutiny (e.g., during the 1975 Emergency).

The President cannot dissolve the lower house (e.g., the US House of Representatives).
• Stable Government: The fixed tenure ensures the government can execute its vision without the constant threat of a no-confidence motion.
• Definiteness in Policies: Stability allows for the formulation and execution of long-term developmental policies.
• Government by Experts: The President can more easily appoint domain experts (technocrats) to lead ministries without worrying about their political electability.
• Conflict between Organs: Frequent deadlocks between the President and the Legislature, especially if they are controlled by rival political parties.
• Non-Responsible: The executive is not dependent on legislative confidence for survival.
• Autocratic Tendencies: Concentrating massive power in the hands of a single individual carries the risk of authoritarianism.

elements.text: 9.2 Why Did India Adopt the Parliamentary System?
During the Constituent Assembly debates, a Presidential system was proposed (notably by Prof. K.T. Shah), but the founding fathers chose the Parliamentary system for four primary reasons:

1. Familiarity with the System: India had grown accustomed to the parliamentary model introduced incrementally during British rule (e.g., the Government of India Acts of 1919 and 1935). K.M. Munshi argued that it would be unwise to discard a system functioning for decades.
2. Preference for Responsibility over Stability: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar explicitly stated that a democratic executive must satisfy two conditions: stability and responsibility. Since no system can guarantee both equally, the Assembly preferred daily and periodic accountability (via questions, debates, and elections) over the absolute stability of a Presidential system.
3. Need to Avoid Legislative-Executive Conflicts: An infant democracy struggling with partition, poverty, and integration could not afford the frequent deadlocks characteristic of the American system. A unified approach to nation-building was required.
4. Nature of Indian Society: India’s extreme diversity (religious, linguistic, ethnic) required a system that could accommodate varied groups within the core power structure (the Council of Ministers), which a single Presidential executive might fail to provide.
9.3 Should India Switch to a Presidential System?
Arguments in Favour of a Switch:
• It would ensure political stability and end the culture of "horse-trading," defections, and coalition blackmail.
• It would allow the direct entry of technocrats and experts into governance instead of relying solely on career politicians.
• Relatively, it would force voters to choose a national leader based on a unified national agenda, rather than fragmented regional, caste, or religion-based voting.
Arguments Against a Switch (The Prevailing View):

• Basic Structure Doctrine: The Supreme Court (in the Kesavananda Bharati case, 1973) held that the Parliamentary system is a part of the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution. Therefore, Parliament cannot amend it into a Presidential system.
• Swaran Singh Committee (1976): Formed to review the Constitution, this committee concluded that the parliamentary system has been doing well and there is no need to replace it.

• Risk of Centralisation: Given India's socio-economic vulnerabilities and vast inequalities, concentrating executive power in one individual could lead to authoritarianism and alienate marginalised regions.

While the parliamentary system in India has suffered from flaws like the criminalisation of politics, defections, and occasional instability, the solution lies in reforming the electoral process and strengthening intra-party democracy, rather than abandoning the system altogether. The Parliamentary framework, enshrined in Articles 74 and 75, with its inherent mechanism of daily accountability, remains best suited to accommodate the vast and pluralistic ethos of the Indian Republic.
Emergency Provisions and Impacts

The Emergency provisions are enshrined in Part XVIII (Articles 352 to 360) of the Indian Constitution. Their primary rationale is to safeguard the sovereignty, unity, integrity, and security of the country, as well as the democratic political system. As Dr. B.R. Ambedkar noted in the Constituent Assembly, the Indian Constitution is unique because it can be "both unitary as well as federal according to the requirements of time and circumstances." During an emergency, the federal structure seamlessly converts into a unitary one without requiring a formal constitutional amendment.
UPSC Mains PYQs

elements.text: 10.3 Judicial Review & Landmark Judgments
The Judiciary has played a monumental role in checking the arbitrary use of Emergency provisions, especially Article 356.

• Minerva Mills Case (1980): The Supreme Court held that the proclamation of a National Emergency (Article 352) is not immune from judicial review. It can be struck down if it is proven to be malafide, absurd, or based on extraneous facts.
• S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): The absolute bedrock judgement for Article 356.
 It held that Article 356 is subject to judicial review.
 The state assembly should only be dissolved after Parliamentary approval.
 A floor test in the assembly is the only definitive test of a majority, not the Governor's subjective assessment.
 Secularism is a "Basic Feature"; dismissing a state government for anti-secular acts is constitutionally valid.

• Nabam Rebia Case (2016 - Arunachal Pradesh) & Harish Rawat Case (2016 - Uttarakhand): The Supreme Court heavily came down on the Centre for the arbitrary imposition of Article 356, physically restoring the ousted state governments and ordered floor test restoration.
 The Court ruled that the Governor's discretionary powers under Article 163 are limited and subject to judicial review.

• Anuradha Bhasin Case (2020): While dealing with the communication lockdown in J&K, the SC ruled that indefinite suspensions (a quasi-emergency measure) are impermissible. Any restriction on fundamental rights must pass the Test of Proportionality.
Test of Proportionality
The Test of Proportionality is a highly significant legal doctrine used by courts to determine whether a government's restriction on a citizen's Fundamental Rights is justified.
In simple terms, it means the government cannot use a "sledgehammer to crack a nut." The restriction placed on a right must be proportionate to the goal the government is trying to achieve.

In India, the Supreme Court formally adopted this test in the landmark K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) case (the Right to Privacy judgment) and extensively applied it in the Anuradha Bhasin (2020) case regarding internet shutdowns in Jammu & Kashmir.
Whenever a government action curtails a fundamental right (like Freedom of Speech, Movement, or Privacy), the courts test that action using a four-pronged framework.
To pass the test and be considered constitutional, the government's action must satisfy all four of the following conditions:
The 4 Prongs of the Proportionality Test
1. Legality (Action backed by Law) The restriction cannot be arbitrary or based on mere executive orders. It must be expressly backed by a valid, enacted law.

 Example: You cannot restrict internet access just because a police officer wants to; it must be done under a specific law like the Telecom Suspension Rules.
2. Legitimate State Aim (Need) The law must seek to achieve a legitimate public or state interest.

 Example: Preventing riots, protecting national security, or stopping the spread of a pandemic are legitimate aims.
3. Rational Connection (Suitability) There must be a logical link between the measure taken and the objective it aims to achieve. The restriction must actually help in solving the problem.

 Example: If the goal is to catch a thief in a neighborhood, imposing a nationwide curfew has no rational connection to the goal.
4. Necessity (Least Restrictive Alternative) This is the most critical step. The government must prove that the measure they chose is the least intrusive way to achieve the goal. If there is an alternative method that achieves the same result while restricting rights less, the government must choose that alternative.

 Example: If stopping a specific violent website is the goal, the government should block just that website (less restrictive) rather than shutting down the entire internet for the whole state (highly restrictive).
10.4 Way Forward: Commission Recommendations

• Sarkaria Commission (1988): Emphasised that Article 356 must be used sparingly and strictly as a "measure of last resort" only when all other constitutional avenues (like issuing warnings under Article 355) have been exhausted

• Punchhi Commission (2010): Localised Emergency: Recommended a constitutional framework for a "Localized Emergency" under Article 355. Instead of dismissing the entire state government and dissolving the assembly under Article 352 or 356, the Centre should be able to take control of only the specific troubled district/area to tackle the crisis locally → never constitutionally implemented

 Codification of Guidelines: Suggested that the guidelines laid down in the S.R. Bommai judgement should be explicitly incorporated into the text of the Constitution to remove any lingering ambiguities.

The Emergency provisions are a necessary "safety valve" to protect the Indian Republic from existential threats. However, the transition from the era of frequent President's Rule (1970s-80s) to the current restrained approach demonstrates the maturation of Indian democracy. Strengthened by the 44th Amendment and the vigilant oversight of the Supreme Court (Bommai and Nabam Rebia cases), these provisions now function closer to Dr. Ambedkar's original vision- a dormant weapon strictly reserved for the ultimate defense of the Constitution, not a political tool for federal subversion.

chapters.title: Comparisons with the USA, UK, France etc

elements.text: Comparisons with the USA, UK, France etc.

As Dr. B.R. Ambedkar famously remarked, the Indian Constitution was drafted after 'ransacking all the known Constitutions of the world'. However, it is not a blind plagiarism of Western models but a brilliant eclectic synthesis. It ingeniously blends the Parliamentary responsibility of the UK with the Judicial Supremacy of the USA, tailored specifically to manage the colossal diversity of the Indian subcontinent. India also borrowed from Ireland, Canada, Australia, Germany, South Africa, etc., to reinforce the “synthesis” idea.
11.1 India v/s United Kingdom (The Westminster Model)
India adopted the British Parliamentary system but completely rejected its foundational premise: the absolute sovereignty of Parliament.

The Indian Constitution provides for a federal structure with a strong unitary bias. Granville Austin described it as "Cooperative Federalism," while K.C. Wheare called it "Quasi-Federal." The Constitution regulates Centre-State relations across three domains: Legislative (Part XI), Administrative (Part XI), and Financial (Part XII).

12.1 Introduction to Indian Federalism

Federalism is a system of government where power is structurally divided between a central authority and constituent units (states/ provinces). In India, Article 1 of the Constitution describes India as a "Union of States." Crucially, the word "Federation" is nowhere mentioned in the Constitution. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar justified the term "Union" to signify two things:

1. The Indian Federation is not the result of an agreement among independent states (unlike the USA).
2. The states have no right to secede from the federation.

India represents a "Holding Together" federation, where a large, diverse nation consciously divides its power between the Centre and States to accommodate administrative convenience and regional diversity, as opposed to a "Coming Together" federation (like the USA) where independent states pooled their sovereignty.
Types/Models of Federalism

1. Cooperative Federalism
2. Competitive Federalism
3. Asymmetric Federalism
4. Fiscal Federalism
Asymmetric Federalism

• Concept: A system where all constituent states do not possess identical powers. The Constitution accommodates unique geographic, ethnic, or historical challenges by granting special status to certain regions.

• Enshrined in Part XXI of the Constitution ("Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions"), Articles 371 to 371-J embody this principle, granting special provisions to 12 states (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, and Karnataka).
Type Characteristics & Constitutional Examples
Vertical Asymmetry (Centre vs. States)

• The Union is indestructible; states are not.
• States have no role in ratifying most constitutional amendments (only those affecting federal structure

require 50% state ratification).
• Existence of Union Territories (UTs) directly governed by the Centre.
Horizontal Asymmetry (State vs. State)

• Rajya Sabha Representation: Unequal, based on population (e.g., UP has 31 seats; Sikkim has 1).
• Article 371 (A-J): Special provisions for specific states (e.g., Naga customary laws in 371A; special

development boards for Vidarbha/Saurashtra).
• 5th & 6th Schedules: Special administrative setups for tribal areas. The 6th Schedule creates
Autonomous District Councils (e.g., in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram).
Among Union Territories

• Delhi & Puducherry: Have legislative assemblies and Chief Ministers.
• J&K: UT with a legislature (currently under transition).
• Other UTs (e.g., Lakshadweep, Andaman): No legislature; ruled purely by central Administrators/Lt.
Governors.
Why Did India Adopt Asymmetric Federalism?

• Protection of Cultural & Ethnic Identity: Recognising that the tribal customary laws and land-holding systems of the Northeast are unique and pre-date the Indian Constitution (e.g., Nagaland and Mizoram).

• Addressing Regional Imbalances (Developmental Asymmetry): To prevent the neglect of historically backward regions within a developed state by creating special development boards and ensuring equitable allocation of funds (e.g., Vidarbha in Maharashtra, Saurashtra in Gujarat, and Kalyana in Karnataka).

• Smooth Political Integration & Law & Order: To manage the transition of newly integrated regions into the Indian Union (e.g., Sikkim) and to handle sensitive border states where the Governor is given special responsibilities for law and order (e.g., Arunachal Pradesh).

12.2 Features of Indian Federalism
Federal Features (Promotes State Autonomy)
Unitary Features (Promotes Strong Centre)
Dual Polity: Clear existence of Union and State governments.
Single Constitution & Citizenship: States do not have their own constitutions or citizenship (unlike the USA).
Written Constitution & Supremacy: Limits the powers of both the Centre and States.
Emergency Provisions: Converts the federal structure into a unitary one overnight without formal amendment (Articles 352 & 356).
Division of Powers: The 7th Schedule divides subjects into Union, State, and Concurrent lists.
Overriding Legislative Power: The Centre has residuary powers (Article 248) and overrides states in the Concurrent List.
Independent Judiciary: The Supreme Court acts as the umpire in Centre-State disputes (original jurisdiction under Article 131).
All India Services: IAS, IPS, and IFoS are recruited by the Centre but serve the states, providing centralised administrative control.

Indian federalism is a unique "holding together" federation that balances state autonomy with a strong Centre to safeguard national unity and administrative efficiency. Its flexible design has enabled India to accommodate vast regional diversity while preserving constitutional stability and cooperative governance.

Principles for Interpreting the Seventh Schedule
Doctrine Meaning / Basis Core Principle / Test
Recent Landmark Case
Doctrine of Pith and Substance

Union of India v. Future Gaming Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (2025): The Supreme Court held that lotteries fall under "betting and gambling" (Entry 62, State List); hence, the Centre cannot levy service tax on lottery distributors, applying the Doctrine of Pith and Substance. Parliament's residuary power cannot override an express State List entry.
Determines the true nature and character of legislation rather than its form or incidental effects. Basis: Articles 245–246 and the Seventh Schedule.
If a law substantially falls within the legislature's competence, incidental encroachment into another List does not invalidate it.
Doctrine of Federal Supremacy (Repugnancy)

Forum for People's Collective Efforts v. State of West Bengal (2021): The Supreme Court struck down WB-HIRA, 2017 as repugnant to the central RERA, 2016 under Article 254(1), holding that both laws occupied the same Concurrent List field, making it a landmark application of the Doctrine of Repugnancy.

Where a valid Union and State law conflict on a Concurrent List subject, the Union law prevails and the State law becomes void to the extent of repugnancy. Basis: Articles 246, 251, 252 & 254 (primarily Article
254).
Repugnancy exists only when there is direct and irreconcilable conflict, both laws occupy the same field, and obedience to one results in disobedience of the other (M. Karunanidhitest).
Doctrine of Harmonious Construction

M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024): The Supreme Court harmonized Articles 14 and 21 by recognizing a right against the adverse effects of climate change, balancing environmental protection with developmental and energy needs, exemplifying the Doctrine of Harmonious Construction.
Apparent conflicts between constitutional or statutory provisions should be reconciled so that both provisions operate harmoniously. Basis: Judicial rule of interpretation.
Courts should avoid conflict, reconcile provisions wherever possible, and avoid rendering any provision redundant.
Doctrine of Colourable Legislation

Animal Welfare Board of India v. Union of India (Jallikattu Case, 2023): The Supreme Court upheld the Tamil Nadu Jallikattu Amendment Act, 2017, rejecting the colourable legislation challenge and holding that legislative competence and true effect - not motive - determine constitutional validity.
Legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly; substance prevails over form. Basis:Articles 245–246 and the Seventh Schedule.
Legislative competence is examined, not legislative motive; if a legislature lacks competence, it cannot disguise the legislation through indirect means.
Doctrine of Ancillary/ Incidental Powers

Union of India v. Future Gaming Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (2025): While primarily a Pith and Substance case, the Supreme Court held that Parliament's residuary/ancillary power (Article 248 & Entry 97, List I) cannot override a specific State List entry, reaffirming the limits of the Doctrine of Ancillary Powers.
Legislature possesses incidental powers necessary for the effective exercise of its principal legislative power.
Legislative power extends to matters reasonably connected with the principal subject; incidental powers must be proximate, not remote.

The Constitutional and Legal Framework for Fiscal Consolidation
Fiscal consolidation refers to the policies undertaken by governments to reduce their deficits and accumulation of debt stock.

• FRBM Act, 2003: Acts as the statutory anchor for deficit reduction. The current glide path targets a Union fiscal deficit of
4.5% by 2025-26 and 3.5% by 2030-31.
• Article 293(3) of the Constitution: Mandates that states must obtain the Union's consent to borrow if they have outstanding central loans.
 The 16th FC strictly enforces this to cap State fiscal deficits at 3% of GSDP.

Curbing Off-Budget Borrowings: The 16th FC mandates integrating all hidden liabilities into state budgets. The CAG is tasked with standardised annual reporting of these liabilities, closing loopholes that states use to bypass FRBM limits.
12.4 GST Council and Fiscal Federalism

The GST Council is a joint constitutional forum of the Centre and the States, established to govern the Goods and Services Tax (GST) - a destination-based indirect tax aimed at creating a ‘One Nation, One Tax’ system.
Constitutional Mandate: Inserted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, under Article 279A.
Objective: To pool the fiscal sovereignty of the Centre and States, ensuring a harmonised indirect tax structure across the country.

elements.text: GST Council

Enshrined under Article 279A via the 101st Constitutional Amendment, the GST Council is India's first truly federal decision-making institution. It represents a historic leap of faith into 'pooled sovereignty', where the Union and the States voluntarily surrendered their exclusive taxation domains to forge a unified national market. However, the Council currently navigates a fragile equilibrium, caught between the constitutional ideal of cooperative federal consensus and the centralising realities of fiscal majoritarianism.

rows.text: Dimension
Details Impact
Basic Structure & Composition (Article 279A)

• Chairperson: Union Finance Minister.
• Members: Union Minister of State for Finance + Finance/Tax Ministers of all States/UTs.
• Institutionalises "cooperative federalism" by forcing the Centre and all 28 States to sit at the same table to decide tax policy
Voting Architecture & Central Veto Loss of Fiscal Autonomy

• Centre’s Weight: 1/3rd of the total votes.
• States’ Weight: 2/3rd (distributed equally among all states).
• Decision Threshold: Requires a 75% majority.
• De Facto Veto: No resolution can pass without the Centre’s support (due to its 33.3% share). Even if all 28 states agree, they cannot pass a decision, reducing a federal forum to what critics call an "appendage of the Union Executive."
• States surrendered roughly 44% of their own-tax revenue mechanisms (VAT, Octroi, etc.) to join the GST regime.
• States lack the fiscal flexibility to adjust tax rates during local economic crises, natural disasters, or post-pandemic stress.
Unshared IGST & Divisible Pool

• Under Article 269A, IGST is levied on interstate commerce. IGST constitutes about 55% of total GST collections.
• Large sums (e.g., ₹2.4 Lakh crore in 2021-22) have historically remained in the "undistributed IGST black box", severely impacting fund-starved states.
GST Compensation Fund Expiry

• States originally agreed to GST on a 5-year revenue compensation guarantee, which expired in June 2022.
• Despite pleas for an extension, the Centre refused. Consequently, states face massive revenue shortfalls (fiscal cliffs) without the power to adjust rates.
Consumer vs. Producer Disparities

• GST is a destination-based consumption tax.
• It structurally harms manufacturing/producer states and rewards consumer states. For instance, Southern states contribute highly to direct/indirect taxes but receive a lower proportion from the central divisible pool.
Reliance on Cesses/Surcharges

The Union government increasingly relies on cesses and surcharges. These are not shared with states via the Finance Commission pool, further shrinking the states' legitimate share of national revenues.

elements.text: Challenges
Challenge Description
The Loss of State Fiscal Autonomy

Before GST, states could raise VAT or excise duties to fund emergency relief (e.g., floods, pandemics) or fulfil local welfare manifestos. Today, they cannot alter tax rates without the Council's approval, leaving them financially paralysed during crises.
The Missing Dispute Resolution Mechanism
Article 279A(11) explicitly mandates the Council to establish a mechanism to adjudicate disputes between the Centre and States, which has not yet been established.
The Veto and Political Partisanship

Opposition-ruled states allege that the Centre uses its 33.33% veto weightage, combined with the votes of ruling party states, to steamroll decisions (like the taxation of essential goods or online gaming), bypassing genuine consensus.
Judicial Interventions & The Transition to "GST 2.0"
Aspect Context & Recommendations Significance for Federalism
Judicial Pushback: The Mohit Minerals Case (2022)

The Supreme Court ruled that GST Council recommendations hold only persuasive value, not binding force. Under Article 246A, Parliament and State legislatures have "simultaneous" and "equal" power to legislate on GST.
Reaffirmed India’s federal architecture. It reminded the Centre that the GST Council must be a space for "collaborative dialogue", not coercive central dictation.
GST 2.0: Justice Kurian Joseph Committee Report
A recent expert committee warned that the current GST framework has eroded the fiscal autonomy of States, advocating for a second generation of reforms (GST 2.0).
Highlights that GST is not just a technical tax mechanism but a constitutional arrangement requiring continuous balance between integration and autonomy.
Reforming Voting Weights
Recommendation: Reduce the Union’s vote share to 20%, or adopt a "one member, one vote" model. Treats the Union as an equal partner rather than a dominant promoter, ensuring true consensus.
Rotational Chairpersonship
Recommendation: Rotate the GST Council chair annually between the Union and State Finance Ministers (similar to the European Union model).
Democratises the agenda-setting process, preventing the Centre from monopolising discussions.
Fiscal Flexibility (Rate Bands)
Recommendation: Allow States to vary their SGST component within a narrow, pre-defined band (e.g., +/- 2%).
Gives states the critical fiscal agency needed to raise emergency funds without breaking the national macro-tax structure.
Independent Dispute Resolution
Recommendation: Establish an independent GST Dispute Settlement Authority chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge.
Neutrally resolves Union-State fiscal conflicts, bypassing the built-in Central veto of the Council.
Way Forward
Reform Area Description
Operationalising the Independent Tribunal

Immediately finalise the formation of the GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) with predominantly judicial (rather than technical) members to resolve Centre-State revenue disputes outside of the highly politicised Council meetings.
Democratizing the Voting Structure

To reduce the perception of a Central dictatorship, experts recommend amending the weightage to require the affirmative vote of at least 50% of the States (14 states) alongside the Centre's vote for any decision to pass, preventing a few large states and the Centre from bullying smaller states.
State-Specific Emergency Levers

Introduce a Constitutional provision allowing states to levy a temporary micro-cess (e.g., 1%) on GST within their own borders strictly for notified natural disasters, restoring a sliver of fiscal autonomy without breaking the national supply chain.
Rate Rationalization & Exemptions

The Council must transition from the complex multi-slab structure (5%, 12%, 18%, 28%) to a simplified three-slab structure (as recommended by various economic committees) to boost compliance, reduce classification disputes, and increase the overall revenue pie for states.

The GST Council was envisioned as the apex temple of cooperative federalism, built on the premise of mutual trust and pooled sovereignty. However, the Supreme Court’s Mohit Minerals judgement serves as a stark reminder that the Council’s survival depends not on constitutional coercion but on political statesmanship.
