Indian federalism is an evolving, asymmetric arrangement tailored to the nation's unique socio-political realities. While a "strong Centre" was historically necessary to ensure national integration, the maturation of Indian democracy demands that states be treated as equal partners. Shifting from a paradigm of "subordination" to one of genuine "cooperation and collaboration" is essential for India's inclusive growth and the realisation of its constitutional ethos.
Inter-State Water Disputes

Inter-state water disputes in India arise when two or more states contest the sharing and use of river waters flowing across political boundaries. Driven by uneven rainfall, growing agricultural demand, and climate change, these disputes pose a major challenge to cooperative federalism and sustainable resource management.

Although water is primarily a State subject under the Constitution, the Union is empowered to regulate inter-state rivers in the national interest. To address such conflicts, Article 262 provides a special constitutional mechanism for adjudication, leading to the enactment of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956. However, delays, ad-hoc tribunals, and procedural inefficiencies continue to weaken the effectiveness of the existing framework.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. Constitutional mechanisms to resolve the inter-state water disputes have failed to
address and solve the problems. Is the failure due to structural or process inadequacy
or both? Discuss. (2013)
13.1 Constitutional and Legal Framework
• Entry 17, State List: Water - supply, irrigation, canals, drainage, embankments, water storage, water power - is primarily a state subject.
• Entry 56, Union List: Gives the Union power to regulate and develop inter-state rivers and river valleys, but only to the extent Parliament declares this "expedient in the public interest."
• Article 262(1): Parliament may by law provide for adjudication of any dispute relating to the use, distribution, or control of inter-state river waters.

• Article 262(2): Parliament may bar the Supreme Court and all other courts from exercising jurisdiction over such disputes - an unusual ouster clause, without direct parallel elsewhere in the Constitution.
13.1.2 Legislation enacted under these provisions:

• River Boards Act, 1956 - allows the constitution of advisory River Boards for integrated basin development. Never operationalised, no River Board has ever actually been constituted in nearly seven decades.
 However, some river boards, commissions, authorities have been constituted through government resolution, agreements,
executive orders or Acts. Example: Andhra pradesh state reorganisation Act, 2014 established - Godavari River management boards and Krishna river management board.

• Inter-State River Water Disputes (ISRWD) Act, 1956 - the primary operative law. A state government requests the Centre to refer a dispute; if negotiation fails, the Centre must constitute a Water Disputes Tribunal. A published tribunal award has the same force as a Supreme Court decree.

• 2002 Amendment (Sarkaria Commission recommendations): Mandated a 1-year deadline to constitute a tribunal and a 3-year deadline (extendable by 2 years) for it to give a decision - deadlines routinely breached in practice.

• State may request Centre to refer a dispute. If negotiations fail, Centre must

• Centre may establish implementation authorities (e.g., CWMA & CWRC) through notified schemes.
Sec. 7–9A Powers & Administrative Framework

• Bars jurisdiction of courts over water disputes under Art. 262(2).
• However, the Supreme Court has exercised appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 (SLP), making the exclusion not absolute.
Sec. 12–14 Miscellaneous & Special Tribunal

• Sections 12–13 contain procedural provisions.

elements.text: 13.2 Issues and Explanation

rows.text: Core Issue
Explanation & Examples
Ad hoc-ism of Tribunals Lack of Hydrological Data

Separate tribunals are created for every dispute, leading to a massive loss of institutional memory. Once an award is given, the tribunal dissolves. There is no universally accepted central repository of water data. States often present conflicting data on river flow and distress years, breeding mistrust.
Inordinate Time Lags
The Godavari tribunal took nearly 10 years, and the Mahadayi (Goa-Karnataka-Maharashtra) tribunal took over 16 years. Justice delayed exacerbates the conflict.
Non-Compliance by States Bypassing Article 262

• Tribunal awards lack a strong enforcement mechanism.
• Example: In the Sutlej-Yamuna Link (SYL) Canal Dispute, despite Supreme Court directives since 2002 to finish the canal, Punjab refuses to comply, citing over-exploited groundwater, declining river flows, and changed hydrological realities.
• In May 2025, the Supreme Court had to step in again, directing Punjab and Haryana to cooperate with the Centre for an "amicable mediation". Though Art 262 bars SC jurisdiction, states routinely bypass this by filing Special Leave Petitions (Article 136) in the Supreme Court (e.g., Cauvery dispute), defeating the purpose of specialised tribunals.

elements.text: 13.3 Way Forward
To fix these archaic issues, the Inter-State River Water Disputes (Amendment) Bill of 2019 (which was lapsed later) proposed revolutionary changes

1. Dispute Resolution Committee (DRC): A mandatory pre-litigation negotiation phase. A dispute will only go to a tribunal if the DRC fails to resolve it amicably within 1 year.
2. Single Permanent Tribunal: Dissolving all existing ad-hoc tribunals to create one permanent tribunal with multiple benches, saving costs and retaining technical expertise.
3. Strict Timelines: Reducing the total adjudication time to a maximum of 4.5 years.
4. National Data Bank: Mandating the Centre to maintain a transparent, national-level data bank for every river basin to eliminate "data wars" between states.
5. Binding Decision: The decision of the bench will automatically become final and binding, removing the requirement for the Centre to officially publish it in the gazette to give it force.
6. Operationalise the River Boards Act so basin-level cooperative planning has a genuine institutional home, rather than remaining entirely dormant.

Inter-state river disputes highlight the tension between federal autonomy and national resource management. A transparent, science-based, and cooperative institutional framework- supported by reliable hydrological data, time-bound adjudication, and effective enforcement - is essential to transform water from a source of conflict into an instrument of cooperative federalism.
5th and 6th Schedules

Part X of the Indian Constitution details the special administrative frameworks for "Scheduled Areas" and "Tribal Areas" under Article 244. The framers recognised that tribal populations, due to their distinct socio-cultural practices and historical disadvantages, required specialised protection to prevent exploitation and land alienation. Consequently, the Constitution deployed Asymmetric Federalism, establishing the 5th Schedule for mainland tribal areas and the 6th Schedule for the uniquely autonomous tribes of the North-East.

rows.text: Dimension Fifth Schedule (Article 244(1))
Sixth Schedule (Article 244(2) & 275(1))
Geographical Extent 10 States in Mainland India: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, and Rajasthan.
4 States in North-East India (AMTM): Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.

Declaration & Alteration The President is empowered to declare an area as a Scheduled Area, alter its boundaries, or revoke the order (in consultation with the Governor). Key Administrative Institution Tribes Advisory Council (TAC) Composition of Institution Maximum 20 members, of which three-fourths (3/4th) must be ST representatives sitting in the State Legislative Assembly. Nature of Institution Purely an Advisory Body Legislative Powers None. The TAC only advises on matters referred to it. The Governor holds the power to make regulations restricting land transfer and money-lending. Executive Control (Role of Governor) The Governor enjoys vast proactive powers to independently direct how state/central laws apply to the area. Applicability of Central/State Laws Acts of Parliament or State Legislature apply by default, unless the Governor issues a specific public notification restricting or modifying them. Judicial Powers No judicial powers. Regular state judiciary applies.

The Governor is empowered to organise and re-organise "Autonomous Districts" and "Autonomous Regions" (alter boundaries and change names). Autonomous District Council (ADC) and Regional Councils. 30 members (4 nominated by Governor, 26 elected by adult franchise for a 5-year term). (Exception: Bodoland Territorial Council has 40 members). Highly autonomous self-governing body (often termed a "state within a state"). Vast. ADCs can make laws on land, forests, shifting cultivation, village administration, inheritance, marriage, and social customs (subject to Governor's assent). The Governor acts primarily as an approving authority for the laws passed by the ADCs and determines the jurisdiction of their courts. Acts of Parliament or State Legislature do not apply automatically (or apply with specified modifications). For Assam, the Governor decides; for other states, the President/Governor decides. ADCs can constitute village councils or courts for the trial of civil/criminal suits between ST members.
Financial Autonomy Highly dependent on the State Government. TAC has no taxation powers.
ADCs can assess and collect land revenue and impose specific local taxes (on professions, trades, animals, vehicles, tolls).

Extension of Local Governance The 73rd Amendment does not apply directly; Parliament enacted the PESA Act, 1996, to empower Gram Sabhas in 5th Schedule areas. Contemporary Challenges & Friction Points
• TACs as Rubber Stamps: Often headed by the CM, stifling independent tribal voices (Xaxa Committee).
• Governor's Inaction: Governors rarely use their proactive powers to stop corporate land grabs.

Neither the 73rd Amendment nor the PESA Act applies, as the ADCs themselves serve as the primary local self-government framework.
• State vs. ADC Conflict: State governments deliberately delay funds (under Article 275(1)) and Governor's assent to ADC bills.
• Exclusion of Minorities: Non-tribals in ADC areas face political alienation (e.g., Bodo vs. non-Bodo clashes).

elements.text: • PESA Dilution: State rules frequently
• Demand for Expansion: Agitations in Ladakh
bypass Gram Sabha consent for mining/ dams.
demanding 6th Schedule status to protect land/ environment.
Way Forward

rows.text: Reform Dimension
5th Schedule
6th Schedule
Institutional & Democratic Reforms

Democratise the TAC: Implement the Xaxa Committee recommendation that the TAC should elect its own chairperson (rather than the CM by default) and mandate a minimum number of meetings per year to ensure genuine tribal representation.

Pass the 125th Amendment Bill: This pending bill aims to significantly increase the financial and executive powers of the ADCs and establish elected Village Municipal Councils to ensure decentralisation doesn't stop at the district level.
Financial Devolution
Direct Funding to Gram Sabhas: Ensure strict adherence to the Tribal Sub-Plan (TSP). Funds should be earmarked and transferred directly to PESA Gram Sabhas, bypassing state-level bureaucratic delays.

Direct Finance Commission Grants: Mandate the Central Finance Commission to allocate funds directly to the ADCs (bypassing the State Government). Introduce mandatory CAG audits to ensure transparency and curb corruption within ADCs
Administrative & Governor's Role

Proactive Discretion: Governors must actively use their constitutional mandate to submit timely, independent reports to the President and veto state mining/land acquisition laws that alienate tribal lands.
Mediation & Timely Assent: The Governor should act as a neutral constitutional mediator to resolve the frequent administrative and financial deadlocks between the State Legislature and the ADCs.
Local Governance & Land Rights

Enforce PESA in Letter & Spirit: Stop the dilution of the PESA Act by state rules. The "Free, Prior, and Informed Consent" (FPIC) of the Gram Sabha must be strictly mandatory before any land acquisition or corporate mining.
Strengthen Village Courts: Standardise and upgrade the customary village courts under the ADCs to ensure speedy, accessible justice while ensuring their practices align with basic Fundamental Rights.
Inclusivity & Conflict Resolution

Harmonise FRA and PESA: Ensure seamless implementation of the Forest Rights Act (FRA,
2006) alongside PESA to guarantee community forest resource rights.

Protect Minorities: Develop political and administrative mechanisms to give a voice to non-tribal minority populations living within ADC jurisdictions to prevent severe ethnic clashes (e.g., in Bodoland or Meghalaya).

elements.text: The ultimate goal of both schedules is democratic decentralisation. Moving forward, the paradigm must shift from a 'Welfare Approach' (treating tribals as passive beneficiaries) to an 'Empowerment Approach' (treating them as active stakeholders in their own development), ensuring that the quest for national economic growth does not result in the marginalisation and displacement of India's indigenous populations.
Union Territories

Under Part VIII (Articles 239 to 241) of the Constitution, Union Territories are administered directly by the Central Government. Unlike states, which share a federal relationship with the Centre, UTs exhibit a unitary relationship. The creation of UTs was necessitated by diverse reasons:

1. Political & Administrative: Delhi and Chandigarh (capital and contentious borders).
2. Cultural Distinctiveness: Puducherry, Daman & Diu, Dadra & Nagar Haveli (former French/Portuguese colonies).
3. Strategic Importance: Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep.
4. Special Treatment & Security: Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh.

15.1 General Administrative Framework of UTs (Articles 239–241)
Dimension Constitutional Provision & Explanation
Executive

Administered by the President through an appointed Administrator (designated as Lieutenant Governor, Chief Commissioner, etc.). The Administrator is an agent of the President, not a Constitutional head of state like a Governor.
Legislature Parliament holds the paramount power to make laws on any subject (including the State List) for any Union Territory.
President’s Regulations (Article 240)

The President can make regulations for the "peace, progress, and good government" of certain UTs (Andaman, Lakshadweep, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, Ladakh). These regulations have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament.
Judiciary Parliament can establish an independent High Court for a UT (e.g., Delhi is the only UT with its own) or place it under the jurisdiction of an adjacent state's High Court.
15.2 The Case of Delhi
Dimension Details
Constitutional Basis
Article 239AA (added by the 69th Amendment Act, 1991, based on the S. Balakrishnan Committee). Designated Delhi as the National Capital Territory (NCT) with a Legislative Assembly.
Legislative Exceptions
The Assembly can legislate on all State/Concurrent List subjects except three: Public Order, Police, and Land (exclusive to the Centre).
Article 239AB

It outlines the provisions in case of a failure of constitutional machinery in the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi. It empowers the President of India to suspend the special administrative mechanisms of Delhi and take direct control over its governance.
The Core Friction Overlapping jurisdictions between the elected Chief Minister and the Centre-appointed LG, leading to massive friction over who controls the bureaucracy ("Services").
2018 SC Judgment

Ruled that the LG is bound by the "aid and advice" of the Council of Ministers (except on the 3 reserved subjects). LG cannot act as an independent adjudicator (invoke the doctrine of "Constitutional Morality").
2023 SC Judgment
Ruled that the Delhi Government has legislative/executive control over Services (Entry 41). Emphasised the "Triple Chain of Accountability" (Civil Servants → Ministers → Legislature → Electorate).
GNCTD (Amendment) Act, 2023

Nullified the 2023 SC ruling by removing "Services" from the Delhi government. Created the NCCSA (CM + Chief Sec + Home Sec) for transfers. With bureaucrats forming the majority, the CM can be outvoted. The LG holds the final say in disputes.
15.3 The Case of Jammu & Kashmir
Dimension Details
The Transition Following the abrogation of Article 370, the J&K Reorganisation Act (2019) downgraded the State to a UT with a legislature, while Ladakh became a UT without a legislature.
Legislative Exceptions
The J&K Assembly can legislate on the State List, EXCEPT TWO: Police and Public Order. (Unlike Delhi, J&K retains control over Land, and these restrictions are statutory, not constitutional).
SC Judgement (Dec 2023)
Unanimously upheld the abrogation of Article 370 as a temporary provision. Directed the EC to hold assembly elections by Sept 2024 (which are now concluded).
Status of Statehood

The SC avoided ruling on the constitutional validity of downgrading a State to a UT under Article
3. It accepted the Centre's assurance that J&K's UT status is "temporary" and directed the earliest restoration of statehood.
15.4 Broad Issues with UT Governance
Issues Details
Democratic Deficit (in UTs without Legislatures)

UTs like Lakshadweep and Andaman are entirely governed by unelected bureaucrats. Example: Recent controversial regulations in Lakshadweep (land development/animal preservation) were introduced without local consultation, sparking massive protests.
Over-centralization & Asymmetric Federalism

Even in UTs with legislatures (Delhi, Puducherry), the ultimate veto lies with the Centre. Example: In Puducherry, the LG frequently bypasses the CM by directly issuing orders to secretaries, causing severe policy paralysis.
Financial Dependence
UTs have virtually no financial autonomy. They are heavily dependent on the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) for grants and cannot independently borrow money in the market like States can.
Role of the LG

The Constitution lacks a clear boundary delineating the LG’s role as a pure "Administrator" versus a "Constitutional Head" in UTs with legislatures, leading to continuous administrative gridlock and endless litigation.
15.5 Way Forward

1. Respecting the Triple Chain of Accountability (SC Recommendation): For UTs with legislatures, the Centre must respect the electoral mandate. The civil service must remain accountable to the elected ministers to ensure effective day-to-day governance, as ruled in the 2023 SC judgment.
2. Implementation of Punchhi Commission Principles: Although the Punchhi Commission focused on Governors, its core principle - that the titular head should not act as a parallel power centre or dictate policies to an elected government - must be legally codified for Lieutenant Governors.
3. Local Democratic Empowerment (Lakshadweep/Andaman Model): For UTs without legislatures, the Centre should strengthen the Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) and Municipalities. Major administrative regulations should be subjected to mandatory public consultation and approval by the local District Panchayats.
4. Time-bound Statehood for J&K: To restore democratic trust and fulfill the assurances given to the Supreme Court, a clear, time-bound roadmap for restoring J&K to full statehood must be initiated by Parliament.

The Union Territory model was designed for regions requiring specialised care, not as a tool for mechanism for excessive centralisation. While the Centre's overarching control is justified for national security (J&K) or protecting the national capital (Delhi), it must be harmonised with the fundamental constitutional ethos of representative democracy and collaborative governance.

chapters.title: Panchayati Raj Institutions, Urban Local Bodies, PESA

elements.text: Panchayati Raj Institutions, Urban Local Bodies, PESA

Decentralisation is the transfer of authority, responsibility, and resources from the central and state governments to local bodies. In India, it is governed by the Principle of Subsidiarity, which dictates that a central authority should perform only those tasks which cannot be performed effectively at a more immediate or local level. Rooted in Article 40 of the Directive Principles of State Policy (organising village panchayats), true democratic decentralisation materialised through the landmark 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts (CAAs) of 1992, transforming India’s federal structure from a two-tier to a three-tier system.
UPSC Mains PYQs

1. Analyse the role of local bodies in providing good governance at local level and bring out the pros and cons of merging the rural local bodies with the urban local bodies. (2024)
2. To what extent, in your opinion, has the decentralisation of power in India changed the governance landscape at the grassroots? (2022)
3. The strength and sustenance of local institutions in India has shifted from their formative phase of ‘Functions, Functionaries and Funds’ to the contemporary stage of ‘Functionality’. Highlight the critical challenges faced by local institutions in terms of their functionality in recent times. (2020)
4. Assess the importance of the Panchayat system in India as a part of local government. Apart from government grants, what sources the Panchayats can look out for financing developmental projects? (2018)
5. In the absence of well – educated and organised local level government system, Panchayats and Samitis have remained mainly political institutions and not effective instrument of governance. Critically Discuss. (2015)
6. Khap panchayats have been in the news for functioning as extra – constitutional authorities, often delivering pronouncements amounting to human right violations. Discuss critically the actions taken by the legislative, executive and judiciary to set the things right in this regard. (2015)
16.1 Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) - 73rd CAA
The 73rd Amendment created a three-tier Panchayati Raj framework across the country (Village, Intermediate/Block, and District levels) and institutionalised grassroots democracy.

rows.text: Core Constitutional Provisions
Explanation
Gram Sabha (Art 243A)
The foundational unit comprising all registered voters in a village. It acts as the "Legislature" at the village level.
3-Tier System

• Gram Panchayat (Village), Panchayat Samiti (Block), and Zila Parishad (District). (States with a population of <20 lakhs may skip the intermediate tier.)
• Further exceptions exist: Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Scheduled Areas (subject to PESA) and certain tribal regions.
Reservations (Art 243D)
Proportional reservation for SCs/STs. At least 1/3rd of total seats and chairperson positions are reserved for Women (many states like Bihar and MP have extended this to 50%).
Independent Institutions

• State Election Commission (SEC): Ensures free, fair, and timely elections every 5 years.
• State Finance Commission (SFC): Recommends the devolution of financial resources from the state to the Panchayats.
The Eleventh Schedule

Added to the Constitution, detailing 29 functional items that fall under the purview of Panchayats, including agriculture, rural development, sanitation, education, and poverty alleviation programmes.

elements.text: 16.1.1 The "3 Fs" Crisis: Bottlenecks in Decentralisation
Dimension Details Examples / Impact
Funds (Over-reliance on Grants & Poor Revenue Generation)
• Negligible OSR (own-source revenue): Gram Panchayats
• The Expendable Agency:

generate less than 1% of their total revenue from local taxes (like property, fairs, or water tax).
• Tied Grants: Over 95% of their budget comes from central/state

Because they lack financial autonomy, PRIs are reduced to mere "implementing agencies" for top-down State/Central schemes rather than self-sustaining local governments capable of solving unique village problems.

grants (e.g., MGNREGA, PM-AWAS), which are "tied" to specific schemes, leaving the Panchayat with zero discretionary spending power.
• SFC Apathy: State governments routinely delay setting up
SFCs, reject their recommendations, or fail to table the reports in the assembly.
Functions Discretionary Devolution (Article 243G)
• The 11th Schedule Illusion: The Constitution lists 29 subjects
• Positive Example: Kerala

(agriculture, health, education) for PRIs. However, Article 243G leaves their actual devolution entirely to the discretion of the State Legislature.
• Lack of Activity Mapping: States formally transfer subjects but

(People's Plan Campaign) devolved all 29 subjects and 30% of its plan budget directly to PRIs.
• Negative Example: States like UP,
do not map the specific activities, leading to overlapping jurisdictions between state departments and the Panchayat.
Punjab, and Bihar have devolved very few subjects. Furthermore, parallel parastatal bodies (like Rural Development Agencies) bypass the Zila Parishad entirely.
Functionaries
• No Independent Cadre: Panchayats do not have their own
• Executive Paralysis: An elected

bureaucracy. They rely on the Block Development Officer (BDO) or Panchayat Secretary, who are State employees. They report to their line ministries, not to the elected Sarpanch.
• Capacity Deficit: A massive lack of technical expertise among

Sarpanch cannot even initiate disciplinary action against an absent village teacher or health worker because those functionaries belong to the State cadre, breaking the chain of local democratic accountability.

elected representatives for tasks like spatial planning or accounting.
• Proxy Representation: The "Sarpanch Pati" syndrome, where male
relatives wield the actual power on behalf of elected women.
Role of Women in Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)
• The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (1992) brought a silent revolution in India’s democratic structure by mandating women's representation at the grassroots.
• Article 243D: Mandates the reservation of not less than one-third (33%) of the total number of seats and offices of Chairpersons at all three levels of Panchayats for women.
• Current Status: Many states (e.g., Bihar, MP, Kerala, and Rajasthan) have legally increased this reservation to 50%. Nationally, women currently hold about 46% of all Panchayat seats (MoPR, 2022).
Impact of Women's Reservation in PRIs (Positive Outcomes)
Theme Outcomes
Political Empowerment

• Elevated economic, social, and political status of women.
• Inspires Aspirations: Grassroots leadership encourages more women to step out of domestic roles
and contest elections independently.
Better Governance Focus
• Women leaders tend to prioritize human development indicators like education, healthcare,
drinking water, and sanitation over purely infrastructure-heavy projects.
Gender-Sensitive Policies

• Increased focus on social welfare policies that directly benefit women and children.
• Examples: Spearheading anti-liquor movements, installing public streetlights for safety, and
leading gender budgeting initiatives (e.g., in Kerala).
Reduction in Corruption
• Studies and anecdotal evidence often suggest that women-led panchayats exhibit higher
transparency and lower instances of systemic corruption.
Way Forward
To move from "de-concentration" of administration to true "devolution" of power, structural reforms must be integrated with recent technological initiatives.
Reform
Solutions
Areas
Financial Autonomy
• Expand and rationalize own-revenue sources: property tax reform (GIS-based property mapping, as

piloted in some states), user charges for water/sanitation services, advertisement tax, market fees
• Reallocate rigid tied grants into untied grants where sectoral saturation has been achieved (per

Standing Committee recommendation) - enabling need-based local spending
• Incentive-linked grants: Centre/States should link a portion of grants to own-revenue mobilization

performance (as practiced in some urban local body reforms under AMRUT), creating a positive fiscal incentive rather than pure dependency
• 16th FC Grants: The 16th Finance Commission (FC) significantly boosted financial grants for

Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) to over ₹4.35 lakh crore for 2026–2031.
• To drive fiscal autonomy, it mandated a 50:50 ratio of tied-to-untied grants, heavily incentivised the
growth of local Own-Source Revenue (OSR), and introduced penalties for delayed state-level fund transfers.
Activity Mapping & Functions
• Clear Devolution Index: The Inter-State Council should penalise states that fail to implement detailed

"Activity Mapping" (specifying exactly what the state does vs. what the Panchayat does). Parastatal bodies must be merged into Zila Parishads.
• Draw on global decentralization models (e.g., Nordic local-government systems where municipalities
manage substantial independent tax revenue) as aspirational benchmarks, adapted to Indian federal context
Empowering Functionaries
• Creation of a Panchayat Cadre: Establish a dedicated local bureaucratic service accountable strictly to

the Zila Parishad and Gram Panchayat.
• Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (RGSA): Aggressively scale up RGSA to provide continuous,
technology-driven capacity building and training for elected representatives, particularly women, to end the "Sarpanch Pati" culture.
Digital Transparency
• e-GramSwaraj & AuditOnline: Mandate 100% compliance on the MoPR’s unified portal for digital
planning, accounting, and online auditing of Panchayats to curb corruption and build state trust in local bodies.

The 73rd Amendment was a watershed moment in India's democratic journey, successfully achieving the political empowerment of marginalised sections and women. However, the next generation of reforms must focus on functional and financial empowerment. By mandating strict activity mapping, building an independent local cadre, and leveraging technology like the SVAMITVA scheme to boost its own-source revenue, PRIs can be transformed from mere administrative appendages of the State into vibrant, self-reliant institutions of grassroots nation-building.
16.2 Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas (PESA) Act 1996

Based on the recommendations of the Dilip Singh Bhuria Committee, Parliament enacted the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA). PESA embodies the highest form of Asymmetric Federalism and Participatory Democracy. Unlike the mainland where the elected Panchayat is supreme, PESA flips the power structure: it makes the Gram Sabha (the community) the absolute, unquestionable authority, recognising that for tribals, the community is the natural unit of governance.
PESA grants extraordinary powers to the Gram Sabha to protect tribal identity and resources

rows.text: Dimension of Power Defining the "Village"
Specific Provisions under PESA A village is not just a geographical boundary; it is defined by "traditions and customs, management of community resources, and customary mode of dispute resolution".
Land Rights

• Mandatory Consultation: The Gram Sabha must be consulted before acquiring land for development projects or resettling affected persons. (This is India's version of Free, Prior, and Informed Consent - FPIC).

elements.text: • Preventing Alienation: Power to prevent the alienation of tribal land and restore any unlawfully
alienated land.
Resource Management
• Minor Forest Produce (MFP): Vests the absolute ownership of MFP (tendu leaves, bamboo, and

honey) in the Gram Sabha.
• Water Bodies & Minerals: Mandatory recommendations from the Gram Sabha are required prior to
granting prospecting licenses or mining leases for minor minerals.
Social & Cultural Control

• Prohibition: Power to enforce prohibition or regulate the sale and consumption of intoxicants.
• Money Lending: Power to exercise control over money-lending to Scheduled Tribes.
• Customary Justice: Power to safeguard the cultural identity and resolve local disputes using
traditional methods.
Administrative Control
• The Gram Sabha holds the power to approve all socio-economic development plans before they are
implemented by the Panchayat, and issues the utilisation certificate for funds.
Despite its revolutionary legal text, PESA has suffered from a massive "governance deficit". State governments and the corporate-bureaucratic nexus have systematically diluted its provisions.
Core Issue Explanation Examples & Impact
Dilution via State Rules
• • The MFP Monopoly: State Forest
• PESA is a central law, but State Legislatures had to

frame rules to implement it. Few states still haven't framed PESA rules. Even states that did (like MP and Gujarat) drafted them cleverly to transfer the Gram Sabha’s powers to the District Collector or Forest Department.
Corporations often retain monopoly rights over trading lucrative MFP, like tendu leaves, depriving the Gram Sabha of its Constitutional revenue source.
Bypassing Consent (The Land Grab)
• Hasdeo Arand (Chhattisgarh): Massive
• The mandatory "consultation" clause for land
acquisition is routinely violated. State governments use the colonial-era Land Acquisition Act or the Coal Bearing Areas Act to bypass PESA. Gram Sabha resolutions are frequently forged.

tribal protests erupted against coal mining, where locals alleged the State and corporates forged Gram Sabha consent resolutions.
• Polavaram Project (AP): Large-scale
displacement occurred with allegations of inadequate Gram Sabha consultation.
Conflict with Other Laws
• PESA frequently clashes with the Indian Forest Act
• Criminalisation of Tribals: Forest
(1927), the Wildlife Protection Act, and even the Forest Rights Act (FRA, 2006). Bureaucrats prefer operating under the Forest Department's rules rather than respecting the Gram Sabha's autonomy.
guards routinely harass tribals collecting minor forest produce inside sanctuaries, citing conservation laws and ignoring PESA/FRA protections.
Functionary / Capacity Deficit
• Bureaucratic Apathy: The Panchayat
• The traditional tribal leadership is often unaware of
the complex bureaucratic procedures required to exercise PESA rights. A Ministry of Panchayati Raj (MoPR) study showed that over 40% of elected ST representatives do not fully understand the Act.
Secretary (a state official) controls the registers and funds, often manipulating them without the actual consent of the tribal Sarpanch or Gram Sabha.
Way Forward
1. Legal & Administrative Reforms

 Enforce Mandatory Consent (FPIC): Amend the PESA Act to explicitly require the "Free, Prior, and Informed Consent" (FPIC) of the Gram Sabha before any land acquisition or mining lease is granted, replacing the weak "consultation" clause.

 Harmonise Conflicting Laws: The Ministries of Tribal Affairs and Panchayati Raj must legally synchronise the PESA Act, the Forest Rights Act (FRA, 2006), and the Land Acquisition Act (LARR, 2013) to create a single, unbreakable tribal rights framework.

 Strict Rule Compliance: Implement the Xaxa Committee's recommendation by empowering the Inter-State Council to penalise 5th Schedule states that have failed to frame or operationalise proper PESA rules.

 Establish a Tribal Ombudsman: Create a dedicated, independent grievance redressal authority at the district level exclusively to handle violations of PESA, FRA, and tribal rights.
2. Transparency & Capacity Building

 Mandate Digital Fund Tracking: Enforce the use of the PESA-GPDP Portal to digitally track fund utilisation. This ensures that bureaucrats cannot forge offline utilisation certificates without the Gram Sabha's actual knowledge.

 Resource Mapping via NTRI: Empower the National Tribal Research Institute (NTRI) and utilise the Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (RGSA) to train tribal youth in digitally mapping their community forest resources to assert their legal ownership over Minor Forest Produce (MFP).
16.3. Urban Local Bodies

India is urbanising at a breakneck pace, with its urban population expected to cross 50% by 2050. To manage this massive demographic shift, the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act (1992) inserted Part IX-A into the Constitution, giving constitutional status to municipalities. The goal was to transform chaotic urban sprawls into systematically planned, self-governing cities based on the Principle of Subsidiarity.
UPSC Prelims PYQs
1. Analyse the role of local bodies in providing good governance at a local level and
bring out the pros and cons of merging the rural local bodies with the urban local
bodies. (2024).
2. "The states in India seem reluctant to empower urban local bodies both functionally
as well as financially." Comment. (2023)

elements.caption: Panchayati Raj Institutions, Urban Local Bodies, PESA — illustration

elements.text: 16.3.1 The Constitutional Framework (Part IX-A)
Constitutional
Explanation & Core Function
Provision
Types of ULBs (Article 243Q)

1. Nagar Panchayat: For a transitional area (rural to urban).
2. Municipal Council: For a smaller urban area.
3. Municipal Corporation: For a larger urban area (Metropolitan cities).
Wards Committees (Article 243S)
Mandatory in municipalities with a population of 3 lakhs or more. It ensures that governance doesn't stop at the city level but reaches the neighbourhood/ward level.
Reservations (Article 243T) Proportional reservation for SCs/STs. A minimum of 1/3rd of total seats and mayoral positions are reserved for Women.
District Planning Committee (DPC -Article 243ZD)
A crucial body that consolidates the plans prepared by both Panchayats and Municipalities in a district to draft an integrated development plan.
Metropolitan Planning Committee (MPC - Article 243ZE)
It is mandatory for metropolitan areas (population >10 lakhs) to draft a unified development plan, ensuring urban and peri-urban areas are planned together.
The 12th Schedule (Article 243W)
Lists 18 subjects (e.g., urban planning, public health, fire services, and solid waste management) to be devolved to the ULBs by the State Legislature.
16.3.2 Challenges in Urban Governance
Dimension Explanation and Impact
Funds Abysmal Revenue & The GST Impact
• 0.6% GDP Contribution: According to the RBI’s 2024 Municipal Finances Report, Indian ULBs

generate only 0.6% of GDP in own-source revenue (compared to 6% in South Africa).
• Property Tax: Due to poor GIS mapping and political reluctance, property tax collection is

staggeringly low.
• Untied vs tied grant rigidity: similar to PRIs, Central/State grants often come earmarked for specific

schemes, limiting local flexibility.
• The Octroi Vacuum: Post-GST, Octroi (a major local tax) was abolished. States promised
compensation, but it has been irregular, leaving many ULBs in India severely cash-strapped.
Functions The Rise of Parastatal Bodies & SPVs
• Bypassing the Elected Body: State governments refuse to devolve the 18 subjects. Instead, they

create unelected parastatal bodies (water boards, urban development authorities) that report to the State CM, not the local Mayor. Also elections are not held regularly.
• Smart City SPVs: Under the Smart Cities Mission, parallel Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) run by

bureaucrats were created, further sidelining the elected municipal council.
• Impact: In Bengaluru, functions are split between the BBMP (elected), BDA, and BWSSB, leading to
disastrous, uncoordinated urban flooding and traffic crises.
Functionaries
• The Mayoral Figurehead: In most Indian cities, the Mayor has a ceremonial 12 to 30 months' term

with zero executive power. Real power lies with the Municipal Commissioner, an IAS officer appointed by and accountable to the State Government.
• Planning Deficit: ULBs lack a dedicated cadre of urban planners, traffic engineers, and environmental
experts, heavily relying on generalist state bureaucrats.
Dysfunctional DPCs and MPCs
• • Unplanned Sprawl: DPCs and MPCs are either not constituted or completely bypassed. Without
them, urban planning is fragmented, resulting in illegal colonies, peri-urban slums, and the destruction of urban wetlands (e.g., Chennai floods).
16.3.3 Way Forward
To transform Indian cities from engines of chaos to engines of economic growth, the following structural reforms must be pursued:
Financial Empowerment:

• GIS-Based Property Tax: Aggressively utilise Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to map all urban properties, digitise records, and automate property tax collection, insulating it from local vote-bank politics.

• Deepening the Municipal Bond Market: Emulate the Pune and Indore models by mandating transparent, double-entry accounting in all ULBs to improve their credit ratings, allowing them to raise capital via Municipal Bonds for large infrastructure.

• Value Capture Financing (VCF): ULBs must be empowered to capture the increased value of private land generated by public infrastructure investments (e.g., levying a betterment charge near a newly built Metro line).
Functional Autonomy

• Abolish Parastatal Encroachment: Systematically absorb unelected parastatal bodies (Development Authorities, Water/ Sewage Boards) into the elected Municipal Corporation under a unified command structure.

• Operationalise MPCs and DPCs: The Inter-State Council must penalise states that fail to constitute and empower Metropolitan and District Planning Committees. Urban planning must be integrated, not piecemeal.
Administrative Overhaul

• The "Strong-Mayor" System: Amend the 74th CAA to mandate a directly elected Mayor with a fixed 5-year term. The Mayor must have full executive control over the municipal budget, the Municipal Commissioner, and city departments (Police, Transport).

• Specialised Municipal Cadre: Create a dedicated, professional urban cadre comprising town planners, environmental engineers, and public health experts who report exclusively to the elected local government.

The 74th Amendment created the structure for urban governance, but state governments have actively starved it of substance. As India aims to become a $5 trillion economy, it cannot rely on cities governed by fragmented, unaccountable parastatal bodies and powerless mayors. True urban decentralisation requires instituting a "Strong-Mayor" framework, merging parallel agencies, and unlocking municipal financial markets to build resilient, world-class cities.
16.4. Role of Local Bodies in Providing Good Governance
Good governance is characterised by participation, responsiveness, equity, and accountability. The 73rd and 74th Amendments institutionalised these pillars at the grassroots:
Governance
Role Played by Local Bodies
Pillar
(PRIs & ULBs)
Participatory & Inclusive
• Institutionalized Inclusion: A 33-50% reservation for women and proportional reservation for SC/

STs ensure marginalised voices shape local policies.
• Direct Democracy: Gram Sabhas and Ward Committees allow citizens to directly participate in
decision-making, rather than just voting every 5 years.
Responsive & Effective
• The Principle of Subsidiarity: Local leaders understand micro-level issues better than state
capitals. A Gram Panchayat is far more effective at identifying local beneficiaries for PM-AWAS or managing a village watershed than a distant state bureaucrat.
Accountable & Transparent
• Social Audit: The Gram Sabha holds the executive accountable by reviewing expenditure and

issuing utilisation certificates.
• Triple Chain of Accountability: Local bureaucrats (in an ideal setup) are accountable to the
Sarpanch/Mayor, who is accountable to the ward/village, preventing administrative impunity.
16.5. Merging Rural and Urban Local Bodies

rows.text: Dimensions
Pros of Merging Rural & Urban Bodies
Cons & Challenges of Merging
Spatial & Infrastructure Planning
Integrated Development: Allows for seamless planning of contiguous infrastructure like solid waste management plants, ring roads, and drainage networks without jurisdictional deadlocks.

Urban Bias (Loss of Rural Voice): Urban priorities (flyovers, commercial zoning) will inevitably overshadow rural agrarian needs (irrigation, livestock health). Rural voices will be outvoted in a merged council.
Resource Management Economic & Administrative Efficiency

Water & Land Equity: Prevents the predatory relationship where cities extract groundwater and dump waste in neighbouring rural Panchayats. Ensures regional ecological balance. Economies of Scale: Reduces the duplication of administrative machinery. A single Metropolitan Planning Committee (MPC) can manage regional transport efficiently.

Taxation Shocks: Rural residents, accustomed to low or negligible property taxes, would suddenly face harsh urban municipal tax rates, causing severe economic distress for small/marginal farmers. Loss of Targeted Grants: PRIs receive specific constitutional grants (e.g., for MGNREGA or agricultural subsidies) that might be legally complicated to disburse or diluted in a merged "Rurban" entity.

elements.text: 16.6. Government Initiatives for Urban Local Bodies

rows.text: Initiative
Objective
Impact/Data/Example
16th Finance Commission
The 16th FC prioritizes strengthening local financial autonomy, emphasizing the modernization of municipal accounting
The ₹3.56 lakh crore allocated to ULBs is part of a larger ₹7.91 lakh crore package for all local bodies, representing a 116% increase in absolute terms from the Fifteenth Finance Commission
15th Finance Commission (XV-FC) Grants NITI Aayog’s framework for million plus cities

Shifted to Tied Grants. ULBs must meet entry conditions: publishing audited accounts online and notifying floor rates for property tax to receive funds. The report identifies persistent governance issues, including weak and fragmented leadership structures, constrained fiscal capacity, and capacity gaps that limit service delivery and urban performance

Data: XV-FC allocated ₹1,21,058 crore (2021-2026). Over 4,500 ULBs now publish financial data on MoHUA’s CityFinance.in portal. Key Recommendations
• Strengthen Urban Leadership: Introduce a directly elected Mayor with a fixed tenure, supported by an empowered Mayor-in-Council system.
• Integrate Urban Services: Bring water supply, sanitation and public transport under city governments for better coordination and accountability.
• Enhance Municipal Finances: Strengthen own-source revenues, ensure timely State Finance Commission transfers, and promote municipal bonds.
• Institutional Reforms: Bring parastatal agencies under city government oversight with clearly defined roles and stronger coordination.
Urban Challenge Fund

• ₹1 lakh crore fund (₹10,000 crore Budget 2025–26 allocation) to promote market-driven, reform-linked urban infrastructure and develop future-ready, economically competitive cities.
• Credit Support: ₹5,000 crore Credit Repayment Guarantee Scheme to improve creditworthiness and facilitate market borrowing by Tier-II/III cities, Northeastern & hilly states, and smaller ULBs.

• Challenge-based Funding: Projects selected competitively and linked to reforms, milestones, KPIs and digital monitoring through a single portal.
• Market-led Financing: At least 50% of project cost to be mobilised through municipal bonds, bank loans and PPPs, with the balance from States/UTs/ULBs.
• Reform Focus: Incentivises reforms in urban governance, municipal finance, operational efficiency, urban planningand greater private sector participation.
• Coverage & Project Verticals: Covers million-plus cities, all State/UT capitals and major industrial cities, focusing on Growth Hubs, Creative Redevelopment, and Water & Sanitation.
Municipal Bond Incentive Scheme

MoHUA, under the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT) scheme, provides an interest subsidy of ₹13 crore for every ₹100 crore raised by ULBs, encouraging entry into capital markets.
Data: Over 10 cities have raised >₹3,840 crore. Pune raised ₹200 crore for water; Vadodara issued Asia's first US Treasury-assisted municipal bond.
Property Tax linked to Circle Rates
The Dept of Expenditure mandates states to link property tax collections to prevailing state circle rates to qualify for additional state borrowing limits.
Impact: Forces political leadership to bypass local vote-bank politics and scientifically assess property taxes (the primary own-source revenue).
AMRUT 2.0 (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation & Urban Transformation)
Focuses on making cities "water secure". Mandates GIS-based master planning for 500 cities to map all utility networks.
Example: Cities like Hyderabad and Ahmedabad utilised this to map underground utilities, drastically reducing water leakage (non-revenue water).
Swachh Bharat Mission - Urban (SBM-U 2.0)
Shifts focus from toilet construction to 100% processing of Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) and remediating legacy dumpsites to create "garbage-free" cities.
Data: Urban MSW processing capacity jumped from 18% (2014) to over 77% today (MoHUA Dashboard). Indore achieved a 7-star rating by monetising waste via bio-CNG.
National Urban Digital Mission (NUDM)
Creates a shared digital baseline (National Urban Innovation Stack) that any ULB can use to offer online civic services (taxes, certificates).
Impact: Drastically reduces IT expenditure for smaller Nagar Panchayats and Municipal Councils that cannot afford private tech contractors.
Smart Cities Mission & ICCCs
Mandated the creation of Integrated Command and Control Centres (ICCCs) to act as the digital nervous system for city administration
Example: Originally used as COVID war rooms (in Surat and Pune), ICCCs are now heavily utilized for real-time traffic management and flood monitoring.
TULIP (The Urban Learning Internship Program)
A joint MoHUA and AICTE initiative to match fresh graduates (engineers, urban planners) with ULBs and Smart City SPVs for internships.
Objective: Directly addresses the acute bureaucratic "capacity deficit" by injecting fresh, tech-savvy human capital into outdated municipal administration.

elements.text: While a complete political merger of PRIs and ULBs may unjustly dilute the rural agrarian voice, administrative and spatial integration is non-negotiable. The solution lies not in merging the bodies, but in strictly empowering the District Planning Committees (DPCs) and Metropolitan Planning Committees (MPCs) (mandated by Articles 243ZD and ZE) to enforce a unified regional development plan that respects both urban growth and rural sustainability.
Separation of Powers Between Various Organs,
Dispute Redressal Mechanisms and Institutions
Separation of Powers

The doctrine of Separation of Powers, propounded by the French political philosopher Montesquieu in The Spirit of the Laws (1748), entails the division of the legislative, executive, and judicial functions of government among distinct organs. This structural demarcation prevents the concentration of power, minimises the possibility of arbitrary governance, and ensures that each organ acts as a check and balance on the others, thereby safeguarding constitutionalism and the rule of law.
UPSC Mains PYQs

1. Judicial legislation is antithetical to the doctrine of separation of powers as envisaged in the Indian Constitution. In this context, justify the filing of large number of public interest petitions praying for issuing guidelines to executive authorities. (2020)
2. Do you think the Constitution of India does not accept the principle of strict separation of powers rather it is based on the principle of ‘checks and balances’? Explain.(2019)
3. Resorting to ordinances has always raised concerns on violation of the spirit of the separation of powers doctrine. While noting the rationales justifying the power to promulgate, analyse whether the decision of the Supreme Court on the issue have further facilitated resorting to this power. Should the power to promulgate the ordinances be repealed? (2015)
17.1 Constitutional Articles Underpinning Separation of Powers
Article Key Provisions Implication for Separation of Powers
Article 50 The State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services.
Core Directive Principle ensuring the judiciary remains free from executive influence.
Articles 53 & 154
The executive power of the Union/State shall be vested in the President/Governor.
Establishes the distinct constitutional existence of the Executive branch.
Articles 121 & 211
No discussion shall take place in Parliament/State Legislature regarding the conduct of any Supreme Court or High Court Judge.
Protects judicial independence by insulating judges from political debates and legislative pressure.
Articles 122 & 212
Courts are barred from enquiring into the validity of any proceedings in Parliament/State Legislature.
Protects the sovereignty of the Legislature in its internal functioning and rule-making.
Article 361
The President or the Governor shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of their official powers
Grants immunity to the nominal executive head, ensuring they can act without fear of legal harassment.
17.2 Checks-and-Balances

• Collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha under Article 75(3)
• Question Hour, Zero Hour, No-Confidence Motion, Censure Motion, Budgetary Control, Parliamentary Committees, approval of government policies and expenditure.

Executive (President/ Council of Ministers)

elements.text: Executive (President/CoM)
Judiciary Appointment of judges; power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, and remissions under Article 72.
Judiciary Legislature Judicial review of laws, striking down unconstitutional legislation, and safeguarding the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
Judiciary Executive Judicial review of executive actions; issuance of writs against executive excesses and arbitrary actions.
Judiciary Parliament & Executive Power to enforce Fundamental Rights under Articles 32 and 226.
President Parliament Veto powers and returning ordinary Bills for reconsideration.
Union Government (Federal Check)
State Governments Directions to states, legislative intervention in specified circumstances, and imposition of the President's Rule.
How do PILs address legislative vacuums and executive apathy?

• The Governance Vacuum: When the legislature fails to enact necessary laws on pressing social issues, or the executive fails to implement them, a vacuum is created that threatens the fundamental rights of citizens.
• The Constitutional Safety Valve: The judiciary steps in through PILs not to permanently usurp the lawmaking function but to provide immediate relief and protect constitutional values.

• Example: The Supreme Court laid down the Vishaka Guidelines to prevent sexual harassment at the workplace, serving as a temporary, necessary framework until the Parliament enacted a formal law years later.
Why are PILs necessary to protect the marginalised and voiceless?

• Relaxing Locus Standi: Under Articles 32 and 226, the traditional rule of locus standi (only the aggrieved party can sue) is relaxed, allowing public-spirited citizens to approach the courts on behalf of those who cannot afford legal recourse.
• Defending the Vulnerable: Under trials, bonded labourers, and impoverished communities often face executive negligence or police excesses but lack the awareness or resources to fight back.

• Upholding Part III: When courts entertain PILs on their behalf, they are not breaching the separation of powers; they are fulfilling their core constitutional duty to enforce Fundamental Rights and directing the executive to discharge its constitutional and statutory obligations.
How do PILs help in enforcing institutional accountability?

• Executive Reluctance: In cases involving massive political corruption, administrative paralysis, or severe environmental degradation, the executive is often perceived as compromised or deeply reluctant to investigate itself.
• Court-Monitored Investigations: Citizens utilise PILs to bypass this apathy and initiate independent, court-monitored investigations.

• Upholding the Rule of Law: In these instances, the courts issue directives compelling executive authorities to act in accordance with the law. This upholds the Rule of Law, which is itself the foundational bedrock of the separation of powers.
• Examples: Court intervention in the 2G spectrum allocation scam and the M.C. Mehta environmental protection cases.
17.3 Significance of the Separation of Powers
Aspect Details
Prevention of Tyranny
Ensures that the immense power of the state to make, execute, and interpret laws does not consolidate in one individual or body, thereby preventing authoritarianism.
Protection of Liberty
Acts as a structural safeguard for Fundamental Rights. If the body making the laws also executes them, there is no defense against oppressive laws.
Functional Efficiency

The modern state is highly complex. Separation allows for institutional specialisation: The legislature specialises in debate, the executive in rapid administration, and the judiciary in legal fairness, at the same moment cooperating with each other.
Judicial Independence

By isolating the judiciary from the executive and legislature (Article 50), it ensures judges can strike down unconstitutional government actions without fear of political retaliation or loss of job security.
Rule of Law Guarantees that the government itself is bound by the laws it creates. The executive cannot act outside legislative authority, and the judiciary enforces this boundary.
17.4 Contemporary Issues and Challenges
Theme Issues & Challenges
Judicial Overreach
The judiciary is crossing the line from "reviewing" law to "making" policy.
• Examples: Imposing the Highway Liquor Ban, managing the cricket board (BCCI) case, etc.
Executive Dominance
Bypassing Parliamentary debate through frequent re-promulgation of Ordinances.
• Example: Passing controversial, substantive legislation by labelling it as a "Money Bill" to bypass
the Rajya Sabha.
Legislative Decline

Rushing bills without debate (e.g., passing farm laws or criminal codes amid opposition walkouts and limited Parliamentary scrutiny). Drastic reduction in the number of bills referred to Parliamentary Committees.
Tribunalisation of Justice
The Executive creating tribunals for specific issues (NGT, SAT) but retaining control over the appointment and tenure of tribunal members, compromising their independence.
Friction over Appointments
The ongoing tug-of-war between the Executive and Judiciary over the Collegium system, resulting in massive delays in judicial appointments and high pendency of cases.
Delegated Legislation
Excessive delegation of rule-making to the executive weakens legislative oversight, potentially diluting parliamentary authority.
Judiciary and Separation of Powers
Theme & Concept Issue Arguments Landmark Case
Separation of Powers vs Checks & Balances - Functional Blending (Rejection of strict watertight compartments)

No. India uses a Parliamentary system that fuses the Executive and Legislature (ministers are MPs). Instead, it relies on Checks and Balances: Legislature questions Executive, Executive appoints Judges, Judiciary reviews both.
Indira Nehru Gandhi vs Raj Narain (1975) (Established separation of power as a basic feature)
Does India have a strict separation of powers like the USA?
Ordinance-Making Power - Executive Usurpation of Legislature (Articles 123 & 213)

Yes, it violates the spirit if misused. Designed only for acute emergencies. Executives often abuse it by repromulgating without debate. No to repeal: Needed for national security/emergencies. Solution: Strict judicial review of the executive's intent.
D.C. Wadhwa (1987) (Banned routine repromulgation) Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) (Ordinances are subject to judicial review.)
Does bypassing Parliament via ordinances violate separation of powers? Should it be repealed?
SC Checking Parliament - Counter - Majoritarian Check (Article 368 vs Article 13)
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) (Basic Structure) Minerva Mills (1980) (Limited amending power)
How does the SC prevent Parliament from using majorities to become a tyrant?

By establishing that Parliament's amending power is limited, not absolute. The SC acts as the ultimate guardian, ensuring that majoritarian governments cannot alter or destroy the secular, democratic, and judicial core of the Constitution.
Judicial Independence - Prerequisite of Democracy (Rule of Law)
Why is independence a prerequisite?

Democracy is not just majority rule; it requires protecting individual rights against state tyranny. The Constitution guarantees this via: Security of tenure (strict impeachment), non-votable salaries (Consolidated Fund), and contempt powers.
NJAC Judgment / 4th Judges Case (2015)
Collegium System: India vs USA - Judicial Primacy vs Executive Nomination

India (Collegium): Evolved via Three Judges Cases. Pros: More independence from politics. Cons: Opaque, oligarchic, lacks public accountability. USA (Exec + Senate): Pros: High democratic accountability and public hearings. Cons: Hyper-partisan, judges often selected for ideological loyalty.
First Judges Case (1981) (Executive primacy) Second/Third Judges Cases (1993/1998) (Created Collegium)
Comparing how apex judges are appointed.
Growth of PIL & SC Power - Relaxation of Locus Standi & Epistolary Jurisdiction

Growth: Driven by mass poverty, illiteracy, and the courts dropping the rigid "only the aggrieved can sue" rule. Most Powerful: Yes, structurally. It recommends the appointment of its own judges, can strike down Unconstitutional amendments, and take suo motu control of executive policies.
S.P. Gupta (1981) (Relaxed locus standi) Sunil Batra (Epistolary jurisdiction)
Why did PILs grow, and did it make the SC the "most powerful"?
PILs & Judicial Legislation - Transformative Constitutionalism vs Judicial Overreach
Vishaka vs State of Rajasthan (1997) (Stipulated sexual harassment at workplace guidelines) D.K. Basu (1997) (Arrest guidelines)

The Justification: Arises due to Executive Vacuum/Apathy. When legislatures fail to act on pressing crises (environment, harassment), the SC can intervene to protect Article 21 (Life/Liberty). It acts as a transitional social catalyst until the State builds capacity.
How to justify the SC making "laws" (guidelines) via PILs?
17.5 How Checks and Balances Complement Separation of Powers
Aspect Principle of Separation of
Complimentary system of checks and balances
Application
Powers
Foundational Philosophy
Compartmentalisation: Rooted in Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws (1748), it dictates that powers (Legislative, Executive, Judiciary) must be strictly separated into distinct branches.
Vigilance against Corruption: Rooted in Lord Acton’s premise that "absolute power corrupts absolutely," it ensures that separated powers actively monitor each other.
Without checks, an isolated branch could grow tyrannical. Checks and balances ensure that each branch exercises vigilance over the others to keep the whole system in balance.
Structural Setup
Interlocking Mechanisms: Provides tools for one branch to intervene in or halt the actions of another, preventing unilateral dominance.
Distinct Functions: The Legislature makes laws, the Executive implements them, and the Judiciary interprets them. They are designed to be "coequal".
The President may return an Ordinary Bill once (except Money and Constitutional Amendment Bills). If Parliament repasses it, assent is mandatory.
Executive & Legislative Overlap
Strict Separation (Presidential System): In the US, the Executive and Legislative branches are kept strictly apart to avoid conflict of interest.

Oversight within Integration (Parliamentary System): In India/the UK, the Executive emerges from the Legislature. Checks and balances legitimize this by ensuring the Executive relies on Legislative support.
The Vice President serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Art. 64), providing an institutional link between the Executive and the Legislature.
Financial Control vs. Gridlock
Independent Mandates: The Executive determines governance and spending needs, while the Legislature holds the "power of the purse".
Mutual Dependency: The Executive cannot spend money without Legislative sanction, forcing cooperation.

Government Shutdowns: Strict separation without compromise leads to gridlock. For example, the 43-day US government shutdown (Oct-Nov 2025) occurred when the legislature refused to sanction executive expenditure.
Role of the Judiciary
Independent Functioning: The Judiciary operates entirely independent of Executive or Legislative pressure to ensure fair trials.
Judicial Review: Empowers the Supreme Court to act as the "guardian and protector of the Constitution" by striking down unconstitutional acts of the other two branches.

Tribunal Reforms Act, 2021: The Supreme Court checked the Executive and Legislature by striking down provisions of this Act because it allowed excessive Executive control over tribunal appointments, which violated the separation of powers.
Final Constitutional Authority
The Constitution is what the Court says it is: The Supreme Court acts as the final arbiter, preventing "legislative/executive overrides" of binding judicial judgements.
Limits on Lawmaking: The Legislature cannot pass arbitrary laws, nor can the Executive issue overriding ordinances unconditionally.
Arbitration of Meaning: The courts ensure that laws and executive actions align with constitutional arrangements.
17.6 Way Forward

rows.text: Theme
Way Forward
Key Cases & Committee Recommendations
Contemporary Examples
Judicial Overreach vs. Restraint

The judiciary must exercise self-restraint and adhere to the "Doctrine of Deference", respecting the policy domain of the executive and the law-making domain of the legislature. PILs should be heavily screened to prevent "Policy by Judiciary."

• 2nd ARC: Emphasised that courts should not cross the boundary of judicial review to assume executive functions.
• Supreme Court (State of Rajasthan v. Union of India): Courts cannot run the government; they must respect coordinate branches.
Example: The SC taking suo motu cognisance of the Kolkata RG Kar case, while necessary for justice, often reignites debates on judicial intervention in executive law-and-order domains.
Executive Dominance (Ordinance & Money Bill Route)

The executive must limit the use of Ordinances (Article
123) only to extreme, unforeseen emergencies. The Speaker’s certification of a "Money Bill" (Article 110) should not be used as a political tool to bypass the Rajya Sabha and should be subject to strict judicial scrutiny.

• D.C. Wadhwa Case (1987) & Krishna Kumar Singh Case (2017): Re-promulgation of ordinances is a "fraud on the Constitution" and is subject to Judicial Review.
• Aadhaar Case (2018): SC upheld the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill but laid down strict parameters for future scrutiny.

A 7-judge Constitutional bench of the Supreme Court is currently reviewing the scope of the Speaker's power to classify legislation as a "Money Bill" (arising from the Finance Act, 2017, tribunal rules).
Arresting Legislative Decline
Parliament must reclaim its supreme deliberative role. Rushing complex legislation without debate undermines the checks on the executive. Pre-legislative scrutiny must be institutionalised.

• NCRWC (Venkatachaliah Commission): Recommended that it should be made mandatory for all major Bills to be referred to Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs).
• Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy (2014): Mandates a 30-day public consultation for all bills (poorly implemented).

The passage of the three new criminal codes (BNS, BNSS, BSA) and the Telecommunications Act, 2023 saw limited debate due to opposition suspensions. Strengthening DRSCs is the most cited "way forward" by constitutional experts today.
Reforming Tribunalisation
To prevent the executive from acting as a "judge in its own cause", the administrative and financial control of tribunals must be completely decoupled from their parent, sponsoring ministries.

• 74th Parliamentary Standing Committee & 272nd Law Commission: Strongly recommended the creation of an independent National Tribunals Commission (NTC) to oversee appointments, infrastructure, and administration of tribunals.
• L. Chandra Kumar Case (1997): Tribunals can supplement, but not supplant, the High Courts.

The Tribunal Reforms Act, 2021 saw friction when the Executive reintroduced provisions (regarding tenure and age of members) that the Supreme Court had previously struck down in the Madras Bar Association cases, showing an ongoing tug-of-war.
Resolving Appointments Friction
The friction over the Collegium system must be resolved through mutual compromise. The Collegium needs to be more transparent, and the Executive must clear recommended names within a fixed timeline.

• 2nd ARC & NCRWC: Supported a National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) model (which was later struck down in 2015).
• Finalization of MoP: A mutually agreed Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) for judicial appointments

The Supreme Court has started publishing the "reasons" for its Collegium resolutions on its website to counter allegations of opacity. However, friction remains over the Executive returning or sitting on reiterated names.

elements.text: Necessity of Coordination Between Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary

While the doctrine of Separation of Powers is essential to prevent the concentration of authority, a strict, watertight compartmentalisation is practically impossible in a modern welfare state. The Indian Constitution embodies a "Doctrine of Checks and Balances", requiring a functional overlap where the three organs act as partners in governance rather than adversaries. Effective administration demands harmonious coordination to achieve constitutional goals.
1. Enhancing Legislative Efficacy (Effective Lawmaking)

 Concept: The judiciary’s interpretation of existing statutes frequently exposes loopholes, ambiguities, or constitutional gaps. This judicial feedback is vital for the legislature to craft precise, future-ready laws.

 Example: The Supreme Court’s landmark Puttaswamy Judgement (2017) recognising the Right to Privacy provided the essential legal scaffolding for the legislature to eventually draft the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.
2. Ensuring Seamless Execution (Smooth Implementation & Delegated Legislation)

 Concept: Clear communication and shared understanding between the executive machinery and the judiciary minimise friction, reduce unnecessary litigation, and ensure legislative intent is translated into action on the ground. Furthermore, the system of delegated legislation explicitly relies on the executive's administrative expertise to implement broad legislative mandates.

 Example: Collaborative workshops for bureaucrats and judicial officers on newly enacted laws (e.g., new labour codes or criminal laws) foster a uniform understanding and better enforcement.
3. Upholding 'Constitutional Objectivity' & Public Trust

 Concept: As emphasised by the Supreme Court, the principle of "Constitutional Objectivity" requires each branch to operate within its designated sphere while cooperating to prevent the absolute accumulation of power. This mutual respect fosters public trust in the rule of law.

 Example: Collaborative and timely efforts between the Executive and the Judicial Collegium to fill judicial vacancies are critical to reducing case pendency and maintaining citizen confidence in the justice system.
4. Bridging Governance Deficits through Institutional Synergy

 Concept: In instances of executive inaction or legislative delay regarding critical social issues, coordination is seen when the judiciary steps in via Public Interest Litigations (PILs) to protect Fundamental Rights until the legislature can formulate a permanent law.

 Example: The Supreme Court issued the Vishaka Guidelines to prevent sexual harassment at the workplace, which seamlessly acted as the law of the land until the legislature enacted the POSH Act in 2013.
5. Facilitating Crisis Management (Swift Action on Critical Issues)

 Concept: National emergencies, disasters, or pandemics demand a synchronised response where executive swiftness is carefully balanced with judicial oversight to ensure due process is not entirely discarded.

 Example: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the executive implemented strict lockdown measures under the Epidemic Diseases Act and Disaster Management Act, while the judiciary expedited hearings to ensure these measures did not arbitrarily violate fundamental rights, balancing public health with individual liberty.
6. Tackling Transnational Challenges (Globalized World)
 Concept: In an interconnected world, modern threats such as cyber-terrorism, cross-border financial fraud, and environmental degradation require a united institutional front.

 Example: Framing effective extradition treaties, adopting international environmental agreements, and establishing cybercrime jurisdictions require the executive to negotiate, the legislature to ratify, and the judiciary to enforce them consistently.

Ultimately, the doctrine of Separation of Powers in the Indian Constitution is not meant to create isolated, watertight compartments, but rather a dynamic system of checks and balances. While the core objective remains the prevention of concentrated power and the protection of liberty, the Constitution envisions a functional overlap to ensure mutual accountability. The success of this democratic framework relies heavily on 'Constitutional Comity' where the Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary exercise institutional self-restraint, respect each other's constitutional domains, and work collaboratively to uphold the Rule of law."

chapters.title: Dispute Redressal Mechanisms (Tribunals, ADRs and Lok Adalats)

elements.text: Dispute Redressal Mechanisms (Tribunals, ADRs and Lok Adalats)

Dispute Redressal Mechanisms (DRMs) are institutional frameworks created outside the traditional, formal judicial hierarchy (courts) to resolve disputes efficiently, cost-effectively, and with specialised expertise. They act as "safety valves" for an overburdened judiciary.

• Tribunals: Quasi-judicial bodies established to deal with specific problems such as tax, administrative, or environmental disputes. They blend judicial fairness with administrative expertise. They are not bound by the strict rules of the Civil Procedure Code (CPC) but are guided by the Principles of Natural Justice.
• Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR): Techniques for resolving conflicts outside the courtroom. The main types are:
 Arbitration: A neutral third party renders a binding decision.
 Mediation: A neutral third party facilitates a negotiated settlement (non-binding until an agreement is signed).

 Conciliation: Similar to mediation, but the conciliator plays a more active role in proposing solutions.
• Lok Adalats (People’s Courts): A forum where disputes/cases pending in the court of law or at the pre-litigation stage are settled/compromised amicably.

rows.text: Dimension Traditional Courts Pendency & Workload Burdened by large case backlogs, causing delays in justice delivery. Bench Composition & Expertise Presided over by legally trained judges with broad judicial expertise. Procedure & Flexibility Follow strict procedures under procedural and evidentiary laws, ensuring legal rigour.

Administrative Tribunals
• Created to reduce court burden by handling specialised disputes (e.g., CAT, NCLT, NGT).
• However, vacancies have led to growing pendency in many tribunals.
• Comprise judicial and technical members, providing sector-specific expertise.

18.2 Alternative Dispute Resolution
Aspect Details
Legal & Statutory Backing
• Article 39A → Mandates equal justice and free legal aid, acts as the Constitutional cornerstone for

Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) mechanisms in India.
• Section 89 of CPC: Mandates courts to refer pending disputes to ADR if settlement elements exist.
• Arbitration & Conciliation Act, 1996: Governs domestic and international arbitration.
• Mediation Act, 2023: Provides statutory backing specifically for mediation.
Data & Examples
• Data: India historically ranks low in "Enforcing Contracts". High-stakes corporate disputes (e.g.,

Vodafone, Amazon-Future Retail) often prefer Singapore (SIAC) or London (LCIA) over India.
• Examples: India International Arbitration Centre (IIAC) and the emerging GIFT City Arbitration centre.
Issues & Challenges
• Over-judicialisation: Indian arbitration has become almost as formal, expensive, and lengthy as regular

court proceedings, defeating its core purpose.
• Judicial Interference: Section 34 of the Arbitration Act is frequently misused by losing parties to

challenge arbitral awards in regular courts, stalling finality.
• Lack of Professionals: A severe shortage of dedicated, globally recognised professional arbitrators (the
space is currently dominated by retired judges).
Way Forward & Committees
• B.N. Srikrishna Committee: Recommended minimising court intervention and creating specialised

arbitration bars to make India an international arbitration hub.
• Institutional Shift: Moving away from ad-hoc arbitration toward institutional arbitration with strict
timelines and professional grading.
Recent Updates
• Mediation Act, 2023: A landmark update that encourages institutional mediation, mandates pre-litigation

mediation in commercial cases, and makes mediated settlement agreements enforceable by law.
• Arbitration Council of India (ACI): Although it was enacted into law as an independent statutory body
via the Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act of 2019, the Union government has faced significant delays in fully forming the council.
