elements.text: Arbitration & Conciliation (Amendment) Act, 2021

The 2021 Amendment (the third amendment to the original 1996 Act) aimed to promote a pro-arbitration regime. However, it inadvertently introduced provisions that experts argue might delay enforcement.

rows.text: Area of Concern
Description Impact
Automatic Stays Ambiguous Terms

Introduced unconditional/automatic stays on arbitral awards if the court is satisfied prima facie that the contract/award was induced by "fraud or corruption". Encourages the losing party to file frivolous allegations just to delay the enforcement of the award. Broad, undefined terms like "fraud" and "corruption" are left to judicial interpretation. Increases judicial intervention, defeating the core purpose of arbitration (which is keeping disputes out of court).
Evidence Threshold

Lack of statutory clarity on what constitutes prima facie evidence needed for fraud claims. Leads to prolonged preliminary hearings (applications under Section 36(2)), increasing costs and burdening courts.
Arbitrator Qualifications Investor Confidence

The amendment deleted Schedule 8 (which specified strict qualifications for arbitrators), transferring the power to frame regulations to the executive/ACI. Removing statutory clarity could dilute the quality and independence of arbitrators if not strictly regulated. Weak/delayed enforcement of contracts due to prolonged stays. Negatively impacts foreign direct investment (FDI) and global commercial trust in Indian jurisdictions.

elements.text: Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Bill, 2024 (Draft)

Aim: Designed to rectify past anomalies, boost institutional arbitration (moving away from ad-hoc arbitration), reduce court intervention, and ensure timely resolution to make India a global arbitration hub.
Key Features & Reforms:
1. Renaming the Act (Omission of Conciliation):
 The Act is to be renamed from the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 simply to the Arbitration Act, 1996.

 Reason: Provisions related to conciliation have been integrated into the newly enacted Mediation Act, 2023, streamlining the legal framework.
2. Emergency Arbitrator:

 Introduces the concept of an "Emergency Arbitrator" to grant urgent interim relief to parties even before the formal arbitral tribunal is fully constituted.
3. Institutional Focus over Ad Hoc:

 Shifts the preference toward institutional arbitration (where disputes are managed by specialized arbitration institutions) rather than ad-hoc arbitration (where parties arrange proceedings themselves), aiming to improve procedural efficiency, consistency, and institutional oversight.
4. Empowering the Arbitration Council of India (ACI):

 The Draft Bill strengthens institutional governance mechanisms and provides for recognition and regulation of arbitral institutions, while revisiting the role envisaged for the Arbitration Council of India under earlier amendments.
5. Virtual Proceedings (Tech Integration):

 Officially permits and legally recognizes video conferencing and virtual arbitration proceedings, accommodating global parties and reducing travel logistics/costs.
6. Appellate Arbitral Tribunal:

 Proposes the creation of an internal appellate mechanism to hear appeals against arbitral awards, minimizing the need for parties to immediately drag the dispute into traditional High Courts.
7. Recognition of Electronic Arbitration Agreements
 Arbitration agreements can be concluded electronically.

 Digital signatures and electronic records are expressly recognised.
8. Reduced Court Intervention

 Courts are encouraged to defer to arbitral tribunals on interim measures and procedural issues.
9. Time-bound Jurisdictional Decisions

 Arbitral tribunals must decide jurisdictional objections within prescribed timelines.
10. Remand of Awards
 Courts may remit awards back to tribunals to cure defects instead of outright setting them aside.
18.3 Lok Adalats
An informal, people-centric forum where disputes are resolved by consensus, not contest, ensuring accessible, compassionate, and timely justice.
18.3.1 Core Philosophy & Features
• Consensus over Contest: Operates on a conciliation model. The effort is not to decide who is right/wrong, but to find a practical, fair, and quick resolution. There are no winners or losers.
• Cost-Effective: No court fee is payable. Furthermore, if a pending court case is settled in a Lok Adalat, the already paid court fee is refunded.
• Binding Nature: The award of a Lok Adalat is final, binding, and deemed to be a decree of a civil court. No appeal is permitted, ensuring quick finality.
18.3.2 Variants of Lok Adalats & their Mandates
Variant Operational Framework & Mandate
National Lok Adalats (NLAs)
• Mission-Mode Delivery: Simultaneous, nationwide sittings held on a single day across all court levels

based on an annual NALSA calendar.
• Process: Extensive pre-Lok Adalat sittings are held to scope out settlements. Disposed cases are

immediately updated on the National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG).
• Scale: They resolve millions of pre-litigation and pending cases in a single day.
Permanent Lok Adalats (PLAs)
• Focus: Dedicated entirely to Public Utility Services (transport, telecommunications, electricity, water, and

postal).
• Jurisdiction & Composition: Pecuniary jurisdiction up to ₹1 crore. The bench comprises a Chairperson

and 2 domain experts.
• Unique Power: Unlike regular Lok Adalats, which just return the case if conciliation fails, PLAs have the
statutory authority to decide the dispute on merits (adjudication), ensuring closure.
E-Lok Adalats
• Digital Adaptation: Born out of the COVID-19 necessity, these allow remote participation through video
conferencing, bringing justice directly into people’s homes and drastically cutting travel time/costs.
18.3.3 Issues & Way Forward
Dimensions Details
Issues & Challenges
• • Quality vs. Quantity: In the rush to show high disposal statistics during National Lok Adalats, poor

litigants are sometimes pressured to accept subpar settlements.
• • Imbalance of Power: In disputes involving banks (loan recovery) or insurance companies, the

individual is at a severe negotiating disadvantage against corporate giants.
• • Lack of Adjudication (in regular Lok Adalats): If parties fail to compromise, regular Lok Adalats
cannot decide the case; they merely return it to the regular court, causing delays.
Way Forward
• • Strict Pre-counselling: Institutionalise rigorous pre-Lok Adalat counselling to ensure consent is

genuine and not obtained through pressure or ignorance of legal rights.
• • Expand PLAs: Promote awareness and utilisation of Permanent Lok Adalats, as their ability to
adjudicate public utility disputes provides guaranteed finality.
18.3.4 NALSA (National Legal Services Authority)
The apex statutory body was constituted to provide free and competent legal services to the weaker sections and coordinate Lok Adalats nationwide.
Aspect Details
Foundation & Hierarchical Architecture
• Origin: Constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987; came into force on 9th

November 1995 to fulfil the mandate of Articles 39A, 14, and 22(1).
• National (NALSA): The Patron-in-Chief is the Chief Justice of India, and the Executive Chairman is

the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court.
• State (SLSA): The Patron-in-Chief is the Chief Justice of the respective High Court, with the senior-

most HC Judge as Executive Chairman.
• District & Taluka (DLSA/TLSC): DLSAs are chaired by the District Judge and operate directly from
the District Court Complexes to ensure grassroots access.
Mandate & Beneficiaries (Section 12 of LSA Act)
• Target Groups: Women, children, SC/STs, industrial workmen, and persons in custody (including

juvenile homes and psychiatric hospitals).
• Disaster Victims: Explicitly covers victims of mass disasters, ethnic violence, caste atrocities, floods,

droughts, and earthquakes.
• Income Ceiling Limits: The annual income limit for availing free legal aid has been strictly defined -

revised up to ₹5,00,000 for matters before the Supreme Court and ₹1,00,000 for High Court matters.
• Income caps are entirely waived if you belong to certain categories. Anyone who is a woman, a child,
or a member of SC/ST automatically qualifies for free legal aid, regardless of their income.
Scope of Services & Key Initiatives
• Beyond Representation: Free legal aid includes payment of process fees, witness expenses, drafting

of legal documents (like Special Leave Petitions), and supplying certified copies of judgements.
• Social Justice Litigation: NALSA actively files Public Interest Litigations (PILs) for matters of

special concern, like prison reforms, human rights, etc.
• Infrastructure Setup: Expanding access by appointing "Legal Aid Counsel" in all Magistrate courts,

establishing Counseling & Conciliation Centers in all districts, and setting up legal aid facilities inside jails.
• Publication: Drives legal literacy through its official newsletter, "Nyaya Deep".
Issues & Challenges
• Awareness Deficit: The most marginalised sections (tribals, undertrials, bonded labourers) remain

completely unaware of their statutory right to free legal aid.
• Quality of Representation: Empaneled legal aid lawyers are often inexperienced, underpaid, or lack

motivation, leading to the critique that "free legal aid often becomes poor legal aid".
• Apathy at Grassroots: District and Taluka-level committees often suffer from poor infrastructure,
delayed funding disbursements, and administrative bottlenecks.
Way Forward
• NALSA Centre for Citizen Services: A dedicated central facility recently set up at Jaisalmer House,

New Delhi, to streamline public access and grievances must be expanded pan-India.
• Tele-Law & Digital Access: Leveraging Common Service Centres (CSCs) at the Panchayat level to

connect marginalised communities with panel lawyers via video conferencing.
• Engaging Senior Counsel: NALSA is actively pushing to integrate Pro Bono Legal Services (via the
Nyaya Bandhu App), encouraging senior advocates to take up cases to ensure high-quality representation for the poor.

elements.text: Lok Adalats have transformed from scattered initiatives into India's most trusted alternative dispute resolution mechanism. By combining the statutory robustness of the LSA Act, 1987, with a deeply humane model of justice, they prove that justice need not be distant or intimidating. They successfully substitute courtroom drama with conversation and negotiation, transforming ordinary court complexes into bustling centres of resolution and rebuilding trust between the citizen and the system.
18.3.5 Gram Nyayalayas

The Law Commission of India, in its 114th Report, had suggested the establishment of Gram Nyayalayas for providing affordable and quick access to justice to the citizens at their doorsteps. The Gram Nyayalayas Bill was passed by the Parliament on 22nd December 2008, and the Gram Nyayalayas Act came into force with effect from 02nd October 2009. The Act extends to the whole of India, except to the States of Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim and to the tribal areas specified in Parts I, II, IIA and III of the paragraph 20 of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution of India within the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, respectively.
Core Foundation: What are Gram Nyayalayas?
• Philosophy: They embody the constitutional mandate of Article 39A (Free Legal Aid) and the democratic decentralisation envisaged by the 73rd Amendment.
• Nature: They are mobile courts that hold proceedings at the headquarters of the intermediate Panchayat and also periodically visit villages to hear cases directly at the grassroots.
• Aim: To provide speedy, inexpensive, and substantial justice to the rural population.
Dimension Details
Statutory Backing
Established under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 (came into force on October 2, 2009). Established by the State Government in consultation with the respective High Court.
Presiding Officer
• Headed by a Nyayadhikari, who is strictly a judicial officer equivalent to a Judicial Magistrate of the

First Class (JMFC).
• Appointed by the State Government in consultation with the High Court.
• The Nyayadhikari shall periodically visit villages and may hear the parties and dispose of the cases at
the place other than its headquarters
Seat The seat of the Gram Nyayalayas shall be located at the headquarters of the intermediate Panchayat.
Guided by PNJ

The Gram Nyayalaya shall not be bound by the rules of evidence provided in the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, but shall be guided by the principles of natural justice subject to any rule made by the High Court.
Dual Jurisdiction
Gram Nyayalayas have jurisdiction over both Civil and Criminal cases.
• Criminal : Offences not punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment > 2 years (follows

summary trial procedure).
• Civil: Property disputes, minimum wages, domestic violence, etc.
Appeal Mechanism

• Criminal Appeals: Go to the Court of Session.
• Civil Appeals: Go to the District Court.
• Crucial Detail: Appeals must be filed and disposed of within a strict timeline of six months.
Issues and Challenges
Challenge Details
Reluctance of Stakeholders

Lawyers & Police: Advocates are reluctant to travel to remote villages to practice in these courts due to low fees. Police officials often do not file charge sheets before Gram Nyayalayas, preferring regular district courts.
Concurrent Jurisdiction Overlap
The jurisdiction of Gram Nyayalayas runs parallel to regular courts. Since litigants (and lawyers) are more accustomed to regular courts, they bypass the Gram Nyayalaya, leaving it underutilised.
Funding & Infrastructure
States complain of a severe lack of funds to build infrastructure (courtrooms, vehicles for mobile courts, and staff salaries). The central assistance provided is often deemed insufficient.
• In the recent National Federation of Societies for Fast Justice case, the argument was provided that
only about five to six per cent of Gram Nyayalayas have been set up till now.
Lack of Awareness
Rural populations remain largely unaware of the existence of Gram Nyayalayas or their power to hear and decide cases locally.
Way Forward

rows.text: Theme Detailed Way Forward
Example
Judicial Intervention The Supreme Court must strictly enforce the operationalisation of the 2008 Act. States must be given hard deadlines to notify and fund these courts.

The Supreme Court (in National Federation of Societies for Fast Justice vs UoI) frequently pilled up State Governments and High Courts, issuing notices for their failure to establish Gram Nyayalayas, calling it a "farce" of the 2008 Act.
Financial Re-structuring The Central Government needs to increase its one-time infrastructural grant and recurring salary assistance to incentivise states.

Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS): The scheme for infrastructural facilities for the judiciary now includes specific, extended funding provisions for Gram Nyayalayas up to 2026. It should be made a permanent feature of the justice system at the grassroots level.

elements.text: Exclusive Jurisdiction
Recommendation: Various legal experts suggest amending the Act to remove concurrent jurisdiction with regular district and sessions courts.
To solve the overlap issue, certain petty civil and criminal matters should be made the exclusive domain of Gram Nyayalayas at the first instance, forcing lawyers and police to utilise them.
Digital Integration
Integrate Gram Nyayalayas with the e-Courts project and Common Service Centres (CSCs) to track case pendency and facilitate virtual hearings where physical mobility is an issue.
Deploying robust, high-speed broadband or satellite-based internet to ensure rural mobile courts and block-level Nyayalayas can upload data to the e-Courts Services platform in real-time
18.4. Designing Innovative Solutions for Holistic Access to Justice (DISHA Scheme)

Modern technology is helping people access the legal system easily and affordably, too. About 2.10 crore people (as on February 28, 2025) were given pre-litigation advice, pro bono services, and legal representation and awareness through the DISHA scheme, which has been implemented from
2021-2026. It is funded by the Government of India and has an outlay of Rs. 250 crore.

elements.text: An effective dispute redressal mechanism must ensure that justice is not only fair but also timely and enforceable. Strengthening institutional independence, ensuring time-bound adjudication, and leveraging technology can enhance public trust and uphold the rule of law.
Parliament and State Legislatures - Structure,
Functioning, Conduct of Business, Powers & Privileges and Issues Arising
Out of These
Indian Parliament

The Parliament at the Union level and the State Legislatures at the State level form the bedrock of India's representative democracy. Operating on the Westminster model of parliamentary democracy, they are not merely law-making bodies but the primary instruments of ensuring executive accountability, financial oversight, and national deliberation.
→ Parliament: Part V (Articles 79–122) → State Legislatures: Part VI (Articles 168–212)

19.1 Structure, Membership, and Elections
The Indian Parliament is designed to balance direct popular representation (Lok Sabha) with the federal representation of the States (Rajya Sabha).

rows.text: Dimension Lok Sabha
Rajya Sabha
System of Elections Direct Elections using the First-Past-The-Post (FPTP) system based on Universal Adult Suffrage
Indirect Elections through Proportional Representation by means of Single Transferable Vote (STV) by State MLAs.

Current Strength 543 elected members. (The provision for 2 nominated Anglo-Indian members was discontinued by the 104th Amendment Act). (Articles 81, 331) Duration of House 5 Years from the first sitting. Can be extended during a National Emergency for 1 year at a time (Article 83)
245 members (233 elected and 12 nominated by the President). (Article 80) Permanent Body (Not subject to dissolution). 1/3rd of its members retire every 2 years.

elements.text: Qualifications Minimum age 25 years; must be an Indian citizen (Article 84).
Minimum age 30 years; must be an Indian citizen (Article 84).
Disqualifications
Disqualified under Article 102, the 10th Schedule (Anti-Defection), or the RPA 1951 (holding an office of profit, unsound mind, or insolvency).
The same disqualification criteria apply as in the case of the Lok Sabha.
19.2 Why do we need Rajya Sabha?
Bicameralism ensures checks and balances. The Rajya Sabha was explicitly designed not to rival the Lok Sabha but to complement it through federal balance and mature deliberation.

rows.text: Rationale Explanation Federal Balance Article 80(1): Allocates seats to states/UTs based on population. It protects state interests in national legislation.
Example In 2015, the Rajya Sabha blocked the Land Acquisition Bill (which states opposed), forcing the government to revise it.

Check on Hasty Legislation Article 107: Acts as a revising chamber to prevent rushed or populist decisions by the Lok Sabha. Continuity & Stability Article 83(1): It is a permanent house, ensuring legislative continuity even when the Lok Sabha is dissolved. Expertise & Experience Article 80(3): Twelve members are nominated by the President for special knowledge in arts, science, literature, and social service.

Both houses must pass ordinary bills, ensuring double scrutiny. Important for national continuity during sudden falls of the Union government. Sachin Tendulkar (nominated in 2012) advocated for sports reforms.
Prevents Autocracy Prevents the absolute majority dominance of a single party that sweeps the Lok Sabha, protecting minority and regional interests.
Forces coalition-building and cross-party consensus on major legislative overhauls.

elements.text: 19.3 Comparison of Powers: Lok Sabha vs. Rajya Sabha
While both houses share identical powers in constitutional amendments and impeachments, the Lok Sabha heavily dominates financial matters and executive accountability.

rows.text: Category of Power
Constitutional Articles
Dominance
Equal Powers

Article 107: Non-money bills require approval from both. Article 368: Equal power to amend the Constitution. Articles 54 & 66: Equal electoral powers (President/VP). Articles 61 & 124(4): Equal impeachment powers (President/Judges).
Absolute Equality. Neither house can override the other.
Unequal Status (Lok Sabha Dominance)

Article 109 (Money Bills): LS has exclusive power to introduce Money Bills. RS has only 14 days to suggest non-binding changes. Article 75(3): The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible only to the LS (No-Confidence Motion). Article 352: Only the LS can pass a resolution to disapprove a National Emergency. Article 108: In Joint Sessions, LS dominates due to numerical superiority (543 vs 245).
Lok Sabha Dominates. The "will of the people" overrides the federal chamber in finance and government survival.
Special Powers of Rajya Sabha

Article 249: Can authorise Parliament to legislate on the State List only if the RS passes a resolution declaring it necessary in the national interest. (requires a 2/3rd majority of members present and voting). Article 312: Can create new All-India Services (requires a 2/3rd majority of members present and voting). Article 67(b): Exclusively initiates the removal of the Vice President.
Rajya Sabha Exclusive. Grants it unique federal vetoes.

elements.text: 19.4 Functioning and Conduct of Business
The daily operations, passage of bills, and scrutiny of the government rely on specific rules of procedure and the committee system.
Dimension Constitutional
Examples Contemporary
Articles
Issues
Sessions & Sittings
Article 85: The President summons the Houses. The max gap between two sessions cannot exceed 6 months.

Issue (Declining Deliberation): The NCRWC recommended at least sittings of 120 days for the Lok Sabha and 100 days for the Rajya Sabha annually, but this has not been implemented, leading to rushed legislation.
According to PRS Legislative Research, the 17th Lok Sabha held only 274 sittings, the lowest for any full-term Lok Sabha in Indian history.
Presiding Officers
Article 93: Speaker & Deputy Speaker (LS). Article 89: Chairman & Deputy Chairman (RS).

Issue (Convention Broken): In the 17th Lok Sabha (2019-2024), the post of Deputy Speaker (traditionally given to the opposition) was left vacant for the entire 5-year term, violating the spirit of Article 93.
The Speaker certifies Money Bills and maintains order.
Departmental Related Standing Committees (DRSCs)
Article 118: Rules of Procedure. There are 24 DRSCs acting as "mini-parliaments".

Data Update: Massive decline in scrutiny. While the 15th LS referred 71% of bills to committees, the 17th LS referred merely 16% (PRS Data). Crucial bills like the Three New Criminal Codes saw limited debate.
Committees ensure bipartisan, technical scrutiny of bills away from the political grandstanding of the main House.
Legislative Process
Articles 107-109 (Ordinary & Money Bills), Article 111 (President's Assent).
Joint Sitting (Art 108): Used only three times in history (e.g., POTA 2002) to resolve deadlocks over ordinary bills.
Issue: Passing major, complex bills via the "Voice Vote" mechanism amid din or mass suspensions of opposition MPs (e.g., 146 MPs suspended in the 2023 Winter Session).
19.5 Powers and Executive Accountability
The Parliament exercises control over the executive (Council of Ministers) primarily through financial powers and Parliamentary devices.

rows.text: Dimension
Constitutional Article
Example
Contemporary Issues
Executive Accountability Financial Control (The Budget) The Money Bill Controversy

Article 75(3): The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Article 112 (Annual Financial Statement), Article 114 (Appropriation Bill), Article 265 (No tax without authority). Article 110: Defines a Money Bill. Article 109: Rajya Sabha cannot reject it

Enforced via Question Hour, Zero Hour, Adjournment Motions, and No-Confidence Motions. Parliament controls the national purse. The PAC (Public Accounts Committee) audits government spending post-facto. Classifying the Aadhaar Act and Tribunal Reforms Act as Money Bills to bypass the Rajya Sabha's scrutiny.

Frequent disruptions and the occasional cancellation of Question Hour (e.g., during the 2020 COVID session) dilutes the opposition's primary tool to hold ministries accountable on a daily basis. In recent years, due to lack of time, up to 70-80% of the Union Budget demands for various ministries have been passed via the "Guillotine" (put to vote directly without any discussion). A 7-judge Constitutional Bench of the Supreme Court is currently reviewing the scope of the Speaker's final authority to classify a bill as a Money Bill under Article 110(3).

elements.text: 19.6 Privileges and Judicial Interventions

Parliamentary privileges are special rights and exemptions enjoyed by the two Houses and their members, necessary to secure their independence. Article 105 of the Constitution was designed to grant Members of Parliament the necessary immunities to discharge their duties fearlessly, free from executive intimidation or civil litigation.
19.6.1 The Dual Nature of Privileges (Article 105 & 194)

rows.text: Dimension & Constitutional Basis Meaning, Purpose & Scope (Articles 105 & 194)

Key Features Landmark Cases / Examples Special rights, immunities and exemptions enjoyed by the Houses, committees and members to ensure legislative independence, dignity and effective functioning. Derived from British parliamentary traditions and conventions.
Criticism Broad and undefined scope creates ambiguity and potential misuse.
Freedom of Speech in the House [Articles 105(1), 105(2), 194(1) & 194(2)]

MPs/MLAs enjoy absolute freedom of speech in the House, subject to House rules. No legal proceedings for anything said or any vote given in the House or its committees. Parliamentary debates, committee proceedings and voting.
Distinct from Article 19(1)(a); debate continues on balancing privilege with accountability.
Immunity from Court Proceedings [Article 105(2)]
Complete immunity for speeches, votes and authorised parliamentary publications. Protection is confined to legislative functions. Members cannot be sued for statements made inside Parliament.
Does not extend to acts outside legislative functions.
Bribery & Parliamentary Immunity [Article 105 – Judicial Interpretation]

Parliamentary privilege cannot shield corrupt acts linked to legislative functions. Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024): MPs/MLAs can be prosecuted for accepting bribes related to speeches or votes, overruling the P.V. Narasimha Rao case (1998).
Strengthened accountability and reinforced that privilege is not a shield against corruption.

elements.text: Freedom from Arrest & Court Attendance [Section 135A, CPC]
Immunity from arrest in civil cases during a session and 40 days before and after it; exemption from appearing as a witness during a session.
Ensures uninterrupted participation in legislative business.
No immunity in criminal cases or preventive detention.
Collective Privileges of the House [Articles 105(3) & 194(3)]
Right to regulate internal proceedings, exclude strangers, hold secret sittings, publish/prohibit publication of proceedings, and punish for contempt or breach of privilege.
Secret sittings, privilege motions and disciplinary proceedings.
Can generate tensions with transparency and media freedom.
Breach of Privilege & Contempt of House [Articles 105 & 194; Parliamentary Rules]
Any act obstructing a member or the House in performing its functions may amount to a breach of privilege or contempt. Houses may reprimand, suspend, imprison or expel offenders.
Privilege proceedings against members, officials or journalists.
Lack of codification creates uncertainty regarding scope and punishment.
Committee of Privileges [Lok Sabha Rule 222; Rajya Sabha Rule 187]
Investigates privilege complaints and recommends action to the House.
Examination of privilege notices and breach allegations.
Criticised at times for politicisation and inconsistent standards.
Judicial Review vs Parliamentary Autonomy [Articles 122 & 212]
Raja Ram Pal v. Lok Sabha (2007): Privilege powers are subject to judicial review in cases of illegality, mala fides or constitutional violations.
Courts generally cannot question parliamentary proceedings on procedural irregularities, but constitutional violations remain reviewable.
Ongoing tension between parliamentary autonomy and constitutional supremacy.
Uncodified Nature of Privileges [Articles 105(3) & 194(3)]
Parliament has the power to define privileges by law, but most remain uncodified and continue to rely on conventions.
Continued reliance on British parliamentary precedents.
Leads to uncertainty, selective interpretation and possible misuse.
Conflict with Fundamental Rights [Articles 105, 194 vis-à-vis Articles 19 & 21]
Privileges protect legislative autonomy, while Fundamental Rights protect citizens and media. Courts seek a constitutional balance between the two.
Searchlight Case, 1959: SC held that legislative privileges can prevail over freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) in certain circumstances.
Concerns that uncodified privileges may chill free speech and democratic scrutiny.
Reforms & Way Forward (NCRWC, 2nd ARC Recommendations)
Codification of privileges, clearer definition of breach of privilege, stronger ethics mechanisms and harmonisation with Fundamental Rights.
Repeated recommendations by constitutional reform bodies.
Need to balance legislative independence with accountability, transparency and constitutionalism.
Assessing the reasons for non-codification
The Constitution (Article 105(3)) explicitly instructed Parliament to define its privileges "by law." Seven decades later, no such
law exists. Why?
1. The Fear of Judicial Review (The Primary Reason): If Parliament enacts a comprehensive "Privileges Act", it will be
classified as a "Law" under Article 13.
 Consequently, this codified law would be strictly subject to Fundamental Rights, especially the Right to Free Speech
[Art 19(1)(a)] and the Right to Life/Liberty [Art 21].
 Currently, because they are un-codified Constitutional conventions, the Supreme Court (in the Searchlight Case,
1959) ruled that parliamentary privileges can override Article 19(1)(a). Parliament refuses to codify them to maintain
this supremacy over the press and citizens.
2. Desire for Absolute Flexibility: Codification rigidly defines what constitutes "contempt of the house". By keeping it
uncoded, Parliament retains the flexible power to decide on a case-by-case basis what offends its dignity.
3. The "British Legacy" Argument: Legislators argue that since the UK House of Commons has not codified its privileges
and relies on evolving conventions, India should do the same to maintain parliamentary sovereignty.
The Consequences of Ambiguity
Why is this a problem for democracy?
• Chilling Effect on the Press: Journalists operate in constant fear. Reporting on parliamentary proceedings or criticising
the Speaker can arbitrarily invite a "Breach of Privilege" notice, stifling journalistic freedom (e.g., the Hindu journalists'
case in Tamil Nadu).
• Violation of Natural Justice: In privilege cases, Parliament acts as the victim, the prosecutor, and the judge. This violates
the core legal principle of Nemo judex in causa sua (no one should be a judge in their own case).
• Institutional Hubris: State legislatures often misuse these powers to settle political scores or arrest critics, wasting legislative
time on perceived slights rather than law-making.
How can this be addressed?
1. Implement the NCRWC Recommendations: The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution
(Venkatachaliah Commission) explicitly recommended that privileges should be defined and delimited for the free functioning
of democracy.
2. Statutory Codification (The Ultimate Solution): Parliament must enact a "Parliamentary Privileges Act." This act must:
 Exhaustively define what specific acts constitute "contempt".
 Remove the archaic power to punish citizens for simply criticising the House outside its walls.
 Formally subject the penal powers of the House to the Fundamental Rights of citizens.
3. The Australian Model: India can adopt the Parliamentary Privileges Act 1987 of Australia, which successfully codified
privileges, defined contempt strictly as actions that cause "substantial interference" with the House's work, and removed
the power to punish for defamatory words against Parliament
19.7 Systemic Issues & Democratic Deficits

Beyond procedural rules, the institutional integrity of the Parliament is facing severe systemic threats. The transition from a "Deliberative Democracy" to "Executive Dominance" requires urgent institutional reforms.

Ordinance Raj

Source: SC (D.C. Wadhwa & Krishna Kumar Singh)
• Misusing Article 123 to pass substantive laws without parliamentary debate. Intended for unforeseen emergencies, it is used as a parallel, convenient law-making tool.

Enforcing Accountability:

• Make it mandatory for the government to lay down a detailed statement of the "extraordinary circumstances" that necessitated the ordinance before the House.

elements.text: 19.8 Office of the Speaker
The Office of the Speaker, enshrined in Article 93, is designed to be the Constitutional embodiment of Parliamentary dignity and absolute impartiality.

rows.text: Theme
Constitutional Provisions & Key Features
Contemporary Issues / High-Value Cases
Nature of Office & Appointment

Art. 93: Lok Sabha elects the Speaker. Presiding officer, custodian of House privileges, interpreter of rules, and representative of the House. Expected to function impartially despite party affiliation.
Debate over the political neutrality of the Speaker in a highly polarised parliamentary environment.
Election & Vacancy Rules
Arts. 93–95: Elected by the Lok Sabha; removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all then members after 14 days' notice. Continues in office until the first sitting of the next Lok Sabha.
The deputy speaker's post remained vacant throughout the 17th Lok Sabha (2019–24), raising concerns over Article 93's requirement to elect one "as soon as may be".
Legislative Powers & Scrutiny
Arts. 108 & 110: Presides over proceedings, decides admissibility of motions, refers bills to committees, certifies money bills, and presides over joint sittings.
The Aadhaar Act (2016) and Finance Acts triggered controversy over money bill certification. Rojer Mathew (2019) case questioned the scope of the speaker's certification power.
Discipline & Disqualification
Tenth Schedule (Para 6), Art. 118: Maintains order, suspends disorderly members, and decides anti-defection petitions.
Kihoto Hollohan (1992): Speaker's decisions subject to judicial review. Nabam Rebia (2016) and Subhash Desai (2023) highlighted concerns over delays and neutrality in disqualification proceedings.
Impartiality & Voting
Art. 100(1): Speaker ordinarily does not vote; exercises a casting vote in case of a tie. Conventionally used to maintain the status quo.
Debate on adopting the UK model, where the Speaker resigns from party affiliation to strengthen neutrality.

elements.text: What is the 'Once a Speaker, Always a Speaker' Convention?

In the UK (Westminster system), the moment an MP is elected as Speaker, s/he formally resigns from his/her political party. S/he completely severs all political affiliations to ensure absolute neutrality. In return for this sacrifice, a healthy political convention exists: major political parties do not field candidates against the Speaker in subsequent general elections, ensuring their unopposed return to the House.
Why is it needed in India?
In India, the Speaker rarely resigns from their party (Neelam Sanjiva Reddy being a rare exception). This creates severe conflicts of interest:

• The Anti-Defection Tribunal: Under the 10th Schedule, the Speaker acts as a tribunal to disqualify defecting MLAs/MPs. Partisan Speakers routinely sit on disqualification petitions of opposition members who defect to the ruling party, paralysing justice.
• Arbitrary Classification of Bills: The Speaker's decision on whether a bill is a "money bill" (Article 110) is final. Partisan Speakers have been accused of classifying controversial ordinary bills as Money Bills to bypass the Rajya Sabha (e.g., the Aadhaar Act controversy).
• Stifling the Opposition: Disproportionate suspension of opposition MPs, biased allocation of time during debates, and refusal to admit Adjournment Motions create a massive trust deficit.
If India were to aggressively adopt this British convention, what would be the impact on our parliamentary business?
Dimensions Positive Implications Challenges
Disciplinary Action & Decorum

Reduced Disruptions: If the Speaker is truly neutral, the opposition will trust their rulings. The need to storm the well or disrupt proceedings out of frustration will drastically decrease, increasing parliamentary productivity.

Lack of Political Culture: Indian political parties lack the maturity to not field candidates against a sitting Speaker. Without this guarantee, a Speaker who resigns from their party risks political suicide in the next election.
Adjudicating Defections (10th Schedule)

Swift Justice: A neutral Speaker would adjudicate disqualification petitions impartially and swiftly, preventing the "horse-trading" of elected representatives and ensuring the stability of governments.

The SC's Alternative: The Supreme Court (in Keisham Meghachandra Singh, 2020) noted that expecting a Speaker to be neutral is unrealistic. They suggested stripping the Speaker of this power entirely and creating an independent tribunal.
Legislative Scrutiny

Empowering Committees: An objective Speaker would prioritise rigorous legislative scrutiny, referring more bills to Department-Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) rather than allowing the ruling party to bulldoze bills through voice votes amid the din.

Coalition Vulnerabilities: In eras of coalition governments, a completely independent Speaker might be viewed as a threat by a weak ruling coalition, leading to frequent attempts to remove them via No-Confidence motions.
Challenges Affecting the Speaker's Office
Despite constitutional protections, the office currently faces several functional and perceptional challenges:

• Politicisation: Increasing perception of partisan conduct, especially concerning the disqualification of MLAs/MPs under the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law) and the certification of controversial bills as Money Bills.
• Procedural Deadlocks: Frequent confrontations between the ruling party and the Opposition erode trust, making consensus-building difficult and leading to parliamentary paralysis.
• Weakening Conventions: Unwritten parliamentary norms that once guaranteed impartial conduct are gradually being overshadowed by tactical, competitive political considerations.
The Procedure for Removal of the Speaker
Aspect Constitutional & Procedural Details
Constitutional Provision
Governed by Article 94(c) of the Indian Constitution.
Procedural Rules Laid down in Rules 200 to 203 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha.
Notice Period A minimum of 14 days' written notice must be submitted to the Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha.
Admission in House Requires the support of at least 50 members for the motion to be admitted and proceed for discussion.
Grounds The resolution must clearly state the specific charges against the Speaker.
Voting Majority Required
Must be passed by a majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha (Effective Majority), not merely those present and voting.
Speaker's Rights during Motion
The Speaker can participate in the debate as a regular member and can vote in the first instance, but cannot cast a tie-breaking vote.
Historical Precedents
Extremely rare. Attempted only thrice: 1954 (G.V. Mavalankar), 1966 (Hukam Singh), and 1987(Balram Jakhar). All three motions failed.
Institutional Challenges and The Way Ahead

rows.text: Core Challenge
Way Ahead
Erosion of Impartiality
Reinforce Institutional Conventions: Political parties must collectively reaffirm the unwritten tradition that the Speaker strictly acts above party lines once elected.
Allegations of Bias in Rulings
Enhance Transparency: Provide clear, reasoned explanations for major decisions (e.g., rejecting discussion requests, certifying Money Bills) to reduce perceptions of partisanship.
Parliamentary Deadlocks Ambiguity in Discretionary Powers

Encourage Structured Dialogue: Foster continuous, structured consultations between the government and the Opposition regarding procedures to reduce confrontations and boost productivity. Codify Best Practices: While parliamentary flexibility is needed, codifying guidelines regarding the Speaker’s discretionary powers (like Anti-Defection rulings) can minimise disputes.

elements.text: While procedural disruptions and executive dominance pose contemporary challenges, the Indian Parliament remains a highly resilient institution. Its future lies not in resisting rapid governance but in modernising its oversight mechanisms. By embracing digital integration (like e-Vidhan), data-driven committee scrutiny, and codified privileges, Parliament is poised to evolve from a traditional deliberative body into a dynamic, 21st-century legislative hub - perfectly balancing executive agility with democratic accountability."
State Legislature

Established under Part VI (Articles 168 to 212), the State Legislature is the primary law-making and deliberative body at the state level in India. While it mirrors the Westminster model of the Union Parliament, it operates with significant federal nuances. Currently, most states have a unicameral legislature (Legislative Assembly), while six states (Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, and Karnataka) operate a bicameral system.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. Discuss the role of Presiding Officers of state legislatures in maintaining order
and impartiality in conducting legislative work and in facilitating best democratic
practices. (2023)
20.1 Structure, Membership, and Elections
Dimension Legislative Assembly Legislative Council
System of Elections
Indirect Elections & Nominations (STV).
Direct Elections (FPTP) based on Universal Adult Suffrage from territorial constituencies.

• 1/3 by Local Bodies (Panchayats/Municipalities).
• 1/3 by MLAs.
• 1/12 by Graduates (3 years standing).
• 1/12 by Teachers (Secondary level+).
• 1/6 Nominated by the Governor.
Current Strength
60 to 500 members depending on population. (Exceptions: Goa, Mizoram and Sikkim have fewer than 60.
A minimum of 40 to a maximum of 1/3rd of the Assembly's strength. (Article 171)
Duration of House
Permanent Body. 1/3rd of its members retire every 2 years.
5 Years from the first sitting. Can be extended during a National Emergency for 1 year at a time.
Qualifications Minimum age 25 years; must be an Indian citizen and registered voter in the state.
Minimum age 30 years; must be an Indian citizen.
20.2 The Bicameralism Debate (Article 169)
Unlike the Rajya Sabha (a federal necessity), the Legislative Council is entirely at the mercy of the Assembly.
Dimension Details
The Article 169 Mechanism
The creation/abolition of a Council requires a Special Majority in the State Assembly (2/3rd present & voting + absolute majority), followed by a Simple Majority in Parliament.
The Utility (Importance of Legislative Council)

1. Check on Hasty Legislation: Acts as a reviewing chamber against populist Assembly decisions.
2. Expertise & Representation: Accommodates teachers, graduates, and Governor's nominees (literature, science, art, cooperative movement) who have fewer chances to be elected from electoral politics.
3. Nurturing Future Leadership - The Council often acts as a training ground for young or inexperienced politicians, allowing them to understand legislative procedures and debates before they dive into the turbulent waters of the Legislative Assembly.
4. Accommodating Diversity & Minorities: Political parties often use the Upper House to provide representation to unrepresented minorities, marginalised communities, or specific linguistic groups.
Issue (Article) Description Reforms / Way Forward
Weak Legislative Powers (Articles 197 & 198)
The Council can only delay ordinary bills (up to 4 months) and has merely recommendatory powers over Money Bills.
Strengthen its role as a revisory chamber through mandatory scrutiny of major bills.
Subordinate Status to Assembly (Articles 197–199)
Unlike the Rajya Sabha, the Council cannot effectively check the Lower House and remains constitutionally weaker.
Recast the Council as an expert deliberative body rather than a rival chamber.
Financial Burden
Maintaining an additional chamber entails expenditure on salaries, staff and infrastructure despite limited powers.
Improve legislative output and committee scrutiny to justify costs.
Political Rehabilitation Centre (Article 171)
Often used to accommodate defeated politicians, ministers without electoral mandates and party loyalists (backdoor entry).
Make nominations merit-based, focusing on experts in literature, science, art, social service and public affairs.
Elite and Narrow Representation (Article 171)
Teacher and graduate constituencies represent limited groups and may not reflect contemporary social realities.
Review composition and broaden representation to newer professional and social sectors.
Indirect Democratic Legitimacy (Article 171)
Most members are indirectly elected, weakening democratic accountability.
Reform electoral composition to improve representativeness and accountability.
Lack of Visibility and Accountability
Proceedings often receive limited public attention, and policy impact remains low.
Improve transparency through live streaming, research support and public outreach.

Uncertain Existence (Article
169)
Creation or abolition depends on Assembly resolutions and Parliamentary approval, often driven by political considerations.
Develop objective criteria for the creation or abolition of Councils.
Declining Deliberative Quality
Intended as a House of revision but often underutilised and affected by disruptions.
Strengthen committee systems, research support and member capacity-building.
Rajya Sabha vs Legislative Council

rows.text: Dimension
Rajya Sabha (Council of States)
Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad)
Status
Upper House of Parliament.
Upper House of a State Legislature.
Constitutional Articles
Articles 79–122 (especially Articles 80, 83, and 84).
Articles 168–212 (especially Articles 169, 171, 172).
Purpose
Represents the States in the Union and acts as a revising chamber.
Acts as a revising chamber at the state level and provides representation to special interest groups.
Creation Maximum Strength
Permanent constitutional body; cannot be abolished. 250 members (currently 245).

Created or abolished by Parliament under Article 169 on the recommendation of the State Legislative Assembly. Cannot exceed 1/3rd of the strength of the Legislative Assembly and cannot be less than 40 members (except in certain states).
Composition
Elected members represent States and UTs; 12 members are nominated by the President for special contributions in art, literature, science and social service.
Members elected by local bodies, graduates, teachers, and MLAs; some nominated by the Governor for special knowledge or practical experience.
Method of Election
Elected by elected MLAs through proportional representation by single transferable vote (STV).
Indirect election through multiple electoral colleges; some nominated by Governor.
Tenure
Permanent House: 1/3rd of members retire every two years; term = 6 years.
Permanent House: 1/3rd of members retire every two years; term = 6 years.
Representation
Represents States in the federal structure.
Represents local bodies, teachers, graduates and eminent persons within a State.
Role in Ordinary Bills
Equal powers with Lok Sabha; can amend, reject or delay bills. Deadlocks may lead to a Joint Sitting (Article 108).
Can only delay Ordinary Bills for a maximum of 4 months (Article 197); Assembly ultimately prevails.
Role in Money Bills
Can only recommend amendments within 14 days; Lok Sabha may accept or reject them (Article 109).
Can only recommend amendments within 14 days; Assembly may accept or reject them (Article 198).
Role in Constitutional Amendments
Equal powers with the Lok Sabha; must approve Constitutional Amendment Bills. No Joint Sitting permitted.
No role in Constitutional Amendments, as amendments are passed by Parliament.
Role in Executive Accountability
Ministers are collectively responsible only to Lok Sabha, but Rajya Sabha can question and scrutinise the government.
The Council of Ministers is responsible only to the Legislative Assembly, but the Council can question and scrutinise the government.
Special Powers
Article 249: Can authorise Parliament to legislate on State List subjects. Article 312: Can create All India Services.
No comparable special constitutional powers.
Federal Significance
Key pillar of Indian federalism.
Not a federal institution; primarily a state-level revisory chamber.
Presiding Officer
The Vice-President of India is the ex officio Chairman (Articles 64 & 89). He is not a member of Rajya Sabha.
Chairman elected by the Council (Article 182). Chairman is a member of the house.
Dissolution
Cannot be dissolved.
Cannot be dissolved, but the entire Council itself can be abolished under Article 169.

elements.text: 20.3 Legislative Process and Federal Friction
The most critical contemporary issue in state polity is the friction between the elected legislature and the Centre-appointed Governor.
Governor and the State Legislature: Legislative Processes and Contemporary Issues
Dimension Constitutional
Contemporary
Articles
Issues
Sessions & Sittings
Article 174: The Governor summons/prorogues. The max gap is 6 months.
Severe Decline: State assemblies meet for an average of just 21-25 days a year (PRS Data). True deliberation is practically non-existent.
The Governor's Assent
• Article 200: The
Issue: Judicial review of Governor's delay in assenting to bills.
Governor can assent, withhold, return, or reserve the bill.
• Tamil Nadu approached the Supreme Court, alleging that the

Governor's prolonged inaction on several Assembly-passed bills stalled governance and undermined democracy, prompting the Court to examine the Governor's duties under Article 200.
• The Nov 2025 Presidential Reference clarified Governors do retain

genuine discretion (not bound by aid/advice in all Art. 200 situations), that courts cannot impose binding timelines, and that "deemed assent" is unconstitutional - while leaving the TN bills' operative outcome undisturbed.

Supreme Court Opinion on Governor's Assent to Bills (Presidential Reference No. 1 of November
2025)
• No Judicial Timelines: The Supreme Court held that courts cannot prescribe fixed timelines for

Governors or the President to decide on State Bills and overturned the timelines laid down in the Tamil Nadu Governor Case (2025).
• No Deemed Assent: A Bill cannot be treated as automatically approved merely because the Governor

or President delays taking a decision.
• Limited Mandamus Allowed: In cases of prolonged, unexplained, and indefinite delay, courts may

issue a limited mandamus directing the Governor to decide the matter within a reasonable time.
• Governor's Powers Generally Non-Justiciable: The exercise of discretionary powers under Article

200 - granting assent, withholding assent, or reserving a Bill for the President- is generally beyond judicial review.
• Separation of Powers Upheld: The judiciary cannot assume or exercise constitutional functions
specifically entrusted to the Governor or the President.
Significance of the SC opinion on Governor’s Assent to Bill
• Reaffirmed the doctrine of Separation of Powers by holding that courts cannot usurp the

constitutional functions of the Governor or President by prescribing mandatory timelines or granting deemed assent.
• Clarified the scope of Article 200, recognising that the Governor possesses limited constitutional

discretion and is not bound by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers in every situation.
• Rejected the doctrine of deemed assent, holding that a Bill cannot become law merely because of

executive inaction or delay.
• Recognised limited judicial review, permitting courts to issue a limited mandamus in cases of

arbitrary, unexplained, or indefinite delay without directing the outcome of the Governor's decision.
• Preserved the constitutional role of the Governor and President, making their discretionary powers

under Articles 200 and 201 generally non-justiciable.
• Highlighted the importance of constitutional morality and cooperative federalism, as the absence

of constitutional timelines requires constitutional authorities to act reasonably and in good faith.
• Provides long-term constitutional clarity by balancing judicial accountability of constitutional
authorities with respect for their institutional autonomy, thereby reducing future Centre–State constitutional conflicts.
Reservation of Bill for President Assent
Article 201: If reserved, the President can assent, withhold, or direct the Governor to return it.
Federal Friction: States complain that the Centre uses Article 201 through the Governor to kill state legislation indefinitely, as there is no constitutional time limit for the President to act.
Address and Messages to Legislature
Articles 175 & 176: Right to Address and Send Messages and Special Address by the Governor.
Controversies over Governors' addresses, omissions of state government-prepared texts, and disputes between elected governments and Governors.
20.4 Speaker of the State Legislative Assembly

The Speaker is the constitutional head and presiding officer of the State Legislative Assembly, responsible for maintaining order, ensuring impartial conduct of legislative business, protecting the privileges of the House, and acting as the adjudicating authority under the Anti-Defection Law. The office is central to legislative autonomy and parliamentary democracy.
Constitutional Provisions
• Article 178 - Election of Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
• Article 179 - Vacation, resignation and removal (effective majority; 14 days' notice).
• Article 180 - Deputy Speaker performs duties during vacancy/absence.
• Article 181 - Speaker cannot preside during proceedings for own removal.
• Article 199 - Speaker certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
• Article 208 - Rules of Procedure of the State Legislature.
• Article 212 - Courts cannot question legislative proceedings on grounds of procedural irregularity.
• Tenth Schedule (Para 6) - Speaker acts as adjudicating authority under the Anti-Defection Law.

rows.text: Aspect
Key Points
Election & Tenure Removal

• Elected by Assembly members from among themselves by simple majority.
• Usually elected immediately after the general election.
• Holds office till dissolution but continues until successor assumes office.
• May resign to the Deputy Speaker.
• Removed by an effective majority (majority of all then members).
• Requires 14 days' prior notice (Art. 179).
• Cannot preside over proceedings concerning own removal (Art. 181).
Major Powers & Functions

• Legislative: Presides over House, maintains order, decides admissibility of motions/questions, regulates debates.
• Procedural: Certifies Money Bills (Art. 199).
• Disciplinary: Suspends disorderly members, exercises casting vote in case of tie.
• Administrative: Head of Assembly Secretariat and controls establishment matters.
• Quasi-Judicial: Decides disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule.
• Custodial: Protects privileges, dignity and rights of the House.
Landmark Judgments Why the Office is Criticised?

• Kihoto Hollohan (1992): Speaker acts as Tribunal; decisions subject to judicial review.
• Ravi S. Naik (1994): Voluntarily giving up membership may be inferred from conduct.
• Rajendra Singh Rana (2007): Speaker's inaction cannot protect defectors.
• Nabam Rebia (2016):Speaker cannot decide disqualification while removal motion is pending (issue referred to larger Bench).
• Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020): Decisions ordinarily within 3 months; suggested independent tribunal.
• Subhash Desai (2023): Criticised delay in Maharashtra case; larger Bench to revisit Nabam Rebia.
• Padi Kaushik Reddy (2025): Speaker is a Tribunal; Article 212 immunity unavailable for quasi-judicial functions; directed disposal within 3 months.
• Speaker usually belongs to ruling party and contests future elections on party ticket.
• No mandatory timeline enables strategic delays in deciding disqualification petitions.
• Defectors continue as legislators/ministers during prolonged pendency.
• Judicial review generally begins only after the Speaker's decision, allowing prolonged inaction.
Way Forward

• Institutional: Constitutionally mandate strict timelines for disposal of defection cases.
• Structural: Transfer adjudication to an independent tribunal/ECI.
• Political: Adopt British convention of political neutrality.
• Legislative: Restrict whip to survival of government.
• Judicial: Continue strict judicial supervision against prolonged inaction.
• Administrative: Public disclosure of pending disqualification petitions and reasons for delay.

elements.text: 20.5 Major Issues and Way Forward

rows.text: Challenge
Description
Way Forward
Defections

Source: 10th Schedule Evasions To bypass anti-defection disqualification, ruling coalition MLAs are induced to simply resign, causing the government to fall. They then immediately fight by-elections on the new ruling party's ticket (e.g., Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka).
Election Commission Suggestion: Amend the RPA/10th Schedule so that any legislator who resigns mid-term is barred from contesting any by-election for the remainder of that assembly's tenure.
Ordinance Raj at State Level
Source: Article 213 State governments bypass the assembly entirely by issuing and re-promulgating ordinances, using it as a parallel legislative tool.
SC (D.C. Wadhwa Case): Re-promulgation of ordinances without placing them before the assembly is a "fraud on the Constitution" and must be struck down.
The Partisan Speaker Criminalization of State Politics

Source: Anti-Defection Adjudication Speakers delay disqualification decisions of defecting MLAs for years to protect the ruling government. Source: ADR State assemblies often have a significantly higher percentage of MLAs with serious criminal records compared to Parliament.

SC (Keisham Meghachandra Case): The SC suggested transferring defection disqualification powers from the Speaker to an Independent Permanent Tribunal headed by a retired judge. Election Commission: Disqualification upon the framing of charges for heinous crimes by a court of law, rather than waiting for final conviction.
Lack of Financial Accountability
Source: CAG Reports: State budgets are passed via a "Guillotine". Furthermore, the convention of offering the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) chairmanship to the Opposition is often bypassed.
NCRWC Recommendation: Mandate a minimum of 90 days of sitting for large state assemblies and strictly empower the Opposition in financial committees.

elements.text: Despite contemporary challenges like executive aggrandisement and federal friction, state legislatures remain the bedrock of grassroots democracy. Their evolution relies on embracing technological integration (like e-Vidhan) and structural reforms (such as independent tribunals and mandated sitting calendars). Ultimately, by transitioning from political battlegrounds to modern, data-driven deliberative chambers, state assemblies will truly drive the cooperative federalism essential for a 'New India'.
Parliamentary Committees

Parliamentary Committees are institutional extensions of the legislature, drawing their authority from Article 105 (Privileges) and Article 118 (Rules of Procedure). Given the sheer volume of legislation and the highly politicised nature of the open House, Parliament cannot effectively scrutinise every policy detail. Committees serve as the vital "deliberative core" of India's democracy.
21.1 Significance of Parliamentary Committees
Dimension Explanation
The Absence of the "Whip"
In the open House, the Anti-Defection Law forces MPs to vote on party lines. In closed-door committees, whips do not apply. This fosters genuine bipartisan consensus and objective analysis.
Domain Expertise
Parliamentarians are generalists. Committees have the power to summon domain experts, civil society members, and bureaucrats to provide technical evidence before finalising laws.

Micro-Scrutiny Parliament is currently sitting for less than 70 days a year. Committees work year-round, performing the heavy lifting of micro-scrutinising complex bills and budgets, saving the floor time of the House.
Executive Accountability
Committees routinely summon high-ranking bureaucrats (Secretaries) to answer for administrative lapses, ensuring the executive remains accountable even when Parliament is not in session.
21.2 Structure of the Committees

The committees are broadly divided into two categories: Ad Hoc Committees (temporary, formed for a specific task like investigating a financial scam or a specific bill) and Standing Committees (permanent, reconstituted annually). The Standing Committees are the backbone of the system.
The Standing Committee Structure:

1. Financial Committees (PAC, Estimates, CoPU) - Scrutinise the national purse.
2. Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) - 24 committees mapping specific ministries.
3. Committees to Inquire (Privileges, Petitions).
4. Committees to Scrutinize & Control (Govt. Assurances, Subordinate Legislation).
5. Housekeeping Committees (Rules, Business Advisory).
21.3 The Big Three Financial Committees

rows.text: Committee
Composition
Role
Public Accounts Committee (PAC)

22 Members (15 LS + 7 RS). Convention: Chaired by a member of the Opposition (convention since
1967).

Role: The ultimate auditor. It examines the CAG reports to ensure money was spent legally, efficiently, and for the intended purpose. Accountability: It establishes accountability by exposing systemic financial irregularities (e.g., exposing the 2G and Coalgate anomalies). CAG acts as the "friend, philosopher, and guide" to the Public Accounts Committee (PAC). CAG assists parliamentarians by preparing a prioritised list of the most urgent financial matters that demand the committee's attention.
Estimates Committee
30 Members (ALL from LS). Convention: Chaired by the Ruling Party.

Role: The "Continuous Economy Committee". It examines budget estimates to suggest alternative, cost-effective policies. Utility: Unlike PAC's post-mortem, it looks at current estimates. It forces the administration to justify its structural efficiency, preventing wasteful expenditure before it becomes a habit.
Committee on Public Undertakings (CoPU)
22 Members (15 LS + 7 RS).
Role: Examines the reports and accounts of PSUs (Public Sector Undertakings) to ensure they are managed following sound business principles, protecting the taxpayer's investment.

elements.text: While financial committees suffer from the inherent limitation of conducting 'post-mortem' analyses of expenditures, their true value lies in their deterrent effect. By institutionalising a culture of rigorous, bipartisan financial auditing, the PAC and Estimates Committee serve as the democratic conscience of the nation. Strengthening their mandate with real-time auditing capabilities will ensure that executive financial accountability remains absolute.
21.4 Department-Related Standing Committees
Introduced in 1993, there are currently 24 DRSCs (each with 31 members: 21 LS, 10 RS). They act as shadow mechanisms for every government ministry.
Dimension Importance
Legislative & Financial Scrutiny

• Conducts clause-by-clause examination of Bills referred to it, improving drafting quality;
• Examines ministry-wise Demands for Grants during Budget session recess, strengthening
Parliament's power of the purse
Executive & Administrative Accountability
• Requires ministries/officials to explain policy, expenditure, and implementation; provides
continuous oversight even when Parliament is not in session, since DRSCs sit year-round
Policy Evaluation & Technical Expertise

• Reviews Annual Reports and Action Taken Reports (ATRs);
• Consults experts, academics, industry bodies, and civil society for evidence-based
recommendations
Bipartisan, In-Camera Deliberation
• Closed-door proceedings reduce political grandstanding and encourage consensus-building across party

lines;
• DRSC chairs are not reserved for opposition (unlike PAC), drawn from various parties by negotiation
Institutional Continuity, Capacity-Building & Transparency

• Builds MPs' sector-specific expertise over time;
• Committee reports are tabled in both Houses, creating a permanent public record of legislative
scrutiny
DRSCs: Major Challenges
Challenge Illustration
Declining Referral of Bills (Bypass Trend)

Share of Bills referred to DRSCs fell sharply from 71% in the 15th Lok Sabha to ~16% in the 17th Lok Sabha (PRS data) - though the 18th Lok Sabha shows some renewal, with the Waqf (Amendment) Bill and Simultaneous Elections Bills referred to Joint Parliamentary Committees
Absence of Mandatory Referral
No constitutional or legal requirement to refer Bills to DRSCs.

rows.text: Lack of Teeth
Recommendations are advisory and not binding on the government. Ministries do not always implement recommendations or ATRs effectively.
Dependence on Bureaucracy Chronic Absenteeism Short Tenure & Frequent Rotation

Committees often rely on information supplied by the same ministries they scrutinise. Lack of dedicated professional researchers and domain experts. Low attendance affects deliberative quality and effectiveness. One-year tenure limits institutional memory and subject specialisation.
Executive Dominance Limited Public Visibility
Strong parliamentary majorities can reduce responsiveness to committee observations. Committee reports receive relatively little media and public attention.

elements.text: 21.5 Parliamentary Committees International Comparison

rows.text: Country
Structure and Membership
Roles and operations
United Kingdom United States
Types: Select, Joint, General, and Grant Committees. Size: 10 to 50 members. Types: Senate, House, Joint, and sub-committees. Size: Senate (7–30 members), House (9–62 members).

Roles: Report on departments, scrutinise proposed laws, and handle regional questions (Scotland, Wales, and North Ireland). Operations: Allow public hearings and televised meetings. elements.text: 21.6 Issues and Proposed Reforms
To transform Parliamentary Committees from "advisory bodies" to true "engines of accountability", critical structural reforms are necessary.
Challenge Way Forward
Short, Non-Renewable Tenure Limits Expertise
• Members' tenure is currently just 1 year, preventing MPs from developing deep domain mastery

before rotation.
• Increase tenure to 2–3 years with continuity of membership, ensuring institutional memory
and specialization (2nd ARC)
No Public/Stakeholder Consultation Mechanism
• Institutionalize a systematic public hearing mechanism, including publishing executive
summaries of Bills in regional languages, to widen the base of stakeholder feedback beyond invited experts alone. - 2nd ARC
No Post-Enactment Review of Laws
• Mandate post-implementation legislative impact assessments (e.g., 5 years after enactment)
so committees evaluate real-world outcomes of laws, not just pre-passage drafting quality -closing the loop between scrutiny and consequence. -2nd ARC
Executive Bypasses Committees via Voice-Vote Passage
• Several Bills with major civil-liberties implications - e.g., the UAPA (Amendment) Act, 2019

and RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 - were passed without DRSC reference.
• Amend House Rules of Procedure to mandate referral of all non-Money Bills unless the
presiding officer records specific, publicly stated reasons for exemption (converting an unwritten convention into an enforceable procedural rule).- PRS Legislative Research
Low Parliamentary Sitting Days Reduce Committee-Floor Linkage
• NCRWC recommended a constitutionally/statutorily mandated minimum of 120 sitting
days for Lok Sabha and 100 for Rajya Sabha - more sitting days create more legislative business requiring committee-stage scrutiny, and more floor time to debate committee reports and ATRs.
Committees Lack Coercive Power to Compel Testimony
• NCRWC recommended strengthening committees' powers to summon officials and enforce
attendance, since currently non-cooperation by ministries/officials faces limited real consequence.
No Institutionalized Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy
• India already has a 2014 Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy requiring draft Bills to be

published for public feedback for a minimum period before introduction - but compliance is inconsistent.
• Make this policy legally binding (not merely an executive guideline) with judicial review
available for non-compliance.
Weak Research Infrastructure for MPs
• Provide additional budgetary support to LARRDIS (Library and Reference, Research,

Documentation and Information Service) so DRSCs can employ dedicated subject-matter research staff - mirroring the House of Commons Library model in the UK, where select committees have permanent specialist staff independent of the civil service.
Opaque Committee Proceedings Reduce Public Accountability
• Televise select committee hearings (excluding sensitive national security/defence matters),
similar to televised US Congressional committee hearings, to build public accountability pressure without compromising the benefits of in-camera deliberation on genuinely sensitive matters.
No "Opposition Day" or Dedicated Oversight Agenda-Setting Time
• Introduce a Westminster-style "Opposition Day" - designated sitting days where the
Opposition sets the floor agenda - allowing structured escalation of unresolved committee findings to full House debate, rather than committee reports simply being tabled and forgotten.

The Department-Related Standing Committees were designed to act as the institutional bulwark against executive overreach, keeping the administration perennially on its toes. However, their increasing marginalisation through bypassed referrals and chronic absenteeism threatens to reduce them to paper tigers.

To restore reverence for parliamentary control, it is imperative to mandate pre-legislative scrutiny, ensuring that Parliament remains a rigorous deliberative democracy rather than a mere majoritarian clearinghouse.
Disqualification of Members of Parliament (MPs)
In the Indian constitutional scheme, the disqualification of an MP is primarily governed by three frameworks to ensure legislative probity and political stability:

1. Constitutional Provisions (Article 102(1))
2. Statutory Provisions (The Representation of the People Act, 1951)
3. Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule / Article 102(2))
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. The role of individual MPs (Members of Parliament) has diminished over the years and
as a result healthy constructive debates on policy issues are not usually witnessed.
How far can this be attributed to the anti-defection law which was legislated but with a
different intention? (2013)
Constitutional Grounds (Article 102(1))
The Constitution lists fundamental grounds under which a person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member of either House of Parliament.
• Office of Profit: If they hold any office of profit under the Union or State government (other than an office exempted by Parliament by law).
• Unsound Mind: If they are of unsound mind and stand so declared by a competent court.
• Undischarged Insolvent: If they are an undischarged insolvent (financially bankrupt).

• Citizenship Issues: If they are not a citizen of India, or have voluntarily acquired the citizenship of a foreign State, or are under any acknowledgement of allegiance or adherence to a foreign State.
• Parliamentary Law: If they are disqualified by or under any law made by Parliament (this paved the way for the RPA, 1951).

elements.text: 22.1 Tenth Schedule

The Tenth Schedule was inserted into the Constitution by the 52nd Amendment Act (1985) to combat the evil of political defections ("Aya Ram Gaya Ram" syndrome) that caused extreme instability in governments.

It aims to ensure that legislators remain loyal to the party ticket on which they were elected, thereby honouring the voters' mandate. It was later modified by the 91st Amendment Act (2003) to plug certain loopholes.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. The role of individual MPs (Members of Parliament) has diminished over the years and
as a result healthy constructive debates on policy issues are not usually witnessed.
How far can this be attributed to the anti-defection law which was legislated but with a
different intention? (2013)
Who Gets Disqualified and How?

rows.text: Category
Provision / Rule Explanation
Grounds: Political Party Members

1. Voluntarily Giving Up Membership Disqualified if a member formally resigns from their party.
• Judicial Stance: The Supreme Court has ruled that "voluntarily giving up" can be inferred from conduct (e.g., publicly campaigning for a rival party or attending opposition rallies) even without a formal resignation letter.
2. Defying the Party Whip Disqualified if a member votes or abstains from voting in the House contrary to the directions (whip) issued by their political party.
• Exception: The disqualification does not apply if the member obtained prior permission or if the party condones the act within 15 days.
Grounds: Independent Members Grounds: Nominated Members

Joining a Party An independently elected member becomes disqualified if they join any political party after the election. Joining a Party After 6 Months A nominated member (e.g., to the Rajya Sabha) is allowed to join a political party within the first six months of taking their seat. They are disqualified if they join a party after the expiry of six months.
Exceptions (No Disqualification)

1. Merger of Parties A member is not disqualified if their original political party merges with another party, provided that at least two-thirds (2/3rds) of the members of the legislature party agree to the merger.
• (Note: The 91st Amendment Act, 2003, deleted the earlier provision that allowed an exemption for a "split" by 1/3rd of the members).
2. Presiding Officers A member elected as the Presiding Officer (Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman, or Deputy Chairman) is exempted if they voluntarily give up their party membership to maintain neutrality and rejoin the party after ceasing to hold that office.
Procedure & Authority
Deciding Authority The Presiding Officer of the House takes the final decision on defection petitions.

Initiation of Process The Presiding Officer cannot take suo motu (on their own) action. The defection process is initiated only when another member of the House submits a petition regarding the defection.
Scope of Judicial Intervention Consequences of Defection

The Tenth Schedule originally barred court intervention. The SC struck this down, allowing Judicial Review of the Speaker's decision on grounds of mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice.
• Limitation: Courts cannot intervene before the Presiding Officer gives a final decision. The 91st Amendment Act (2003) A disqualified defector is subject to severe constitutional penalties until they get re-elected:
• Article 75(1B) / 164(1B): Cannot be appointed as a Minister at the Centre or in the States.
• Article 361B: Cannot hold any remunerative political post (e.g., Chairman of a Board/Corporation with a government salary).

22.2 Judicial Evolution and Landmark Judgements
Landmark Case SC’s Ruling/Impact
Kihoto Hollohan vs. Zachillhu (1992)
The Bedrock Judgement.

1. Upheld the constitutional validity of the 10th Schedule.
2. Ruled that the Speaker acts as a "Tribunal" while deciding cases.
3. Consequently, the Speaker's decision is subject to Judicial Review (on grounds of mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice).
Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020)
The "Independent Tribunal" Fix.
• Noted that Speakers are acting partisanly. The SC recommended Parliament amend the

Constitution to strip the Speaker of this power and vest it in an Independent Permanent Tribunal headed by a retired SC/HC judge.
• It also ruled that Speakers must decide disqualification petitions within a "reasonable time"
(ideally 3 months).
Subhash Desai vs. Principal Secy (2023) (Maharashtra Crisis)

The "Whip" Clarification. The SC ruled that the "Whip" must be appointed by the Political Party, not just the Legislature Party (the group of MLAs). An internal faction cannot arbitrarily appoint its own whip to claim a merger or split.
22.3 How the Law is Bypassed & Misused
Despite the law, political engineering continues unabated. The 10th Schedule has largely failed to prevent defections while successfully destroying intra-party democracy.
Issue Description
The "Resign & Re-elect" Circumvention

• Instead of defecting and facing disqualification, MLAs are induced to simply resign from the House.
• This lowers the total strength of the House, causing the ruling government to fail the floor test. The
resigned MLAs then immediately fight by-elections on the new ruling party's ticket.
The Tyranny of the Whip

• The law forces legislators to vote exactly as the party bosses dictate on every single bill.
• Impact: It has reduced MPs/MLAs to mere "headcounts". They cannot vote according to their
conscience or the specific interests of their constituency, killing 'Deliberative Democracy'.
Delay in Decision Making by Speaker

• The Tenth Schedule sets no time limit for the Speaker to decide a disqualification petition.
• Speakers deliberately sit on petitions against defectors who joined the ruling party until the assembly's
term naturally expires.
The "Merger" Fiction
• The 2/3rd exception assumes that mass defections represent an ideological shift rather than greed. In
reality, it simply means "retail defection is illegal, but wholesale defection is perfectly legal."
22.4 Way Forward
To salvage the true intent of the anti-defection law, several committees have proposed concrete reforms.

• Transfer the power to decide disqualification from the Speaker to the President/Governor, who shall act strictly on the binding advice of the Election Commission of India (similar to Article 103 for holding an Office of Profit).
Curbing Whip Tyranny

Dinesh Goswami Committee & Law Commission.
• Limit the issuance of the "Whip" only to matters threatening government survival (e.g., No-Confidence Motions, Money Bills). For all other ordinary legislation, allow MPs to vote freely.
Closing the "Resignation" Loophole

2nd ARC
• Amend the Representation of the People Act (RPA). Any legislator who is disqualified or resigns mid-term should be barred from holding any ministerial post or contesting any by-election for the remainder of that assembly's tenure.

Supreme Court (Suggested in various rulings).
• SC suggested amending the 10th Schedule to legally bind the Speaker to decide defection petitions within a maximum of 3 months in the Keisham Meghachandra Singh case.
