chapters.title: The Executive - President, PM, Governor, CoM

elements.text: The Executive – President, PM, Governor, CoM
India's dual-executive structure operates at both the Union and State levels to ensure institutional synergy. While the President and
PM represent sovereign democratic will, the Governor uniquely acts as both a constitutional head and a federal link, balancing state
autonomy with national integration.
23.1 The President

Enshrined in Part V (Articles 52-62), the President of India is the Head of the State and the symbol of national solidarity. By adopting the Westminster model, the Constitution deliberately designed the Presidency not as an independent centre of power (like the US President), but as a de jure head. The President embodies the sovereign dignity of the State, while the real executive machinery is driven by the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. Compare and contrast the President’s power to pardon in India and in the USA. Are
there any limits to it in both countries? What are ‘preemptive pardons’? (2025)
23.1.1 The Evolution of Article 74 (Aid and Advise)
Constitutional Phase Impact
Original Constitution (1950)

• Article 74: "There shall be a CoM with the PM at the head to aid and advise the President."
• Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974): The SC ruled that the President is merely a

formal head and must act on the advice of the CoM in almost all matters.
• Ambiguity: It did not explicitly state whether this advice was legally binding.
The 42nd Amendment (1976)
• Article 74 was amended to explicitly state that the President shall act in accordance with

such advice.
• Impact: Legally stripped the President of any Constitutional wiggle room.
• Cemented the absolute supremacy of the Executive over the de jure head during the
Emergency.
The 44th Amendment (1978)
• Added a crucial proviso: The President can require the CoM to reconsider such advice

once. If sent back, the President must accept it.
• Impact: Empowered the President to act as a "Constitutional Brake". Returning advice

sends a powerful, public moral message against hasty or unconstitutional executive actions.
• Example (1997): President K.R. Narayanan returned the Gujral cabinet's advice to impose
President's Rule in UP. The cabinet reconsidered and dropped the move.
23.1.2 Discretionary Powers (Situational)

rows.text: Situational Vacuum
The President's Action Conventions / Guiding Principles
Hung Parliament (No party has a clear majority in Lok Sabha) Loss of Confidence

Discretion to appoint the Prime Minister. The President must find a leader capable of commanding a stable majority. Sarkaria Commission Guidelines:
1. Pre-poll alliance leader.
2. Largest single party making a claim with others.
3. Post-electoral coalition. Discretion to dismiss the Council of Ministers if they lose the majority in the Lok Sabha and refuse to resign. Prevents an illegitimate government from clinging to power.
Dissolution of Lok Sabha

Discretion to dissolve the Lok Sabha if a government loses its majority and no alternative government can be formed. If a PM who has already lost majority advises dissolution, the President is not bound by that advice and can explore other government formations.

elements.text: 23.1.3 The Pardoning Power and the Delay Debate

Under Article 72, the President has the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment. This is not an act of private grace but an act of Constitutional duty performed on the "aid and advice" of the council of ministers mainly through the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).

The Core Issue: Presidents have historically kept mercy petitions pending for years (sometimes over a decade). This delay has triggered a massive debate on whether a constitutional time limit must be imposed.
Arguments FOR Specifying a Time Limit
Arguments AGAINST Specifying a Time Limit
(Why delay is a denial of justice)
(Why a rigid clock is dangerous)
Violation of Article 21 (Right to Life): Keeping a convict in constant suspense about their execution is a form of psychological torture, internationally recognised as the "Death Row Phenomenon".

Complexity of Scrutiny: The President acts as the absolute last resort to correct judicial errors. Imposing a strict deadline might force the MHA to hurriedly process files, leading to a hasty, mechanical rejection of mercy, defeating the very purpose of Article 72.

Defeats the Purpose of Justice: Penology states that punishment should be swift to be an effective deterrent. An unexplained delay of 8-10 years mocks the criminal justice system and erodes public faith.

Executive Prerogative: The power under Article 72 is an executive clemency dependent on political, social, and national security inputs (gathered by various ministries), which take time to compile. A rigid constitutional clock undermines this executive flexibility.
Political Motives: Delay is often not due to complex scrutiny but political expediency. Governments delay deciding on high-profile terrorists or political assassins to avoid electoral backlash.

The Supreme Court's Solution: The SC has already provided a judicial remedy. Fixing a time limit in the Constitution is unnecessary when the judiciary has empowered itself to commute sentences if the delay is deemed unreasonable.
The Supreme Court's Interventions:

1. Shatrughan Chouhan vs Union of India (2014): The Supreme Court ruled that an inordinate and unexplained delay by the President in deciding mercy petitions causes excruciating mental agony, violating Article 21. Therefore, such delay is a valid ground for the Supreme Court to commute the death sentence to life imprisonment.
2. Epuru Sudhakar Case (2006): The SC ruled that the President's pardoning power is not absolute and is subject to Judicial Review if exercised with mala fide intent or on political grounds.
3. Kehar Singh v. Union of India (1989): The Supreme Court addressed whether the President's rejection of a mercy petition is open to judicial review.

a. While the Court reaffirmed that it can review the President's decision to ensure it doesn't violate constitutional bounds (as established in Maru Ram), it clarified that the President is not a higher appellate court. b. The President can examine the evidence and form a different conclusion on the merits of a case, but the executive clemency process cannot be transformed into a judicial retrial.
4. Maru Ram v. Union of India (1980): The Supreme Court ruled that the President's (Article 72) and Governors' (Article 161) powers of pardon and remission are not absolute, unfettered personal discretions.

a. They must be exercised with the aid and advice of the federal or state Council of Ministers. b. Furthermore, these executive powers remain subject to judicial review to prevent arbitrary or irrational decisions.
23.1.4 Veto Powers of the President (Article 111 & 201)
The Veto power is not designed to make the President a dictator but rather to prevent hasty, ill-considered legislation and to stop unconstitutional bills from becoming law.

rows.text: Type of Veto
Scope & Constitutional Limitations
Significance & Examples
Absolute Veto Suspensive Veto Pocket Veto

• Withholding assent completely, causing the bill to die.
• Limits: Used for Private Member Bills OR if the cabinet resigns after passing the bill but before the President signs it (and the new cabinet advises withholding assent).
• Returning an ordinary bill for reconsideration. If Parliament passes it again (with or without amendments), the President must sign it.
• Limits: Cannot be used for Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills (24th Amendment Act made assent mandatory for the latter).
• The Constitution sets no time limit for the President to decide. They can simply keep the bill pending indefinitely.
• Limits: The US President has a 10-day limit; the Indian President's pocket is "larger".

• Significance: Prevents legislation that does not have the backing of the current executive.
• Example: Dr. Rajendra Prasad withheld assent to the PEPSU Appropriation Bill (1954) because President's Rule was revoked before he could sign it.
• Significance: Acts as a moral and political brake. Returning a bill forces a public debate and forces the government to rethink.
• Example: APJ Abdul Kalam returned the Office of Profit Bill (2006).
• Significance: A massive silent weapon against controversial legislation that threatens fundamental rights.
• Example: Gyani Zail Singh used the pocket veto on the controversial Indian Post Office Amendment Bill (1986), which threatened press freedom.
The Federal Veto (Article 201 - State Bills)

• Under Article 200, a Governor can reserve a state bill for the President's consideration.
• Under Article 201, the President can direct the Governor to return the bill. However, even if the State Assembly passes it a second time, the President is NOT bound to give assent.

• Acts as a Union check on Unconstitutional state laws.
• Federal Friction: The Union Executive exercises veto over state legislatures, often delaying assent indefinitely (e.g., NEET exemption bills).

elements.text: Comparison of Pardon Powers: India vs. USA
Features Indian President USA President
Constitutional Source
Article 72 of the Indian Constitution. Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution.
Jurisdiction Applies to offenses under Union law, court-martial sentences, and all death sentences.
Applies strictly to federal offenses against the United States.
State Offenses & Death Penalty
Can pardon death sentences even if imposed under State laws.
Cannot pardon state crimes; this power operates upon offenses against the United States as distinguished from offenses against the states.
Executive Discretion
Bound by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.
Exercises independent and plenary authority.
Judicial Review
Subject to limited judicial review for arbitrariness, mala fide intent, or improper considerations.
Generally not subject to legislative control, and Congress cannot substantively constrain the President's pardon authority through legislation.
Limits
• Impeachment Exception: The U.S.
• The President is bound by the advice of the Council

of Ministers and cannot exercise pardon powers independently (Maru Ram v. Union of India, 1981).
• Pardon decisions are subject to limited judicial

President cannot grant pardons in impeachment cases.
• Federal Jurisdiction Only: Pardon
review if found arbitrary, mala fide, or based on irrelevant considerations (Epuru Sudhakar v. Govt. of A.P., 2006).
power applies only to federal offences, not state crimes.
Preemptive Pardons: A preemptive pardon is an act of clemency issued by a head of state before any trial, conviction, or formal judgment takes place.
Application in the USA:
• Preemptive pardons are legally recognized and constitutionally permitted in the United States for past actions.
• In the 1866 case Ex parte Garland, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that a pardon may be exercised either before legal proceedings are taken, during their pendency, or after conviction and judgment.
Application in India:
• Preemptive pardons are not permitted under the Indian constitutional framework.
• Under Article 72, the constitutional language explicitly states that the President has the power to grant pardons to any person "convicted of any offence".
• This specific phrasing mandates that a formal legal process must conclude and result in a conviction before a pardon can be legally granted.
23.1.5 Ordinance-Making Power (Article 123)
Article 123 grants the President the power to promulgate Ordinances during the recess of Parliament. This is the most extraordinary
power, as it vests legislative authority in the Executive.
1. Constitutional Scope and Limitations
• Condition: Can only be promulgated when either one House or both Houses of Parliament are not in session.
• Rationale: To handle "unforeseen emergencies" that require immediate action when Parliament cannot deliberate.
• Co-extensive Power: An ordinance can only be issued on subjects Parliament can legislate on, and it is subject to the
same constitutional limitations (it cannot violate Fundamental Rights).
• Lifespan: Must be approved by Parliament within 6 weeks of its reassembly. The maximum theoretical life is 6 months
+ 6 weeks.
Ordinances were meant to be an exception, but they are frequently used as a routine tool to bypass parliamentary debate, bypassing
the Rajya Sabha or escaping opposition scrutiny.
Landmark Case Key Constitutional Principle Established
R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) (Bank Nationalization Case)
• Judicial Review of Intent: The Supreme Court ruled that the President's decision to

promulgate an ordinance is not absolute.
• If an ordinance is passed in a circumstance that clearly does not require 'immediate action', it
can be challenged in a court of law to test its constitutionality and check for mala fide intent.
44th Constitutional Amendment Act (1978)
• Legislative Affirmation: Reaffirmed the R.C. Cooper stance. It clarified that the satisfaction of
the President (Article 123) and Governor (Article 213) to issue an ordinance is subject to judicial review and is not final or conclusive.
Dr. D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987)
• Fraud on the Constitution: The Court struck down the practice of "mechanical re-
promulgation" of ordinances without seeking the legislature's approval. It ruled that bypassing the legislature is unconstitutional unless there is a genuine emergency or extreme paucity of time.
Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017) (7-Judge Constitution Bench)
Mandatory Legislative Oversight:
• It is absolutely mandatory to place the ordinance before the Legislature; failure to do so is a

constitutional infraction.
• Enduring Rights Theory: If an ordinance lapses or ceases to operate, any act, right, privilege,

or liability created by it will only survive if it passes three strict tests:
1. The effect of the ordinance is completely irreversible.
2. Reversing the consequences of the ordinance is highly impractical.
3. There is a compelling public interest to continue the effect of the ordinance.
Ordinance-Making Power: President vs Governor
Dimension President (Article 123) Governor (Article 213)
Legislative Recess
Can promulgate an ordinance when either one or both Houses of Parliament are not in session.
Can promulgate an ordinance when the Legislative Assembly (or both Houses in a bicameral legislature) are not in session.
Condition Immediate action must be necessary. Immediate action must be necessary.
Legislative Scope
Can legislate only on subjects within Parliament's legislative competence.
Can legislate only on subjects within the State Legislature's competence.
Legal Status Has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament.
Has the same force and effect as an Act of the State Legislature.
Validity Invalid if Parliament itself lacks competence to enact such a law.
Invalid if the State Legislature lacks competence to enact such a law.
Withdrawal May withdraw the ordinance at any time.
May withdraw the ordinance at any time.
Nature of Power
Exercised on the aid and advice of the Union Council of Ministers.
Exercised on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers.
Legislative Approval
Must be laid before both Houses of Parliament.
Must be laid before the State Legislature.
Duration Ceases after 6 weeks from reassembly of Parliament unless approved earlier.
Ceases after 6 weeks from the reassembly of the State Legislature unless approved earlier.
Prior Approval Requirement
Must obtain the President's instructions if a similar Bill would require Presidential sanction, reservation for the President, or Presidential assent.
No prior approval required.
Contemporary Issues

rows.text: Contemporary Issue
Example
Description
Bypassing Parliament
Three Farm Laws Ordinances (2020)
Bypassed detailed Parliamentary/Committee scrutiny; later repealed (2021), highlighting the risks of legislating without broad consensus.
Separation of Powers
Government of NCT of Delhi (Amendment) Ordinance, 2023
Overturned the SC Constitution Bench verdict on Delhi Services by creating the National Capital Civil Service Authority, raising concerns over executive overreach.
Repromulgation Federal Concerns

Securities Laws (Amendment) Ordinance (2013–14), Indian Medical Council (Amendment) Ordinance (2010), Land Acquisition (Amendment) Ordinance (2014–15), Commission for Air Quality Management Ordinance (2020–21) Jammu & Kashmir Reservation (Amendment) Ordinance (2019)

Re-promulgated multiple times despite judicial censure (D.C. Wadhwa), undermining parliamentary supremacy and democratic accountability. Politically significant ordinance affecting Centre–State/UT relations, raising concerns over federal balance.
Legitimate Emergency Use
Manipur GST (Amendment) Ordinances (2025)
Used during President's Rule to ensure continuity of GST administration, illustrating that ordinances remain a valid emergency governance tool when immediate legislative action is necessary.

elements.text: 23.1.6 Procedure for Impeachment of the President (Article 61)
Aspect Details
Ground for Removal Violation of the Constitution’ (Note: The term is nowhere defined in the Constitution).
Initiation Can be initiated by either House of the Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha).
Notice Period A 14-day advance notice must be given to the President.
Condition for Notice The resolution containing charges must be signed by at least 1/4th members of the initiating House.
Passage in First House Requires a special majority: 2/3rd of the total membership of that House.
Role of Second House Acts as the investigating body. Investigates the charges or constitutes a committee to do so. The President has the right to appear and defend themselves.
Final Passage & Removal
If the Second House sustains the charges and passes the resolution by 2/3rd of its total membership, the President stands impeached from that date.

Ultimately, the Indian President is not a mere titular head but the indispensable 'conscience-keeper' of the Constitution. By balancing executive advice with moral authority, the office acts as a vital brake against hasty governance. Moving forward, the Presidency remains the ultimate symbol of national unity and democratic resilience, ensuring that India's governance is continuously guided by constitutional propriety rather than mere political expediency.
23.1.7 Vice President

Modelled broadly on the American lines, the office of the Vice-President (Article 63) is the second-highest constitutional office in India. However, unlike the US Vice-President who ascends to the Presidency for the unexpired term if the office falls vacant, the Indian Vice-President merely acts as a temporary stopgap.

The true, everyday essence of this office lies in Article 64, which mandates the Vice-President to act as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, serving as the custodian of dignity and federal debate in the Upper House.

rows.text: Aspect
Details
Value Addition
Electoral College
Consists of all members of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha (both elected and nominated). MLAs are not included.

Constitutional Rationale (Dr Ambedkar): The President represents the whole nation (hence MLAs vote), but the VP's primary role is presiding over the Council of States. Thus, only Parliament’s mandate is required. Comparison: Unlike the President's election, nominated MPs participate here.
System of Election Qualifications
Proportional Representation (PR) by means of a Single Transferable Vote (STV) via Secret Ballot. Citizen of India, 35+ years of age, eligible for Rajya Sabha, no Office of Profit.

Analytical Insight: Ensures the winner has an absolute majority (consensus) rather than just a relative majority (as in First-Past-The-Post). The secret ballot ensures MPs vote on conscience, not party lines. Why Rajya Sabha eligibility? Because the VP serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Exception: Sitting President, VP, Governors, and Ministers are legally exempt from the "Office of Profit" disqualification.
Value of Votes
Every MP's vote has the same value: 1.
Comparison: In the Presidential election, an MP's vote value is derived from the total population of States, reflecting federal parity. For the VP, it is a straightforward parliamentary parity.
Nomination & Deposit
Requires 20 Proposers and 20 Seconders. Security deposit of ₹15,000 (forfeited if less than 1/6th of votes are secured).

Democratic Check: Increased from earlier numbers (5 proposers/ seconders) via amendment to the 1952 Act to deter non-serious, frivolous candidates and maintain the dignity of the constitutional office.
Whip & Defection Law Winning Quota
Political parties cannot issue whips. The Anti-Defection Law (10th Schedule) does not apply.

Upholds the independence of the Constitutional mechanism. It ensures the election is driven by the candidate's stature and cross-party acceptability, immune from partisan disciplinary action. Significance: In a fractured parliament, this quota forces political parties to build consensus and alliances, preventing a polarised or minority-supported candidate from winning.

elements.text: Election Disputes

Constitutional Safeguard (Article 71): Vests exclusive original jurisdiction in the Supreme Court. 11th Amendment Act (1961): Crucially established that the VP's election cannot be challenged on the ground of any vacancy in the electoral college (e.g., if a Lok Sabha seat is vacant).
Challenged only in the Supreme Court by a candidate or 10+ electors, within 30 days of the result.
Term & Vacancy

Constitutional Gap vs. the US: Unlike the US Vice-President who automatically becomes President for the remainder of the term if the office falls vacant, the Indian VP merely acts as President for a maximum of 6 months until a new President is elected.
5-year term. Continues to hold office until a successor takes over. No formal line of succession.
Role of the Vice President as Chairman of Rajya Sabha

elements.caption: The Executive - President, PM, Governor, CoM — illustration

elements.text: 23.2. Prime Minister

While Article 52 vests the executive power in the President, Articles 74, 75, and 78 establish the Prime Minister as the real, de facto executive of the Indian Republic. The framers of the Constitution envisioned the PM as primus inter pares (first among equals) within the Cabinet. However, the Prime Minister is not merely a coordinator; they are the central gravitational force of the government.

elements.caption: The Executive - President, PM, Governor, CoM — illustration

elements.text: 23.2.1 Presidentialisation of Indian PM
The Core Debate: Is the shift toward a highly centralised, personality-driven executive a necessary evolution for modern governance or a dangerous erosion of India's parliamentary democracy?
Evaluating the Presidentialisation of the PM
Dimension of Governance
Arguments FOR Presidentialisation (The Benefits / Administrative Necessity)
Arguments AGAINST Presidentialisation
(The Democratic Deficits)
Executive Decisiveness vs. Deliberative Governance

FOR: A strong, dominant PM ends "Policy Paralysis." Complex modern challenges (like national security or economic reforms) require swift, decisive action. A highly centralised executive cuts through bureaucratic red tape and inter-departmental turf wars.

AGAINST: It dilutes "Collective Responsibility." The Cabinet is reduced from a supreme deliberative body to an executive rubber stamp. Sweeping national decisions are taken unilaterally by a tight inner circle, bypassing rigorous multi-stakeholder scrutiny.
Electoral Clarity vs. Erosion of the MP's Role

FOR: It provides the electorate with a clear, identifiable national leader, ensuring a decisive political mandate and government stability (curing the instability of the 1990s coalition era). Voters know exactly who is in charge of the nation's trajectory.

AGAINST: It turns general elections into a "Personality Cult" plebiscite. Local constituency issues are completely ignored, and MPs are reduced to mere "ticket-holders" of the PM's brand, destroying their independent legislative relevance.
Institutional Synergy vs. The Unaccountable PMO

FOR: The rise of the PMO as a "Super-Cabinet" is a modern administrative necessity. It provides vital inter-ministerial coordination and fast-tracks national infrastructure projects that a fragmented Cabinet finds difficult to efficiently manage.

AGAINST: It shifts policy-making power from elected Cabinet Ministers to unelected bureaucrats within the PMO. Because PMO officials are generally shielded from direct parliamentary questioning, it severely undermines the daily accountability of the executive to the legislature.
Global Diplomacy vs Centralisation of Credit

FOR: In a highly globalised world, foreign policy is universally centralised around the Head of Government. A "Presidential" PM projects a strong, unified national image on the global stage, crucial for strategic negotiations.

AGAINST: It leads to an extreme "centralisation of credit". All welfare schemes and government achievements are heavily branded around the PM’s individual persona, bypassing traditional party structures and creating a patron-client relationship with voters.

The 'presidentialisation' of the Indian Prime Minister reflects the complex demands of 21st-century governance, where electoral stability and rapid executive decisiveness are highly prized. However, this efficiency must not come at the cost of constitutional checks and balances. To ensure the survival of true parliamentary democracy, a delicate institutional equilibrium must be restored: the Prime Minister must utilise the PMO as a strategic facilitator while actively reviving the Cabinet as the supreme, rigorous deliberative body it was constitutionally envisioned to be.
23.3 The Council of Ministers
India's Westminster model replicates the exact same parliamentary structure at the Union and State levels, with one massive constitutional exception regarding discretionary power.
Feature Union State Analytical Difference
Aid and Advice
Article 74: There shall be a CoM with the PM at the head to aid and advise the President. The President shall act in accordance with such advice.
Article 163: There shall be a CoM with the CM at the head to aid and advise the Governor, except in so far as he is required to exercise his functions in his discretion.

The Exception: The Constitution explicitly grants discretionary power to the Governor, but NOT to the President. If a conflict arises on whether a matter falls under discretion, the Governor's decision is final.
Appointment and responsibility
Article 75: PM is appointed by President; other Ministers appointed by President on PM's advice. CoM is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
Article 164: CM is appointed by Governor; other Ministers appointed by Governor on CM's advice. CoM is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha).
(Identical Principle) At both levels, the executive is daily accountable to the directly elected lower house.
Duty to Communicate
Article 78: It is the duty of the PM to communicate all decisions of the CoM relating to administration and legislation to the President.
Article 167: It is the duty of the CM to communicate all decisions of the CoM relating to administration and legislation to the Governor.
The Link: The PM/CM acts as the principal Constitutional channel between the titular Head of State and the real executive machinery.
Strength
Article 75(1A): Specifically mandates the 15% maximum limit based on the total strength of the Lok Sabha
Article 164(1A): Specifically mandates the 15% maximum limit (based on the Legislative Assembly's strength) and the 12-member minimum limit
Identical principles at both levels. This ceiling is enforced by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003.
23.4 Has the Cabinet Marginalised Parliament?

In the classical Westminster model, Parliament is supreme and holds the Cabinet accountable. However, modern political realities have inverted this relationship, leading to what constitutional expert Ramsay Muir called "Cabinet Dictatorship".
Mechanisms of Marginalization
The Retained Supremacy (How Parliament still fights back)
(How the Cabinet Dominates)

The Tyranny of the Whip (10th Schedule): The Cabinet decides the policy, issues a whip, and MPs are generally expected to follow the party whip on important votes, and defiance may attract disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.

The Ultimate Sanction: The Cabinet survives only as long as it enjoys the confidence of the Lok Sabha. A no-confidence motion remains the ultimate weapon of parliamentary supremacy (e.g., the fall of the government in 1999).

Control over the Legislative Agenda: The Cabinet dictates when Parliament meets, what bills are introduced, and how much time is allotted. Controversial bills are frequently passed via the "Guillotine". Critics have argued that some legislation has been classified as Money Bills to reduce Rajya Sabha scrutiny.

Committee Scrutiny: While the floor of the House is dominated by the Cabinet, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and DRSCs require ministries and senior officials to explain expenditure, policies and implementation.

Ordinance Raj (Article 123): The Cabinet frequently uses the President's ordinance-making power to implement laws immediately, presenting Parliament with a fait accompli (a done deal) and bypassing prior legislative deliberation.

Question Hour & Daily Accountability: Despite disruptions, mechanisms like Question Hour, Zero Hour, and Adjournment Motions force Cabinet Ministers to publicly defend their administrative actions on a daily basis.

Delegated Legislation: Modern laws are passed by the Cabinet merely as "skeletons". The actual rules, regulations, and implementation details are crafted later by the Cabinet-controlled bureaucracy, receiving comparatively less parliamentary scrutiny than primary legislation.

Judicial Checks on Executive Aggrandisement: The Supreme Court increasingly acts as a check on the Cabinet's attempts to bypass Parliament (e.g., striking down repeated ordinances in Krishna Kumar Singh,
2017).

The growing centralisation of executive power has undoubtedly enhanced decisiveness and administrative efficiency, but it also raises concerns about weakening collective responsibility, Cabinet government, and parliamentary accountability. The constitutional challenge is to preserve an effective executive while reinforcing institutional checks, ensuring that efficiency operates within the framework of constitutional morality and parliamentary democracy.
23.5 Governor

Enshrined in Part VI (Articles 153-167), the Governor is designed to be the titular head of the state executive. Unlike the President, the Governor is not elected but appointed by the Union. This creates a highly complex Dual Role:

1. The Constitutional Head of the State: Bound by the 'aid and advice' of the State Council of Ministers (Article 163).
2. The Federal Sentinel (Link to the Centre): Acting as the Union's representative to ensure the state government functions strictly within the bounds of the Constitution (Article 355/356). The conflict arises when the "Federal Sentinel" begins acting as the "Political Agent" of the ruling party at the Centre.

elements.caption: The Executive - President, PM, Governor, CoM — illustration

elements.text: 23.5.1 Discretionary Powers
Unlike the President, Article 163 expressly recognises limited areas where the Governor may act at his/her discretion.

rows.text: Type of Discretion Constitutional Provision / Situation
Contemporary Misuse & Friction Points
Constitutional (Article 200) Reservation of Bills: Reserving a state bill for the President's consideration (mandatory if it threatens the High Court; discretionary for others).
Friction: Used to delay state legislation (e.g., Tamil Nadu NEET exemption bill) as the President has no time limit to decide under Article 201
Constitutional (Article 356) Report for President's Rule: Recommending the dismissal of the state government due to the failure of constitutional machinery.
Friction: Historically misused as a political weapon to topple opposition-ruled state governments (largely curbed post-SR Bommai judgement).

Situational (Hung Assembly) Appointing the Chief Minister when no party commands a clear majority in the Assembly. Situational (Floor Test) Ordering the CM to prove their majority on the floor of the House if the Governor feels the government has lost confidence Constitutional (Sixth Schedule) Governor enjoys special discretionary responsibilities in certain tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

Friction: A partisan description. Governors have frequently ignored the single largest party or pre-poll alliance and invited the ruling party to form the government (e.g., the Goa and Karnataka government formations). Friction: Disputes often arise regarding the timing and circumstances under which Governors direct floor tests, particularly during periods of political instability and defections. Debate over balancing tribal autonomy with democratic accountability.

elements.text: 23.5.2 Ordinance by Governor

Under Article 213, the Governor possesses extraordinary legislative powers to promulgate ordinances. However, this is not a parallel power of legislation but a "conditional" power meant strictly for unforeseen emergencies.
Essential Conditions for Promulgating an Ordinance
Condition Description
Absence of Session Can only be promulgated when the Legislative Assembly (or both Houses, in bicameral states) is not in session.
Subjective Satisfaction

The Governor must be "satisfied" that circumstances exist rendering immediate action necessary. (Note: This satisfaction is based on the aid and advice of the CoM, which is not completely immune from judicial review.).
Co-extensive Jurisdiction
Ordinances can only be issued on subjects the State Legislature is competent to make laws on (State List and Concurrent List).
Presidential Restraint

The Governor cannot issue an ordinance without prior instructions from the President if a similar Bill would have required the President’s previous sanction (e.g., affecting inter-state trade) or if the Governor would have deemed it necessary to reserve it under Article 200 (e.g., affecting the High Court).
23.5.3 Evaluating the Governor: Roles, Issues and Institutional Fixes

rows.text: Role
Contemporary Issue
Supreme Court Intervention
The Way Forward
Appointment & Tenure (Articles 155 & 156) Appointed by the Centre; serves during the "pleasure of the President."
Partisan Appointments & Arbitrary Removal: Politicians aligned with the Centre are appointed. Regimes frequently dismiss Governors arbitrarily upon coming to power at the Centre.
B.P. Singhal Case (2010): The SC ruled that the "pleasure doctrine" is not absolute. A Governor cannot be removed arbitrarily, capriciously, or merely because the Centre's ruling party changed.

Sarkaria Commission: Must be an eminent person from outside the state; CM must be consulted. Punchhi Commission: Give them a fixed 5-year tenure with their removal based on an impartial process rather than the discretion of the Central Government.

elements.text: Government Formation (Article 164 -Situational Discretion) Appoints the CM when there is a hung assembly.
Partisan Discretion: Ignoring pre-poll alliances to invite the Centre's ruling party, thereby facilitating "Operation Lotus" (poaching MLAs).
Sarkaria Commission: Established a strict order of preference: 1. Pre-poll alliance → 2. Largest single party → 3. Post-poll coalition.
S.R. Bommai Case (1994): The SC ruled that a majority is tested only on the floor of the House, not in the subjective confines of the Raj Bhavan.
Assent to State Bills (Article 200 -Constitutional Discretion) Grant assent, return, or reserve bills for the President.

Weaponising assent to bills: Indefinitely sitting on bills passed by the assembly, effectively paralysing the elected government's legislative mandate (recently Tamil Nadu & Kerala Governors held assent to state bills).
State of Punjab vs Principal Secy (2023): The SC ruled that Governors cannot "veto" bills by sitting on them indefinitely. If they withhold assent, they must return the bill "as soon as possible".
Punchhi Commission: Amend Article 200 to establish a strict time limit of six months within which the Governor must decide on a bill.
Summoning the Assembly (Article 174) Summons/prorogues the House on the aid and advice of the CoM.
Executive Overreach: Refusing the State Cabinet's advice to summon the assembly if it is perceived to politically disadvantage the opposition.
Nabam Rebia Case (2016): The SC unequivocally ruled that the Governor cannot refuse the CM's advice to summon the House as long as the CM enjoys a majority.
Punchhi Commission: Article 163 (Discretion) is not a general power. It must be strictly limited to choices explicitly mentioned in the Constitution.
Promulgating Ordinances (Article 213)
Bypassing the Legislature: State governments using the Governor to continually re-promulgate ordinances without ever placing them before the assembly for a vote.
Krishna Kumar Singh (2017): Placing an ordinance before the legislature is a Constitutional obligation. Successive re-promulgation is a "fraud on the Constitution".
The SC in the D.C. Wadhwa case famously stated that the power to promulgate ordinances is to be used in exceptional circumstances, not as a substitute for the law-making power of the legislature.
Issuing emergency laws when the assembly is not in session.
Statutory Role as University Chancellor (By State Laws) Appointing Vice-Chancellors (VCs).
Politicisation of Education: Friction over VC appointments has led state governments to pass bills stripping the Governor of the Chancellor's role entirely.
Punchhi Commission: The Governor should not be burdened with the role of University Chancellor, as it inevitably drags the constitutional office into daily political controversies.
SC and Various High Courts rulings upheld UGC norms, but the underlying political conflict remains.

Ultimately, the Office of the Governor must transcend its contemporary misuse as a partisan proxy to reclaim its true constitutional mandate as the detached linchpin of India's cooperative federalism. By institutionalising the Punchhi Commission's safeguards - such as fixed tenures and strict timelines for legislative assent - the office can be effectively insulated from daily political friction. This will ensure the Governor functions not as a parallel power centre but as a vital, stabilising constitutional sentinel.

chapters.title: The Judiciary - Supreme Court, High Courts and Subordinate Courts

elements.text: The Judiciary - Supreme Court, High Courts and Subordinate Courts
24.1 The Supreme Court

Enshrined in Part V (Articles 124–147) of the Constitution, the Supreme Court of India stands at the apex of the country's integrated judicial system. Envisioned by the framers as the ultimate guardian of Fundamental Rights, the final interpreter of the Constitution, and the protector of its Basic Structure, it functions not merely as a court of law but as a 'sentinel on the qui vive' - the vigilant guardian of constitutional governance and the rule of law.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. Discuss the evolution of the collegium system in India. Critically examine the advantages
and disadvantages of the system of appointment of the Judges of the Supreme Court of
India and that of the USA. (2025)
2. Explain the reasons for the growth of public interest litigation in India. As a result of it,
has the Indian Supreme Court emerged as the world’s most powerful judiciary?. (2024)
3. The most significant achievement of modern law in India is the constitutionalization of
environmental problems by the Supreme Court. Discuss this statement with the help
of relevant case laws. (2022)
4. Critically examine the Supreme Court’s judgement on ‘National Judicial Appointments
Commission Act, 2014’ with reference to appointment of judges of higher judiciary in
India (2017)

elements.caption: The Judiciary - Supreme Court, High Courts and Subordinate Courts — illustration

elements.text: 24.1.1 The Multi-Faceted Jurisdiction
Type of Jurisdiction
Constitutional Scope & Articles
Why it matters
Original (Article 131)
Exclusive power to resolve federal disputes (Centre vs. State, State vs. State).
It is the ultimate federal umpire, ensuring the Constitutional balance between the Union and the States
Writ Jurisdiction (Article 32)
Power to issue writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, etc.) to enforce Fundamental Rights.
Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 the "heart and soul" of the Constitution. It makes the SC the direct guarantor of civil liberties.
Appellate (Articles 132-136)
SLP (Article 136) gives the SC extraordinary residual power to grant an appeal from any court or tribunal in India to prevent gross injustice.
Appeals in constitutional, civil, and criminal matters. Includes Special Leave Petition (SLP - Article 136).
Advisory (Article 143)
The President can seek the SC's opinion on questions of law or fact of public importance.
Acts as a pre-emptive constitutional check to avoid future legislative friction (e.g., Berubari Union Reference (1960)).
Court of Record (Article 129)
Supreme Court is a Court of Record with power to punish for contempt.
Preserves judicial authority and ensures compliance with its orders.
24.1.2 Does the Supreme Court have the right to create new laws to fill "Constitutional Silences" (gaps in the Constitution), or is that overreach?
The Battle over the Election Commission (Article 324)
The Phase Event and SC Ruling The Executive Pushback
The Constitutional Silence

Article 324 states that the Election Commissioners (ECs) shall be appointed by the President subject to any law made by Parliament. For 70 years, Parliament made no law, leaving appointments effectively under executive control through the aid-and-advice mechanism
(No pushback, Executive enjoyed the monopoly).
The Judicial Intervention

Anoop Baranwal vs. Union of India (2023): The SC ruled that leaving EC appointments solely to the executive threatens free elections. It created an interim Selection Panel (PM, Leader of Opposition, and the CJI) to appoint ECs until Parliament makes a law.
This was hailed as progressive judicial activism to secure institutional independence.
The Executive Pushback

The Current Friction: Parliament, under Article 324(2), enacted a statutory appointment framework different from the one prescribed by the Court. By replacing the CJI with a Cabinet Minister, the Executive enhanced its majority in appointing the umpires of India's elections.

Parliament quickly passed the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. It established a new panel: The PM, the LoP, and a Union Cabinet Minister (completely removing the CJI).
24.1.3 Judicial Appointments: Evolution and Friction

rows.text: Issue
Legal Reality
Impact
The Original Constitutional Design
Article 124(2): Judges shall be appointed by the President (Executive) "in consultation" with the CJI and other judges.
The framers wanted a balance. The Executive would appoint, but the Judiciary would guide, ensuring neither branch had an absolute monopoly over appointments.
The Evolution of the Collegium

Through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, and 1998), the SC re-interpreted the word "consultation" to mean "concurrence" (agreement). It created the Collegium: The CJI + 4 senior-most judges who exclusively decide appointments.

Through judicial interpretation, the Court transformed the meaning of "consultation" into judicial primacy. It grants the Judiciary a dominant role in judicial appointments, leaving the Executive with a limited consultative role.

elements.caption: The Judiciary - Supreme Court, High Courts and Subordinate Courts — illustration

elements.text: The Institutional Clash (NJAC)

The 99th Amendment (2014): Parliament passed the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) to replace the Collegium with a panel comprising the CJI, judges, Law Minister, and eminent persons. The Strike Down (2015): In the 4th Judges Case, the SC struck down NJAC, citing it threatened "judicial independence" (a basic structure).

The SC successfully insulated itself from executive packing. However, critics argued that the judgement gave insufficient weight to the near-unanimous Constitutional Amendment passed by Parliament and ratified by a majority of States.
The Core Issues with the Current Collegium

1. Opacity & Nepotism: No public secretariat and no defined criteria for selection, leading to accusations of the "Uncle Judges Syndrome" (favouritism).
2. Lack of Diversity: Severe under-representation of women, Dalits, and marginalised communities in the higher judiciary.
Operates via unwritten conventions and closed-door meetings.
Contemporary Friction

Executive Evasion: The government frequently uses an informal "pocket veto" - sitting on files of uncomfortable judges for months or selectively clearing names to disrupt the seniority of judges, contributing to judicial vacancies and concerns regarding judicial efficiency
The government cannot reject a Collegium recommendation if it is reiterated. However, there is no time limit for the government to act on the file.
The Memorandum of Procedure (MoP)
The Stalemate: Years later, the revised MoP remains unfinalised because the Government wants a "national security" clause to veto any judge, which the SC refuses to accept.
The MoP is the official rulebook for appointments. Post-NJAC, the SC and the Government agreed to draft a new MoP to induce transparency.
Judicial Independence vs Accountability
The collegium protects judicial independence by minimising executive influence
Creates a trade-off between independence and transparency/accountability

India's Collegium vs USA's Presidential Nomination System

rows.text: Aspect India’s Collegium System Core Philosophy Emphasises judicial independence and minimises executive interference in judicial appointments. Primary Appointers The Collegium recommends names, while the President formally makes the appointments → Judges are selected through the Collegium comprising the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and senior Supreme Court judges. Key Advantages Protects the judiciary from political and executive pressure, thereby safeguarding judicial independence and enabling impartial adjudication. Key Disadvantages Criticised for lack of transparency, perceived favouritism or nepotism, and delays leading to judicial vacancies. Transparency & Scrutiny Relatively low transparency; deliberations occur behind closed doors, and selection criteria are not formally codified. Accountability Limited external accountability, as appointments are primarily controlled by the judiciary itself.

USA’s Presidential Nomination System Emphasizes democratic legitimacy through a system of checks and balances between the executive and legislature. The President nominates judges, while the Senate confirms appointments through a formal approval process. Ensures democratic accountability through elected institutions and subjects nominees to legislative scrutiny before appointment. Often criticised for excessive politicisation, ideological polarisation, and partisan battles during confirmation. High transparency; nominees undergo public hearings and extensive scrutiny before the Senate Judiciary Committee. Greater accountability through oversight by elected branches, though lifetime tenure increases the long-term impact of appointments.
Diversity & Representation Concerns persist regarding adequate representation of women, SC/ST communities, minorities, and regional groups.
Greater scope for promoting demographic and social diversity through conscious nomination policies of successive Presidents.
Nature of Decision-Making Based on peer evaluation and judicial expertise within the higher judiciary.
Based on a combination of executive choice, political considerations, and legislative approval.
Constitutional Basis Evolved through the First Judges Case (1981), Second Judges Case (1993) and Third Judges Case (1998) interpretations of Articles 124 and 217.
Rooted in the Appointments Clause of the U.S. Constitution, requiring Presidential nomination and Senate consent.
Removal of Judges Parliamentary impeachment process
Congressional impeachment process
Major Criticism Seen by critics as a system of judicial overreach/ self-selection lacking transparency and accountability.
Seen by critics as excessively politicised, with ideological considerations sometimes overshadowing merit.

elements.text: Both India's Collegium system and the U.S. Presidential Nomination system embody different constitutional priorities. The Collegium emphasises judicial independence by limiting executive influence, while the U.S. model emphasises democratic accountability through public scrutiny and institutional checks.

Going forward, India would benefit from greater transparency and accountability in appointments, while the United States would benefit from reducing excessive politicisation and restoring broader bipartisan trust. A balanced combination of these strengths can help build a more resilient, diverse, and trusted judiciary.

rows.text: Judicial Independence: A Prerequisite for Democracy
Aspect Protector of Fundamental Rights Upholding Rule of Law Federal Equilibrium Safeguarding Electoral Process

WHY IT IS A PREREQUISITE (THE PHILOSOPHY) Constitutional Backing Examples / Judgements Acts as a bulwark against majoritarian tyranny, protecting individual liberties via Articles 32 & 226. Puttaswamy Case (2017): SC protected citizens' Right to Privacy against potential State overreach. Ensures constitutionalism through Judicial Review (Article 13, 32, 226, etc.), striking down arbitrary executive or legislative actions. Shreya Singhal Case (2015): SC struck down Section 66A of the IT Act to protect free speech from arbitrary police arrests. Impartially resolves disputes between the Centre and States through its Original Jurisdiction (Article 131). Kerala vs. Union of India (2020): Kerala invoked Article 131 to challenge the constitutionality of the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA). Cleanses the democratic process to ensure free, fair, and transparent elections. Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (2024): SC struck down the Electoral Bonds scheme as unconstitutional to protect the voter's right to information.

elements.text: CONSTITUTIONAL GUARANTEES (THE MECHANISM)
Security of Tenure

Justice V. Ramaswami (1993): The only SC judge to face impeachment; the motion failed, proving how strictly tenure is protected against political whims. Also, removal requires a special majority in both Houses of Parliament.
Judges can only be removed via a stringent parliamentary impeachment process (Article 124(4)).
Mode of Appointment
The Collegium System ensures the executive does not have absolute control over appointments.
Fourth Judges' Case (2015): SC struck down the 99th Amendment (NJAC), citing that executive interference in appointments violates the Basic Structure.
Financial Independence
Salaries and pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 112 (3)). - SC Article 125 (SC judges' salaries) Article 221 (HC judges' salaries)
Salaries and allowances cannot be varied to the disadvantage of judges after appointment, except during a Financial Emergency (Article 360).
Power to Punish for Contempt
Prashant Bhushan Case (2020): SC exercised this power to penalise statements deemed to lower the authority of the court.
SC and HCs are courts of record and can be punished for their contempt (Articles 129 & 215).
Conduct Cannot be Discussed
Parliament is barred from discussing the conduct of judges in the discharge of their duties (Article 121).
MPs cannot debate the merits of a judge's ruling on the floor of the House unless an impeachment motion is active.
Separation from Executive
CrPC Reforms (1973): Stripped Executive Magistrates (like Collectors) of judicial trial powers, transferring them to Judicial Magistrates.
Directive Principle mandating the State to separate the judiciary from the executive (Article 50).
Administrative Independence
Articles 146 & 229 Service conditions cannot be altered to the disadvantage of judges after appointment (except during a financial emergency).

The current deadlock over judicial appointments is a symptom of a systemic institutional trust deficit. While the Collegium protects judicial independence, its opacity breeds a severe democratic deficit. The way forward lies in finalising a revised Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) that establishes an independent, permanent secretariat for the Collegium.

elements.text: 24.1.4 Judicial Review

Judicial Review is the foundational power of the Supreme Court to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders. If they violate the Constitution (especially Part III - Fundamental Rights), they are declared ultra vires (null and void).
The Constitutional Basis: While the phrase "Judicial Review" is nowhere explicitly mentioned in the Constitution, it is deeply embedded in several articles:
• Article 13: Declares that any law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights is void.
• Articles 32 & 226: The power to issue writs for the enforcement of rights.
• Articles 131–136 (judicial powers)
• Article 141 (law declared by SC binding)
• Article 142 (complete justice)
Landmark instances of Judicial Review

rows.text: Landmark Case
What the SC Reviewed
Impact
Minerva Mills (1980)
Struck down Section 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which gave Parliament unlimited power to amend the Constitution.
Established that "Judicial Review" itself is a Basic Structure of the Constitution. Parliament cannot amend it away.
Shreya Singhal Case (2015)
Struck down Section 66A of the IT Act, which allowed police to arrest people for "offensive" online posts.
A classic review of statutory law protecting the Fundamental Right to Free Speech (Article 19) against arbitrary executive policing.
4th Judges' Case (2015)
Struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act (NJAC).
Proved that the SC will use judicial review even against a unanimous Parliamentary mandate if it threatens institutional independence.

elements.text: Contempt of Court
Definition: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, defines contempt and divides it into two categories:
• Civil Contempt: Willful disobedience to any judgement, decree, direction, or order of a court, or willful breach of an undertaking given to a court.
• Criminal Contempt: The publication of any matter or the doing of any act which scandalises the court, prejudices any judicial proceeding, or interferes with the administration of justice.
Constitutional Backing:
• Article 129: Declares the Supreme Court as a Court of Record with the power to punish for its contempt.
• Article 215: Vests similar powers in the High Courts.
• Article 142(2): Enables the Supreme Court to investigate and punish any person for its contempt to ensure complete justice.
• Article 19(2): Places "Contempt of Court" as a reasonable restriction on the Fundamental Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression under Article 19(1)(a).
The Need for Contempt Power

• Upholding Court Honour: The judiciary relies on public trust. In Pritam Lal v. The High Court of M.P., the SC held that punishing contempt is the duty of the Court to preserve the authority of courts and public confidence in the administration of justice.
• Sustaining the Rule of Law: Disobedience of court orders directly violates the Rule of Law. Thus, contempt power acts as the glue holding the basic structure of the Constitution together.
• Ensuring Equality Before Law: It acts as an equaliser, forcing powerful entities, the rich, and the executive to strictly comply with judicial orders.
• Protecting Judicial Independence: It shields judges and ongoing proceedings from undue public pressure, political interference, and media trials.

• Preserving Justice Administration: As noted in Brahma Prakash Sharma v State of UP (1954), one does not need to prove actual interference; the mere tendency to interfere with justice is sufficient to invoke contempt.
Established Defenses Against Contempt
Over the years, the law and the judiciary have evolved specific safeguards to prevent the misuse of contempt powers:

1. Fair and Accurate Reporting: Responsible media reporting of judicial proceedings (Sahara India Real Estate v. SEBI, 2012).
2. Fair Criticism: Constructive and fair criticism of judicial orders or the judiciary's functioning (PN Dua v. Shiv Shankar, 1988).
3. Truth as a Defense: Following the 2006 Amendment to the Act, truth was introduced as a valid defense, provided it is made in the public interest and is bona fide (Subramanian Swamy v. Arun Shourie, 2014).
4. Slight Harm (Section 13): The Contempt of Courts Act states that no court shall impose a penalty unless the contempt is of such a nature that it substantially interferes with the due course of justice.
The Mulgaonkar Principles (1978)

In the landmark case In Re: S. Mulgaokar (1978), the Supreme Court laid down essential principles to guide the use of contempt powers, emphasising judicial restraint to balance authority with free speech:
• Exercise of Restraint: Contempt powers should be used sparingly and only when absolutely necessary to uphold the administration of justice.
• Tolerance of Criticism: Fair, reasonable, and even outspoken criticism of the judiciary should not invite contempt proceedings.
• Avoidance of Hypersensitivity: Judges must not be overly sensitive to criticism and should maintain composure and broad shoulders in the face of public scrutiny.
• Real Threat Requirement: Contempt action is only warranted when criticism crosses the line and poses a real threat to the judicial process or public confidence.
Despite the safeguards (like those highlighted in the Law Commission's 274th Report), the power of contempt remains controversial.
Criticism Way Forward
Vague Grounds ("Scandalising the Court"): Terms like "scandalising" are highly subjective, opening the door for arbitrary use by individual judges.
Precise Definitions: Parliament should amend the Act to define contempt more precisely, removing subjective terms like "scandalising" (which the UK abolished in 2013).
Chilling Effect on Free Speech: Fear of contempt stifles legitimate criticism of the judiciary, reducing democratic accountability.
Protecting Accountability: Establish a clearer legal distinction between constructive criticism of a judge/ judgement and actual obstruction of justice.
Violation of Natural Justice: Contempt proceedings often involve the judge acting as both the victim and the adjudicator (Nemo judex in causa sua - no one should be a judge in their own cause).
Independent Review Panels: Establish an independent judicial or peer panel to review contempt cases instead of the aggrieved judge hearing the matter.
Delay in Proceedings: Contempt cases often drag on beyond the one-year limitation period, defeating the purpose of swift justice.
Strict Time Limits: Ensure strict enforcement of the one-year limitation limit and timely, expedited disposal of contempt petitions.
Outdated Global Practice: In modern democracies (like the USA and UK), public discussion and harsh criticism of the judiciary are heavily protected by free speech laws.

Adopt Global Best Practices: India should evolve its jurisprudence to support judicial dignity without gagging speech, trusting that the judiciary's authority stems from its judgements, not the fear of punishment.

elements.text: 24.1.5 Public Interest Litigation

In the late 1970s and 1980s, visionary judges like Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer and Justice P.N. Bhagwati shattered this rule, allowing any public-spirited individual or NGO to file a case on behalf of those who are socially or economically disadvantaged.
The Evolution and impact of PIL
Dimension How PIL transformed the Judiciary Key Cases
Epistolary Jurisdiction
The SC began treating ordinary letters, telegrams, and newspaper reports as formal writ petitions.
Sunil Batra Case (1978): A letter from a prisoner about the torture of a fellow inmate was treated as a PIL, revolutionising prison reforms.
Undertrials & Speedy Justice
PIL exposed the horrifying reality of poor undertrials languishing in jails for periods longer than their maximum possible sentence.
Hussainara Khatoon (1979): The first major PIL. Led to the release of 40,000 undertrials and established the Right to Speedy Trial under Article 21.
Environmental Protection
PIL allowed activists to challenge industrial pollution and deforestation on behalf of the public and future generations.
M.C. Mehta Cases: Resulted in the introduction of lead-free petrol, the protection of the Taj Mahal, and the cleaning of the Ganga.

elements.text: Evaluating the Relevancy of PILs Today
During the recent 9-judge Constitution Bench hearings on the Sabarimala issue, the Centre took an unprecedented stance: urging
the Supreme Court to entirely remove the concept of PIL. The debate centred on whether "strangers" (non-devotees) should have
the locus standi to challenge religious practices.
The Centre's Argument (Why PIL should be abolished)
The Supreme Court's Response (Why it must be retained, but cautiously)

The Access Deficit is Resolved: The original justification for PILs was poverty and illiteracy preventing access to courts. The Centre argues this has been structurally addressed through tech (e-filing) and robust statutory bodies like NALSA and DLSAs (Legal Services Authorities).

The Filtering Mechanism: Chief Justice Surya Kant clarified that the Court has evolved over the last two decades. It no longer accepts PILs blindly. It applies strict parameters to test the "real cause" and issues notices only when there is undeniable Constitutional substance.

Surrogate & Agenda-Driven Litigation: PILs have degraded into "Publicity/Private Interest Litigation." They are increasingly filed at the behest of undisclosed interests, displacing the truly aggrieved parties from the centre of Constitutional adjudication.

Grave Constitutional Issues: While acknowledging misuse, the Court maintains that certain issues transcend individual grievances. For instance, the 2018 Sabarimala verdict allowed judicial intervention in matters involving fundamental rights (like women's rights across religions), regardless of strict locus standi.

Docket Explosion: The Centre highlighted a catastrophic expansion (from 25,000 filings in 1985 to over 70,000 recently). It argued that the "exception has swallowed the rule" and operates in a factual vacuum, urging a return to ordinary principles of locus standi.

Judicial Prudence over Blanket Removal: The Court agreed that it must be highly cautious about petitioners with hidden agendas. However, instead of removing the constitutional device altogether, the solution lies in judicial self-restraint and dismissing frivolous cases at the threshold.
• Rising PIL Backlog: Parliament informed that 3,525 PILs are pending before the Supreme Court, with 698 pending for over 10 years.
 The Government admitted that there is no data on average disposal time of PILs, highlighting institutional gaps in monitoring PIL outcomes.
 M.C. Mehta Case: One of the oldest environmental PILs, filed in 1985, was finally closed in 2026 after nearly 39 years, exposing the problem of perpetual litigation.
 Long-term judicial supervision may blur the separation of powers, consume judicial resources, and contribute to mounting case pendency.
 The challenge is balancing effective enforcement of Fundamental Rights through continuing mandamus while avoiding judicial overreach and endless litigation.

The advent of Public Interest Litigation fundamentally democratised access to justice in India, breathing life into Article 21. However, as the recent Union Government submissions highlight, the proliferation of 'agenda-driven' surrogate litigation threatens to clog the Constitutional courts and displace genuine grievances. While dismantling the PIL framework entirely would be a regressive step against marginalised communities, the Supreme Court's current stance of exercising extreme 'judicial prudence' is the correct path.
24.1.6 Judicial Activism vs. Judicial Overreach
Judicial Activism: 'Judicial activism' refers to an expansive interpretation of Constitutional provisions to protect Rights and address governance gaps where other organs have failed to act.

Judicial Overreach (Adventurism): When the judiciary crosses the Constitutional boundary of the Separation of Powers and starts performing the functions of the Executive (day-to-day administration) or the Legislature (policy-making).

elements.caption: The Judiciary - Supreme Court, High Courts and Subordinate Courts — illustration

elements.text: Activism vs. Overreach
Classification Rationale for Classification Landmark Case Law / Example
Judicial Activism (Positive)
Addressing a Legislative Vacuum: There was no law protecting women from workplace harassment. The SC didn't just judge a case; it created binding laws until Parliament acted.
Vishaka vs State of Rajasthan (1997): The SC laid down the "Vishaka Guidelines", effectively creating temporary legislation to protect women's dignity (Article 21).
Judicial Activism (Positive)
Electoral Transparency: Parliament was unwilling to force politicians to declare their criminal records. The SC stepped in to protect the voter's "Right to Know" (Article 19).
ADR vs. Union of India (2002): Mandated candidates to disclose criminal, educational, and financial antecedents.
Judicial Overreach (Negative)
Encroaching on Executive Policy: Imposing blanket bans based on morality rather than constitutional law, destroying state revenues and local businesses without legislative backing.
The Highway Liquor Ban (2016): The SC invoked Article 142 to ban liquor sales within 500 metres of all national highways, crippling the hospitality sector.
Judicial Overreach (Negative)
Encroaching on the Legislature: Critics argued that the Court entered the domain of symbolic policy-making and cultural regulation by making administrative rules for private entertainment venues.
Shyam Narayan Chouksey (2016): The SC made it mandatory to play the National Anthem in cinema halls (later walked back after massive criticism of overreach).
Why is Overreach Dangerous?

1. Lack of Expertise: Judges are legal experts, not economists, environmental scientists, or urban planners. Policy decisions made from the bench often have disastrous, unforeseen economic consequences (e.g., cancelling 122 telecom licenses in the 2G case caused massive foreign investment flight).
2. No Accountability: If the Executive makes a bad policy, they can be voted out. If the SC makes a bad policy, they are completely unaccountable to the electorate, though they remain accountable through Constitutional reasoning, review jurisdiction and public scrutiny.
Does Judicial Activism Undermine Parliamentary Democracy?
Dimension Arguments: YES (It Undermines / Threatens Democracy)
Arguments: NO (It Strengthens / Upholds Democracy)
Representation vs Accountability
Unelected Nature: Judges are neither elected by the people nor directly answerable to them. Courts are not representative bodies reflecting the popular will.
Reason-Based Accountability: Judges are accountable through the reasoning in their judgements. Flawed decisions are openly criticised, set aside, or reviewed.
Separation of Powers vs Checks and Balance
Constitutional Trespass: It violates the Doctrine of Separation of Powers (Article 50). Law-making and policy formulation are the core responsibilities of the legislature and executive.
Checks and Balances: It is an inevitable response to check the arbitrary or unconstitutional exercise of public power by the State.
Governance Aspect
Lack of Technical Expertise: Courts lack the resources, data, and technical competence to draft complex economic, environmental, or administrative policies.
Filling the Governance Vacuum: When the executive/legislature are apathetic, lax, or incompetent, the judiciary must step in to protect the basic rights of citizens.
Impact on Institutions
Diminishes Institutional Respect: Frequent interventions can demoralize the bureaucracy and reduce the legislature to a secondary role.
Protects the Marginalized: Mechanisms like PILs (Public Interest Litigation) give a voice to the voiceless, ensuring constitutional promises reach the grassroots.
Has the Judiciary Taken Over the Role of the Executive and Legislature?

elements.text: The Way Forward

rows.text: Principle
Explanation & Application
Primacy of Legislature

Just as the "independence of the judiciary" is a part of the Basic Structure, Parliamentary democracy and separation of powers are also components of the basic structure. Interference is not always justified.
Judicial Restraint

Judges should not indulge in "judicial romanticism" or pass ad hoc decisions without sound backing. The Supreme Court itself noted in Aravali Golf Club v. State of Haryana that judges must know their limits and not try to run the government.
Exceptional Use

Activism should be the exception, not the rule. It must be limited to:
1. Furthering the mandates of the Constitution.
2. When a legal norm is urgently required by society and the legislature is unable/unwilling to act.
3. When there is a clear gap in statutory law.
Final Conclusion

Judicial Activism is like a life-saving drug, not daily bread. While judicial review is essential to protect democracy from majoritarian tyranny, continuous overreach risks undermining the very parliamentary democracy the Constitution seeks to protect.

elements.text: While Judicial Activism serves as a vital constitutional safety valve during times of legislative inertia, it must not devolve into Judicial Adventurism. The Constitution is anchored in the delicate Separation of Powers; courts are equipped to test the legality of a policy, but they lack the socio-economic expertise and democratic mandate to formulate it.
24.2 High Courts
While the SC is the highest appellate court, High Courts are Coordinate Constitutional Courts.
• The SC has no administrative control over the High Courts.
• A High Court judge is not a subordinate of a Supreme Court judge.
24.2.1 Structural Framework

rows.text: Element
Constitutional aspect
Difference from SC
Number of Judges (Strength) (Article 216) Qualifications of HC Judge (Article 217)

Every HC consists of a Chief Justice and such other judges as the President may from time to time deem necessary to appoint.
1. Citizen of India.
2. Held a judicial office for 10 years OR been an advocate of a High Court for 10 years.

Parliament determines the strength of the Supreme Court, but the President (Executive) determines the strength of the High Courts based on workload. There is no fixed constitutional maximum for HCs. The Constitution allows a "distinguished jurist" to be appointed to the Supreme Court. However, there is no provision to appoint a distinguished jurist to a High Court.
The Appointment Process (Article 217) Oath of Office (Article 219)

Appointed by the President. The Consultation Mechanism: The President consults the CJI, the Governor of the State, and the Chief Justice of that HC. Administered by the Governor of the State (or their appointee).

The HC Collegium Nuance: To appoint an HC judge, the SC Collegium (CJI + 2 senior-most judges, not 4) considers the recommendation sent by the HC Collegium (HC CJ + 2 senior-most HC judges) and the State Government. An HC judge is appointed by the President and removed by the President but takes their oath before the Governor.

elements.text: 24.2.2 Independence and Accountability Mechanism
Element The High Court Rule & Associated Acts
Significance & Issues
Tenure & Resignation
Retires at the age of 62 years (unlike SC judges who retire at 65). Can resign by writing to the President.
Law Commissions have repeatedly recommended raising the HC retirement age to 65 to retain talent, reduce pendency, and bring parity with the SC, but constitutional amendments for this have stalled.
Removal / Impeachment (Article 217 read with Article 124(4))

An HC judge can be removed from office by the President in the exact same manner as a Supreme Court judge. Grounds: Proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Law: The Judges (Enquiry) Act, 1968, governs the process (requires a special majority in both Houses of Parliament).
The process is deliberately made extremely rigid. No HC judge has ever been successfully impeached in Indian history.
Post-Retirement Restrictions (Article 220)
Ensuring Neutrality: Prevents a retired judge from practicing in the very court where they once sat, preventing them from using their past influence over junior judges or lawyers.
A permanent judge of a High Court cannot plead or act in any court or before any authority in India... except the Supreme Court and other High Courts.
Acting & Additional Judges (Articles 223 & 224)
The President can appoint duly qualified persons as Additional Judges for a temporary period (not exceeding 2 years) to clear arrears of work.
This is a crucial administrative tool used to tackle the vacancies in heavily burdened courts like Allahabad and Bombay without permanently expanding the sanctioned strength.
24.2.3 Writ Jurisdiction of the High Court
Dimension
Supreme Court
High Court (Article 226)
Significance
(Article 32)
Scope of Writs

The Wider Umbrella: The HC's writ jurisdiction is vastly wider than the SC's. It acts as the primary constitutional shield for citizens against all forms of administrative overreach, not just fundamental rights violations.
Can issue writs ONLY for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights (Part III).
Can issue writs for Fundamental Rights AND "for any other purpose" (ordinary legal rights).
Territorial Reach
Federal Accessibility: HCs ensure that constitutional remedies are geographically accessible, preventing Delhi from becoming the sole arbiter of justice.
Pan-India jurisdiction.
Restricted to its territorial borders (or where the cause of action arises).
Discretionary Nature
The Doctrine of Exhaustion: The SC increasingly uses this to force litigants to approach HCs first, preventing the apex court from becoming a glorified trial court.
Article 32 is a Fundamental Right itself. The SC generally cannot refuse to hear a valid petition.
Article 226 is a discretionary power. The HC can refuse to hear a petition if an alternative remedy exists.
24.2.4 Constitutional Powers
Constitutional
Core Power
Significance Landmark Case / Example
Provision
Article 226 (Writ Jurisdiction)
The Wider Umbrella: Makes the HC the primary constitutional shield against administrative overreach. It is geographically accessible, preventing the SC from becoming the sole arbiter of justice.
Power to issue writs for Fundamental Rights AND "any other purpose" (ordinary legal rights).
General Doctrine of Exhaustion: SC forces litigants to approach HCs first.
Article 227 (Supervisory Jurisdiction)
Checking Tribunalisation: Prevents the Executive from bypassing the HC via specialised tribunals. Appeals from tribunals must go through the HC before reaching the SC.
Power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals throughout the state's territory.
L. Chandra Kumar Case (1997): SC ruled that HC judicial review under 226/227 is a Basic Structure.
Article 228
Ranadeb Choudhuri vs. Land Acquisition Judge (1971): Calcutta HC established that if a subordinate court is dealing with a matter of a Constitutional issue, the High Court can withdraw the case.
Withdrawal of cases involving substantial constitutional interpretation from subordinate courts.
Ensures constitutional questions are decided by High Courts.
Article 235 (Control over Subordinate Courts)
Insulating the Lower Judiciary: Prevents the State Executive (Chief Minister/Governor) from blackmailing, punishing, or transferring district judges who rule against the government.
Vests "control" (posting, promotion, and leave) of district judges exclusively in the High Court.
Constitutional safeguard for Judicial Separation of Powers at the grassroots
RPA, 1951 (Original Jurisdiction)
Guarantor of Electoral Purity: Vests monumental democratic power in the HC to act as the ultimate umpire of India's legislative elections.
Allahabad HC (1975): Famously convicted then-PM Indira Gandhi of electoral malpractices.
The HC is the frontline court to hear election petitions challenging the election of an MP or MLA.
