elements.text: 24.3 Challenges Faced by Judiciary

rows.text: The Systemic Crisis The Core Issue
The Proposed Institutional Fix / SC Ruling

The Pendency Crisis With over 5 crore pending cases (87% in subordinate courts), the system suffers from an "Adjournment Culture." This violates the Fundamental Right to Speedy Trial (Article 21) and deters foreign investment due to contract enforcement delays. Subordinate Vacancies & AIJS The Friction: High Courts and State Public Service Commissions fail to conduct timely exams, leading to massive judicial vacancies at the district level. The Federal Roadblock: States oppose the All India Judicial Service (AIJS), arguing that it may dilute states' role in judicial recruitment and reduce sensitivity to local linguistic and social conditions.

Shift from litigation to Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR), institutionalise Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) for petty cases, and strictly enforce time limits under the Civil Procedure Code (CPC) for adjournments. Implement a modified AIJS that includes strict linguistic proficiency tests for state-specific cadres, ensuring national talent is recruited without compromising local linguistic comprehension.
The Tribunalisation of Justice (Articles 323A /323B)

The Friction: Tribunals were created for speed and domain expertise, but they have resulted in the "Bureaucratisation of Justice." Because the Executive controls their appointments and funding, they lack independence. Furthermore, they initially tried to bypass High Courts.

L. Chandra Kumar Case (1997): SC ruled tribunals cannot bypass High Courts' writ jurisdiction (Article 226). Madras Bar Association v. Union o f India (2025): The Supreme Court struck down the Tribunals Reform Act, 2021, holding it unconstitutional and violative of the Constitution's basic structure. Structural Fix: Strengthen tribunal independence through autonomous appointment, administration and financial mechanisms.
Appointment of Judges
The Collegium System faces repeated criticism for its lack of transparency, opacity in candidate selection, and delays in processing appointments.
Transition to a more transparent, consensus-based, and time-bound mechanism for judicial appointments to address the high vacancy rates
Infrastructure Excessive Government Litigation Deep Gender and Social Imbalance

Many subordinate courts lack basic technology, proper courtrooms, and secure linkages with jails, hindering efficient day-to-day operations. The state is the largest single litigant, filling courts with inter-departmental disputes. The higher judiciary suffers from severe lack of diversity; women represent fewer than 15% of High Court judges, with some states having zero or only one female judge.

Launch a centralised National Judicial Infrastructure Authority to fast-track and standardise court funding. Enforce a strict National Litigation Policy to resolve government disputes internally without filing lawsuits. Create institutional reservation or formal, transparent targets for under-represented communities and women during the recruitment of subordinate and higher judiciary members.
Language and Accessibility Barriers
Court proceedings and judgements in the High Courts and Supreme Court are conducted primarily in English, alienating the majority of rural litigants who cannot comprehend the process
Mandate the use of translation tools like the Bhashini AI platform to provide judgements in all regional scheduled languages simultaneously with English.
Transfer of Judges (Article 222)

President (via the SC Collegium) can transfer a judge from one HC to another. → Sudden, opaque transfers of independent-minded judges are viewed as punitive victimisation, reducing co-ordinate judges to transferable civil servants.
K. Ashok Reddy Case (1994): The SC ruled transfers must only be for "public interest" (not punishment) and are subject to limited Judicial Review.
Interference in status of High Courts

HCs are not structurally or administratively subordinate to the Supreme Court. The SC sometimes acts as a routine appellate court, micromanaging state issues and diluting the Constitutional autonomy of the High Courts.
Tirupati Balaji Developers (2004): The SC explicitly affirmed that HCs are "Coordinate Constitutional Courts" whose autonomy must be protected.

elements.text: 24.4 How Judicial accountability could be ensured?
Dimension Aspect Key Details, Case Laws, and Impact
Constitutional and Legal Mechanisms
Impeachment (Articles 124(4) & 217(1)(b))
Removal strictly for "proved misbehaviour or incapacity".
Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 Rigid process: Motion by 100 LS / 50 RS members → 3-member probe committee → requires 2/3rd special majority in Parliament.
Institutional Mechanisms
In-House Procedure

SC's internal inquiry mechanism. Case Law: K. Veeraswami v. UoI (1991) – The court ruled that no First Information Report (FIR) can be registered against a sitting judge without the prior sanction of the Chief Justice of India (CJI)
Ethical Framework Restatements of Judicial Values (1999): Adopted by the judiciary as a moral code of conduct.

rows.text: Critical Issues (Flaws) High Threshold & Politics
The rigid statutory requirement makes removal almost impossible. Example: Justice V. Ramaswami (1993) impeachment failed due to political abstentions.
The "Resignation Loophole"
Judges resign to abruptly halt investigations and escape formal public findings. Examples: Justice Soumitra Sen and Justice P.D. Dinakaran.
Lack of Intermediate Sanctions
The current law is "all-or-nothing". There is no provision for lesser penalties like censure, private reprimand, or temporary suspension.
Opaque Internal Probes
The SC’s in-house mechanism lacks statutory backing, operates entirely in secret, and its decisions are not publicly disclosed.
Reforms Independent Oversight Body Introduce Lesser Penalties Close Escape Routes Enforce Transparency

Establish a body with non-judicial members to oversee conduct (UK Model). Action: Revive the lapsed Judicial Standards & Accountability Bill,
2010. Amend the Judges (Inquiry) Act to allow intermediate sanctions (reprimands/suspensions), similar to the US Federal Judicial Councils. Amend laws to ensure investigations continue to their logical conclusion even if a judge resigns, and publish the final findings. Mandate the public disclosure of assets/liabilities, clearly define "misbehaviour" to include corruption, and set strict statutory timelines for probes.

elements.text: 24.5 Way Forward
To rescue the Indian Judiciary from institutional gridlock, reforms must move beyond piecemeal vacancy-filling and focus on
structural, procedural, and technological re-engineering:
• Enacting a National Litigation Policy: The State (Union and State governments) is the largest single litigant in India, responsible for nearly 46-50% of all pending cases.
 A strict policy must be enforced to stop government departments from filing frivolous appeals and routinely dragging employees to court over minor service disputes.
• Establishing a National Tribunals Commission (NTC): To cure the "bureaucratisation" of tribunals, an independent NTC
must be created. This body would oversee appointments, infrastructure, and financial autonomy for all tribunals, completely removing the Executive's leverage over them.

• Technological Integration (e-Courts Phase III): Move beyond mere digitisation of records. The system requires AI-assisted case management, smart scheduling and digital translation tools and the scaling of SUVAS (Supreme Court Vidhik Anuvaad Software) to instantly translate judgements into vernacular languages.

• Mainstreaming Pre-Institution Mediation: Taking a cue from the Commercial Courts Act, expand pre-institution mediation, particularly in commercial, family and property disputes before they are allowed to enter the formal court system, filtering out millions of reconcilable cases.

• Infrastructure & Financial Autonomy: The subordinate judiciary operates in severe infrastructural deficit. The Union must increase funding under Centrally Sponsored Schemes to build better courtrooms and digital infrastructure, decoupling the lower judiciary's efficiency from the fiscal constraints of individual state governments.
Ultimately, the Indian Judiciary must balance its proactive role as the sentinel of Constitutional rights with strict adherence to the
separation of powers. Moving forward, addressing structural bottlenecks like pendency, opaque appointments, and executive
encroachment is imperative to ensure justice remains accessible, timely, and truly independent.
Pressure Groups

Pressure groups are organized associations formed to protect and promote specific socio-economic, political, or ideological interests. Unlike political parties, they do not seek to directly capture political power or contest elections; instead, they operate "behind the scenes" to influence government policy, legislation, and public opinion in their favour.

how the business associations contribute to public policies. (2021)
2. How do pressure groups influence the Indian political process? Do you agree with
this view that informal pressure groups have emerged as more powerful than formal
pressure groups in recent years? (2017)

elements.text: Salient Features
Of The Representation
Of People’s Act
Representation of People Acts

While Article 324 of the Constitution vests the Election Commission with the sweeping power of 'superintendence, direction, and control,' it provides only the skeletal framework of India's democracy. It is the Representation of the People Acts (1950 and 1951) that provide the operational muscle, translating the constitutional promise of Universal Adult Suffrage into a tangible, legally enforceable democratic reality.
UPSC Mains PYQs

1. Discuss the ‘corrupt practices’ for the purpose of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. Analyze whether the increase in the assets of the legislators and/or their associates, disproportionate to their known sources of income, would constitute ‘undue influence’ and consequently a corrupt practice. (2025)
2. Discuss the procedures to decide the disputes arising out of the election of a Member of the Parliament or State Legislature under The Representation of the People Act, 1951. What are the grounds on which the election of any returned candidate may be declared void? What remedy is available to the aggrieved party against the decision? Refer to the case laws. (2022)
3. “There is a need for simplification of procedure for disqualification of persons found guilty of corrupt practices under the Representation of Peoples Act”. Comment. (2020)
4. On what grounds a people’s representative can be disqualified under the Representation of People Act, 1951? Also mention the remedies available to such person against his disqualification. (2019)

rows.text: Statutory Provision RPA, 1950 (The Preparation Phase) RPA, 1951 (General) (The Execution Phase)

Description Deals with the foundational setup: Allocation of seats, delimitation of constituencies, qualifications of voters, and preparation of electoral rolls. Deals with the actual combat: Qualifications/disqualifications of candidates, conduct of polls, counting of votes, and resolving election disputes.

Analysis & Supreme Court Judgments Demographic Justice: Ensures the constitutional promise of "One Person, One Value." It creates the level playing field before the electoral battle begins. Electoral Purity: Acts as the primary statutory shield to filter out tainted candidates and regulate the ethical conduct of politicians during the campaign.
Sections 8, 9, 10 (RPA 1951) (Disqualification)

• Sec 8: Conviction for crimes (Immediate disqualification if sentence is 2+ years).
• Sec 8A: Found guilty of corrupt practices.
• Sec 9/9A: Dismissal for corruption/disloyalty or holding government contracts.
• Sec 10A: Failure to lodge election expenses.

The Criminalization Battleground:
• Lily Thomas Case (2013): SC struck down the protective shield of Sec 8(4), meaning an MP/MLA now loses their seat immediately upon a 2-year conviction. (Pending Reform: ECI demands disqualification upon framing of charges for heinous crimes, not just conviction.)
• The law heavily penalises criminality and financial opacity.The Remedy: The aggrieved person can appeal to higher courts (HC/SC). Furthermore, under Section 11, the Election Commission of India (ECI) has the extraordinary statutory power to remove or reduce the period of disqualification (e.g., invoked for Sikkim CM P.S. Tamang in 2019).

elements.text: Section 29A (RPA 1951) (Political Parties)

The Inner-Party Democracy Deficit: The law allows the ECI to register parties but gives it no statutory power to deregister them for failing to hold internal democratic elections, leading to dynastic centralisation.
Mandates the registration of political parties with the Election Commission of India (ECI).
Section 123 (RPA 1951) (Corrupt Practices)
Protecting the Secular Mandate:
Defines illegal campaign tactics, including bribery, undue influence, booth capturing, and appealing to voters on the grounds of religion, race, caste, or language.
• Abhiram Singh Case (2017): SC ruled that appealing
to the religion/caste of the candidate, rival, or the voter is a corrupt practice, strictly enforcing elections as a secular exercise. Lok Prahari Case (2018) :
• The Supreme Court h eld that concealing assets,

liabilities, or income sources misleads voters and amounts to a "fraud on the voter."
• Such non-disclosure interferes with the voter's free

choice and constitutes "Undue Influence" under Section 123(2) of the RPA, 1951.
• Therefore, suppression of material financial information
is a corrupt practice and can be a ground for voiding an election.
Election Petitions (Dispute Resolution)

Delayed Justice: While Article 329 prevents courts from stalling an ongoing election, High Courts often take years to resolve these petitions, rendering the mechanism toothless by the time a verdict is reached.
The only legal mechanism to challenge a rigged election or corrupt practice is by filing an Election Petition in the High Court after the results are declared.
Section 80A & Section 100 (Election Disputes & Voiding Elections)
• Sec 80A: Election disputes
• Procedure: The HC tries the petition as an original suit. If

can only be heard by the High Court via an Election Petition (filed within 45 days).
• Sec 100 (Grounds to Void):

grounds under Sec 100 are met, the HC declares the election void.
• Remedy: The aggrieved party can file a statutory appeal to

the Supreme Court under Section 116A of the RPA.
• Case Law: Indira Gandhi vs. Raj Narain (1975)
1. Corrupt practice committed by the candidate/agent. 2. Improper acceptance/ rejection of nomination. 3. Non-compliance with the Constitution or RPA.
(Allahabad HC voided the PM's election for corrupt practices); Abhiram Singh (2017) (SC expanded the definition of religious appeal as a corrupt practice).
26.2 RPA 1951 Contemporary Issues

rows.text: Contemporary Issue
The Core Friction
ECI/Judicial Stance
The "Party Loophole" in Finance (Section 77)

The Limitless War Chest: The law caps election expenditure for individual candidates (₹95 Lakhs for LS) but places zero limits on how much a political party can spend in a constituency, rendering candidate limits meaningless and favouring corporate-backed parties.
The ECI Stance: The ECI has repeatedly demanded that this loophole be closed by bringing political party expenditure under a statutory ceiling.
The MCC Statutory Vacuum (No RPA Backing)
Teeth vs. Agility: The Model Code of Conduct (MCC) is merely a moral consensus without legal teeth. While civil society demands adding it to the RPA to criminalise violations, the ECI opposes this.

The ECI Argument: If the MCC is made statutory, every violation requires a lengthy judicial trial. The ECI prefers the current system, which allows for immediate, summary administrative action (e.g., 48-hour campaign bans)
Disenfranchisement of Prisoners (Section 62(5))

The Undertrial Paradox: The RPA bans anyone in police custody or prison from voting. Since over 70% of Indian prisoners are undertrials (innocent until proven guilty), this systemically disenfranchises millions of marginalized citizens, violating Article 14 (Equality).
Anukul Chandra Pradhan Case (1997): The SC upheld this ban, ruling that voting is a statutory right, not a fundamental one, and citing the logistical impossibility of setting up booths in prisons.
Digital Subversion of the Silence Period (Section 126)

The 20th Century Law: Section 126 bans public meetings and TV/radio broadcasting 48 hours before polling. However, it does not explicitly cover the internet or social media, allowing parties to target voters via social media during the "silence period".
The ECI Challenge: The ECI struggles to enforce jurisdiction over offshore tech servers, relying on voluntary codes of ethics from social media platforms rather than hard law.

elements.text: 26.3 Important Electoral Reforms & Judicial Interventions under the RPA 1951
Provision / Issue Statutory Basis / Case Significance
Candidate Disclosure of Criminal, Financial and Educational Background
ADR Case (2002) + Section 33A, RPA 1951
Supreme Court held that voters have a Right to Know about candidates. Mandatory disclosure of criminal antecedents, assets, liabilities and educational qualifications in nomination affidavits.
Right to Know as Part of Free Speech
PUCL v. Union of India (2003)
Court held that voters' right to information regarding candidates flows from Article 19(1)(a). Section 33B of RPA (which attempted to dilute disclosures) was struck down.
None of the Above (NOTA)
PUCL v. Union of India (2013)
Introduced NOTA in EVMs, strengthening voter choice and electoral participation while preserving the secrecy of voting.
Electoral Bonds Judgment
Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (2024)
The Supreme Court struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme and related amendments to the RPA, Companies Act and IT Act, citing violation of voters' Right to Information under Article 19(1)(a).
Disclosure of Political Donations
RPA Sections 29B & 29C
Political parties may receive contributions, but donations above the prescribed threshold must be reported to the Election Commission. Promotes transparency in political funding.
Paid News
ECI Guidelines + RPA Framework
Paid news distorts voter choice and may be treated as unaccounted election expenditure. ECI has repeatedly sought stronger statutory provisions.
Proxy Voting for Overseas Electors
RPA Amendments & ECI Proposals
NRIs can register as overseas electors, but practical voting participation remains limited. Various reforms, including proxy and remote voting, have been debated.
Election Expenditure Monitoring
Section 77, RPA 1951
Requires maintenance of election expenditure accounts by candidates. Failure may attract disqualification under Section 10A.
False Affidavits Section 125A, RPA 1951 Providing false information or concealing material facts in nomination affidavits is a punishable offence.
26.4 Way Forward
Issue & Statutory Focus Committee / Source Specific Recommendation
Campaign Finance (Section 77 of RPA)

Ceiling on Parties: Amend Section 77 to impose a strict statutory ceiling on party expenditure, not just candidate expenditure. Auditing: Mandate concurrent auditing of party accounts by the CAG. State Funding: Transition to partial state funding of elections (in-kind subsidies like free fuel, voter slips, and media airtime).
255th Law Commission Report Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998)
Digital Campaigning (Section 126 of RPA)
Umesh Sinha Committee (2019)

Digital Intermediaries: Explicitly amend Section 126 to include "Social Media Platforms". Strict Enforcement: Platforms must be legally bound to take down violative political content within 3 hours during the 48-hour silence period.
Decriminalization (Section 8 of RPA)
Election Commission of India (ECI)

Framing of Charges: Do not wait for a final conviction. Amend Section 8 to disqualify candidates the moment a competent court frames charges against them for heinous crimes (punishable by 5+ years), provided charges are framed at least 6 months before the election.
Undertrial Voting Rights (Section 62(5) of RPA)
General Reform Proposal

Postal Ballots: Since physical polling booths in prisons are a logistical nightmare, the RPA must be amended to extend the Postal Ballot facility to undertrials. The State bears a positive obligation to protect their statutory right to vote before they are proven guilty.

The RPA must transition from a 20th-century procedural statute into a proactive shield against modern electoral subversions like digital manipulation and opaque campaign finance. Implementing these structural reforms is no longer optional but a democratic imperative to preserve the absolute purity of India's electoral mandate.
Delimitation Commission
The Delimitation Commission serves as the institutional bedrock of India's representative democracy, translating the
constitutional ideal of 'One Person, One Value' into tangible electoral geography.
Core Mandate: To redraw parliamentary and state assembly constituencies based on the latest Census to ensure equitable
representation.
• Article 82: Parliament enacts a Delimitation Act after every Census (Union Level).
• Article 170: States are divided into territorial constituencies based on the Census.
• Articles 330 & 332: The Commission holds the sole authority to identify and reserve seats for SCs/STs based on population proportion.
27.1 The Anatomy of the Commission

rows.text:
Feature Structure Establishment A statutory body appointed by the President of India, operating independently but closely associated with the Election Commission of India (ECI). Composition
1. A serving or retired Supreme Court Judge (Chairperson).
2. The Chief Election Commissioner (or their nominee).
3. The State Election Commissioner (of the respective state).

Significance Historical Timeline: Despite the constitutional mandate (after every census), it has only been constituted four times: 1952, 1963, 1973, and 2002. Blends high judicial integrity with the logistical expertise of the electoral machinery.

Associate Members Includes 5 MPs (LS) and 5 MLAs from the respective state. Power
• Article 329(a) bars challenging delimitation laws (made under Arts. 327/328).
• Section 10(2) of the Delimitation Act, 2002: The orders of the Delimitation Commission have the force of law and cannot be challenged in any court.

Associate members only have an advisory role. They have no voting rights in the final decisions of the Commission. This absolute immunity prevents frivolous litigation from stalling elections indefinitely.

The impending post-2026 unfreezing of seats represents a severe stress test to Indian Federalism, triggering a high-stakes collision between demographic realities and political equity.

• Individual MPs will see their legislative influence

The Federal Imbalance (North vs. South)
• The "Demographic Penalty": Progressive states feel

Northern states (UP, Bihar and MP) will gain new Lok Sabha seats due to their massive population boom.
• Southern states will lose their relative

penalised for successfully implementing state policies (healthcare, education, family planning).

27.3 Judicial Review of Delimitation
Case Core Principle Impact
Constitutional Mandate (Article 329(a))
Absolute Bar (General Rule) to ensure elections are not derailed by litigation.
Expressly bars courts from interfering in electoral matters, including the validity of delimitation laws or seat allotments.
Gujarat High Court (Earlier Stance)
Strict Compliance with the absolute bar on judicial interference.
Adhered strictly to Article 329(a) and dismissed petitions challenging delimitation.
SC in Meghraj Kothari Case
Clarified the purpose of the bar: it is meant to prevent endless litigation from stalling the electoral process.
The SC decision solidified the inviolability of the Delimitation Commission's orders concerning the delimitation of constituencies.
SC in DMK v. State of T.N. (2020)
Established Exceptions: Courts can intervene if the exercise of power is mala fide (bad faith) or arbitrary.
Balanced Article 329(a) with the principles of justice, explicitly rejecting a total ouster of judicial review.
SC in Kishorchandra Rathod Case (2024)
Current Stance: Constitutional courts retain the power to review Delimitation Commission orders if they are "manifestly arbitrary" or violate Constitutional values.
Cemented the exceptions based on the "Basic Structure" doctrine.
27.4 Way Forward
Proposed Solution Mechanism
Expanding the Pie (The "848 Solution")
• Do not take seats away from the South. Instead, dramatically increase the total number of

Lok Sabha seats (e.g., to 848, utilising the new Parliament building's capacity).
• Allocate the new seats to the North based on population, ensuring the South retains its
absolute numbers, even if its relative percentage drops
Asymmetric Federalism (The Rajya Sabha Fix)
• To compensate the Southern states for their loss of relative power in the Lok Sabha, the
Constitution can be amended to guarantee them equal or disproportionately higher representation in the Rajya Sabha (similar to the US Senate model), creating a true federal balancing chamber.
Fiscal Compensation (via Finance Commission)
• Ensure the Finance Commission aggressively rewards states with strong demographic
performance via specific fiscal transfers. This offsets their loss of political capital with enhanced financial autonomy.
Constitutional Upgrades (Autonomy & Transparency)

1. Digital Transparency: Introduce a digital portal for the Delimitation Commission to actively solicit real-time public feedback on boundary drafts, neutralising fears of gerrymandering.
2. Elevated Status: Grant the Commission constitutional status (similar to the ECI/UPSC) to enhance its institutional autonomy.

Ultimately, the impending post-2026 delimitation is not merely an exercise in electoral cartography but the ultimate crucible for Indian federalism. To preserve the Republic’s unity, Parliament must ensure the Commission's pursuit of demographic justice is harmonised with bold constitutional compromises that protect progressive states from a demographic penalty.
Election Commission

The Election Commission of India (ECI) is an autonomous Constitutional authority established on January 25, 1950, under Article
324. It ensures free, fair, and impartial elections for the Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of the President and Vice President. By managing electoral rolls and enforcing the Model Code of Conduct, the ECI independently safeguards the democratic fabric of the world's largest electorate.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. Examine the need for electoral reforms as suggested by various committees with
particular reference to “one nation – one election” principle. (2024)
2. Discuss the role of the Election Commission of India in light of the evolution of the
Model Code of Conduct. (2022)
3. In the light of recent controversy regarding the use of Electronic Voting Machine
(EVM), what are the challenges before the Election Commission of India to ensure the
trustworthiness of elections in India? (2018)
4. To enhance the quality of democracy in India the Election Commission of India has
proposed electoral reforms in 2016. What are the suggested reforms and how far are
they significant to make democracy successful? (2017)
5. ‘Simultaneous election to the Lok Sabha and the State Assemblies will limit the
amount of time and money spent in electioneering, but it will reduce the government’s
accountability to the people.' Discuss. (2017)
28.1 Constitutional Mandate

rows.text: Article/ Dimension
Constitutional Provision
Significance
Article 324
Vests the power of superintendence, direction, and control of elections (Parliament, State Legislatures, President, and Vice-President) in the ECI.

The "Reservoir of Power": The Supreme Court ruled in Mohinder Singh Gill (1977) that Article 324 is a "reservoir of power". If the RPA is silent on an issue, the ECI can invoke Article 324 to take any administrative action necessary for free elections.
Article 325 Article 326

One general electoral roll for every constituency. No person can be included or excluded on grounds of religion, race, caste, or sex. Universal Adult Suffrage. Elections must be held on the basis of adult franchise (voting age reduced from 21 to 18 via the 61st Amendment, 1988).
The Secular Bedrock: Eradicates the colonial legacy of separate communal electorates (like the 1909 Morley-Minto reforms). Ensures political equality, regardless of property, education, or wealth.
Articles 327 & 328
Empowers Parliament (327) and State Legislatures (328) to make laws regarding elections (delimitation and preparation of rolls).
This is the source power for the Representation of the People Acts (1950 & 1951).
Article 329
Bars the interference of courts in electoral matters (delimitation, allotment of seats). Elections can only be challenged via an Election Petition.
Prevents judicial delays from derailing the massive logistical exercise of a nationwide election.
Appointment & Independence
Constitution leaves appointments to the President (Executive), prescribing no qualifications and no bar on post-retirement jobs.

Anoop Baranwal (2023): SC mandated a Collegium (PM, LoP, CJI) to stop executive capture. The Friction: Parliament enacted the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, replacing the CJI with a Union Cabinet Minister, increasing executive influence in the appointment process.
Internal Equality & Removal
The CEC is protected (removed like an SC judge). The other two ECs lack this protection and can be removed on the CEC's recommendation.

T.N. Seshan Case (1995): The SC ruled the CEC is just the "first among equals" and all decisions require a majority vote. Reform Needed: The 255th Law Commission demands equal removal protection for all three ECs.
