28.2 Basics of CEC Removal
Feature Details
Context/Trigger Opposition parties considering a motion against the CEC over allegations of biased conduct.
Constitutional Provision Article 324(5) guarantees security of tenure and independence to the CEC.
Manner of Removal The CEC can be removed only in the same manner as a Supreme Court Judge.
Grounds for Removal strictly limited to two specific charges: 1. Proved Misbehaviour or 2. Incapacity.
Constitutional Terminology
The formal term is "Removal". (The term "Impeachment" is constitutionally reserved only for the President under Article 61).
Statutory Backing Governed procedurally by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, and aligned with the recent CEC and other ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
Other Safeguards

• Service conditions cannot be altered to the CEC's disadvantage after appointment.
• Other Election Commissioners/Regional Commissioners can only be removed on the
recommendation of the CEC.
Step-by-Step Removal Procedure (Quasi-Judicial)
Stage Action / Procedure Key Requirements & Conditions
Initiation
A removal motion stating the grounds is introduced and submitted to the Presiding Officer (Speaker/Chairman).
Can be initiated in either House. Requires signatures of:

• 100 members in Lok Sabha, OR
• 50 members in Rajya Sabha.
Admission & Investigation
The Presiding Officer may either admit or refuse the motion. If admitted, an investigative committee is formed.

The 3-Member Committee comprises:
1. A Supreme Court Judge
2. A High Court Chief Justice
3. A Distinguished Jurist
Inquiry & Report

• If Not Proved: The motion is dropped; process ends.
• If Proved: The guilty report is submitted back to the House where the motion originated.
The committee investigates the charges. The CEC is given the right to defend themselves.
Parliamentary Voting
The House takes up the motion for consideration based on the committee's guilty report.
Must be passed by a Special Majority in both Houses during the same session:

• Majority of the total membership of the House, AND
• Majority of > 2/3rd of members present and voting.
Final Order
If the motion successfully passes both Houses, a formal address is presented to the Executive head.
The President of India issues the official order for the removal of the CEC.
Scope of Judicial Interference in Electoral Processes

Context: The Supreme Court recently dismissed a plea challenging the rejection of a nomination paper for a Rajya Sabha election, reaffirming the strict constitutional bar on judicial intervention while an election process is ongoing.
• Constitutional Bar on Interference: Article 329(b) of the Constitution imposes a strict, blanket ban on judicial interference in electoral matters once the election process has commenced.

 It dictates that no election to Parliament or a State Legislature can be called into question except by an Election Petition presented to the appropriate authority (the High Court) after the election process concludes.
 Once the election notification is issued, the writ jurisdictions of both the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Article 226) stand excluded regarding the conduct of the election.

• Nature of Electoral Rights: Not a Fundamental Right → The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the right to vote, the right to contest an election, and the right to dispute an election are purely Statutory Rights, not Fundamental Rights or common law rights.

 Implication for Article 32: Because the right to contest is not a Fundamental Right, an aggrieved candidate cannot bypass the standard electoral laws to seek immediate relief directly from the Supreme Court under Article 32.

• The Statutory Remedy: RPA, 1951 → Section 100(1)(c) of the RPA: This section specifically addresses the issue of nominations. It states that the "improper rejection of any nomination" is a valid statutory ground to declare an election void, but this can only be invoked via an Election Petition after the election results are declared.

• The Debate on Exceptions: "Manifest Illegality" → The Petitioner’s Argument (The Exception Rule): Candidates often argue that courts should intervene if a Returning Officer's rejection is completely arbitrary or a "patent illegality," arguing that intervention would facilitate rather than obstruct the democratic process.
 The Supreme Court's Stance (Strict Adherence): The Court has expressly refused to carve out any exceptions for "glaring" or manifest illegalities.

 Reasoning: Allowing exceptions would incorrectly split election disputes into two categories (those requiring immediate intervention vs. those requiring election petitions). This would inevitably delay and derail the time-sensitive election schedule, which the Constitution seeks to prevent.
• Key Judicial Precedents

 N.P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer (1952): A landmark judgement establishing that the word "election" in Article 329(b) covers the entire continuous process from the issuance of the notification to the final declaration of results. Judicial review is barred during this entire window.
 Jyoti Basu v. Debi Ghosal (1982): Cemented the doctrine that electoral rights (including the right to be elected) are strictly statutory creations, subject to statutory limitations.

 Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner (1977): Clarified that while courts shouldn't intervene to obstruct the election, the Election Commission has broad powers under Article 324 to ensure free and fair elections where laws are silent, but this doesn't override the Article 329(b) bar for candidates seeking court injunctions.
28.3 Electoral Challenges and Reforms
Challenge Mechanism Way Forward
The MCC Conundrum (Non-Statutory Code)

Freebies (Subramaniam Balaji): SC ordered the ECI to include manifesto guidelines in the MCC. Digital Era: The Umesh Sinha Committee recommends legally holding social media platforms liable during the 48-hour silence period.
The MCC has no legal backing. The ECI prefers it this way, using summary powers (Article 324) to ban campaigners for 48 hours rather than waiting for lengthy court trials.
Trust Deficit in Tech (EVMs & VVPATs)
SC 2024 Directive: Rejected 100% VVPAT slip counting due to delays, but mandated that Symbol Loading Units (SLUs) be sealed and stored for 45 days post-election for potential auditing.
EVMs use standalone, One-Time Programmable chips (no Wi-Fi/Bluetooth hacking possible). Machines undergo First-Level Checks (FLC) and software randomisation.
Political Funding (The Corporate Nexus)

The Reality: A major challenge due to deep-rooted issues with opaque funding sources, uneven financial power among parties, unregulated campaign expenses, and the potential for corporate corruption. These factors severely distort the democratic process. Also, party expenditure has no legal ceiling under Section 77 of the RPA.

Indrajit Gupta Committee: Transition to partial state funding of elections. Law Commission: Amend Sec 77 to cap party expenditure and mandate CAG audits of party finances. Also, Electoral Bonds were struck down in 2024 for violating the Right to Know.
Criminalization of Politics ("Winability" Factor)
The Reality: Criminals exploit judicial delays. Disqualification currently only happens upon a final conviction of 2+ years (Section 8 of RPA).
ECI 2016 Proposal: Disqualify candidates the moment a competent court frames charges against them for heinous crimes (6 months prior to polls).
Perennial Election Cycle (Simultaneous Elections)
The Debate: Constant elections cause policy paralysis and drain exchequers, but forcing synchronisation threatens state-level federal accountability.

Kovind Committee (2024): Implement simultaneous elections in phases. Crucially, if a state government falls early, hold mid-term polls only for the remainder of the term to preserve the synchronised cycle.
28.4 Evolution of Electoral Playing Field Since Independence

rows.text: Era/Committee Reforms Implemented
Significance
1988 (61st Amendment) Lowering the Voting Age: Reduced the voting age from 21 years to 18 years.
Radically expanded Universal Adult Suffrage, forcing political parties to integrate the youth demographic into policy-making.

1990 (Dinesh Goswami Committee)
1. Restricting Contesting Seats: Capped the number of constituencies a candidate can contest simultaneously to two.
2. Proposers: Mandated 10 proposers for independent/unrecognised candidates. 1996 (National Honour Act) Disqualification: A person convicted under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, is disqualified for 6 years.
Checked the proliferation of non-serious/ dummy candidates who contested solely to confuse voters or split vote banks. Enforced a baseline of Constitutional patriotism for aspiring legislators.

2003 (Transparency & Subsidies)
1. Media Time: Equitable sharing of time on state electronic media based on past performance.
2. Tax Relief: Mandated reporting of contributions above ₹20,000 to claim IT exemptions. 2009 (Electoral Sanity) Exit Poll Ban: Prohibited conducting and publishing exit polls while elections are ongoing.

An early, primitive step toward partial state funding (in-kind subsidies) and financial transparency. Prevented the "bandwagon effect", where early exit polls manipulated voter behaviour in the later phases of multi-phase elections.

elements.text: 28.5 How have recent laws created new democratic paradoxes?

rows.text: Provision
Rule
Issue
The "Jail Paradox" (2013 RPA Amendment)

Parliament amended the RPA after the Supreme Court's Jan Chaukidar (2013) judgement and clarified that a person confined in prison or police custody does not cease to be an elector merely because of such confinement.

Under Section 62(5), a prisoner cannot vote, yet an undertrial or person in lawful custody may still contest elections (unless disqualified upon conviction), creating the paradox of being eligible to stand for election while being ineligible to cast a vote.
Corporate Funding (2017 Finance Act) Foreign Funding (FCRA Amendment)

Removed the cap on corporate contributions (previously restricted to 7.5% of net profit) and allowed loss-making companies to donate. Retrospectively amended the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, to allow political parties to receive foreign funds.

Legalised unlimited corporate interference in elections, directly undermining shareholder interests and exacerbating increased scope for corporate influence. Opened the floodgates for foreign interference in domestic policy-making through opaque corporate routing.

elements.text: 28.6 Electoral Reforms Still Pending Today

rows.text: Issue Reform
How it Enhances the Democracy
Contesting Multiple Seats Amend the RPA to restrict candidates to contesting from only one constituency (down from the current limit of two).
Saves public money. Currently, if a leader wins both seats, they resign from one, forcing a costly and unnecessary by-election on the exchequer.

Government Advertising Prohibit government "achievement advertisements" for a period of six months prior to the expiry of the House. Anti-Defection Adjudication Shift the power to decide disqualifications under the 10th Schedule from the Speaker to the President/Governor acting on the binding advice of the ECI.

Prevents the ruling party from using taxpayer funds to run disguised political campaigns just before the Model Code of Conduct kicks in. Removes the partisan bias of the Speaker, ensuring swift, neutral justice against defecting MLAs/MPs.
Protecting Voter Privacy Introduce totaliser machines that aggregate votes from 14 EVMs before revealing the count.
Currently, parties know exactly which polling booth voted against them, leading to targeted post-poll violence or denial of development funds. Totalisers mask booth-level voting patterns.

elements.text: Bogus Voters & Duplication
Link citizen identification databases (like Aadhaar) with the EPIC (Voter ID) card network.
Cleanses the ERONET database by weeding out duplicate voters registered across different states (e.g., migrant workers holding IDs in both UP and Delhi).
The Campaign Expenditure Trap
Revoke the "Star Campaigner" status under Paragraph 16A of the Symbols Order for severe MCC violations.
Deprives the offending party of the financial loophole that exempts Star Campaigner travel costs from the candidate’s expenditure limit.
28.7 Special Intensive Revision (SIR) vs. Special Summary Revision (SSR)

rows.text: Feature
SSR
SIR
Nature of Exercise Methodology
Routine, annual updating of the existing voter list. Relies on voters voluntarily submitting Form 6 (Additions) or Form 7 (Deletions) based on draft rolls.

A complete, ground-up rebuilding of the electoral roll. Proactive door-to-door enumeration by Booth Level Officers (BLOs). Voters must submit fresh enumeration forms and photographs to remain on the list.
The Documentation Rule
Standard address and age proof

The 2003 Benchmark: In the 2025-2026 SIR, voters registered before January 2003 need only provide the 2003 roll extract. However, voters registered after 2003 are required to submit additional eligibility and citizenship documents.
Frequency
Conducted every year before January 1st.
Extremely rare. The last nationwide SIR was conducted in 2001-2004. Triggered only when the ECI believes the rolls are fundamentally compromised by migration, urbanisation, or illegal immigration.

elements.text: 28.7.1 SIR Issues
The deletion of lakhs of voters has triggered profound administrative and legal battles, testing the limits of the Election Commission's mandate.

rows.text: Theme of Friction
The Core Issue & ECI's Rationale
Democratic Critique & Judicial Challenge
Citizenship Checks

• The Issue: SIR requires legacy documents (pre-2003 residency) in certain states.
• ECI Rationale: Rapid migration and border-state demographics (e.g., West Bengal, Assam) necessitate strict document checks to weed out foreign illegal immigrants holding duplicate IDs.

• The Critique: Places an impossible burden of proof on marginalised communities (Dalits, Adivasis, migrant labourers).
• ADR & Ors. v. ECI (2026): SC ruled that while the ECI has the authority to verify non-citizenship to maintain roll integrity (under Section 16 of the RPA), it cannot act as a de facto citizenship adjudicatory authority.
Mass Deletions vs. Universal Suffrage Administrative Timelines vs. ECI Autonomy

• The Issue: Over 5.5 cro re voters were removed across states.
• ECI Rationale: Vital for cleaning the democratic mandate by excising millions of duplicate, shifted, and deceased individuals (over 60 lakh dead voters removed).
• The Issue: The June 2025 ECI notification mandated strict, rapid deadlines to ensure rolls were ready before the 2026 assembly elections.
• ECI Rationale: Under Article 324(1), the ECI asserts absolute authority over the preparation of electoral rolls and insists courts cannot dictate its methodological timelines.

• The Critique: Opposition parties term it "Selective Ideological Removal," alleging massive purges disproportionately target minority enclaves.
• Constitutional Friction: Argued as an indirect violation of Articles 325 & 326, effectively disenfranchising the undocumented poor and denying Universal Adult Suffrage.
• The Critique: State Chief Electoral Officers (e.g., Maharashtra) red-flagged the tight timelines. (The 2002 SIR took 13 months).
• Rushing through complex verifications leads to high error rates, wrongful deletions and denies voters adequate time to appeal.

elements.text: Way Forward for SIR
• Separate ECI and Citizenship Functions: Maintain a clear firewall between electoral roll verification by the ECI and citizenship determination under the Citizenship Act, 1955.
• Ensure Inclusive Verification: Adopt flexible documentary standards and retain a rebuttable presumption of validity for existing voters to prevent exclusion of genuine electors.
• Strengthen Transparency & Appeals: Publish district-wise deletion reasons, provide accessible online/offline grievance mechanisms, and empower Booth Level Agents (BLAs) for greater transparency.
• Institutionalise Independent Oversight: Conduct independent post-revision audits and preserve judicial review against arbitrary or wrongful deletions.
• Adopt Realistic, Phased Timelines: Fix state-specific timelines, implement phased revisions, and provide dedicated error-correction windows before finalising electoral rolls.
• Leverage Reliable Technology: Use robust de-duplication and verification systems, disclose methodologies, and periodically audit technological processes to minimise erroneous deletions.
Recent initiatives by ECI

rows.text: Initiative ECINET (2025) cVIGIL App 100% Webcasting EVM Microcontroller Verification EVM–VVPAT Reconciliation Automatic Death Database Linkage Duplicate EPIC Removal SVEEP Home Voting

Key Features Integrated digital platform for voters, election officials and political parties; facilitates technology sharing with Election Management Bodies (EMBs). Enables citizens to report Model Code of Conduct (MCC) violations through geo-tagged photos/videos for quick Flying Squad action. Real-time monitoring of polling stations nationwide to enhance transparency and electoral integrity. Enhanced post-election verification, including checks on 5% of EVMs, to strengthen confidence in EVMs. Strengthened verification procedures for EVM-VVPAT data mismatches. Enables automatic removal of deceased voters from electoral rolls. Eliminates duplicate Elector Photo Identity Card (EPIC) numbers across states. Flagship voter awareness programme promoting participation of youth, women and first-time voters. Home voting facility for 80+ senior citizens and Persons with Disabilities (PwDs).
Reduced Polling Station Size
Voter limit reduced from 1,500 to 1,200 per polling station to reduce congestion.
Fast-Track EPIC Delivery Redesigned Voter Information Slip
Voter ID cards delivered within 15 days. Improved readability with clearer serial and part numbers for easier verification.
Mobile Deposit Counters
Counters outside polling stations to enforce the no-mobile-phone rule inside booths.
Additional Urban Booths
More polling stations established in high-rise residential complexes for better accessibility.
Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
Comprehensive electoral roll revision launched in Bihar (2025) and expanded to 12 States/ UTs; upheld by the Supreme Court (2026).
Delisting of Inactive Political Parties Photo ID Cards for BLOs
Removal of inactive and unrecognised political parties from the electoral registry. Identity cards introduced for Booth Level Officers (BLOs) to improve accountability during roll revision.

elements.text: Model Code of Conduct
Aspect Details
Meaning & Nature
• A non-statutory set of guidelines issued by the Election Commission of India (ECI) under Article

324 to regulate the conduct of political parties, candidates and governments during elections, ensuring free and fair elections.
• It comes into force immediately after the election schedule is announced and remains effective until
the electoral process concludes.
Historical Evolution

• 1960: First adopted in Kerala
• 1962: Extended nationwide by ECI
• 1974: Formal MCC issued
• 1979: Expanded to regulate the party in power
• 1991: Strict enforcement under T.N. Seshan
• 2013: Manifesto guidelines added following SC directions
• 2018: cVIGIL app launched
• 2024: Extended to social media campaigns
• 2025: AI-generated/deepfake campaign content required to be labelled.
Major Provisions

• General Conduct: No caste/communal appeals, bribery, intimidation or personal attacks
• Meetings & Processions: Prior permission and coordination required
• Polling Day: Code of conduct for candidates and polling agents
• Party in Power: No misuse of official machinery, government advertisements, scheme

announcements or official visits for campaigning
• Transfers: No transfer/posting of election officials without ECI approval
• Manifestos (2013): Promises should not unduly influence voters and must indicate feasible means
of implementation.
Enforcement Mechanism
• Though not legally enforceable, violations may attract action under the Representation of the

People Act, 1951, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (earlier IPC) and other laws.
• Complaints can be filed with the Returning Officer, CEO, ECI or through cVIGIL.
• ECI issues notices, deploys Observers, Flying Squads and video surveillance, and may censure
candidates, suspend party recognition, disqualify candidates or postpone/cancel polls in exceptional cases.
Major Criticisms
Recommendations

• Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990): Statutory backing for MCC
• 2nd ARC (2008): Strengthen ECI's enforcement powers
• Parliamentary Standing Committee (2013): Incorporate MCC into the RPA, 1951
• Law Commission (255th Report, 2015): Legal enforceability with penalties
• ECI's View: Opposes full legalisation, arguing that court-based enforcement would delay elections
within the short electoral timeline.

The Election Commission of India’s initiatives and the evolving framework of the Model Code of Conduct reflect a proactive, technology-driven approach to maintaining electoral integrity in an increasingly complex digital landscape. While these measures significantly enhance transparency and accessibility, the ongoing debate regarding statutory backing versus flexible moral authority highlights the challenge of balancing robust enforcement with the need to ensure the efficient conduct of elections.
Appointment to Various
Constitutional Posts,
Powers, Functions and
Responsibilities of Various
Constitutional Bodies
Union Public Service Commission

Enshrined in Part XIV of the Constitution, the Public Service Commissions serve as the institutional watchdogs of meritocracy in India. Designed to insulate the recruitment of civil servants from the vagaries of political patronage and executive aggrandisement, the UPSC, SPSCs, and JSPSCs form the bedrock of an impartial, permanent executive capable of delivering objective governance in a complex federal democracy.
Constitutional
UPSC SPSC JSPSC
Aspect
Creation Mandate
Statutory Creation: Created by an Act of Parliament upon the request of two or more state legislatures.
Direct Constitutional Creation (Article 315).
Direct Constitutional Creation (Article 315).
Appointment
The President of India appoints the Chairman and members.
The Governor of the State appoints the Chairman and members.
The President of India appoints the Chairman and members.
Composition Limit
Not specified in the Constitution. Usually 9 to 11 members (President's discretion)
Not specified. Left to the Governor's discretion.
Not specified. Left to the President's discretion.
Tenure & Age Limit
6 years or until the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier (Article 316).
6 years or until the age of 62 years, whichever is earlier.
6 years or until the age of 62 years, whichever is earlier.
Removal Authority
Removed only by the President (after an SC inquiry).
Removed by the President (after an SC inquiry).
Appointed by the Governor, but can only be removed by the President (after SC inquiry).
Post-Retirement Bar
The chairman cannot hold any other government employment. Members can become UPSC Chairman or SPSC Chairman.
Chairman can become UPSC Chairman/Member. Cannot hold other government jobs.
Same as SPSC.
29.1 Indian Civil Services
Constitutional Framework
• Part XIV of the Constitution (Articles 308 to 323): This part deals comprehensively with the services under the Union and the States.
• Article 309: Empowers the Parliament and State legislatures to regulate the recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to public services under the Centre and States, respectively.

• Article 310 (Doctrine of Pleasure): Civil servants hold office during the pleasure of the President (for Union services) or the Governor (for State services). This allows the government to terminate the employment of public servants at will.
 Doctrine of Pleasure operates subject to constitutional safeguards under Article 311.

• Article 311: Provides constitutional safeguards to civil servants. It protects them against arbitrary dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank without a proper inquiry and an opportunity to be heard.
Theme Details
All India Services (AIS) (Article 312)

Creation: Parliament can create new AIS, but it strictly requires a Rajya Sabha resolution (2/3rd majority). Evolution: ICS & IP were replaced by IAS & IPS in 1947. The Indian Forest Service (IFS) was added in 1966. Control: Officers serve both Centre and States. Immediate control lies with the State, while ultimate control lies with the Centre. Rationale: Maintains high administrative standards and systemic uniformity and facilitates Centre-State cooperation.
Accountability, Transparency & Redressal

CVC: Investigates corruption complaints against AIS and Group A Central officers. RTI Exemptions: Officials can legally withhold information citing the AIS Conduct Rules (1968) and Official Secrets Act (1923). Tribunals (Art 323A): Administrative Tribunals (established 1985) ensure speedy dispute resolution for civil servants regarding recruitment and service conditions.
Proposed Reform: All India Judicial Service (AIJS)

Constitutional Backing: The 42nd Amendment (1976) empowered Parliament to create an AIJS under Article 312. Not yet created. Condition: Cannot include any post inferior to that of a district judge. Need: Aims to resolve high vacancies and varying standards caused by state-wise recruitment by creating a dedicated, standardised professional judicial cadre.
29.2 Challenges and Reforms

rows.text: Challenge Description
Way Forward

Examination Integrity & Certificate Fraud The Issue: Evolving methods of fraud and administrative hurdles in verifying caste/income claims undermine equitable access. Example: The Puja Khedkar Case (2024), involving allegations of fake OBC and disability certificates to gain reservation benefits and extra attempts. Opaque Evaluation & Antiquated Cycles The Issue: Aspirants criticise the lack of early answer key disclosure and opaque moderation techniques. Judicial Stance: In UPSC vs. Angesh Kumar (2018), the SC backed the UPSC, ruling that disclosing keys before final results would compromise exam confidentiality. Lateral Entry & Bypassing the Mandate The Issue: Recruiting specialists directly at Joint Secretary/Director levels bypasses the rigorous UPSC CSE process, raising severe concerns about transparency, vetting, and the bypassing of constitutionally mandated SC/ST/OBC reservation rosters. The Vernacular & Urban-Rural Divide The Issue: Despite reservations, structural inequalities (like poor translation quality in papers and the high cost of urban coaching) systemically disadvantage rural and vernacular-medium aspirants.

Digital Integrity & Verification: Leverage AI and Blockchain technologies to instantly verify the authenticity of EWS/OBC/Disability certificates, aligning the process with the Digital India mandate to eliminate forged documents. Examination Modernisation: Transition the CSE to assess 21st-century analytical skills over rote memorisation. Baswan Committee (2016): Urgently implement logistical improvements to reduce the gruelling exam cycle duration and address high absenteeism. Advisory Empowerment & Transparency: Reduce the exemptions given to the Executive under the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations. The government must provide transparent, written justifications to Parliament whenever it recruits outside the standard framework or rejects the Commission's advice. Enhancing Inclusivity: Actively boost access by dramatically improving translation quality in question papers and providing state-sponsored, high-quality coaching to level the playing field against affluent urban candidates.

elements.text: The Public Service Commissions are not merely administrative recruitment agencies; they are the Constitutional custodians of equal opportunity and administrative neutrality. To effectively meet the governance challenges of a rising digital India, the UPSC and SPSCs must evolve beyond their traditional paradigms - embracing technological verification to eliminate fraud, ensuring radical transparency in evaluation, and fiercely defending the sanctity of merit against political and systemic subversions.
Comptroller and Auditor General

Described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the most important officer under the Constitution of India, the CAG serves as the supreme guardian of the public purse. While the Election Commission secures the democratic mandate, the CAG secures democratic accountability - ensuring that the Executive remains financially subservient to the Legislature, thereby preventing the arbitrary aggrandisement of public resources.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. “The duty of the Comptroller and Auditor General is not merely to ensure the legality of
expenditure but also its propriety.” Comment. (2024)
2. “The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has a very vital role to play.” Explain how
this is reflected in the method and terms of his appointment as well as the range of
powers he can exercise. (2018)
3. Exercise of CAG’s powers in relation to the accounts of the Union and the States is derived
from Article 149 of the Indian Constitution. Discuss whether audit of the Government’s
policy implementation could amount to overstepping its own (CAG) jurisdiction (2016)
30.1 Framework
Constitutional
Description Significance
Provision
Article 148 (Appointment & Independence)
Appointed by the President. Removed only in the same manner as a Supreme Court Judge.
Provides iron-clad security of tenure (6 years or until attaining 65 years of age). To prevent post-retirement bias, the CAG is ineligible for further government office after stepping down.
Article 149 (Duties & Powers)
The Scope: Audits all expenditures from the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, and Public Accounts of both the Union and the States.
Performs duties prescribed by Parliament. This led to the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971.
Article 150 (Form of Accounts)
The accounts of the Union and the States shall be kept in such form as the President may, on the advice of the CAG, prescribe.
Ensures standardisation and prevents states/ departments from hiding fiscal deficits through creative accounting.
The PAC Nexus: The CAG's reports act as the foundational document for the Public Accounts Committee (PAC). The CAG acts as a "friend, philosopher, and guide" to the PAC.
Article 151 (Audit Reports)
Submits audit reports to the President (for Parliament) and to the Governor (for State Legislatures).
30.2 Challenges

rows.text: Challenge The "Post-Mortem" Limitation Performance Audit vs. Policy Overreach

Description
• Unlike the UK's CAG, India's CAG is merely an "Auditor General," not a true "Comptroller." Money can be drawn from the Consolidated Fund without the CAG's approval.
• The audit happens ex-post facto (after the money is already spent), meaning the CAG conducts a "post-mortem" of financial disasters rather than preventing them.
• The Friction: Beyond checking receipts (Compliance Audit), the CAG conducts Performance / Propriety Audits to check the wisdom and economy of government spending.
• The Controversy: During the 2-G Spectrum and Coalgate reports, the Executive accused the CAG of overstepping into policy-making (estimating "presumptive losses").
• SC Stance: In Arvind Gupta vs. UoI, the Supreme Court upheld the CAG's authority to conduct
performance audits to ensure public resources are not squandered.
The PPP and NGO Blindspot Delay & Denial of Information

• With the state transitioning from a "provider" to an "enabler", massive public funds are routed through Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs), Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs), and NGOs.
• Private entities fiercely resist CAG audits, creating massive blind spots in national financial scrutiny (e.g., disputes over auditing DISCOMs).
• The CAG relies on government departments to provide files. Departments routinely delay or deny access to crucial documents (e.g., defense procurements), crippling the audit process, as the CAG has no punitive power to compel document production.

elements.text: 30.3 Way Forward

rows.text: Reform Area
Recommendation
The Appointment Collegium

• Currently, the CAG is appointed solely by the Executive, which violates the principle that the auditor should not be chosen by the auditee.
• Reform: Implement a Collegium system (PM, Chief Justice, and Leader of Opposition) for CAG appointments to ensure absolute neutrality.
Amending the DPC Act (1971)

• Amend the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act to grant the CAG statutory punitive powers to fine or penalise government departments that fail to produce required documents within a stipulated timeframe.
Bringing PPPs under the Ambit

• Explicitly amend the DPC Act to bring all Public-Private Partnerships, SPVs, and government-funded NGOs under the mandatory audit jurisdiction of the CAG to prevent the privatisation of profits and socialisation of losses.
Transitioning to Real-Time Digital Auditing

• Shift from sample-based, post-mortem auditing to 100% data-driven auditing using Big Data, Artificial Intelligence, and the integration of government financial portals (like PFMS) to flag financial anomalies in real-time.

elements.text: In an era characterised by complex public-private financial architectures and massive welfare expenditures, the CAG can no longer be restricted to the role of a traditional accountant conducting post-mortem compliance checks. To preserve the sanctity of legislative control over the executive, the CAG must be statutorily empowered to audit PPPs, modernised with real-time data analytics, and shielded by a collegium-based appointment, ensuring it remains the ultimate bulwark of India's financial integrity.
Finance Commission

Enshrined under Article 280 of the Constitution, the Finance Commission serves as the supreme Constitutional architect of fiscal federalism in India. Designed to correct the inherent vertical and horizontal imbalances of a 'holding-together' federation, the Commission acts as the balancing wheel, ensuring that the political autonomy of the States is not suffocated by financial dependency on the Union.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. How have the recommendations of the 14th Finance Commission of India enabled the
States to improve their fiscal position? (2021)
2. How is the Finance Commission of India constituted? What do you know about the
terms of reference of the recently constituted Finance Commission? Discuss. (2018)
31.1 The Core Framework and Responsibilities

rows.text: Constitutional Provision
Description
Significance
Article 280 (Composition)
Comprises a Chairman and 4 members. Parliament determines their qualifications (usually experts in public affairs, economics, and high court judges).
Ensures the body has a blend of judicial impartiality, macroeconomic expertise, and administrative foresight.
Article 280(3) (The Core Duties)

1. Tax Devolution: Distribution of net tax proceeds between Centre and States (Vertical) and among the States (Horizontal).
2. Grants-in-Aid (Art 275): Principles governing grants to states in need.
3. Local Body Augmentation: Measures to supplement state resources for Panchayats/ Municipalities.
The Evolution: Following the 73rd and 74th Amendments, the FC's role expanded massively from merely balancing Centre-State relations to empowering grassroots democratic institutions (Local bodies).
Article 281 (Recommendations)
The President shall cause every recommendation made by the Finance Commission to be laid before each House of Parliament, along with an explanatory memorandum on the action taken.

Advisory but Authoritative: The recommendations are technically advisory, not legally binding on the government. However, by convention, the formula for tax devolution is universally accepted to prevent federal collapse.

elements.text: 31.2 16th Finance Commission Recommendations

rows.text: Dimensions Recommendations
Impact

Vertical Devolution Retained at 41% of the divisible pool (unchanged from the 15th FC). Grants-in-Aid
• Massive Shift: The 16th FC entirely discontinued Revenue Deficit Grants, Sector-specific, and State-specific grants.
• Funds are now strictly routed to Local Bodies and Disaster Management.

The "Grand Bargain" Debate: States demanded an increase to 50% due to the shrinking divisible pool caused by the Centre's heavy reliance on cesses and surcharges. The FC opted for stability over an increase.
• Ends the era of "bailout" grants. States with poor fiscal management will no longer be cushioned by Revenue Deficit grants, forcing them to increase their own-source revenues.

elements.text: Urbanization & Local Bodies
Urban Local Body (ULB) share increased to 45% of all local grants. Introduced an Urbanisation Premium (for merging peri-urban villages) and tied grants to wastewater management.
Acknowledges India's rapid demographic shift (projected 41% urbanization by 2031) and forces states to proactively manage rural-to-urban transitions rather than reacting to slum formations.
Fiscal Discipline & Subsidies
• Rationalise Freebies: It strongly urged states to review
• A direct strike against the populist

and rationalise their subsidy expenditure.
• Strict Debt Rules: States capped at 3% fiscal deficit.
"freebie culture." By forcing off-budget borrowings onto the main ledger, it prevents states from masking their true debt-to-GDP ratios.
Ordered a complete halt to Off-Budget Borrowings, bringing all hidden debts onto official books.
31.3 Challenges
Challenge Description
The North-South Divide (The Demographic Penalty)
• The Issue: Since the 15th FC (and continuing into the 16th FC debates), the Commission uses the

2011 Census (instead of 1971) to allocate funds.
• The Friction: Southern states (like TN and Kerala) argue this heavily penalises them for
successfully stabilising their populations, while rewarding Northern states (like UP and Bihar) for demographic failure, threatening the "cooperative" spirit of federalism.
The "Cess and Surcharge" Loophole (Article 271)
• The Issue: Under Article 271, Cesses and Surcharges levied by the Centre do not form part of the

divisible pool (states get no share).
• The Friction: The Centre has aggressively increased cesses (from roughly 10% of gross tax
revenue a decade ago to over 20% today). This artificially shrinks the pie available for states, rendering the FC's high devolution percentages (e.g., 41%) practically much lower on the ground.
Conditionality of Grants
• The Issue: The FC increasingly ties Grants-in-aid to specific sectoral reforms (e.g., power sector

reforms or "One Nation One Ration Card").
• The Friction: States view this "performance-based" funding as a backdoor encroachment by the
Union into State Subjects, undermining their fiscal autonomy.
Lack of Institutional Continuity
• The Issue: Being a temporary body constituted every 5 years, the FC lacks a permanent

secretariat.
• Once a Commission submits its report, it is dissolved, leaving no institutional mechanism to
monitor whether the Centre actually releases the recommended funds or compliance.
31.4 Way Forward

rows.text: Reform Area
Recommendations
Capping the Cess & Surcharge Levy

Reform: Amend the Constitution or establish a binding statutory ceiling to cap the total collection of cesses and surcharges at a maximum of 10% of the Union’s Gross Tax Revenue. Anything collected beyond this must be mandatorily routed into the divisible pool.
Rewarding Performance (Weightage)

Reform: To appease progressive states and neutralise the "demographic penalty", the 16th Finance Commission must assign significantly higher weightage to criteria like Demographic Performance, Tax Effort, and Ecological Stewardship (forest cover), shifting the focus from purely need-based equalisation to efficiency-based incentivisation.
Permanent Secretariat for the FC

Reform: Upgrade the Finance Commission into a permanent body with a standing secretariat. This will ensure institutional memory, allow for real-time monitoring of fund utilisation by states, and provide continuous macroeconomic advisory.
Rationalizing Discretionary Grants

• Reform: The Centre often bypasses the FC by using Article 282 (Discretionary Grants) for massive centrally sponsored schemes.
• The mandate of the FC should be expanded to review and rationalise all discretionary transfers to ensure they do not undermine the statutory devolution formula.

elements.text: As India navigates widening economic disparities and aggressive demographic transitions, the Finance Commission can no longer operate merely as a quinquennial accounting body. To safeguard the structural integrity of the Republic, it must transform into a permanent institution of fiscal equity - one that surgically plugs the 'cess and surcharge' loopholes, rewards progressive governance, and ensures that the pursuit of national equalisation does not inadvertently penalise the very states driving India's economic engine.

chapters.title: Attorney General of India and Advocate General of State

elements.text: Attorney General of India and Advocate General of State

Enshrined under Article 76 and Article 165 of the Constitution, the Attorney General and the Advocate General serve as the primary legal conduits between the Executive and the Judiciary. They are entrusted with a unique dual mandate: to fiercely defend the policies of the elected government while simultaneously upholding the absolute supremacy of constitutional morality as impartial officers of the court.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. The Attorney General of India plays a crucial role in guiding the legal framework of the
Union Government and ensuring sound governance through legal counsel.” Discuss his
responsibilities, rights and limitations in this regard. (2025)
2. “The Attorney-General is the chief legal adviser and lawyer of the Government of India.”
Discuss (2019)
32.1 Constitutional Architecture

rows.text: Constitutional Aspect
Attorney General of India (AGI)
Advocate General of State (AGS)
Significance
Constitutional Mandate Qualifications
Article 76 Must be qualified to be a Supreme Court Judge (5 yrs HC Judge / 10 yrs HC Advocate / Eminent Jurist).
Article 165 Must be qualified to be a High Court Judge (10 yrs Judicial Office / 10 yrs HC Advocate).
Created to ensure the government acts strictly within legal bounds. Ensures the highest calibre of legal expertise equivalent to the apex judiciary.
Appointment Tenure & Removal Resignation
By the President (on advice of the Union Cabinet). No fixed tenure. Holds office during the "Pleasure of the President." Often resigns following a change in government.
By the Governor (on advice of the State Cabinet). No fixed tenure. Holds office during the "Pleasure of the Governor." Often resigns following a change in government.

Structurally, they are political appointees, not career bureaucrats The Vulnerability: They lack the security of tenure enjoyed by the ECI or CAG, making them subservient to executive whims. Reinforces the reality that the office is co-terminus with the political executive.

elements.text: 32.2 Roles of Attorney General

rows.text: Functional Domain
Details
Primary Advisory Role
Legal Advisor: Advises the Union on complex matters (e.g., GST, amendments). President's Assignments: Drafts legal documents and renders opinions.
Representation of the Union
Court Advocate: Defends the Centre in SC/HCs (e.g., Aadhaar, CAA, NRC). Art. 143: Represents the Govt. in Presidential advisory references to the SC.
Constitutional & Parliamentary
Interpretation: Assists courts in clarifying constitutional laws (e.g., Privacy case). Art. 88: Participates in Parliament (no vote) to aid complex law-making.
Strategic & Reformative
International Guidance: Advises on global treaties (like Paris Climate Agreement). Legal Reforms: Suggests improvements to existing laws and judicial processes.

elements.text: 32.3 Powers and Limitations
Rights Limitations
Right of Audience: The AGI has the right of audience in all courts in the territory of India. (AGS has it before any court within the State).
No Anti-Government Advice: Cannot appear against the Government without permission.
Legislative Privileges (Art 88 / Art 177): They have the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of both Houses of Parliament/State Legislature or any joint sitting/committee.
No Criminal Defense: Cannot defend accused persons in criminal prosecutions without the explicit permission of the Government.
Immunity: Enjoys all the privileges and immunities available to an MP/MLA, despite not being a member of the House.
Corporate Board Bar: Cannot accept appointments as a director in any company or corporation without Government permission.
The Private Practice Loophole: They are not full-time government servants. They are allowed to continue their private legal practice.
The Friction: This private practice allowance is heavily criticised for creating conflicts of interest between private corporate clients and public duty.
32.4 Challenges
Challenge Description
The "Pleasure Doctrine" & Partisanship

The Issue: Because the AGI/AGS can be dismissed instantly without cause, they often function as political mouthpieces rather than independent legal advisors. Impact: They are sometimes forced to defend clearly unconstitutional laws or executive overreach in the Supreme Court to appease the ruling party.
Conflict of Interest (Private Practice)

The Issue: Allowing the top government lawyer to maintain a private practice creates massive ethical grey areas. Impact: An AGI might represent the government on Monday and represent a corporate giant on Tuesday. Even with safeguards, the sheer access to classified government policy creates an unparalleled advantage in private practice.
Shielding the Executive from Scrutiny

The Issue: Governments increasingly use the AGI/AGS to file "sealed cover" reports in courts, shielding controversial executive decisions (like electoral bonds or security procurements) from public transparency and adversarial judicial scrutiny.
32.5 Way Forward
Aspect Description
Statutory Security of Tenure
• Implement a fixed statutory tenure (e.g., 3 or 5 years) that survives changes in government,
removing the Damocles sword of the "Pleasure Doctrine".
Banning Private Practice
• The Law Commission has debated whether the AGI/AGS should be made full-time
government servants. Prohibiting private practice entirely during their tenure would eliminate all corporate conflicts of interest.
The UK Model (Separating Politics from Prosecution)
• In the UK, the Attorney General is a political figure (Cabinet Minister), but the actual

prosecutions are handled by an independent Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP).
• India should establish an independent DPP with constitutional backing to handle criminal
matters neutrally, leaving the AGI to handle constitutional advice.
Enhancing Transparency
• Limit the AGI's use of "sealed cover jurisprudence". The office must prioritise its duty as an
officer of the court over its duty as a defender of the executive by advising the government to drop unconstitutional bills before they become law.

The Attorney General and Advocate General serve as the indispensable "first law officers" to the Union and State executives respectively, providing vital constitutional continuity and legal counsel across both tiers of governance. Operating under a fusion-of-powers model, they act as the essential bridge between the political executive and the judiciary by defending state interests and assisting legislatures on complex legal questions.

chapters.title: Social Justice Commissions: NCSC, NCST, & NCBC

elements.text: Social Justice Commissions: NCSC, NCST, & NCBC

Enshrined in Part XVI of the Constitution, the National Commissions for SCs, STs, and Backward Classes represent the institutional bulwark of India's affirmative action framework. Evolving from a single Special Officer to a triad of robust constitutional bodies, they are mandated to oversee the socio-economic empowerment of marginalized communities, ensuring that the constitutional promise of equality is translated from legal text to lived reality.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. Discuss the role of the National Commission for Backward Classes in the wake of its transformation from a
statutory body to a constitutional body. (2022)
33.1 Constitutional Evolution & Architecture

rows.text: Commission
Constitutional Evolution & Article
Composition & Appointment Significance
NCSC (Scheduled Castes)
Article 338: Originally, there was only one Special Officer. The 65th Amendment (1990) created a combined multi-member commission for both SCs and STs.

1 Chairman, 1 Vice-Chairman, 3 Members. Appointed by the President (warrant under hand and seal). The foundational body. Mandated to investigate specific complaints regarding the deprivation of rights of the scheduled castes.
NCST (Scheduled Tribes)
Article 338A: The 89th Amendment (2003) bifurcated the combined commission, creating a separate NCST to focus exclusively on tribal nuances.

Same as NCSC (1+1+3). Appointed by the President. The Tribal Nuance: Created because tribal issues (forest rights, displacement, PESA) are geographically and culturally distinct from the untouchability issues faced by SCs.
NCBC (Backward Classes)

Article 338B: Previously a mere statutory body under an Act of
1993. Elevated to constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment (2018).

Same as NCSC (1+1+3). Appointed by the President. The Parity Shift: Brought the NCBC on par with the NCSC/NCST, giving it the power to hear specific grievances of OBCs, rather than just advising on inclusion/exclusion in the central list.

elements.text: 33.2 Core Powers (The Civil Court Authority)
All three Commissions share the exact same investigative powers under the Constitution.
• Powers of a Civil Court: When investigating any matter or enquiring into any complaint, they have the powers of a civil court trying a suit, specifically regarding:
 Summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person and examining them on oath.
 Requiring the discovery and production of any document.
 Receiving evidence on affidavits.

 Requisitioning any public record from any court or office.
• Mandatory Consultation: The Union and every State Government shall consult the respective Commission on all major policy matters affecting SCs, STs, or SEBCs (Socially and Educationally Backward Classes).
33.3 Challenges
Challenge Details
The "Toothless Tiger" Critique
• The Issue: Despite having the powers of a civil court to summon, they have absolutely no power to
penalise. Their reports are purely recommendatory. Governments routinely ignore their findings, and Action Taken Reports (ATRs) are delayed for years in Parliament.
The Sub-Categorization Dilemma
• The Issue: The most burning contemporary debate. The Commissions are struggling to address

"elite capture" within reservations.
• Context: Demands from the Madiga community (NCSC) and the findings of the Justice Rohini
Commission (NCBC) point to the need to sub-categorise quotas so that the most marginalised within the SC/OBC categories get their due, challenging the Commissions to redefine backwardness.
The NCBC & Federal Friction (105th Amendment)
• The Issue: The 102nd Amendment initially caused chaos by implying states lost the power to

identify their own backward classes.
• The Fix: Parliament had to pass the 105th Amendment (2021) to clarify and restore the power of
State Governments to maintain their own SEBC lists, showcasing a friction between central oversight and federal autonomy.
Vacancies and Bureaucratic Apathy
• The Issue: These commissions frequently operate without a full quorum. Furthermore, they lack an
independent investigative cadre (relying entirely on state police to investigate atrocities), leading to severe delays and compromised fact-finding in various cases.
33.4 Way Forward
Reform Area Strategy
Statutory Teeth for Recommendations

Amend the respective constitutional articles to mandate that the Executive must table the Action Taken Report (ATR) in Parliament within a strictly fixed timeframe of six months. Unreasonable rejection of recommendations should be subject to judicial review.
Independent Investigative Cadre

Establish a dedicated, permanent investigative wing for all three commissions, drawing officers on deputation who are structurally insulated from state-level political pressure, ensuring unbiased probes into atrocities (SC/ST PoA Act violations).
Proactive Policy Formulation

Shift focus from reactive grievance redressal to proactive policy design. The commissions must aggressively audit the implementation of Sub-Plans (SCSP/TSP) and utilise big data to identify micro-communities facing extreme intersectional vulnerability.
Convergence and Joint Sittings

Address jurisdictional overlaps (e.g., a tribal woman facing custodial violence falls under NCST, NCW, and NHRC) by institutionalising joint task forces to prevent bureaucratic ping-pong and ensure swift justice for intersectional victims.

The constitutional elevation of the NCSC, NCST, and NCBC signifies India's enduring commitment to restorative justice. However, a constitutional tag without punitive teeth renders these commissions as mere spectators to systemic discrimination.

To truly safeguard the marginalised, Parliament must empower these bodies with binding investigative authority and independent administrative machinery, transforming them from passive advisory boards into formidable engines of socio-economic egalitarianism.
Statutory, Regulatory
and Various Quasi-Judicial Bodies
National Human Rights Commission

Established on 12th October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA) and inspired by the Paris Principles (1991/1993), the NHRC serves as India’s principal statutory guardian of life, liberty, equality, and dignity. However, as former Chairperson Justice H.L. Dattu aptly observed, the NHRC is largely a "moral compass". Because its enforcement powers are constrained, its true efficacy is realised only when it acts as an aggressive complement to the Judiciary, civil society, and other accountability mechanisms to promote SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions).
34.1 How Does the NHRC Use its Mandate to Support and Reduce the Burden on Constitutional Courts and Other Statutory Bodies?

rows.text: Function
Framework
Complements Judiciary
Inquiry & Investigation

Suo motu or petition-based inquiries equipped with Civil Court powers (CPC
1908). Upholds Article 21.

Complementing Courts: Reduces judicial pendency by doing ground-level fact-finding. Example: Issued notice to Odisha over delays in custodial death compensation, aiding the enforcement of the SC's D.K. Basu guidelines.
Judicial Intervention
Can intervene in ongoing human rights proceedings with the prior approval of the court.

Complementing Courts: Acts as an amicus curiae (friend of the court). Example: The NHRC relies on the compensatory jurisprudence established in the Nilabati Behera case to investigate custodial deaths and human rights violations, subsequently recommending that State governments pay monetary relief to the victims' families.
Institutional Oversight
Mandated by Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA) to visit jails, detention centres, and state hospitals to assess living conditions.

Complementing State Machinery: Issued notice to the UP government over the reported deaths of three prisoners in Varanasi jails. Its 1998 Jail Reform Guidelines complement the SC's R.D. Upadhyay (2006) judgement on prison reforms.
Policy Review & Advocacy
Reviews safeguards under international covenants (ICCPR, ICESCR) and recommends policy shifts.

Complementing Statutory Commissions: Advocated for the Idate Commission Report (2017) for Denotified Tribes (DNTs). Note: NHRC coordinates with NCST, whose chief is an ex-officio member to prevent overlapping jurisdictions.

elements.text: 34.2 Synergies with Accountability Mechanisms
Institutional Partner How the NHRC Complements Them Landmark Examples
The Judiciary (Supreme/High Courts)

Fact-Finding vs. Adjudication: Courts are burdened with pendency and strict procedural laws. The NHRC complements them by conducting rapid, on-ground fact-finding missions. It often approaches the Supreme Court to enforce its findings when the government ignores them.

The Gujarat Riots (2002): The NHRC intervened in the Supreme Court, leading to the transfer of key trial cases outside the state. Encounter Killings: SC mandated that all encounter killings must be reported to the NHRC within 48 hours for independent review.
Other Statutory Commissions (NCSC, NCST, NCW)

Intersectional Justice via Ex-Officio Members: Human rights violations are rarely one-dimensional (e.g., violence against a Dalit woman involves gender and caste). The PHRA mandates that the Chairpersons of the NCSC, NCST, NCW, and Minorities Commission sit as ex-officio members of the NHRC, ensuring a coordinated, intersectional approach rather than bureaucratic turf wars.
Custodial Violence: If a tribal youth dies in custody, the NCST and NHRC can pool their investigative resources to establish a systemic pattern of abuse.
Civil Society & NGOs
Institutionalizing Activism: NGOs have grassroots intelligence but lack official power. The NHRC acts as a bridge, utilizing NGOs as its eyes and ears to bypass apathetic state police networks.
Regular interactions with human rights defenders to monitor illegal mining, bonded labor, and manual scavenging.
34.3 Recent NHRC Initiatives

rows.text: Area Initiative
Details
Women & Labor Rights Foxconn Case & National Symposium Vulnerable Groups Comprehensive Advisories (2023-24)

Ordered a reinvestigation into gender bias in hiring (Foxconn); held symposiums on workplace safety, female labour force participation, and gig worker rights. Issued specific directives on widows' rights, anti-begging (integration with the SMILE scheme), mental health, and child protection (CSAM).
Transgender Rights National Conference (2025) & Policy
Evaluated 'Garima Greh' shelters to improve infrastructure; issued advisories for comprehensive welfare and livelihood support.
Justice & Custodial Safety Relief for Custodial Deaths & Prison Reforms Social Protection Anti-Trafficking Push

Recommended ₹4.5 cr compensation in 89 cases; held a national conference advocating the transformation of prisons into reform spaces. Directed states to appoint senior nodal officers explicitly to combat human trafficking after alarming state-level reports.
Grievance Redressal Aggressive Case Resolution (2024-25) Outreach & Fast-tracking Camp Sittings & Public Hearings Awareness & Education Competitions & Specialized Training

Handled over 73,849 complaints (including 108 suo motu cases), recommending around ₹9 crore in monetary relief to victims in 210 cases. Held regional sittings (e.g., Guwahati, Shimla) to fast-track pending human rights cases and engage local police/NGOs directly. Organised awareness contests (short films/photography on LGBTQ+ and caste); conducted human rights training in sensitive regions like Manipur.

elements.text: Issues and Way Forward with the Functioning of NHRC

rows.text: Issue
Evidence (GANHRI SCA, 2025–26) Way Forward
Conflict of Interest in Investigations Executive Influence in Administration

NHRC relies on government-seconded police officers to investigate custodial torture and police excesses; concern repeatedly flagged since 2017. Amend PHRA, 1993 to create an independent investigative wing with forensic, legal and human rights experts. The Secretary General is a government-deputed civil servant, undermining NHRC's independence. Allow NHRC to independently appoint its Secretary General and senior officials.
Lack of Diversity & Vacancies

2 of 6 Commissioner posts vacant; only 93 women out of 339 staff; inadequate representation of SC/ STs, minorities, PwDs and LGBTQ+ persons. Ensure time-bound appointments and adopt transparent diversity benchmarks in appointments.
Opaque Appointment Process
Selection process remains executive-dominated, limiting institutional autonomy. Broaden the selection committee to include judiciary and civil society with transparent, merit-based selection.
Weak Action on Systemic Violations

Limited action on custodial deaths, shrinking civic space, Human rights defenders (HRDs), surveillance concerns; most cases end with compensation rather than prosecution. Publish periodic thematic reports, institutionalise civil society consultations, and recommend prosecution & disciplinary action in serious violations.
Institutional Credibility Concerns
NHRC questioned the Paris Principles/GANHRI accreditation instead of addressing deficiencies. Implement GANHRI recommendations and strengthen compliance to restore global credibility.

elements.text: The NHRC remains the cornerstone of India's human rights protection architecture. Strengthening its independence, enforcement powers, and institutional capacity is essential to transform it from a recommendatory body into an effective guardian of constitutional rights.
Central Vigilance Commission
The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) is the apex statutory vigilance institution of the Government of India, mandated to combat corruption and ensure integrity in public administration.

• Origin: It was established in 1964 via an executive resolution based on the recommendations of the Santhanam Committee on Prevention of Corruption (1962–64).
• Statutory Status: Originally an advisory body, it was granted statutory status by Parliament through the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, following the Supreme Court’s directives in the landmark Vineet Narain case (1997).
• Nature: It is an independent body, free of control from any executive authority, responsible only to Parliament.
35.1 Structure and Composition

rows.text: Aspect
Details
Composition
Multi-member body: 1 Central Vigilance Commissioner (Chairperson) + Maximum of 2 Vigilance Commissioners.
Appointment

Appointed by the President on the recommendation of a high-powered committee comprising:
1. Prime Minister (Chairperson)
2. Union Minister of Home Affairs
3. Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha
Tenure
4 years or until they attain the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier. They are not eligible for reappointment in any Central/State government agency, ensuring post-retirement neutrality.
Removal

Removed by the President on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity only after an inquiry by the Supreme Court. The President can also remove them for insolvency, paid outside employment, or moral turpitude.
Independence
Their salary, allowances, and service conditions are identical to those of the UPSC Chairman and Members, charged to the Consolidated Fund of India.

elements.text: 35.2 Issues and Challenges

rows.text: Issue
Challenges & Data Points
1. Massive Pendency in Trials & Appeals

• Trial Delays: 7,072 corruption cases pending trial (379 pending for >20 years; 2,660 for >10 years).
• Appellate Bottlenecks: 13,100 appeals/revisions pending in High Courts and the Supreme Court (606 pending for >20 years).
2. Delays in Investigation by CBI

• Unmet Timelines: While investigations should ideally conclude within 1 year, 529 corruption cases are pending investigation (56 for >5 years).
• Complex Scrutiny: Prolonged time required to scrutinise voluminous records, especially in economic offences and bank frauds.
• Logistical Hurdles: Delays in locating and examining witnesses in remote areas.
3. Administrative & Procedural Bottlenecks

• Prosecution Sanction: Delays by competent authorities in granting sanction to prosecute corrupt officials act as a major shield for the corrupt.
• Letters Rogatory (LRs): Extreme delays in obtaining international cooperation and responses to LRs in cross-border corruption cases.
4. Manpower and Capacity Constraints

• Resource Crunch: The report explicitly cites "inadequate manpower" and "excessive work" as primary reasons for delayed investigations.
• CVO Dependency: CVC heavily relies on the Chief Vigilance Officers (CVOs) of respective departments, who often face a conflict of interest or lack adequate staff.
5. Declining Conviction Rates

• Dip in Success: The conviction rate in corruption cases dropped to 69.14% in 2024 from 71.47% in 2023, indicating potential gaps in evidence gathering or prolonged trials weakening cases over time (witnesses turning hostile/dying).
6. "Toothless Tiger" (Advisory Nature)

• Lack of Punitive Power: The CVC is fundamentally an advisory body. Central Government departments are free to either accept or reject its advice regarding disciplinary actions against corrupt officials.
• It does not have the power to register criminal cases; it only exercises "superintendence" over the CBI for Prevention of Corruption Act (PCA) cases.

elements.text: 7. Lack of an Independent Investigation Wing
• Borrowed Personnel: The CVC lacks its own dedicated investigative machinery. It is entirely
dependent on the CBI or departmental CVOs for field investigations, limiting its direct operational control.
8. Jurisdictional Limitations
• Limited Scope: The CVC's jurisdiction primarily covers Group 'A' officers of the Central
Government and higher-ups in PSUs/Public Sector Banks. It does not comprehensively cover all government employees or state-level machinery.
35.3 Way Forward
Category of Reform Solutions & Recommendations
1. Tackling Judicial Pendency & Trial Delays
• Dedicated Fast-Track Courts: Establish special CBI courts mandated to conduct day-to-

day hearings without arbitrary adjournments.
• Strict Appellate Timeframes: Create specialised benches in High Courts and the Supreme

Court with a statutory time limit (e.g., 6–12 months) for disposing of appeals under the Prevention of Corruption Act (PCA).
• Digitisation of Evidence: Leverage the e-Courts project to digitise voluminous charge
sheets and evidence to prevent delays caused by misplaced physical files.
2. Reforming the Investigation Process (CBI & CVOs)
• Augmenting Expertise: Directly recruit subject-matter specialists (chartered accountants,

cyber forensics experts, financial analysts) to expedite the scrutiny of complex economic offences.
• Enforcing Deadlines: Strictly monitor the CVC's 1-year investigation completion deadline;

hold Investigating Officers (IOs) accountable for unjustified delays through performance reviews.
• Streamlining Letters Rogatory (LRs): Establish a dedicated MEA-MHA cell to fast-track
mutual legal assistance and LRs to prevent stalling in cross-border probes.
3. Institutional Empowerment of the CVC
• From Advisory to Binding Authority: Amend the CVC Act so that if a Ministry rejects the

CVC’s recommendation for disciplinary action, it must record the reasons in writing and table them before Parliament.
• Independent Investigative Wing: Provide the CVC with its own dedicated, independent

investigative cadre to reduce its over-reliance on the CBI and departmental CVOs.
• Protecting CVOs: Ensure CVO independence by mandating that their Annual Confidential
Reports (ACRs) are written entirely by the CVC, shielding them from departmental pressure.
4. Addressing Administrative Bottlenecks
• Enforcing 'Deemed Sanction': Strictly enforce the 3-month statutory limit for competent

authorities to grant prosecution sanction. If they fail to decide, it should be legally treated as "deemed sanction" so trials can commence.
• Protecting Honest Officers: Implement Hota Committee recommendations to protect honest
civil servants from harassment for bona fide administrative errors, preventing 'policy paralysis'.
5. Leveraging Technology & Preventive Vigilance
• AI for Document Scrutiny: Deploy Artificial Intelligence and Big Data analytics to scan

millions of pages of bank records and procurement documents to detect anomalies swiftly.
• Minimising Human Interface: Expand the scope of e-Procurement, GeM (Government
e-Marketplace), and Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT) to eliminate the root causes of systemic bribery.

To transform the CVC from an advisory "toothless tiger" into a formidable anti-corruption bulwark, it is imperative to grant its recommendations binding statutory authority and equip it with an independent investigative cadre. Ultimately, coupling this institutional empowerment with technological integration and fast-tracked judicial processes is vital to ensuring swift accountability and upholding the highest standards of integrity in India's public administration.
Lokpal
The Lokpal is India's premier independent statutory anti-corruption ombudsman, established to enquire into allegations of corruption against certain categories of high-ranking public servants.
36.1 Evolution and Statutory Framework
Aspect Details
Global Origin The concept originated with the Ombudsman in Sweden (1809) and the term "Lokpal" was coined by L.M. Singhvi in 1963.
First Recommendation
In 1966, the 1st Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) (headed by Morarji Desai) recommended setting up a Lokpal at the Centre and Lokayuktas in States.
Subsequent Endorsements

Recommended by the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (NCRWC,
2002) and the 2nd ARC (2005) under Veerappa Moily.
Legislative Attempts
Between 1968 and 2011, eight separate Lokpal Bills were introduced in Parliament but repeatedly failed to pass due to political deadlocks.
Final Momentum The "India Against Corruption" movement led by Anna Hazare in 2011 forced the government to fast-track the legislation.
Statutory Backing
The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, was passed by Parliament and received Presidential assent on January 1, 2014.
36.2 Structure, Composition, and Tenure
Feature Details
Composition Consists of a Chairperson (former CJI/SC Judge or eminent person) and a maximum of 8 members.
Representation Mandate
50% must be judicial members. Furthermore, at least 50% of total members must be from SC, ST, OBC, minorities, or women.
Selection Committee
Comprises: 1. Prime Minister (Chair), 2. Speaker of Lok Sabha, 3. Leader of Opposition (LS), 4. Chief Justice of India (or SC judge nominee), 5. Eminent jurist nominated by the President.
The LoP Amendment (2016)
Due to the absence of a recognised LoP (requiring 10% of seats), the Act was amended to include the Leader of the Single Largest Opposition Party in the Selection Committee.

Search Committee The Selection Committee must form a Search Committee of at least 7 persons to prepare a panel of names. Note: The 50% reservation rule (SC/ST/OBC/Women) applies to this committee as well.
Term & Conditions 5 years or until 70 years of age. Salaries and allowances are equivalent to the CJI (for the Chairperson) and Supreme Court Judges (for members).
Strict Post-Tenure Bar

Members are barred from any diplomatic assignment, appointment to any territory/state as Administrator/Governor, or contesting any election (President/VP/MP/MLA) for 5 years after ceasing to hold office.
36.3 Jurisdiction and Operational Functions
Aspect Provisions, Scope, and Exemptions
Public Servants Covered
Prime Minister, Union Ministers, MPs, and Group A, B, C, and D officers of the Central Government.
NGOs and Societies
Jurisdiction extends to anyone managing a society/trust/NGO that receives a government grant above ₹1 crore or foreign contributions above ₹10 lakh (under FCRA).
PM Exceptions Cannot enquire into allegations against the PM related to: International Relations, External/Internal Security, Public Order, Atomic Energy, and Space.
MPs' Privilege Exemption
Does not have jurisdiction over any speech made or vote given by an MP in Parliament (protected under Article 105).
Asset Confiscation Vested with the power to provisionally attach and confiscate property, assets, and receipts acquired by corrupt means, even during the pendency of prosecution (before conviction).
Transfer of Officers Can recommend the transfer or suspension of public servants connected with corruption allegations to prevent evidence tampering.
Limitation Period The Lokpal cannot enquire into any complaint made after the expiry of 7 years from the date on which the offense was committed.
36.4 Issues and Way Forward
Issues / Limitations Suggested Reforms
No Suo Motu Power: The Lokpal cannot initiate enquiries on its own; it can only act on complaints filed in the prescribed format.
Grant Suo Motu Cognisance: Empower the Lokpal to take up cases based on media reports or intelligence, similar to the NHRC or Supreme Court.
Exclusion of the Judiciary: The Lokpal Act completely excludes the higher judiciary from its ambit.
Judicial Standards Bill: Enact a separate, robust mechanism (like the Judicial Standards and Accountability Bill) to address judicial corruption.
Lack of Independent Machinery: Relies heavily on the CBI and CVC. The CBI continues to be administratively controlled by the DoPT (Executive).
Dedicated Investigation Cadre: Equip the Lokpal with its own independent investigative wing to free it from executive pressure.
Anonymous Complaints Barred: The Act severely punishes "false and frivolous" complaints (up to 1-year imprisonment) and bans anonymous complaints, deterring honest whistleblowers.
Operationalise Whistleblower Act: Fully implement the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014, and protect the identity of complainants to encourage reporting.
Administrative Friction: Overlap of duties between CVC (handling vigilance for Group C & D) and Lokpal.
Institutional Synergy: Clearly define the hierarchy. Make the CVC an explicit investigative arm and strengthen coordination between Lokpal and CVC.

The Lokpal represents the culmination of decades of efforts to create an independent and credible anti-corruption watchdog at the national level. While the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 has strengthened accountability in public life, its effectiveness remains constrained by institutional and operational limitations. Empowering the Lokpal with greater functional autonomy, independent investigative capacity, and stronger whistleblower protection can transform it into a robust pillar of transparent, ethical, and citizen-centric governance.
Lokayukta
The Lokayukta is India's adaptation of the Swedish Ombudsman (established 1809; the word means "legal representative"). The First
Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC, 1966–70) under Morarji Desai, in its landmark report on "Problems of Redress of
Citizens' Grievances," first recommended independent authorities at both the Union (Lokpal) and state (Lokayukta) levels.

• Maharashtra (1971): First state to establish a Lokayukta under the Maharashtra Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayuktas Act, 1971; widely regarded as India's first Lokayukta institution (Odisha's 1970 Lokpal used different nomenclature).

• Karnataka (1984): Introduced the most powerful Lokayukta model, featuring independent police powers, suo motu jurisdiction, and special courts; often considered the gold standard for anti-corruption ombudsman institutions.
Feature Standard Provisions & State Variations
Appointment Appointed by the Governor of the respective state.
Consultation Process
Different states have different procedures. In most states, the Governor must consult the Chief Justice of the State High Court and the Leader of Opposition (LoP) in the State Legislative Assembly.

Qualifications Generally restricted to individuals with a high judicial background (e.g., a former Supreme Court Judge or a former Chief Justice of a High Court). Some states allow eminent non-judicial members.
Tenure Typically 5 years or until the age of 65/70. Variation: States like Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan previously had Lokayukta's tenure set to 8 years.
Removal Process
Enjoys security of tenure. Cannot be dismissed or transferred by the state executive. Removal requires an impeachment-style motion passed by the state legislature, ensuring independence.
Jurisdiction and Operational Powers

rows.text: Aspect
Provisions, Scope, and Exemptions
The Chief Minister

Included: States like Himachal Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat bring the CM under the Lokayukta's ambit. Excluded: States like Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan explicitly exempt the CM from its jurisdiction.
Public Servants Covered
Usually includes State Ministers, MLAs, members of local authorities, statutory bodies, and all state government officers.
Investigative Mechanism
Most Lokayuktas lack their own independent investigation wing. They must rely on state agencies like the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) or the State CID, which creates a conflict of interest.
Nature of Action
Their powers are predominantly advisory/recommendatory. After an inquiry, the Lokayukta submits an annual consolidated report to the Governor.
Legislative Accountability

The Governor is constitutionally bound to lay this report before the State Legislature, accompanied by an explanatory memorandum detailing the government's action (or reasons for inaction) on the recommendations. → This obligation arises from respective state Lokayukta Acts, not directly from the Constitution.

elements.text: Lokayukta remains one of India's most important instruments for promoting transparency, integrity, and citizen-centric governance. Experiences from states such as Karnataka demonstrate that a well-designed and empowered Lokayukta can serve as an effective check on corruption. With greater institutional independence, stronger investigative capacity, and uniform standards across states, the institution can evolve into a cornerstone of accountable and ethical governance in India's federal framework.
